questions.stem: Which type of neuron sends signals away?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Axon**

- **A. Bipolar** — Bipolar, unipolar, and pseudounipolar refer to types of neurons. All of these have axons and are therefore capable of sending signals away.
- **B. Unipolar**
- **C. Pseudounipolar**
- **D. Axon** — The axon is the portion of a neuron that carries nerve impulses away from the cell body. Although the question was asking for a type of neuron, this remains to be the best answer because it is the only one that specifically answers the question.

questions.stem: Bobby was involved in a physical altercation wherein she got stabbed on the face, injuring his parotid gland. Which muscle is pierced by the parotid and is also likely affected?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Buccinator**

- **A. Masseter** — The masseter muscle is found anterior to the parotid gland; hence, this muscle may be damaged by the stab. However, the question specifically asks for a muscle pierced by the parotid gland.
- **B. Zygomaticus** — The zygomaticus muscle extends from the zygomatic bone to the angle of the mouth. It is not closely related to the parotid gland.
- **C. Buccinator** — The Stensen’s duct traverses anterior to the masseter muscle then pierces the buccinator, moving medially to open into the oral cavity near the 2nd upper molar. This muscle, being a muscle of facial expression, is relatively superficial, making it susceptible to the stab as well.
- **D. Risorius** — The risorius muscle, deemed as the “smiling muscle,” is usually found in the superficial layer of the facial muscles on either side of the lips, overlying the buccinator muscle.

questions.stem: In the previous situation involving a stab wound affecting the parotid gland, which cranial nerve is likely injured?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — CN VII**

- **A. CN V** — The auriculotemporal nerve, a branch of CN V3, is closely related to the parotid gland and passes superior to it with the superficial temporal vessels to innervate the parotid sheath. Nevertheless, this is not the best answer as only one of the branches of CN V is related to the parotid.
- **B. CN VII** — Embedded within the parotid gland, from superficial to deep, are the parotid plexus of the facial nerve (CN VII) and its branches. Hence, injury to the gland will likely result in facial nerve injury as well.
- **C. CN IX** — The parasympathetic component of the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) supplies presynaptic secretory fibers to the otic ganglion. The postsynaptic parasympathetic fibers are conveyed from the ganglion to the parotid gland by the auriculotemporal nerve. Hence, although it supplies the parotid, this is not the best answer.
- **D. CN X** — CN X is not closely related to the parotid gland.

#### Salivary gland ducts and innervation

| Gland | Duct | Innervation | Special features |
|---|---|---|---|
| Parotid gland | Stensen’s duct | CN IX | Stensen’s duct pierces the buccinator muscle; the facial nerve passes through the gland but does NOT innervate it |
| Submandibular gland | Wharton’s duct | CN VII | - |
| Sublingual gland | Duct of Rivinus | CN VII | - |

questions.stem: Which is NOT part of the Tetralogy of Fallot?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — LVH**

- **A. RVOT obstruction** — RVOT obstruction from a pulmonary stenosis is part of the Tetralogy of Fallot.
- **B. LVH** — TOF presents with right ventricular hypertrophy (not left) due to increased work from having to pump blood against an obstructed right ventricular outflow tract.
- **C. VSD** — VSD is a component of TOF.
- **D. Dextroposition of the aorta** — Dextroposition of the aorta is a component of TOF.

questions.stem: Which presents as a boot-shaped heart on chest xray?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — TOF**

- **A. TAPVR** — Total anomalous pulmonary venous return (TAPVR) presents with the snowman sign.
- **B. TOF** — Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) presents as a boot-shaped heart.
- **C. Truncus arteriosus** — Truncus arteriosus presents with moderate cardiomegaly with pulmonary plethora as a result of collateral formation.
- **D. TGA** — Transposition of great arteries (TGA) presents with the classic “egg on a string” appearance.

questions.stem: If an OBGYN resident performing dilatation and curettage accidentally pierces the anterior part of the uterus, what structure is likely affected?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Bladder**

- **A. Bladder** — The uterus lies immediately posterosuperior to the bladder, hence it can be injured when the anterior surface of the uterus is pierced.
- **B. Rectum** — The rectum lies posterior to the uterus.
- **C. Uterine artery** — The uterine artery crosses the ureters laterally to the internal os of the cervix. It is not found anterior to the uterus.
- **D. Broad ligament** — The broad ligament is a double layer of peritoneum attaching the sides of the uterus to the pelvis. It is not found anterior to the uterus.

questions.stem: Regardless of anastomoses, if the superior mesenteric artery is ligated, what anatomical structure will likely be ischemic?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Ascending colon**

- **A. Ascending colon** — The superior mesenteric artery (SMA) supplies the midgut derivatives, from the proximal duodenum to the proximal 2/3 of the transverse colon. Hence, the ascending colon will be affected if blood supply from the SMA is removed.
- **B. Transverse colon** — The distal 1/3 of the transverse colon is supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery (IMA), hence it will not be entirely ischemic if blood supply from the SMA is disrupted.
- **C. Descending colon** — The descending colon is supplied by the IMA, hence it will not be affected.
- **D. Sigmoid colon** — The sigmoid colon is supplied by the IMA, hence it will not be affected.

questions.stem: Dermis is full of what kind of tissue?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Collagenous**

- **A. Fibrous** — The specific dominant component of dermis is collagen. Fibrous and soft tissues are too nonspecific, hence not the best answers for this question.
- **B. Soft**
- **C. Collagenous** — The dermis of the skin contains dense irregular connective tissue, consisting of little ground substance, few cells (mostly fibroblasts), and abundant collagen in randomly arranged fibers.
- **D. Fatty** — Fatty tissue is more associated with the hypodermis than the dermis.

#### Connective tissue proper

| Type | General organization | Major functions | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| Loose (areolar) connective tissue | Much ground substance; many cells and little collagen, randomly distributed | Supports microvasculature, nerves, and immune defense cells | Lamina propria beneath epithelial lining of digestive tract |
| Dense irregular connective tissue | Little ground substance; few cells (mostly fibroblasts); much collagen in randomly arranged fibers | Protects and supports organs; resists tearing | Dermis of skin, organ capsules, submucosa layer of digestive tract |
| Dense regular connective tissue | Almost completely filled with parallel bundles of collagen; few fibroblasts, aligned with collagen | Provide strong connections within musculoskeletal system; strong resistance to force | Ligaments, tendons, aponeuroses, corneal stroma |

#### Collagen types

| Type | Examples |
|---|---|
| I | Dermis, bone, tendon, fibrocartilage |
| II | Hyaline and elastic cartilages |
| III | Reticular fibers during wound healing |
| IV | Basal lamina |
| V | Fetal membrane |

questions.stem: A mass on the upper inner quadrant of the breast will drain to which lymph nodes?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Internal thoracic**

- **A. Supraclavicular** — The supraclavicular lymph nodes drain the neck, thorax, and abdomen. More specifically, the right supraclavicular lymph nodes drain the breast, lung and upper esophagus, while the left supraclavicular lymph nodes have more extensive drainage sites and drain distant regions such as the kidney, cervix, testes, and pancreas.
- **B. Internal thoracic** — The medial aspect of the breast drains into the parasternal nodes, also known as the internal mammary or internal thoracic nodes.
- **C. Pectoral** — Pectoral nodes are also called anterior axillary nodes. These receive drainage from the lateral aspect of the breast and abdominal wall.
- **D. Inguinal** — Inguinal nodes receive drainage from the lower extremity, genitals, dorsal perineum, and the inferior aspect of the anterior abdominal wall.

questions.stem: A surgeon performing prostatectomy ligates what artery to achieve hemostasis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Inferior vesical artery**

- **A. Superior vesical artery** — The superior vesical artery supplies the superior part of the urinary bladder.
- **B. Inferior vesical artery** — The inferior vesical artery is the main arterial supply to the prostate gland.
- **C. Middle vesical artery** — The middle vesical artery is not commonly described in textbooks, but in some sources, it can be a variation of a branch of the superior vesical artery. It is also referred to as the vesiculodeferential artery, which supplies the seminal vesicles.
- **D. External iliac artery** — The external iliac artery gives off the inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac branches, which supply the muscle and fascia of the anterior abdominal wall.

#### Branches of the internal iliac artery

**Posterior division**

- Iliolumbar
- Lateral sacral
- Superior gluteal – supplies gluteal muscles and tensor fascia lata

**Anterior division**

- Pudendal (internal) – muscles of the anal canal; skin and muscles of perineum
- Inferior vesical (male) – base of UB, prostate, seminal vesicle, ductus deferens, lower ureter
- Uterine (female) – uterus
- Middle rectal – rectum, anal canal
- Vaginal (female) – vagina and base of UB
- Obturator – pelvic muscles; medial compartment of thigh
- Umbilical – obliterates and becomes the medial umbilical ligament
- Superior vesical – superior part of UB
- Inferior gluteal – supplies gluteus maximus, piriformis and quadratus femoris muscles

questions.stem: Alex presents in the ER with sudden loss of gag reflex as a consequence of a skull base fracture from a head injury. Which is affected?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — CN IX**

- **A. CN IX** — CN IX provides the sensory (afferent) limb of the gag reflex. Damage therefore leads to complete loss of the reflex, especially with skull base trauma; recall that CN IX exits via the jugular foramen together with CN X and XI.
- **B. CN X** — CN X provides the motor (efferent) limb of the gag reflex. However, A is still the best answer since damage to CN IX leads to total loss of gag reflex as compared to when only the efferent limb is affected.
- **C. CN VII** — CN VII is the efferent limb of the corneal reflex.
- **D. CN III** — CN III is the efferent limb of the pupillary light reflex.

choices.text: At the level of the umbilicus
In the right lower quadrant of the abdomen

questions.stem: During suprapubic aspiration of urine in a neonate, the needle should be inserted at which location?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Just above the symphysis pubis**

- **A. Below the symphysis pubis** — The bladder cannot be accessed below the symphysis pubis.
- **B. Just above the symphysis pubis** — The bladder, when distended, can be accessed just above the symphysis pubis.
- **C. At the level of the umbilicus** — The umbilicus is already too high to find the bladder.
- **D. In the right lower quadrant of the abdomen** — The bladder is typically seen more midline.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a border of the Hesselbach triangle?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Deep inguinal ring**

- **A. Inferior epigastric vessels** — The inferior epigastric vessels form the superolateral border of the triangle.
- **B. Rectus abdominis** — The lateral end of the rectus abdominis forms the medial border of the triangle.
- **C. Deep inguinal ring** — The deep inguinal ring lies lateral to the Hesselbach triangle. It does not form any of its borders.
- **D. Inguinal ligament** — The inguinal ligament forms the inferolateral border of the triangle.

questions.stem: The follicles of the thyroid gland are lined by which type of epithelium?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Simple cuboidal epithelium**

- **A. Simple squamous epithelium** — When inactive or atrophic, thyroid follicles can appear flat, resembling squamous epithelium.
- **B. Simple cuboidal epithelium** — Under normal, moderate activity conditions, the follicles of the thyroid gland are lined by a simple cuboidal epithelium. This is the best answer.
- **C. Simple columnar epithelium** — During periods of high thyroid stimulation, active follicles may transition into simple columnar cells.
- **D. Stratified cuboidal epithelium** — Stratified cuboidal epithelium is not typically seen in thyroid follicles; these are seen lining ducts of sweat glands, salivary glands, and mammary glands.

questions.stem: Goosebumps are caused by the contraction of which muscle?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Arrector pili muscle**

- **A. Pilosebaceous muscle** — These are distractors and are not formal anatomical terms.
- **B. Dermal papilla smooth muscle**
- **C. Superficial cutaneous muscle**
- **D. Arrector pili muscle** — Goosebumps are caused by the contraction of the arrector pili muscle. These are tiny smooth muscles attached to hair follicles. When they contract, they cause the hair to stand up and make the skin appear bumpy.

questions.stem: In a peripheral blood smear, a large cell with abundant grayish cytoplasm and a kidney bean-shaped, frosted glass-appearing nucleus is observed. Which type of cell is this?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Monocyte**

- **A. Lymphocyte** — Lymphocytes are typically smaller with a round, dense nucleus and a thin rim of basophilic cytoplasm.
- **B. Monocyte** — Monocytes have abundant, grayish-blue cytoplasm. Their nuclei are characteristically kidney bean-shaped or indented with a delicate, lace-like appearance (“frosted-glass” appearance).
- **C. Neutrophil** — Neutrophils are smaller than monocytes and are recognized by their multilobed nucleus and pale cytoplasm with fine granules.
- **D. Eosinophil** — Eosinophils have a bilobed nucleus and prominent eosinophilic cytoplasmic granules.

questions.stem: Which of the following refers to the specialized macrophages found in the liver?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Kupffer cells**

- **A. Microglia** — Microglial cells are seen in the CNS.
- **B. Alveolar macrophages** — Alveolar macrophages are seen in the lungs.
- **C. Kupffer cells** — Kupffer cells are specialized macrophages in the liver.
- **D. Osteoclasts** — Osteoclasts are seen in the bone.

#### Mononuclear phagocyte system

- Monocyte - Blood
- Macrophage – CT, lymphoid organs, Lungs
- Kupffer cell - Liver
- Microglia - CNS
- Langerhans cell – Skin
- Osteoclast – Bone
- Placenta - Hofbauer

questions.stem: What is the most common site of ectopic pregnancy?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Ampulla**

- **A. Ampulla** — Nearly 95% of ectopic pregnancies implant in the fallopian tube’s various segments. The ampulla is the most frequent site (70%).
- **B. Fimbriae** — The rate for ectopic pregnancy at the fimbriae is 11%.
- **C. Isthmus** — The rate for ectopic pregnancy at the isthmus is 12%.
- **D. Previous CS scar** — 5% of ectopic pregnancies are nontubal, which include implantation in the ovary, peritoneal cavity, cervix, or prior cesarean scar.

questions.stem: The medial umbilical ligament is the adult derivative of which fetal structure?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Umbilical artery**

- **A. Urachus** — The urachus becomes the median umbilical fold.
- **B. Umbilical vein** — The left umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres or round ligament of the liver.
- **C. Umbilical artery** — The umbilical artery develops into the medial umbilical ligament.
- **D. Ductus venosus** — The ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum of the liver.

questions.stem: Where does sperm mature?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Epididymis**

- **A. Epididymis** — The epididymis is a coiled tube where sperm is stored for maturation prior to ejaculation.
- **B. Testes** — The testes are where spermatogenesis occurs.
- **C. Vas deferens** — The vas deferens is a thick-walled muscular tube that transports spermatozoa from the epididymis to urethra.
- **D. Seminal vesicle** — The seminal vesicles produce secretions which comprise the seminal fluid. Secretions include fructose, ascorbic acid, amino acids, and prostaglandins.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT found in the posterior mediastinum?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Phrenic nerve**

- **A. Thoracic aorta** — The thoracic aorta is found in the posterior mediastinum.
- **B. Azygos vein** — The azygos vein is found in the posterior mediastinum.
- **C. Phrenic nerve** — The phrenic nerve is part of the middle inferior division, not the posterior mediastinum.
- **D. Esophagus** — The esophagus and esophageal nerve plexus are found in the posterior mediastinum.

#### Posterior mediastinum contents mnemonic: POST-DATES

- D – Descending aorta (thoracic aorta)
- A – Azygos and hemiazygos veins
- T – Thoracic duct
- E – Esophagus
- S – Sympathetic trunk/ganglia

questions.stem: Which among the layers of the meninges is made up of dense fibrous membrane and continues up to the spinal cord?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Dura mater**

- **A. Pia mater** — The pia mater is the innermost meningeal layer consisting of delicate loose connective tissue.
- **B. Meninges** — This term refers collectively to all three layers (dura mater, arachnoid mater, and pia mater).
- **C. Dura mater** — The dura mater, particularly the meningeal layer, is composed of dense strong fibrous membrane. It is continuous with the dura of the spinal cord.
- **D. Arachnoid mater** — The arachnoid mater is composed mainly of avascular connective tissue. It has delicate collagen and elastic fibers.

questions.stem: A patient presents with a heart murmur caused by the inability to maintain constant tension on the atrioventricular (AV) valve cusps. Which of the following structures is most likely damaged?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Chordae tendinae**

- **A. Crista terminalis** — The crista terminalis is a muscular ridge in the right atrium separating the smooth posterior wall (sinus venarum) from the rough anterior wall containing pectinate muscles. It does not contribute to AV valve function.
- **B. Septomarginal trabecula** — Its main role is conducting electrical impulses, not maintaining AV valve tension.
- **C. Chordae tendinae** — The cusps of the tricuspid and mitral valves correspond with the papillary muscles which give off the chordae tendinae that attach to the respective cusps.
- **D. Pectinate muscle** — The pectinate muscle refers to parallel ridges of myocardium found mainly in the atria, especially the right atrium and auricles. It increases atrial contraction efficiency but do not interact with valve cusps.

questions.stem: What is the period when male and female mammary glands are similar?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Pre-puberty**

- **A. Reproductive** — During the reproductive period and lactation, the female mammary glands undergo further enlargement and functional differentiation.
- **B. Lactation** — During the reproductive period and lactation, the female mammary glands undergo further enlargement and functional differentiation.
- **C. Puberty** — At puberty, under the influence of estrogen and progesterone, the female breast develops, while the male breast remains rudimentary.
- **D. Pre-puberty** — Before puberty, male and female mammary glands are identical in structure, consisting mainly of lactiferous ducts with little to no glandular tissue.

questions.stem: Where does the diaphragm insert?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Central tendon**

- **A. Central tendon** — The diaphragm is a dome-shaped muscle that consists of a peripheral muscular part and a central tendon, where it inserts.
- **B. Inferior ribs** — The costal part of the diaphragm originates from the internal surfaces of the inferior six ribs and their costal cartilages, not inserts on them.
- **C. Xiphoid process** — The sternal part of the diaphragm originates from the posterior aspect of the xiphoid process.
- **D. Lumbar vertebrae** — The lumbar part of the diaphragm arises from the right and left crura attached to the upper lumbar vertebrae (L1–L3).

questions.stem: A patient is diagnosed with Brown-Séquard syndrome following a spinal cord hemisection. Which of the following neurologic disturbances will be observed on the contralateral side of the lesion?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Loss of pain and temperature sense from level of lesion downwards**

- **A. Loss of discriminative touch and pressure sensation below the level of lesion** — Loss of discriminative touch and pressure sensation below level of lesion are carried by the dorsal columns. This does not describe the Brown-Séquard syndrome.
- **B. Loss of pain and temperature sense from level of lesion downwards** — In Brown-Séquard syndrome, the contralateral neurologic disturbance observed below the level of the lesion is loss of pain and temperature sensation, due to involvement of the spinothalamic tract.
- **C. UMN paralysis below the level of lesion** — Spinal hemisection causes ipsilateral upper motor neuron paralysis below the lesion, not contralateral.
- **D. LMN paralysis below the level of lesion** — Below the lesion, paralysis is UMN type, not LMN.

questions.stem: Which cells produce erythropoietin in the kidney?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Juxtaglomerular cells**

- **A. Mesangial cells** — Mesangial cells are located between capillaries within the glomerulus and provide structural support, phagocytic activity, and help regulate glomerular filtration.
- **B. Juxtaglomerular cells** — Juxtaglomerular cells primarily secrete renin, but the peritubular interstitial fibroblast-like cells (closely associated with JG cells) are the main source of erythropoietin (EPO) in adults.
- **C. Podocyte** — Podocytes are specialized epithelial cells that line the visceral layer of Bowman’s capsule and form filtration slits with their foot processes.
- **D. Macula densa** — The macula densa consists of specialized distal convoluted tubule (DCT) cells that sense Na⁺ concentration in the tubular fluid.

questions.stem: If a kidney stone is lodged at the lower 2/3 of the ureter, where will the pain LEAST likely radiate to?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Flank**

- **A. Thigh** — Pain from a lower ureteric stone can radiate to the thigh.
- **B. Flank** — Flank pain is observed more in proximal stones than distal ones. It corresponds to upper ureter or renal pelvis involvement (T10-T12).
- **C. Anterior abdomen** — The anterior abdomen is a typical site for pain when the stone is in the middle third of the ureter.
- **D. Groin** — Pain from a lower ureteric stone can radiate to the groin and/or external genitalia.

questions.stem: A patient with a long-standing gallbladder stone develops erosion of the posterior wall of the gallbladder fundus. Which part of the colon is most likely affected?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Transverse colon**

- **A. Ascending colon** — The ascending colon lies inferior to the liver on the right side of the abdomen, but it is not in direct contact with the gallbladder.
- **B. Transverse colon** — The posterior wall of the fundus of the gallbladder closely lies anterior to the transverse colon.
- **C. Descending colon** — The descending colon lies on the left side of the abdomen, far from the gallbladder (which is on the right upper quadrant).
- **D. Sigmoid colon** — The sigmoid colon is located in the lower left quadrant and is not in anatomical relation to the gallbladder or liver.

questions.stem: The coronary artery arises from the?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Ascending aorta**

- **A. Ascending aorta** — The ascending aorta gives off the right and left coronaries just above the aortic valve.
- **B. Arch of the aorta** — The arch of the aorta gives rise to major arteries of the head, neck, and upper limbs: brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid artery, and left subclavian artery.
- **C. Descending aorta** — The descending aorta supplies thoracic and abdominal organs, not the heart. Branches include the intercostal arteries, subcostal arteries, celiac trunk, SMA, and IMA.
- **D. Subclavian artery** — The subclavian artery supplies the upper limb, neck, and thoracic wall: vertebral artery, internal thoracic artery, thyrocervical trunk, and costocervical trunk.

questions.stem: What structures pass through BOTH the annulus of Zinn and superior orbital fissure?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Oculomotor nerves, abducens nerve, and nasociliary nerve**

- **A. Nasociliary nerve, frontal nerve, lacrimal nerve** — The frontal and lacrimal nerves pass outside the annulus of Zinn but within the superior orbital fissure.
- **B. Nasociliary nerve, frontal nerve, superior ophthalmic vein** — The frontal nerve and ophthalmic vein pass outside the annulus of Zinn but within the superior orbital fissure.
- **C. Nasociliary nerve, oculomotor nerve, ophthalmic artery** — The ophthalmic artery passes through the annulus of Zinn and optic canal, not the superior orbital fissure.
- **D. Oculomotor nerves, abducens nerve, and nasociliary nerve** — The annulus of Zinn is a fibrous ring that serves as the origin of the four rectus muscles, while the superior orbital fissure is a gap between the greater and lesser wings of the sphenoid bone. Structures that pass through both of them are the nasociliary nerve (branch of CN V1), abducens nerve, and oculomotor nerve.

questions.stem: Which of the following supplies the bronchopulmonary segment?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Tertiary bronchi**

- **A. Terminal bronchiole** — The terminal bronchioles are the last part of the conducting portion of the airway and supply pulmonary lobules, not bronchopulmonary segments.
- **B. Primary bronchi** — Primary bronchi are too proximal to supply individual bronchopulmonary segments.
- **C. Primary bronchiole** — Primary bronchioles (or lobular bronchioles) arise from segmental bronchi and supply lobules, not entire bronchopulmonary segments.
- **D. Tertiary bronchi** — A bronchopulmonary segment is supplied by a tertiary (segmental) bronchus. This bronchus provides the airway for the segment, and its distribution defines the segment's boundaries.

questions.stem: In its course through the brainstem, the corticospinal tract is in close anatomical relations with the roots of which cranial nerves?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — CN III, VI, XII**

- **A. CN III, IV, VI** — Although the corticospinal tract is adjacent to CN III in the midbrain and CN VI in the pons, CN IV emerges from the dorsal midbrain and does not course near the ventral brainstem where the corticospinal tract descends.
- **B. CN III, VI, XII** — As the corticospinal tract descends through the brainstem, it is in close anatomical relation to the roots of cranial nerves III (oculomotor), VI (abducens), and XII (hypoglossal). These nerves, like the corticospinal tract, are located medially in the midbrain, pons, and medulla respectively.
- **C. CN VII, X, XII** — Although CN XII is adjacent to the corticospinal tract in the medulla, CN VII is lateral in the pons and CN X emerges posterolaterally in the medulla, placing both far from the ventral pathway of the corticospinal tract.
- **D. CN IX, X, XI** — CN IX, X, and XI all emerge from the posterolateral medulla, which is away from the anterior pyramids where the corticospinal tract descends.

questions.stem: Decussation of the central auditory pathway occurs in which segment of the CNS?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Pons**

- **A. Medulla** — Although the cochlear nuclei are located in the medulla, the major decussation of the central auditory pathway does not occur here; the fibers primarily cross after synapsing in the superior olivary complex, which is in the pons.
- **B. Midbrain** — The midbrain contains the inferior colliculus, a higher auditory relay center, but the major crossing of auditory fibers has already occurred earlier in the ascending pathway.
- **C. Pons** — Decussation of the central auditory pathway occurs in the pons, specifically at the level of the trapezoid body where fibers from the cochlear nuclei cross to the contralateral side.
- **D. Spinal cord** — The spinal cord carries somatosensory and motor tracts but no auditory fibers. It plays no role in the auditory pathway or its decussation.

#### Mnemonic

Can’t hear the call without passing through C-O-LL-Coll:

- **C** — Cochlear Nuclei
- **O** — Olivary nuclei
- **L** — Lateral Lemniscus
- **Coll** — Inferior Colliculi

questions.stem: What separates the carotid triangle from the submandibular triangle?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Posterior belly of digastric**

- **A. Posterior belly of digastric** — The posterior belly of the digastric separates the submandibular triangle from the carotid triangle.
- **B. Anterior belly of digastric** — The anterior belly of the digastric separates the submental triangle from the submandibular triangle.
- **C. Superior belly of omohyoid** — The superior belly of the omohyoid separates the carotid triangle from the muscular triangle.
- **D. Inferior belly of omohyoid** — The inferior belly of the omohyoid separates the supraclavicular triangle from the occipital triangle.

questions.stem: The circumflex artery supplies which of the following?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Left atrium and ventricle**

- **A. Interventricular septum** — The interventricular septum is mainly supplied by the anterior interventricular (left anterior descending or LAD) artery.
- **B. Right atrium and ventricle** — The right atrium and ventricle are primarily supplied by the right coronary artery (RCA).
- **C. Left atrium and ventricle** — The left circumflex artery winds around left margin of the heart to supply the left atrium and left ventricle.
- **D. Apex** — The apex of the heart is usually supplied by the anterior interventricular (LAD) artery.

#### Heart structure blood supply

| Heart structure | Blood supply |
|---|---|
| Right atrium | Right coronary artery |
| Right ventricle | Anterior interventricular artery, right marginal branch |
| Left ventricle | Anterior interventricular artery, left circumflex artery |
| Left atrium and left ventricle | Circumflex branch of left coronary |
| Interventricular septum and apex | Anterior interventricular artery |

choices.text:
Inability to communicate verbally despite having
normal muscle for speech

Inability to understand spoken and or written words
despite having normal auditory pathway
Inability to perform rapidly alternating movements

Inability to detect sensation from parts of the body
and face

questions.stem: A 55-year-old right-handed man is brought to the clinic after suffering a left-sided parietal stroke. A lesion involving Brodmann areas 3, 1, 2 will produce which neurological deficit?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Inability to detect sensation from parts of the body and face**

- **A. Inability to communicate verbally despite having normal muscle for speech** — This describes Broca’s aphasia affecting Brodmann areas 44 and 45, in the inferior frontal gyrus.
- **B. Inability to understand spoken and or written words despite having normal auditory pathway** — This describes Wernicke’s aphasia affecting Brodmann area 22 in the superior temporal gyrus.
- **C. Inability to perform rapidly alternating movements** — This describes dysdiadochokinesia, a cerebellar lesion sign.
- **D. Inability to detect sensation from parts of the body and face** — Brodmann areas 3, 1, and 2 make up the primary somatosensory cortex, located in the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe. A lesion here causes loss or impairment of fine touch, pain, temperature, vibration, and proprioception from the contralateral body and face.

questions.stem: Which nodes to the ureters drain into?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Lateral aortic and iliac nodes**

- **A. Common iliac nodes** — Although the ureters pass near the common iliac vessels, their primary lymphatic drainage is to the lumbar (lateral aortic) nodes and to iliac nodes, not exclusively to the common iliac nodes.
- **B. Mediolateral iliac nodes** — This is not a standard anatomical term for a primary group of lymph nodes the ureters drain into.
- **C. Lateral aortic and iliac nodes** — The ureters drain into the lateral aortic (lumbar) nodes along the abdominal portion and into various iliac nodes (common, external, and internal) along the pelvic portion.
- **D. None of the above** — Choice C is correct.

choices.text: Locate a region devoid of haustra
Trace the taenia coli on the cecum

questions.stem: Which of the following techniques could you use to precisely locate the appendix?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Trace the taenia coli on the cecum**

- **A. Locate a region devoid of haustra** — Haustra are sacculations of the colon formed by the taeniae coli and circular muscle tone. The appendix itself does not have haustra, but the absence of haustra is not a reliable landmark for finding it, since this feature is also seen in the rectum and small intestine.
- **B. Trace the ileocolic artery** — Tracing arteries directly is not practical during surgery to locate the appendix because the artery is small and variable in course.
- **C. Trace the right colic artery** — The right colic artery supplies the ascending colon, not the appendix. Following this artery will not lead to the appendix.
- **D. Trace the taenia coli on the cecum** — All three taeniae coli (longitudinal muscle bands of the colon) converge at the base of the appendix, hence can be used to locate the appendix.

choices.text:
Between ACA and MCA and between the anterior spinal
level and posterior iliac cerebellar artery
Between ACA, MCA, and between the PCA and MCA

questions.stem: Which of the following are considered “watershed” areas of the brain?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Between ACA, MCA, and between the PCA and MCA**

- **A. Between ACA and MCA** — This is partially correct because the cortical border zone between ACA and MCA is a classic cortical “watershed” area. However, it is not the only watershed region, so this is incomplete.
- **B. Between ACA and MCA and between the anterior spinal level and posterior iliac cerebellar artery** — Although the ACA–MCA cortical border zone is a watershed area, the latter is not.
- **C. Between ACA and PCA** — There is no significant border zone between the ACA and PCA. The PCA primarily supplies the occipital lobe, whereas ACA supplies the medial frontal and parietal lobes; there is no defined watershed territory between them.
- **D. Between ACA, MCA, and between the PCA and MCA** — The two main cortical watershed areas of the brain are:

  1. Between the ACA and MCA — involving the superior frontal and parietal regions.
  2. Between the MCA and PCA — involving the parieto-occipital region.

  These regions are vulnerable to ischemia during systemic hypotension, which is the hallmark of watershed infarcts.

choices.text:
The quadrate and caudate lobes are functionally part of
the left lobe.

The triangular ligament connects the liver to the
pancreas.

It receives highly oxygenated blood from the hepatic
portal artery.

The lymphatic drainage is to the superior mesenteric
nodes.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is CORRECT about the liver?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — The quadrate and caudate lobes are functionally part of the left lobe.**

- **A. The quadrate and caudate lobes are functionally part of the left lobe.** — Although the quadrate and caudate lobes appear to belong anatomically to the right lobe (based on surface anatomy and the falciform ligament), functionally and surgically, they are part of the left hepatic lobe, as they receive blood from and drain bile into the left hepatic duct.
- **B. The triangular ligament connects the liver to the pancreas.** — The triangular ligaments (right and left) are peritoneal folds that connect the liver to the diaphragm, not to the pancreas.
- **C. It receives highly oxygenated blood from the hepatic portal artery.** — The liver receives oxygen-rich blood primarily from the hepatic artery proper, not the portal vein. The portal vein brings nutrient-rich, deoxygenated blood from the gastrointestinal tract.
- **D. The lymphatic drainage is to the superior mesenteric nodes.** — The lymph from most of the liver drains initially to the hepatic lymph nodes located in the porta hepatis, then to the celiac lymph nodes.

questions.stem: The submucosal layer is seen in the following organs, EXCEPT?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Gallbladder**

- **A. Duodenum** — The duodenum, like the rest of the small intestine, contains a submucosal layer that supports blood vessels, lymphatics, and submucosal glands.
- **B. Gallbladder** — The gallbladder is the only organ of the GIT without a submucosal layer. The mucosa of the gallbladder is directly attached to the muscularis layer.
- **C. Small intestine** — The small intestine has a prominent submucosal layer containing Brunner’s glands (in the duodenum) and Meissner’s plexus, making it a key structural layer.
- **D. Esophagus** — The esophagus lacks a serosa layer, but has 4 layers including mucosa, submucosa, muscularis propria, and adventitia.

questions.stem: Which of the following veins has no impression on the lungs?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Internal jugular vein**

- **A. Internal jugular vein** — The internal jugular vein is located in the neck, within the carotid sheath, alongside the common carotid artery and vagus nerve. It does not contact the lungs.
- **B. Azygos vein** — The azygos vein arches superiorly over the root of the right lung before emptying into the superior vena cava, creating a distinct groove (impression) on the mediastinal surface of the right lung.
- **C. Superior vena cava**
- **D. Inferior vena cava** — The inferior vena cava (IVC) passes through the central tendon of the diaphragm and forms a vertical impression on the mediastinal surface of the right lung, near its base.

questions.stem: What type of epithelium allows for protection for organs constantly exposed to abrasions?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Stratified squamous**

- **A. Pseudostratified** — Pseudostratified epithelium is typically found in respiratory passages providing secretion and ciliary movement. It does not provide strong protection against abrasion.
- **B. Stratified squamous** — Stratified squamous epithelium, either keratinized or non-keratinized, consists of multiple layers of cells, allowing the superficial layers to be sloughed off without damaging the underlying tissue. It is the common origin of dental, oral mucosal, and cutaneous tissues. It is well-suited for protection against mechanical stress and abrasion.
- **C. Simple cuboidal** — Simple cuboidal epithelium is a single layer of cube-shaped cells, typically involved in secretion and absorption (e.g., kidney tubules, glands) but does not protect against abrasion, as it lacks multiple layers.
- **D. Transitional epithelium** — Transitional epithelium is seen in the urinary bladder and ureters and is specialized to accommodate stretching, not mechanical abrasion.

choices.text: Posterior segment of the right upper lobe
Posterior segment of the right lower lobe
Superior segment of the right lower lobe
Inferior lingular segment of the left upper lobe

questions.stem: Sammy was lying down watching Netflix while eating peanuts, when suddenly she choked. Where did the peanut likely go?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Superior segment of the right lower lobe**

- **A. Posterior segment of the right upper lobe** — This happens when lying on the right side.
- **B. Posterior segment of the right lower lobe** — This happens when sitting or standing.
- **C. Superior segment of the right lower lobe** — This happens when supine.
- **D. Inferior lingular segment of the left upper lobe** — This happens when lying on the left side.

#### Aspiration site by position

| Position | Bronchopulmonary segment (BPS) affected |
|---|---|
| Sitting / standing | Posterior basal BPS of the right lower lobe |
| Supine | Superior BPS of the right lower lobe |
| Lying on the right side | Posterior BPS of the right upper lobe |
| Lying on the left side | Inferior lingular BPS of the left upper lobe |

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman undergoes a total abdominal hysterectomy for symptomatic uterine fibroids. During the operation, the surgeon carefully identifies and ligates the uterine arteries near the lateral aspect of the cervix. However, great care is taken to avoid injury to the ureters, which pass close to the uterine arteries at this level. Accidental ligation of the ureter during this step can lead to urinary leakage or obstruction postoperatively. What is the position of the ureter relative to the uterine artery at the level of the pelvis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Below and behind**

- **A. Below and behind** — In the female pelvis, the ureter passes inferior (below) and posterior (behind) to the uterine artery as it approaches the lateral fornix of the vagina and the base of the broad ligament.
- **B. Above and behind** — The ureter does not pass superior to the uterine artery at the level of the cervix.
- **C. Above and in front of** — The ureter is posterior to the uterine artery, not anterior, and it is inferior, not superior.
- **D. Below and in front of** — Although the ureter is inferior to the uterine artery, it passes posterior to it, not in front.

questions.stem: A trauma patient sustained a laceration injury at the spinal cord at the level of L4. Which of the following is NOT affected?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Lateral horns**

- **A. Dorsal horns** — The dorsal horns are related to sensation and are present at all cord levels.
- **B. Lateral horns** — The gray matter is divided into the dorsal, lateral, and ventral horns. The lateral horns are related to the sympathetic (thoracolumbar) nervous system, and is found in T1-L3 levels only.
- **C. Ventral horns** — The ventral horns are related to motor movement (contain anterior horn cell) and are present at all cord levels.
- **D. White matter** — White matter is present at all cord levels.

questions.stem: What presents as pale red-orange reflex on fundoscopy?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — CRAO**

- **A. CRAO** — CRAO typically presents with sudden, painless, monocular vision and visual field loss that occurs over seconds, due to acute ischemia of the inner retina. The classic finding is a cherry-red spot at the fovea surrounded by a pale retina, with the latter giving rise to a pale ROR.
- **B. Retinal detachment** — Retinal detachment involves the separation of the retina from the underlying choroid. On fundoscopy, it appears as a gray, folded, and opaque retina, but not characteristically pale red-orange.
- **C. Papilledema** — Papilledema refers to the swelling of the optic disc seen as blurred or indistinct disc margins, and not as a pale ROR. This condition results from increased intracranial pressure and increased CSF pressure in the extension of the subarachnoid space around the optic nerve.
- **D. Astigmatism** — Astigmatism is a refractive error, and the ROR remains normal and symmetric because the media are clear and the retina is normal.

#### Clinical correlation: central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO)

- Because terminal branches of the central retinal artery are end arteries, obstruction of them by an embolus result in instant and total blindness.
- Presentation: sudden, painless, unilateral, vision loss that occurs over seconds.
- On ophthalmoscopy: Retina appears diffusely pale with cherry red macular spot.

questions.stem: What is the upper border of the bladder trigone?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Interureteric ridge**

- **A. Interureteric ridge** — The bladder trigone is a smooth triangular area on the posterior wall of the bladder, bounded by three openings: two ureteric orifices at the superolateral angles and the internal urethral orifice at the inferior angle. The upper border of the bladder trigone is formed by the interureteric ridge, which connects the two ureteric orifices.
- **B. Pubovesical ligament** — The pubovesical ligament extends from the pubis to the neck of the bladder and is responsible for supporting the bladder anteriorly.
- **C. Rectovesical ligament** — The rectovesical ligament extends from the bladder to the sides of the rectum and sacrum and serves as another supporting structure of the bladder.
- **D. Urethral orifice** — The urethral orifice makes up the inferior angle of the bladder trigone, not the upper border.

questions.stem: What skin malignancy involves keratinocytes invading the dermis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Squamous cell CA**

- **A. Basal cell CA** — Basal cell carcinoma arises from the basal layer of the epidermis and is composed of basaloid cells with hyperchromatic nuclei arranged in peripheral palisading patterns. Although it can locally invade underlying tissues, it rarely metastasizes and is not characterized by malignant keratinocytes invading the dermis.
- **B. Squamous cell CA** — Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the skin involves malignant proliferation of keratinocytes that breach the basement membrane and invade the dermis. Histologically, invasive SCC shows variable differentiation—well-differentiated tumors exhibit keratin pearls and intercellular bridges, reflecting keratinocyte origin.
- **C. Melanoma** — Melanoma is a malignant tumor of melanocytes, the pigment-producing cells of the basal epidermis. Histology shows atypical melanocytes invading the dermis and epidermis (“pagetoid spread”). Hence, melanoma involves dermal invasion, but by melanocytes, not keratinocytes.
- **D. Adenocarcinoma** — Adenocarcinoma refers to malignant tumors of glandular epithelium, not epidermal keratinocytes. In the skin, adenocarcinomas may originate from sweat or sebaceous glands. Dermal invasion by keratinocytes does not occur in adenocarcinoma.

**Basal cell carcinoma · Squamous cell carcinoma**

questions.stem: Which is NOT part of the triceps coxae?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Piriformis**

**Piriformis**
- Action: hip external rotation
- Insertion: greater trochanter

- **A. Piriformis** — The triceps coxae, or “triceps of the hip,” is a tricipital (three-headed) collection of muscles which occupies the gap between the piriformis and the quadratus femoris. It is formed by the superior gemellus, inferior gemellus, and obturator internus. The piriformis is not part of it.
- **B. Superior gemellus** — The superior gemellus, inferior gemellus, and obturator internus are all part of the triceps coxae.
- **C. Inferior gemellus**
- **D. Obturator internus**

questions.stem: A patient suffers a hip dislocation after being involved in a motor vehicle collision. What is the most common direction of hip dislocation?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Posterior**

- Most common direction of hip dislocation: POSTERIOR
- Mechanism: FLEXION, ADDUCTION, INTERNAL ROTATION

- **A. Anterior** — Anterior is not the most common direction of hip dislocation.
- **B. Posterior** — The most common direction of acquired hip dislocation is posterior, which usually occurs when the hip is flexed, adducted, and medially rotated.
- **C. Inferior** — Inferior is not the most common direction of hip dislocation.
- **D. Superior** — Superior is not the most common direction of hip dislocation.

questions.stem: Atlantoaxial joint is what kind of joint?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Trochoid/pivot**

- **A. Trochoid/pivot** — Examples of pivot/trochoid joints include the atlantoaxial joint and radioulnar joints.
- **B. Plane** — Examples of plane joints include sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular joints.
- **C. Ginglymus** — Examples of ginglymus/hinge joints include the elbows, knees, and ankles.
- **D. Condyloid** — Examples of condyloid joints include the metacarpophalangeal joints.

| Example | Type of joint |
|---|---|
| Atlantoaxial joint | Pivot or trochoid |
| Radiocarpal joint | Condyloid or ellipsoid joint |
| Sacrococcygeal joint | Symphysis |

*Figure: atlanto-occipital and atlanto-axial joints, anterior view.*

| Example | Type of joint |
|---|---|
| Distal radioulnar joint | Pivot or trochoid |
| Elbow joint | Hinge |

questions.stem: What kind of joint are the sacrum and coccyx?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Symphysis**

- **A. Synchondrosis** — Synchondroses are immovable joints (synarthrosis) where bones are connected by hyaline cartilage. An example is the joint between the diaphysis and epiphysis of a growing long bone.
- **B. Syndesmosis** — Syndesmoses are slightly movable joints (amphiarthrosis) comprised of bones held together by an interosseous membrane. An example is the distal tibiofibular joint.
- **C. Symphysis** — Symphyses or symphyseal joints are slightly movable joints (amphiarthrosis) where bones are united by a layer of fibrocartilage. Examples are the joints between vertebral bodies, including the sacrum and the coccyx.
- **D. Synarthrosis** — A synarthrosis refers to immovable joints. Examples are the sutures found between skull bones.

#### Structural classification of joints (connecting medium)

- **Fibrous**
  - Bones united by fibrous connective tissue
  - Generally immovable
  - Types: suture, syndesmosis, gomphosis
- **Cartilaginous**
  - Bones held together by cartilage
  - Slightly moveable
  - Types: synchondroses, symphyses
- **Synovial**
  - Contain synovial fluid
  - Freely moveable

#### Functional classification of joints (mobility)

- **Synarthroses** — immovable joints
  - Types: suture (skull), syndesmosis (distal tibiofibular), gomphosis
- **Amphiarthroses** — slightly moveable joints
  - Primary = synchondrosis (hyaline): epiphyseal cartilage plates, manubriosternal
  - Secondary = symphysis (fibrocartilage): pubic symphysis, intervertebral disks
- **Diarthroses** — freely moveable joints

questions.stem: What is the most distal muscle innervated by the C5 root?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Brachioradialis**

- **A. Pronator teres** — The pronator teres is innervated by the median nerve (C6, C7).
- **B. Biceps brachii** — The biceps brachii is innervated by the musculocutaneous nerve (C5, C6, C7). It attaches to the scapula proximally and to the radial tuberosity and fascia of forearm distally.
- **C. Brachioradialis** — The brachioradialis muscle is the only flexor innervated by the radial nerve (C5, C6). It attaches to the supraepicondylar ridge of the humerus proximally and to the lateral surface of distal end of the radius proximal to the styloid processes distally.
- **D. Coracobrachialis** — The coracobrachialis muscle is innervated by the musculocutaneous nerve (C5, C6, C7). It attaches to the coracoid process of the scapula proximally and to the middle third of the medial surface of the humerus distally.

questions.stem: After amputation, which technique will allow better muscle contraction and effectiveness?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Myodesis**

- **A. Myoplasty** — Myoplasty refers to suturing of muscle to the periosteum or fascia of opposing musculature. This produces less effective muscle contraction.
- **B. Myofascial closure** — These also produce less stable muscle attachments, hence resulting in less effective muscle contraction.
- **C. Myofascial release** — These also produce less stable muscle attachments, hence resulting in less effective muscle contraction.
- **D. Myodesis** — Myodesis refers to suturing of muscle or tendon to bone. It provides a stronger insertion, helps maximize strength, and minimizes atrophy since myodesed muscles continue to counterbalance their antagonists, thereby preventing contractures and maximizing residual limb function.

*Figure reference: myoplasty, myofascial closure, myodesis, myofascial release.*

questions.stem: A nurse was injecting antibiotics into the gluteal area of a patient, inadvertently hitting a nerve which led to numbness on the anterolateral area of the ipsilateral leg as well as foot drop. What structure was affected?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Common peroneal branch**

- **A. Sciatic nerve** — The sciatic nerve passes through the greater sciatic foramen, usually inferior to the piriformis, to enter the gluteal region. It then descends to supply the posterior aspect of the thigh and the entire leg and foot. Though it is the one directly susceptible to injury with gluteal injections, this is not the best and most specific answer for this question.
- **B. Common peroneal branch** — The common peroneal nerve is a branch of the sciatic nerve which innervates the muscles of the anterior compartment of the leg. These muscles dorsiflex the foot. Hence, damage to the common peroneal nerve is commonly associated with foot drop. It also provides sensory innervation to the leg through its branches. Specifically, the superficial fibular nerve innervates the skin of the anterolateral leg and dorsum of the foot. Although it is a terminal branch of the sciatic nerve, its proximal fibers can still be injured which can lead to the specific symptoms stated in the question. To avoid injuries from gluteal IM injections, it must be done in the superolateral quadrant of the buttocks or superior to a line extending from the PSIS to the superior border of the greater trochanter.
- **C. Deep fibular nerve** — The deep fibular or deep peroneal nerve is a terminal division of the common peroneal nerve. It innervates the muscles responsible for dorsiflexing the foot as well as extending the toes at the MTP and IP joints. It also provides cutaneous innervation to the skin of the first webspace on the dorsum of the foot but not the anterolateral leg, hence making it the less likely answer for this question.
- **D. Sural nerve** — The sural nerve provides cutaneous innervation over the posterolateral leg and foot. It does not have a motor innervation.

#### Clinical correlation: intramuscular injections

- To avoid injury to the underlying sciatic nerve, the injection should be given well forward on the upper outer quadrant of the buttock.
- Superior to a line extending from PSIS to the superior border of the greater trochanter (approximating the superior border of the gluteus maximus).

questions.stem: After a night of partying, Rizza was walking home when she lost her balance and fell elbow-first. What structure is likely fractured?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Olecranon**

- Most common mechanism: DIRECT BLOW/FALL ON ELBOW

- **A. Olecranon** — The olecranon is the part of the ulna that cups the lower end of the humerus, creating a hinge for elbow movement. The bony point of the olecranon can easily be felt beneath the skin since it does not have much protection from muscles or other soft tissues. Thus, it can break easily as a consequence of a direct blow to the elbow or a fall onto the tip of the elbow.
- **B. Radius** — The radius is less likely to be injured in this situation.
- **C. Styloid process** — The styloid process is less likely to be injured in this situation.
- **D. Humerus** — The humerus is less likely to be injured in this situation.

questions.stem: What is the lateral muscle of the pelvis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Obturator internus**

- **A. Piriformis** — *Posterior pelvic wall.* The piriformis muscle, though a lateral rotator like the obturators, is not the main component of the lateral walls of the pelvis. It is located more posteriorly, originating at the sacrum and inserting into the greater trochanter.
- **B. Obturator internus** — The lateral pelvic walls are formed by the right and left hip bones, each of which includes an obturator foramen closed by an obturator membrane. The fleshy attachments of the obturator internus muscles cover and thus pad most of the lateral pelvic walls.
- **C. Rectus femoris** — *Anterior thigh compartment.* The rectus femoris is part of the quadriceps femoris muscle group of the thigh.
- **D. Gluteus maximus** — *Gluteal and posterior thigh compartment.* The gluteus maximus is a large muscle located at the buttocks.

questions.stem: What kind of joint is the distal radioulnar joint?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Pivot**

| Example | Type of joint |
|---|---|
| Distal radioulnar joint | Pivot or trochoid |

- **A. Pivot** — Examples of pivot/trochoid joints include the atlantoaxial joint and radioulnar joints.
- **B. Condyloid** — Examples of condyloid joints include the metacarpophalangeal joints.
- **C. Plane** — Examples of plane joints include sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular joints.
- **D. Ball and socket** — Examples of ball and socket joints include the hip joint, where the spherical head of the femur rotates within the socket formed by the acetabulum of the hip bone.

questions.stem: Teddy, a 65-year-old woman, presents with a 6-month history of back pain associated with a feeling that she got short. Calcium, phosphate, and alkaline phosphatase are within normal limits. What will her spine x-ray show?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Radiolucency**

- **A. Skip lesions** — Skip lesions are more classically seen in metastatic cancer or in Pott’s disease.
- **B. Radiolucency** — This is a case of osteoporosis, which involves decreased bone strength associated with bone demineralization. This would present on a radiograph as radiolucency or decreased cortical thickness in the early stages.
- **C. Demineralization** — Demineralization refers to the general pathologic process observed in osteoporosis, but it is not a specific radiographic finding per se.
- **D. Abscess** — Abscess formation is seen in infectious processes such as tuberculous or pyogenic infection. This would also present with systemic symptoms and localized tenderness.

Quick associations:
- Skip lesions: metastasis, abscess
- Increased radiolucency: osteoporosis

questions.stem: You notice Tyra Banks with an unusual gait while she sashayed on the runway. When her weight is on her right leg, her pelvis drops on the left side. Which structure is likely affected?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Gluteus medius**

**Trendelenburg sign**
- Affected stance leg
- Superior gluteal nerve injury
- Gluteus medius weakness

- **A. Gluteus medius** — Injury to the superior gluteal nerve results in gluteus medius weakness, causing weakened abduction of the thigh and subsequent drop of the contralateral pelvis. This results in the characteristic Trendelenburg gait, a compensatory mechanism for the loss of gluteus medius action.
- **B. Gluteus maximus** — The gluteus maximus extends the hip. It is not involved in Trendelenburg gait.
- **C. Adductor longus** — The adductor longus adducts the hip. It is not involved in Trendelenburg gait.
- **D. Tensor fascia lata** — The tensor fascia lata contributes to the medial rotation of the hip. It is not the main structure involved in the Trendelenburg gait.

questions.stem: Which of the following does NOT comprise the acetabulum?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Sacrum**

- **A. Ilium** — The ilium, pubis, and ischium form the acetabulum.
- **B. Pubis** — The ilium, pubis, and ischium form the acetabulum.
- **C. Ischium** — The ilium, pubis, and ischium form the acetabulum.
- **D. Sacrum** — The sacrum does not form the acetabulum.

questions.stem: What bone maintains the transverse arch of the foot?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Cuneiform**

- **A. Cuboid** — The cuboid is part of the transverse arch of the foot; however, it is not the keystone.
- **B. Cuneiform** — The transverse arch of the foot is composed by the bases of metatarsal bones, cuboid, and cuneiforms; its keystone is the intermediate cuneiform.
- **C. Calcaneus** — Calcaneus is part of the medial and lateral transverse arch.
- **D. Talus** — Talus is part of the medial longitudinal arch.

#### Arches of the foot

- **Medial longitudinal arch**: calcaneum, talus, navicular, three cuneiforms, 1st–3rd metatarsals
- **Lateral longitudinal arch**: calcaneum, cuboid, 4th–5th metatarsals
- **Transverse arch**: bases of metatarsal bones, cuboid, medial, intermediate, and lateral cuneiforms

questions.stem: Pain is elicited when the patient tucks his thumb inside his fingers when making a fist, with the wrist deviated ulnar. What is likely the diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Tenosynovitis**

- **A. Gamer’s thumb** — “Gamer’s thumb” is an informal or colloquial term often referring to De Quervain’s tenosynovitis caused by repetitive thumb use (e.g., gaming, texting). While related, the formal clinical term is tenosynovitis, not “Gamer’s thumb.”
- **B. Tenosynovitis** — De Quervain’s tenosynovitis refers to the excessive friction of APL and EPB on their common sheath resulting in fibrous thickening of the sheath and stenosis of the osseofibrous tunnel. Pain is elicited via the Finkelstein test.
- **C. Carpal tunnel syndrome** — Carpal tunnel syndrome involves compression of the median nerve under the flexor retinaculum. Symptoms include numbness, tingling, and pain in the lateral 3½ digits, weakness in thenar muscles, and difficulty with thumb opposition.
- **D. Radial tunnel syndrome** — Radial tunnel syndrome results from compression of the posterior interosseous nerve (a branch of the radial nerve) as it passes through the supinator muscle. It presents with deep, dull pain in the proximal forearm, often mistaken for lateral epicondylitis.

#### Clinical correlation: De Quervain’s tenosynovitis

- APL and EPB
- Finkelstein test
- Excessive friction of APL and EPB on their common sheath results in fibrous thickening of the sheath and stenosis of the osseofibrous tunnel
- Caused by repetitive forceful use of the hands during gripping and wringing (e.g., squeezing water out of clothes)
- Pain in the wrist that radiates proximally to the forearm and distally toward the thumb
- Local tenderness over the common flexor sheath on the lateral side of the wrist

#### Related conditions

- **Gamekeeper’s thumb** — ulnar collateral ligament
- **Carpal tunnel syndrome** — median nerve; FDS (4), FDP (4), FPL
- **Radial tunnel syndrome** — posterior interosseus nerve

questions.stem: The patency of which arteries are checked in Allen’s test?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Radial and ulnar**

- **A. Brachial and radial** — Allen’s test is not used to assess the brachial artery, since it lies proximal to the hand’s collateral circulation.
- **B. Radial and ulnar** — The Allen’s test is used to determine patency of the ulnar and radial arteries.
- **C. Ulnar and brachial** — The ulnar artery supplies the superficial palmar arch, while the brachial artery terminates higher in the forearm, making this combination irrelevant for Allen’s test.
- **D. Subclavian and brachial** — These vessels are too proximal to evaluate hand perfusion and are not tested in Allen’s test.

#### Clinical correlation: Allen test

- Used to determine patency of the ulnar and radial arteries
- Compress radial artery and ask the patient to tightly clench the fists
- Ask to open the hands; normally blood quickly flows into the arches through the ulnar arteries, causing the palms to promptly turn pink (ulnar artery patent)
- Repeat the test by compressing the ulnar artery to establish patency of the radial artery

questions.stem: What innervates the webspace between the first and second toes?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Deep peroneal**

- **A. Deep peroneal** — The deep peroneal nerve innervates the adjacent sides of the big and second toes.
- **B. Superficial peroneal** — *Anterolateral leg, foot dorsum.* The superficial peroneal (fibular) nerve supplies the skin on the dorsum of the foot and toes, except for the first interdigital cleft.
- **C. Tibial** — The tibial nerve provides motor supply to the posterior compartment of the leg and cutaneous innervation to the heel and plantar surface of the foot, not the dorsum or web spaces.
- **D. Sural** — *Posterolateral leg, lateral foot.* The sural nerve supplies sensory innervation to the lateral side of the foot and little toe, not the web space between the first and second toes.

questions.stem: Which muscle in the medial compartment of the thigh that can flex the knee joint?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Gracilis**

- **A. Adductor magnus** — *Hip adduction; assist hip ER; hip extension.* While the adductor part primarily adducts and flexes the thigh, the hamstring part extends the thigh, not the knee. It does not flex the knee joint.
- **B. Adductor brevis** — *Hip adduction; assist hip ER.* Adductor brevis acts mainly to adduct the thigh and assist in flexing the hip. It does not cross the knee joint, so it cannot flex the knee.
- **C. Adductor longus** — *Hip adduction; assist hip ER.* Adductor longus also primarily adducts the thigh and assists in hip flexion, but it does not act on the knee joint because it does not cross it.
- **D. Gracilis** — *Hip adduction; knee flexion.* The gracilis muscle adducts the thigh at the hip joint and flexes the leg at the knee joint.

questions.stem: A patient presents with a ruptured calcaneal (Achilles) tendon following a sudden forceful push-off while running. Which of the following movements can the patient tendon no longer perform?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Plantarflexion**

**Gastrocsoleus**
- Common insertion: Achilles tendon
- Common action: ankle plantarflexion

- **A. Dorsiflexion** — Dorsiflexion is performed by the anterior compartment muscles.
- **B. Inversion** — Inversion is produced by the tibialis anterior and tibialis posterior muscles.
- **C. Plantarflexion** — The Achilles tendon is the most powerful tendon in the body. It connects the gastrocnemius, soleus, and plantaris muscles to the posterior surface of the calcaneus. Its primary function is to plantarflex the foot at the ankle, hence rupture will lead to inability to plantarflex the foot.
- **D. Eversion** — Eversion is done by the peroneus longus and peroneus brevis muscles.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man presents to the clinic after falling off his motorcycle and landing directly on his right shoulder. On examination, there is a visible flattening of the shoulder contour and atrophy of the deltoid muscle. Sensory testing reveals loss of sensation over the lateral aspect of the shoulder. Which nerve is most likely injured?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Axillary nerve**

#### Nerve injuries — quick reference

- Radial nerve: wrist drop
- Suprascapular nerve: weak abduction and external rotation
- Musculocutaneous nerve: weak elbow flexion, sensory loss on lateral forearm

- **A. Radial nerve** — A radial nerve injury classically produces wrist drop due to paralysis of the wrist and finger extensors and sensory loss over the posterior forearm and dorsum of the hand, not over the lateral shoulder. It does not innervate the deltoid, so it would not cause deltoid atrophy.
- **B. Axillary nerve** — The axillary nerve (C5–C6) passes through the quadrangular space and supplies the deltoid and teres minor muscles, and provides sensation via the superior lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm. Injury commonly occurs due to fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus or dislocation of the glenohumeral joint, and manifests as deltoid paralysis with a flattened shoulder contour, loss of abduction from 15° to 90°, and loss of sensation over the lateral shoulder.
- **C. Suprascapular nerve** — Suprascapular nerve injury causes weakness of supraspinatus and infraspinatus, leading to impaired initiation of abduction and weak external rotation. It does not affect the deltoid nor does it produce sensory loss.
- **D. Musculocutaneous nerve** — Musculocutaneous nerve injury presents with weakness in elbow flexion and supination, and sensory loss over the lateral forearm, not shoulder, through the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old male construction worker falls on his outstretched right hand. He complains of pain and swelling around the elbow. On examination, movement at the elbow joint is limited, but the radiocapitellar and ulnohumeral articulations are intact. Imaging is done to assess for fracture or dislocation involving the elbow joint components. Which of the following is NOT a component of the elbow joint?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Lateral epicondyle**

- **A. Capitulum** — The articulation of the elbow joint occurs between the trochlea and capitulum of the humerus, and the trochlear notch of the ulna, and head of the radius respectively.
- **B. Lateral epicondyle** — The lateral epicondyle is an anatomical landmark and site of muscle attachment, but it is not an articular component of the elbow joint itself.
- **C. Trochlea** — The articulation of the elbow joint occurs between the trochlea and capitulum of the humerus, and the trochlear notch of the ulna, and head of the radius respectively.
- **D. Trochlear notch** — The articulation of the elbow joint occurs between the trochlea and capitulum of the humerus, and the trochlear notch of the ulna, and head of the radius respectively.

questions.stem: Bea was diagnosed with a medial epicondyle injury. Which nerve is likely affected?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Ulnar nerve**

- **A. Radial nerve** — In relation to the elbow, the radial nerve runs laterally, near the lateral epicondyle.
- **B. Median nerve** — In relation to the elbow, the median nerve passes anteriorly through the cubital fossa.
- **C. Ulnar nerve** — The ulnar nerve is closely related to the medial epicondyle of the humerus, hence any injury to this area results in damage to the said nerve.
- **D. Musculocutaneous nerve** — The musculocutaneous nerve ends above the elbow, becoming the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.

Related terms: cubital tunnel syndrome, claw hand.

choices.text: More commonly injured than the PCL

Attached to the lateral side of the medial femoral
condyle
Attached to the intercondylar area of the tibia
Runs upward, backward, and laterally to the femur

questions.stem: Which is INCORRECT regarding the anterior cruciate ligament?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Attached to the lateral side of the medial femoral condyle**

- **A. More commonly injured than the PCL** — The ACL is weaker and thus more commonly injured than the PCL.
- **B. Attached to the lateral side of the medial femoral condyle** — The ACL attaches to the medial side of the lateral epicondyle of the femur, whereas the PCL attaches to the lateral side of the medial femoral condyle.
- **C. Attached to the intercondylar area of the tibia** — The ACL arises from the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia, just posterior to the attachment of the medial meniscus.
- **D. Runs upward, backward, and laterally to the femur** — The ACL extends superiorly, posteriorly, and laterally to attach to the posterior part of the medial side of the lateral epicondyle of the femur.

#### ACL vs. PCL (both intracapsular ligaments)

| Feature | Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) | Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) |
|---|---|---|
| Tibial attachment | Attached below to the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia | Attached below to the posterior intercondylar area of the tibia |
| Femoral attachment | Passes upward, backward, and laterally to attach to the lateral femoral condyle | Passes upward, forward, and medially to attach to the medial femoral condyle |
| Function | Prevents forward sliding of the tibia on the femur (or posterior displacement of the femur on the tibia); prevents hyperextension of the knee joint | Prevents backward sliding of the tibia on the femur (or anterior displacement of the femur on the tibia); limits hyperflexion of the knee |
| Tension | Taut during knee extension; lax during knee flexion | Taut during knee flexion; lax during knee extension |
| Mechanism of injury | Blow on the lateral side of the knee, hyperextension, landing with the knee flexed | — |
| Special test | Anterior drawer sign, Lachman test, lateral pivot shift test | Posterior drawer sign |

questions.stem: What type of joint is the radiocarpal joint?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Condyloid**

| Example | Type of joint |
|---|---|
| Radiocarpal joint | Condyloid or ellipsoid joint |

- **A. Hinge** — Hinge joints allow movement in one plane only (flexion-extension). Examples of hinge joints include the elbow, knee, and ankle joints.
- **B. Plane** — Plane joints allow gliding/sliding between relatively flat surfaces and only small, limited movements. Examples of plane joints include the sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular joints.
- **C. Condyloid** — The radiocarpal or wrist joint is classified as a condyloid, specifically an ellipsoid, synovial joint. It allows movement in two planes: flexion-extension and abduction-adduction, which when combined, produce circumduction.
- **D. Saddle** — Saddle joints (e.g., carpometacarpal joint of the thumb) have reciprocally concave–convex surfaces permitting biaxial movement but with a distinct saddle shape. The radiocarpal joint’s articular geometry is ellipsoid/condyloid rather than saddle-shaped.

questions.stem: Which muscle is the main shoulder abductor?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Supraspinatus**

- **A. Supraspinatus** — The supraspinatus, which is part of the rotator cuff muscles, initiates shoulder abduction for the first 15 degrees, after which the deltoid muscle takes over as the main abductor for the remainder of the movement.
- **B. Subscapularis** — The subscapularis is also part of the rotator cuff, but its primary function is to medially (internally) rotate the arm.
- **C. Teres minor** — The teres minor is a rotator cuff muscle that functions mainly to laterally (externally) rotate the arm along with the infraspinatus.
- **D. Infraspinatus** — The infraspinatus, another rotator cuff muscle, functions primarily to laterally (externally) rotate the arm along with the teres minor.

#### Rotator cuff muscles

| Muscle | Nerve supply | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Supraspinatus | Suprascapular nerve | Abducts arm and stabilizes shoulder joint |
| Infraspinatus | Suprascapular nerve | Laterally rotates arm and stabilizes shoulder joint |
| Teres minor | Axillary nerve | Laterally rotates arm and stabilizes shoulder joint |
| Subscapularis ★ | Upper and lower subscapular nerves | Medially rotates arm and stabilizes shoulder joint |

questions.stem: Which ligament prevents hyperextension of the vertebral column?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Anterior longitudinal ligament**

| Ligament | Description |
|---|---|
| Anterior longitudinal ligament | Runs from the skull (occipital bone) to the sacrum on the anterior surface of the vertebral bodies and intervertebral disks. Limits extension of the vertebral column. Wide and strongly attached to the front and sides of the vertebral bodies and to the intervertebral discs. |
| Posterior longitudinal ligament | Interconnects the vertebral bodies and intervertebral disks posteriorly. Limits flexion of the vertebral column. Weak and narrow, attached to the posterior borders of the discs. |
| Ligamentum flavum | Connects the laminae of two adjacent vertebrae. |
| Ligamentum nuchae | Triangular-shaped median fibrous septum between the muscles on the two sides of the posterior aspect of the neck. Thickened supraspinous and interspinous ligaments in the cervical region. |
| Interspinous ligament | Between two adjacent spinous processes. |
| Intertransverse ligament | Between two adjacent transverse processes. |
| Supraspinous ligament | Between tips of two adjacent spinous processes. |

- **A. Ligamentum flavum** — The ligamentum flavum connects adjacent laminae and helps preserve normal curvature and assist in extension. It limits abrupt flexion of the vertebral column. It does not prevent hyperextension.
- **B. Anterior longitudinal ligament** — The anterior longitudinal ligament runs along the anterior surfaces of the vertebral bodies and intervertebral discs from the skull to the sacrum. It is the only ligament that strongly resists hyperextension.
- **C. Posterior longitudinal ligament** — The posterior longitudinal ligament runs along the posterior surfaces of the vertebral bodies within the vertebral canal. It prevents hyperflexion and helps redirect herniated disc material.
- **D. Interspinous ligament** — The interspinous ligament lies between adjacent spinous processes. It limits flexion of the vertebral column, not extension.

questions.stem: A person falls from a height and fractures the T12 vertebra. He develops loss of ankle dorsiflexion but intact knee extension. Which nerve root is most likely injured?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — L5**

| Myotome | Index Muscle | Action |
|---|---|---|
| C5 | Biceps brachialis | Elbow flexors |
| C6 | Extensor carpi radialis | Wrist extensors |
| C7 | Triceps | Elbow extensors |
| C8 | Flexor digitorum profundus | Finger flexors (FDP of middle finger) |
| T1 | Abductor digiti minimi | Small finger abductor |
| L2 | Iliopsoas | Hip flexors |
| L3 | Quadriceps | Knee extensors |
| L4 | Tibialis anterior | Ankle dorsiflexors |
| L5 | Extensor hallucis longus | Long toe extensors |
| S1 | Gastrocnemius | Ankle plantarflexors |

- **A. L3** — An L3 nerve root injury would produce weak hip flexion and partial loss of knee extension, not isolated ankle dorsiflexion weakness. Since knee extension is intact, an L3 nerve root injury is unlikely.
- **B. L4** — Injury to the L4 nerve root will affect knee extension and foot inversion. Since knee extension is intact, an L4 nerve root injury is unlikely.
- **C. L5** — The L5 nerve root primarily contributes to ankle dorsiflexion and toe extension. An injury would produce foot drop (loss of dorsiflexion) with preserved knee extension, as seen in the patient in this case.
- **D. S1** — The S1 nerve root contributes to plantar flexion and ankle eversion. Injury produces difficulty walking on toes and reduced Achilles reflex, not isolated dorsiflexion loss.

questions.stem: What among the following structures is the earliest to disappear?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Right umbilical vein**

- **A. Right umbilical vein** — In early embryonic development, both right and left umbilical veins carry oxygenated blood from the placenta to the sinus venosus. However, as development progresses, the right umbilical vein and the proximal part of the left umbilical vein disappear—the right umbilical vein is the first to regress, typically by the 5th to 7th week of development.
- **B. Right umbilical artery** — The right and left umbilical arteries persist much longer than the right umbilical vein because they continue to carry deoxygenated blood from the fetus to the placenta throughout fetal life.
