questions.stem: A previously healthy 65-year-old man who was admitted to the hospital yesterday after having fevers for a week at home. On admission, his temperature was 39.7°C, heart rate was 68 beats/min, and blood pressure was 110/60. Examination of his skin reveals a faint, salmon-colored, blanching, maculopapular rash located primarily on the trunk and chest. He complains of moderate abdominal pain and nausea. While blood culture reveals no organisms; a bone marrow culture grows gram-negative rods. The bacteria produce acid on glucose fermentation, reduce nitrates, and do not produce cytochrome oxidase or ferment lactose. Closer inspection shows that they are motile by means of flagella. Which of the following organisms is the patient most likely infected with?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Salmonella typhi**

- The patient is infected with a Salmonella species (Choice D), most likely Typhi or Paratyphi. His rash is “rose spots,” the rash of enteric fever due to S. typhi or Salmonella paratyphi. Salmonella species do not ferment lactose. Further, this patient has striking relative bradycardia, a dissociation between the heart rate and presence of fever. Most patients with such a degree of fever will be tachycardic; however, approximately 50% of patients with Salmonella infections will manifest this relative bradycardia.
- Clostridium difficile (Choice A) does not present with rash and typically not bradycardia. Escherichia coli (Choice C) infection from ingested food can be considered; however, the microbial characteristics rule out the other choices. Clostridium (Choice A) is a gram-positive rod, and Entamoeba histolytica (Choice B) is a protozoan, not a bacteria.

Harrison, T. R., Wiener, C., Bloomfield, G. S., Brown, C., Schiffer, J. T., & Spivak, A. M. (2004). Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, Self-Assessment and Board Review.

choices.text: Treatment of prior head and neck cancer

questions.stem: All of the following have been identified as risk factors for the development of squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck EXCEPT:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Treatment of prior head and neck cancer**

- Second head and neck malignancies are usually not therapy-induced (Choice D); they reflect the exposure of the upper aerodigestive mucosa to the same carcinogens that caused the first cancer.
- Alcohol and tobacco (Choice B/C) use are the most significant risk factors for head and neck cancer, and when used together, they act synergistically. Smokeless tobacco is an etiologic agent for oral cancers. Other potential carcinogens include marijuana and occupational exposures such as nickel refining, exposure to textile fibers, and woodworking. Some head and neck cancers have a viral etiology. Epstein-Barr virus infection (Choice A) is frequently associated with nasopharyngeal cancer. The human papilloma virus is also associated with a rising incidence of tumors arising from the oropharynx, that is, the tonsillar bed and base of tongue.

Harrison, T. R., Wiener, C., Bloomfield, G. S., Brown, C., Schiffer, J. T., & Spivak, A. M. (2004). Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, Self-Assessment and Board Review.

questions.stem: What is the most affected joint in gout?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — First metatarsophalangeal joint**

- Gout flare is typically monoarticular, often occurring in the lower extremities. The most commonly involved joint is the first metatarsophalangeal joint (Choice A).
- The talar, subtalar, ankle (Choice B), and knee (Choice C) can also be involved in some cases. Additionally, gout can occur in axial joints such as sacroiliac joints (Choice D) and the spine, though much less common than peripheral involvement, leading to diagnostic confusion.

Harrison, T. R., Wiener, C., Bloomfield, G. S., Brown, C., Schiffer, J. T., & Spivak, A. M. (2004). Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, Self-Assessment and Board Review.

choices.text: >2000 mL when the fluid develops rapidly
250 mL when the fluid develops rapidly

questions.stem: What is the amount of blood necessary to produce cardiac tamponade?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — >2000 mL in slowly developing effusions**

The quantity of fluid necessary to produce cardiac tamponade may be as small as 200 mL when the fluid develops rapidly to as much as >2000 mL in slowly developing effusions, when the pericardium has had the opportunity to stretch and adapt to an increasing volume (Option C). Other options are wrong.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman has hypertension that is difficult to control. She was diagnosed at age 26. Since that time she has been on increasing amounts of medication. Her current regimen consists of labetalol 1000 mg bid, lisinopril 40 mg qd, clonidine 0.1 mg bid, and amlodipine 5 mg qd. On physical examination she appears to be without distress. Blood pressure is 168/100, and heart rate is 84 beats/min. Cardiac examination is unremarkable, without rubs, gallops, or murmurs. She has good peripheral pulses and has no edema. Her physical appearance does not reveal any hirsutism, fat maldistribution, or abnormalities of genitalia. Laboratory studies reveal a potassium of 2.8 mEq/dL and a serum bicarbonate of 32 mEq/dL. Fasting blood glucose is 114 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Conn syndrome**

- **A. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia** — The patient has no physical features that suggest congenital adrenal hyperplasia.
- **B. Cushing syndrome** — The patient has no physical features that suggest Cushing syndrome. In addition, there is no glucose intolerance as is commonly seen in Cushing syndrome.
- **C. Conn syndrome**
  - This patient presents at a young age with hypertension that is difficult to control, raising the question of secondary causes of hypertension. The most likely diagnosis in this patient is primary hyperaldosteronism, also known as Conn syndrome.
  - The findings of hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis in the presence of difficult-to-control hypertension yield the likely diagnosis of Conn syndrome.
  - Diagnosis of the disease can be difficult, but the preferred test is the plasma aldosterone/renin ratio. This test should be performed at 8 a.m., and a ratio greater than 30–50 is diagnostic of primary hyperaldosteronism. Caution should be made in interpreting this test while the patient is on angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor therapy, as ACE inhibitors can falsely elevate plasma renin activity. However, a plasma renin level that is undetectable or an elevated aldosterone/renin ratio in the presence of ACE inhibitor therapy is highly suggestive of primary hyperaldosteronism.
- **D. Pheochromocytoma** — The lack of episodic symptoms and the labile hypertension make pheochromocytoma unlikely.

questions.stem: The following are insulin secretagogues, EXCEPT:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Exenatide**

- **A. Tolbutamide**
  - 1st generation sulfonylurea
  - Insulin secretagogue
- **B. Exenatide**
  - GLP-1 agonist
  - Incretin modulator, rather than a secretagogue
- **C. Glipizide**
  - 2nd generation sulfonylurea
  - Insulin secretagogue
- **D. Meglitinide**
  - Insulin secretagogue

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most abundant receptor on a platelet and therefore a target for antiplatelet therapy?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa**

- **A. Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa**
  - The platelet glycoprotein (Gp) IIb/IIIa (αIIbβ3) complex is the most abundant receptor on the platelet surface.
  - Platelet activation converts the normally inactive Gp IIb/IIIa receptor into an active receptor, enabling binding to fibrinogen and von Willebrand factor (vWF).
  - Because the surface of each platelet has about 50,000 Gp IIb/IIIa–binding sites, numerous activated platelets recruited to the site of vascular injury can rapidly form an occlusive aggregate by means of a dense network of intracellular fibrinogen bridges.
  - Because this receptor is the key mediator of platelet aggregation, it has become an effective target for antiplatelet therapy.
- **B. Protein C** — Protein C is a plasma glycoprotein that is activated by thrombin and acts to inactivate factors V and VIII.
- **C. Tissue factor**
  - Tissue factor binds the cofactor VIIa and can act to directly activate factor X, or it can activate factor IX, which in turn acts with factor VIIIa to activate factor X.
  - Activated factor X then converts prothrombin to thrombin, which in turn has positive feedback on the coagulant system by activating factor XI (the classic intrinsic pathway).
- **D. von Willebrand factor** — The vWF is a very large multimeric protein that is found in both the plasma and in the extracellular matrix of the subendothelial vessel wall.

choices.text: Frequent elevation of the lower extremities.

questions.stem: All of the following are appropriate therapeutic steps for varicose veins EXCEPT:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Aspirin**

- **A. Aspirin** — Varicose veins usually are treated with conservative measures.
- **B. Avoid prolonged standing.** — Symptoms often decrease when the legs are elevated periodically, prolonged standing is avoided, and elastic support hose are worn.
- **C. Frequent elevation of the lower extremities.** — See explanation in option B.
- **D. Graduated compression stockings.**
  - External compression with elastic stockings or stretch bandages provides a counterbalance to the hydrostatic pressure in the veins.
  - Although compression garments may improve symptoms, they do not prevent progression of varicose veins.
  - Graduated compression stockings with pressures of 20–30 mmHg is suitable for most patients with simple varicose veins, although pressures of 30–40 mmHg may be required for patients with manifestations of venous insufficiency such as edema and ulcers.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT part of the triad of Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Hypertension**

Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) is a clinical syndrome characterized by the triad of microangiopathy hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia and acute renal damage. It is one of the most common causes of acute renal damage in children.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the earliest plain radiographic finding of rheumatoid arthritis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Juxta-articular osteopenia**

- Joint imaging is a critical tool for both diagnosis and monitoring of disease status in rheumatoid arthritis (RA).
- Plain radiographs, because of their ready availability and ease of film comparison, are most commonly ordered.
- The earliest clinical sign of RA is juxta-articular osteopenia (Option A), although this may be difficult to appreciate on newer, digitized films.
- Other findings include soft tissue swelling (Option C), symmetric joint space loss (Option B), and subchondral erosions (Option D), most frequently in the wrists, metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, and metatarsophalangeal joints.

Harrison, T. R., Wiener, C., Bloomfield, G. S., Brown, C., Schiffer, J. T., & Spivak, A. M. (2004). *Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, Self-Assessment and Board Review.*

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has come to the clinic to discuss options in therapy. He is concerned about potential side effects, in particular weight gain. He has a history of myocardial infarction and subsequently lost 40 lb with diet and exercise. His heart function is normal now. He has previously tried metformin but did not tolerate it due to diarrhea and nausea. He had hypoglycemia with glipizide. Which of the following medications would be best for him to try next?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Exenatide**

- **A. Exenatide** — Exenatide would avoid the weight gain the patient is concerned about and hypoglycemia that the patient has experienced in the past.
- **B. Glimepiride** — Weight gain occurs with most (insulin, insulin secretagogues like glimepiride and repaglinide, thiazolidinediones like rosiglitazone) but not all (metformin, α-glucosidase inhibitors, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists like exenatide, dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors) therapies. Hypoglycemia can occur with glimepiride and repaglinide so they would not be preferred in this patient.
- **C. Repaglinide** — See explanation in Option B.
- **D. Rosiglitazone** — See explanation in Option B.

Harrison, T. R., Wiener, C., Bloomfield, G. S., Brown, C., Schiffer, J. T., & Spivak, A. M. (2004). *Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, Self-Assessment and Board Review.*

questions.stem: Jian complains of a 12-year history of heartburn. He is on proton pump inhibitor with poor compliance. He now complains of gradual food dysphagia over the last 6 months associated with lessening heartburn attacks. What is the MOST likely complication present in this patient?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Peptic stricture**

- **A. Peptic stricture** — A prolonged history of heartburn from chronic reflux preceding the onset of dysphagia is more likely suggestive of a mechanical obstruction such as a peptic stricture. Peptic stricture is one of the most common structural causes of dysphagia. Specifically, it presents as progressive dysphagia, first for solids, as in this case, then for liquids.
- **B. Achalasia** — Achalasia is a motility disorder presenting as impaired deglutitive LES relaxation and absent peristalsis. Clinical manifestations may include intermittent solid and liquid food dysphagia. However, achalasia is not a direct complication of chronic heartburn.
- **C. Esophageal dysplasia** — Esophageal squamous dysplasia is the precursor lesion of esophageal squamous cell cancer, the most common type of esophageal malignancy worldwide. However, it does not typically cause dysphagia on its own, unless it has progressed to invasive squamous cell carcinoma.
- **D. Barrett's esophagus** — Barrett's esophagus is specialized columnar metaplasia that replaces the normal squamous mucosa of the distal esophagus in some persons with GERD. Barrett's esophagus increases the risk of developing esophageal adenocarcinoma, however, it is less likely to cause dysphagia.

(HPIM 21st)

questions.stem: One hour after getting stung by a bee for the first time, Anja complained of itchy rashes, progressive difficulty of breathing, and dizziness. At the ER, her BP is 80/60, HR 102 bpm, RR 32/min, with a temperature of 36.5. Which information does NOT support a diagnosis of anaphylaxis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — First time bee sting**

Repeated exposure to the allergy-causing antigen is an important risk factor to keep in mind when evaluating patients with anaphylaxis. This generates an allergen-specific IgE, which is the end result of sensitization via the adaptive immune system. Thus, a first-time exposure such as to a bee sting (Choice A) is less likely supportive of a diagnosis of anaphylaxis. Difficulty breathing (Choice B), itchy rashes (Choice C), and hypotension (Choice D) are all clinical clues to anaphylaxis.

(HPIM 21st, p. 2727)

questions.stem: Which is NOT a risk factor for developing deep vein thrombosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Thrombocytopenia**

Deep vein thrombosis is usually caused by prothrombotic states, including cancer (Choice A), obesity, cigarette smoking, systemic arterial hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic kidney disease, blood transfusion (Choice B), long-haul air travel, air pollution, estrogen-containing contraceptives, pregnancy (Choice C), postmenopausal hormone replacement, surgery, and trauma. Sedentary lifestyle is increasingly prevalent. Thrombocytopenia or low platelet count is not considered a risk factor of DVT.

(HPIM 21st, p. 2092)

questions.stem: Endoscopy done by GI specialist reveals peptic ulcer and Helicobacter pylori infection. You start your patient on triple therapy with the following drugs, EXCEPT
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Misoprostol**

Current regimens for H. pylori infection consist of a PPI and two or three antimicrobial agents given for 10–14 days. Omeprazole (Choice D) is a proton pump inhibitor, while amoxicillin (Choice A) and clarithromycin (Choice B) are antibiotics used to kill the underlying infection of H. pylori. Misoprostol (Choice C) is not included in the commonly recommended regimens, as seen below:

**Commonly Recommended Treatment Regimens for Helicobacter pylori**
*(Adapted from Table 163-2. Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine. 21st ed. 2022)*

| Regimen (Duration) | Drug 1 | Drug 2 | Drug 3 | Drug 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Regimen 1: OCM (14 days) | Omeprazole (20mg bid) | Clarithromycin (500mg bid) | Metronidazole (500mg bid) | -- |
| Regimen 2: OCA (14 days) | Omeprazole (20mg bid) | Clarithromycin (500mg bid) | Amoxicillin (1g bid) | -- |
| Regimen 3: OBTM (14 days) | Omeprazole (20mg bid) | Bismuth subsalicylate (2 tabs qid) | Tetracycline HCl (500mg qid) | Metronidazole (500mg bid) |
| Regimen 4: Concomitant (14 days) | Omeprazole (20mg bid) | Amoxicillin (1g bid) | Clarithromycin (500mg bid) | Tinidazole (500mg bid) |
| Regimen 5: OAL (10 days) | Omeprazole (20mg bid) | Amoxicillin (1g bid) | Levofloxacin (500mg bid) | -- |

(HPIM 21st, p. 1283)

questions.stem: Julian, 25/M complains of fever and pain behind scrotum. Rectal exam showed tender prostate. Management of acute bacterial prostatitis includes the following, EXCEPT.
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Prostatic Massage**

Acute bacterial prostatitis presents as dysuria, frequency, and pain in the prostatic pelvic or perineal area. If acute bacterial prostatitis is suspected, antimicrobial therapy (Choice C) should be initiated after urine and blood are obtained for cultures. Therapy can be tailored to urine culture results and should be continued for 2–4 weeks. Suprapubic cystostomy (Choice A) may be done for acute urinary retention in which a urethral catheter cannot be passed. In such cases, hospitalization (Choice D) is also warranted. Prostatic massage (Choice B) should not be done in acute prostatitis as it may further release bacteria into the bloodstream.

(HPIM 21st, p. 1073)

questions.stem: Trousseau sign is appreciated in patients with _____.
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Hypomagnesemia**

The Trousseau sign is carpal spasm caused by reduction of blood supply to the hand with a tourniquet/BP cuff inflated to 20 mmHg above SBP applied to the forearm for 3 minutes. Three main causes include hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, and metabolic alkalosis.

(HPIM 21st, p. 358)

questions.stem: Which is NOT associated with right-sided heart failure?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Orthopnea**

Symptoms of right heart failure (HF) are typically related to systemic venous congestion. Weight gain and lower extremity edema from fluid retention (Choice B) may be the initial manifestations, followed by a range of gastrointestinal symptoms due to edema of the bowel wall and hepatic congestion. Abdominal bloating, anorexia (Choice C), and early satiety are common.

The congestion in the systemic veins, particularly in the superior and inferior vena cava, also leads to an increase in venous pressure (Choice A), which manifests as jugular venous distension, hepatomegaly, and peripheral edema. Some patients develop right upper quadrant pain related to stretching of the hepatic capsule, with nausea and vomiting. For patients with refractory right HF, the development of massive edema involving the entire body with recurrent pleural effusions and/or ascites is termed anasarca.

Orthopnea (Choice D) refers to dyspnea that occurs in the recumbent position, and it is more commonly associated with left-sided heart failure. Moreover, for some patients with right-sided HF from worsening left-sided HF, orthopnea may even diminish as symptoms of right HF appear.

| Left-sided CHF symptoms | Right-sided CHF symptoms |
|---|---|
| Dyspnea predominates | Fluid retention predominates |
| Left-sided S3/S4 gallop | Right-sided S3/S4 gallop |
| Bilateral basilar rales | JVD |
| Pleural effusions | Hepatojugular reflux |
| Pulmonary edema | Peripheral edema |
| Orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea | Hepatomegaly, ascites |

(HPIM 21st, p. 1936)

questions.stem: Jenny, 42/F diabetic, has been started on pharmacologic therapy two years prior. She now complains of easy fatiguability and bipedal edema. Electrocardiogram and 2D Echo are within normal limits. What drug may have caused her condition?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Pioglitazone**

Thiazolidinediones (e.g., pioglitazone, rosiglitazone) reduce insulin resistance by binding to the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ (PPAR-γ) nuclear receptor found at highest levels in adipocytes. They may cause peripheral edema, CHF, weight gain, fractures, macular edema. The other choices are not typically associated with bipedal edema or fluid retention.

(HPIM 21st, p. 3110)

questions.stem: Justine, 20/F, consults your clinic for easy fatiguability. Physical examination reveals a loud holosystolic murmur at the left parasternal 3rd-4th intercostal space. What is your initial impression?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Ventricular septal defect (VSD)**

- **A. Tricuspid stenosis (TS)** — The mid-diastolic murmur associated with tricuspid stenosis is best heard at the lower left sternal border and increases in intensity with inspiration. This murmur is very difficult to hear and most often is obscured by left-sided acoustical events.
- **B. Ventricular septal defect (VSD)** — Holosystolic murmurs begin with S1 and continue through systole to S2. They are usually indicative of chronic mitral or tricuspid valve regurgitation or a VSD. The holosystolic murmur of a VSD is loudest at the mid- to lower-left sternal border and radiates widely. A thrill is present at the site of maximal intensity in most patients. There is no change in the intensity of the murmur with inspiration. With large defects, the ventricular pressures tend to equalize, shunt flow is balanced, and a murmur is not appreciated.
- **C. Atrial septal defect (ASD)** — Significant left-to-right intracardiac shunting due to an ASD leads to an increase in pulmonary blood flow and a grade 2–3 mid-systolic murmur at the middle to upper left sternal border, attributed to increased flow rates across the pulmonic valve with fixed splitting of S2.
- **D. Mitral stenosis (MS)** — The murmur of MS is a low-pitched mid-diastolic murmur and thus is best heard with the bell of the stethoscope. It is loudest at the left ventricular apex and often is appreciated only when the patient is turned in the left lateral decubitus position. It is usually of grade 1 or 2 intensity but may be absent when the cardiac output is severely reduced despite significant obstruction.

| Valve | Where Best Auscultated | Associated Murmurs |
|---|---|---|
| Aortic | Right, 2nd ICS, lateral to sternum | **Systolic murmur:** aortic stenosis, flow murmur (e.g. physiologic murmur), aortic valve sclerosis |
| Pulmonic | Left, 2nd ICS, lateral to sternum | **Systolic ejection murmur:** pulmonic stenosis, atrial septal defect, flow murmur |
| Tricuspid | Left, 4th-5th ICS over left sternal border | **Holosystolic murmur:** tricuspid regurgitation, ventricular septal defect. **Diastolic murmur:** tricuspid stenosis |
| Mitral | Left, 5th ICS MCL (apex) | **Holosystolic murmur:** mitral regurgitation. **Systolic murmur:** mitral valve prolapse. **Diastolic murmur:** mitral stenosis |
| -- | Left sternal border | **Diastolic murmur:** aortic regurgitation (valvular), pulmonic regurgitation. **Systolic murmur:** hypertrophic cardiomyopathy |

(HPIM 21st, p. 278-284; table adapted from *First Aid for the USMLE Step 1*, 2020)

choices.text: FEV1 increased by at least 200 mL

questions.stem: Air flow obstruction such as in bronchial asthma is suggested via spirometry when values after the administration of a bronchodilator results in the following findings EXCEPT?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Reduced FEV1/FVC ratio**

Both increase in FEV1 by at least 200 mL (Choice C) AND 12% increase in FEV1 (Choice A) after bronchodilator administration should be observed to determine reversibility of airflow obstruction.

In this case, Choice B (reduced FVC/FEV1 ratio) would decrease since FEV1 is assumed to increase post-dilator. It follows then that FVC/FEV1 would decrease since FEV1 is the denominator. Choice D then (Reduced FEV1/FVC), should not apply post-dilator, is part of the PRE-DILATOR criteria for diagnosis, and is the correct answer.

**Spirometry Criteria in Asthma**

- Evidence of Obstruction
  - FEV1/FVC < LLN (using lower limit of normal from GINA 2022/HPIM 21st Ed)
  - FEV1/FVC is < 0.75-0.80 (using fixed cutoffs from Philippine Asthma guidelines and local centers)
- Evidence of variable expiratory airflow limitation (reversibility criteria) can be done 3 ways:
  - Spirometry w/ post bronchodilator test (most recommended)
    - FEV1 that increases by >12% and by at least 200 ml from baseline post bronchodilator with salbutamol
    - FEV1 that increases by >12% and by at least 200 ml from baseline after 2-4 weeks on steroid trial (30-40 mg oral prednisone or prednisolone)
  - Peak Expiratory Flow (using Peak Flowmeter and PEF diary at home, new in GINA 2022)
    - >20% increase in PEF, 15 minutes after 2 puffs salbutamol
    - Improvement of PEF + Symptoms after 4 weeks of ICS
  - Bronchoprovocation Test
    - Decrease in FEV1 by 20% with methacholine or histamine – test for airway hyperresponsiveness

(HPIM 21st, p. 2132)

questions.stem: The degree of left-to-right shunting in patients with ventricular septal defect (VSD) is dependent on the presence of _____.
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Size of VSD**

The amount of shunting in VSD is dependent on the size of the defect relative to the size of the aortic valve. Classically, defects that are <30% of the size of the aortic annulus do not lead to significant shunting, those between 30% to 65% of aortic annulus size will lead to LA and LV volume overload and may lead to pulmonary hypertension, while those >65% of aortic annulus size will invariably lead to LA and LV volume overload and pulmonary hypertension unless closed early in life. Note that pulmonary hypertension is a consequence, not a cause.

(Hurst's The Heart 15th)

questions.stem: Chris has been complaining of chronic, productive cough. In order to diagnose him with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), you need to see the following reduced findings on spirometry, EXCEPT ___.
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Residual volume**

The hallmark of COPD is airflow obstruction. Pulmonary function testing shows airflow obstruction with a reduction in FEV1 (Choice D) and FEV1/FVC (Choice A). Spirometry values that satisfy COPD under the GOLD criteria is FEV1/FVC < 0.7 and FEV1 ≥ 80% predicted. Residual Volume (Choice C) is an unmeasured quantity in spirometry.

**Obstructive vs Restrictive Lung Pattern**

| | Obstructive | Restrictive |
|---|---|---|
| FEV1 | ↓↓↓ | ↓ |
| FVC | ↓ | ↓ |
| FEV1/FVC ratio | ↓ | Normal or ↑ |
| Common causes | COPD, asthma | IPF |

(HPIM 21st, p. 2182)

choices.text: Increase incidence of nausea and vomiting
Prevent the development of response fluctuation

questions.stem: Carbidopa is added to levodopa in the management of Parkinson's disease in order to
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Decrease extracerebral breakdown of levodopa**

- **A. Increase incidence of nausea and vomiting** — Acute dopaminergic side effects of levodopa include nausea, vomiting, and orthostatic hypotension. These are usually transient and can generally be avoided by starting with low doses and gradual titration. If they persist, they can be treated with additional doses of a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor (e.g., carbidopa), administering with food, or adding a peripheral dopamine-blocking agent such as domperidone. Thus, carbidopa decreases the incidence of nausea and vomiting.
- **B. Increase levodopa dose noted** — Since carbidopa decreases peripheral metabolism of levodopa, its combination helps to avoid having to increase the dose of levodopa.
- **C. Decrease extracerebral breakdown of levodopa** — Levodopa is routinely administered in combination with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor (e.g., carbidopa) to prevent its peripheral metabolism to dopamine and the development of nausea, vomiting, and orthostatic hypotension due to activation of dopamine receptors in the area postrema (the nausea and vomiting center) that are not protected by the blood brain barrier (BBB).
- **D. Prevent the development of response fluctuation** — Chronic levodopa treatment is associated with the development of motor complications which consist of fluctuations in motor response ("on" episodes when the drug is working and "off" episodes when parkinsonian features return as drug wears off) and involuntary movements known as dyskinesias. Long-term double-blind studies show that these can be minimized by using the lowest dose of levodopa that provides satisfactory benefit and using polypharmacy to avoid the need for raising the dose of levodopa.

(HPIM 21st, p. 3393-3394)

questions.stem: Levothyroxine might be needed to be increased if the following drugs are concurrently administered, EXCEPT _____.
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Teduglutide**

Teduglutide (Choice B) is a GLP-2 analog used for the treatment of short bowel syndrome. It increases levels of levothyroxine and may increase absorption of concomitant PO medications.

Drugs such as calcium carbonate, aluminum-containing antacids, sucralfate (Choice C), iron supplements (Choice A) impair the absorption of levothyroxine. Phenytoin (Choice D) is an inducer hence enhances metabolism of levothyroxine. Thus, levothyroxine dose may need to be increased with concomitant use of these drugs.

**Mnemonic for Cytochrome P450 Inducers:** "Smoke Sa BGC, PRE!"

- St. John's Wort
- Barbiturates (EXCEPT Secobarbital)
- Griseofulvin
- Carbamazepine
- Phenytoin
- Rifampicin
- Ethanol

questions.stem: Before initiating therapy, you need to assess a patient diagnosed with hypothyroidism for the following conditions, EXCEPT _____.
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Menstrual irregularity**

Thyroid hormone replacement may exacerbate adrenal insufficiency (Choice A). Patients with cardiovascular risk, such as in elderly patients with coronary artery disease (Choice C), usually require lower doses of levothyroxine. There exists an inverse relationship between levels of thyroid function and airway beta adrenergic responsiveness such that hypothyroidism may improve coexisting bronchial asthma (Choice B). As such, correction of hypothyroidism may worsen asthma symptoms and make controlling asthma more difficult. Thus, before beginning therapy with thyroid hormone, the hypothyroid patient requires clinical assessment and further management of adrenal insufficiency, asthma, and CAD.

While it is still prudent to evaluate for menstrual irregularities, restoring normal thyroid hormone levels with thyroid hormone replacement can improve menstrual irregularities (Choice A) in patients with hypothyroidism. Thus, this is the best answer to this question compared to the other choices.

(HPIM 21st, p. 2936-2937)

questions.stem: Lara suddenly develops tachycardia with a heart rate of 200 beats per minute. She is diagnosed with heart failure. What drug is effective in treating SVT BUT is contraindicated in patients with heart failure?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Verapamil**

- **A. Flecainide** — Class IC agents (flecainide, propafenone) possess slow kinetics and high potency. Chronic therapy with flecainide is an option if prophylactic therapy of SVT is needed to reduce frequency of episodes in some patients.
- **B. Procainamide** — Class IA agents, including procainamide and quinidine, possess intermediate binding kinetics and potency. It can be used to treat SVT.
- **C. Verapamil** — Calcium channel blockers (verapamil or diltiazem) are effective in SVT but may cause hypotension before and after arrhythmia termination and have a longer duration of action. They exert negative inotropic effects in patients with HFrEF and destabilize previously asymptomatic patients, and thus are generally avoided in these patients.
- **D. Adenosine** — Intravenous adenosine can terminate the vast majority of PSVT episodes by transiently blocking conduction in the AV node. Adenosine may produce transient chest pain, dyspnea, and anxiety. It is contraindicated in patients with prior cardiac transplantation due to potential hypersensitivity due to surgical sympathetic denervation. It may aggravate bronchospasm. Adenosine precipitates AF, which is usually brief, in up to 15% of patients.

(HPIM 21st, p. 1898-1899)

questions.stem: After 3 months of taking methotrexate for Rheumatoid Arthritis, Danee is still symptomatic. Prescribe the second line drug for Danee's condition.
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Leflunomide**

- **A. Leflunomide** — DMARDs slow or prevent structural progression of RA. The conventional DMARDs include hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine, methotrexate, and leflunomide; they exhibit a delayed onset of action of ~6–12 weeks. Methotrexate is the DMARD of choice for the treatment of RA and is the anchor drug for most combination therapies. The clinical efficacy of leflunomide, an inhibitor of pyrimidine synthesis, appears similar to that of methotrexate; it has been shown in well-designed trials to be effective for the treatment of RA as monotherapy or in combination with methotrexate and other DMARDs.
- **B. Tocilizumab** — Tocilizumab is a monoclonal antibody directed against the membrane and soluble forms of the IL-6 receptor. Clinical trials attest to the clinical efficacy of these therapies for RA, both as monotherapy and in combination with methotrexate and other DMARDs.
- **C. Sulfasalazine** — Sulfasalazine is another DMARD and has been shown in randomized, controlled trials to reduce radiographic progression of disease.
- **D. Tofacitinib** — Tofacitinib is a selective JAK1 and JAK3 inhibitor with minor inhibitory effects on JAK2 and Tyk2. JAK inhibitors can be used as monotherapy or in combination with methotrexate.

(HPIM 21st, p. 2761-2764)

questions.stem: Which complication of systemic lupus erythematosus is NOT treated with corticosteroid?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Leukopenia**

Lymphopenia may be clinically silent or associated with increased risk of infections and/or active SLE. The treatment of lymphocytopenia is mainly directed at treating the SLE. In rare cases with severe lymphocytopenia, it may be appropriate to use prophylactic antibiotics against organisms such as Pneumocystis jirovecii, but there is a lack of high-quality data to support this approach. Lymphopenia by itself usually does not require therapy. Corticosteroids are used in the management of the other choices.

(UpToDate: Hematologic Manifestations of SLE)

questions.stem: Emergency surgery is NOT indicated in the following cases of acute mitral regurgitation
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Rheumatic mitral regurgitation**

Clinical settings in which acute, severe MR occur include (1) papillary muscle rupture (Choice A) complicating acute myocardial infarction (MI), (2) rupture of chordae tendineae (Choice B) in the setting of myxomatous mitral valve disease, (3) infective endocarditis (Choice C), and (4) blunt chest wall trauma.

Rheumatic mitral regurgitation is not an indication for emergency surgery.

(HPIM 21st, p. 242)

questions.stem: Which is NOT a Medical therapy used in the management of persistent acromegaly after surgery?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Serotonin antagonist**

Surgical resection of GH-secreting adenomas is the initial treatment for most patients.

- **A. GH receptor antagonist** — Combined treatment of GH receptor antagonist with monthly somatostatin analogues and weekly or biweekly Pegvisomant injections has been used effectively in resistant patients.
- **B. Dopamine agonist** — Very high doses of cabergoline (0.5 mg/d), a dopamine agonist, may achieve short-lived and modest GH therapeutic efficacy. Combined treatment with octreotide and cabergoline may induce additive biochemical control compared with either drug alone.
- **C. Serotonin antagonist** — This is not primarily used in the treatment of acromegaly.
- **D. Somatostatin analog** — Somatostatin analogues are used as adjuvant treatment for preoperative shrinkage of large invasive macroadenomas, immediate relief of debilitating symptoms, and reduction of GH hypersecretion; in frail patients experiencing morbidity; and in patients who decline surgery or, when surgery fails, to achieve biochemical control.

(HPIM 21st, p. 2913-2914)

questions.stem: The following interventions can be used in the treatment of psoriasis EXCEPT:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Antibiotics**

- **A. Antibiotics** — Antibiotics are not part of psoriasis management.
- **B. Emollient** — All patients should be instructed to avoid excess drying or irritation of their skin and to maintain adequate cutaneous hydration. Thus, emollients are typically recommended.
- **C. Topical corticosteroids** — Most cases of localized, plaque-type psoriasis can be managed with mid-potency topical glucocorticoids, although their long-term use is often accompanied by loss of effectiveness (tachyphylaxis) and atrophy of the skin. Oral glucocorticoids should not be used for the treatment of psoriasis due to the potential for development of life-threatening pustular psoriasis when therapy is discontinued.
- **D. Vitamin D analogues** — A topical vitamin D analogue (calcipotriene) and a retinoid (tazarotene) are also efficacious in the treatment of limited psoriasis and have largely replaced other topical agents such as coal tar, salicylic acid, and anthralin.

(HPIM 21st, p. 378)

questions.stem: Untreated atrial fibrillation can lead to the following, EXCEPT
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Resolution of arrhythmia**

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a cardiac arrhythmia characterized by seemingly disorganized, rapid, and irregular atrial electrical activation, resulting in loss of organized atrial mechanical contraction. AF is not a benign condition, with a 1.5- to 1.9-fold increased risk of mortality after controlling for underlying cardiac disease. If untreated, it can persist and worsen. Thus, resolution of arrhythmia is least likely to happen if the condition is not properly managed. The other choices are all likely complications of persistent and unmanaged atrial fibrillation.

(HPIM 21st, p. 1903)

questions.stem: Hilda, 30/female, is suspected to have pheochromocytoma. Assay for plasma fractionated from metanephrine can be erroneously affected by which drug?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Tricyclic antidepressant**

In the diagnosis of pheochromocytoma, measurements of plasma metanephrine are the most sensitive and are less susceptible to false-positive elevations from stress, including venipuncture. However, physiologic stress responses and medications that increase catecholamine levels still can confound testing. Because the tumors are relatively rare, borderline elevations are likely to represent false-positive results. In this circumstance, it is important to exclude dietary or drug-related factors (withdrawal of levodopa or use of sympathomimetics, diuretics, tricyclic anti-depressants (Choice C), alpha and beta blockers) that might cause false-positive results and then to repeat testing or perform a clonidine suppression test.

The other choices were not directly mentioned in Harrison's.

(HPIM 21st, p. 2977)

questions.stem: Alexandra, 44F, is admitted in the hospital for recurrent pancreatitis. What is the likely cause?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Cholelithiasis**

Gallstones and alcohol account for 80–90% of identified cases of acute pancreatitis in the United States. Gallstones continue to be the leading cause of acute pancreatitis in most series (30–60%). The risk of acute pancreatitis in patients with at least one gallstone < 5 mm in diameter is fourfold greater than that in patients with larger stones.

Patients with gallstone pancreatitis are also at increased risk of recurrence, and consideration should be given to performing a cholecystectomy during the same admission or within 4–6 weeks of discharge.

(HPIM 21st, p. 2658)

questions.stem: In patients with catastrophic antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (APAS), a three-pronged intervention is done using the ff EXCEPT.
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Aspirin**

Patients with catastrophic APAS (CAPS) should be treated with combination therapy with glucocorticoids (Choice C), an anticoagulant such as heparin, and plasma exchange (Choice A) or IVIG (Choice D) together with appropriate management of triggering events such as infections. For refractory CAPS, B-cell depletion (e.g., with rituximab) or complement inhibition (e.g., with eculizumab) therapies are alternative options. Aspirin (Choice B) is an antiplatelet, NOT an anticoagulant.

(HPIM 21st, p. 2751)

questions.stem: What drug that can cause drug-induced systemic lupus erythematosus?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Hydralazine**

**Mnemonic for Drug-Induced Lupus:** "Lupus Makes my HIPS Extremely Painful"

- Methyldopa
- Minocycline
- Hydralazine
- Isoniazid
- Procainamide
- Sulfonamides (e.g. Sulfamethoxazole)
- Etanercept
- Procainamide

Delirium alternating with period of calm

questions.stem: Which clinical presentation is NOT compatible with the CNS stage (encephalitic form) of rabies infection?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Muscle rigidity and tremor**

Two acute neurologic forms of rabies are seen in humans: the encephalitic (furious) in 80% and the paralytic form in 20%.

**Clinical Stages of Rabies**
*(Adapted from Table 208-1. Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine. 21st ed. 2022)*

| Stage | Typical Duration | Symptoms and Signs |
|---|---|---|
| Incubation period | 20-90 days | None |
| Prodrome | 2-10 days | Fever, malaise, anorexia, nausea, vomiting; paresthesia, pain, or pruritus at the wound site |
| Acute Neurologic Disease — Encephalitic (80%) | 2-7 days | Anxiety, agitation, hyperactivity, bizarre behavior, hallucinations, autonomic dysfunction, hydrophobia |
| Acute Neurologic Disease — Paralytic (20%) | 2-10 days | Flaccid paralysis in limb(s) progressing to quadriparesis with facial paralysis |
| Coma, death | 0-14 days | -- |

- **A. Autonomic stimulation like increase salvation** — Autonomic dysfunction is common in rabies and may result in hypersalivation, gooseflesh, cardiac arrhythmia, and priapism.
- **B. Painful laryngeal spasm on drinking water** — Rabies encephalitis is distinguished by early brainstem involvement, which results in the classic features of hydrophobia (involuntary, painful contraction of the diaphragm and accessory respiratory, laryngeal, and pharyngeal muscles in response to swallowing liquids) and aerophobia (the same features caused by stimulation from a draft of air). The combination of hypersalivation and pharyngeal dysfunction is responsible for the classic appearance of "foaming at the mouth."
- **C. Delirium alternating with period of calm** — In encephalitic rabies, episodes of hyperexcitability are typically followed by periods of complete lucidity that become shorter as the disease progresses.
- **D. Muscle rigidity and tremor** — About 20% of patients have paralytic rabies in which muscle weakness predominates and cardinal features of encephalitic rabies (hyperexcitability, hydrophobia, and aerophobia) are lacking. There is early and prominent flaccid muscle weakness (NOT muscle rigidity), often beginning in the bitten extremity and spreading to produce quadriparesis and facial weakness.

(HPIM 21st, p. 1620-1621)

questions.stem: Joe is a known asthmatic rushed to the ER for difficulty of breathing. ABG was requested. Impending respiratory failure in a patient with exacerbation of bronchial asthma is seen in a patient with respiratory acidosis and
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Increased PaCO2**

Arterial blood gas (ABG) is the gold standard for diagnosing respiratory failure. Respiratory acidosis occurs as a result of severe pulmonary disease, respiratory muscle fatigue, or abnormalities in ventilatory control and is recognized by an increase in PaCO2 and decrease in pH. HCO3- obtained from an ABG is a calculated value and may be inaccurate. Analysis of an ABG may performed using a measured HCO3- obtained from a basic metabolic panel.

(HPIM 21st, p. 338)

questions.stem: What is the drug of choice for hypercalcemia of malignancy?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Alendronate**

- **A. Calcitonin** — Previously used agents such as calcitonin and mithramycin have little utility now that bisphosphonates and other agents are available to treat hypercalcemia of malignancy.
- **B. Vitamin D** — Chronic hypocalcemia due to hypoparathyroidism is treated with calcium supplements (1000–1500 mg/d elemental calcium in divided doses) and either vitamin D2 or D3 (25,000–100,000 U daily) or calcitriol.
- **C. Cinacalcet** — Cinacalcet (30 mg PO bid to 90 mg PO qid) stimulates calcium-sensing receptors to suppress PTH secretion and is therefore applicable in parathyroid carcinoma and rare cases of ectopic PTH-producing tumors.
- **D. Alendronate** — The mainstays of therapy in hypercalcemia are bisphosphonates, which are potent inhibitors of bone resorption. Zoledronic acid (e.g., 4 mg IV over ~30 min) and pamidronate (e.g., 60–90 mg IV over 2–4 h) are bisphosphonates that are commonly used for the treatment of hypercalcemia of malignancy in adults. Bisphosphonates like Alendronate can reduce serum calcium within 1–2 days and suppress calcium release for several weeks.

(HPIM 21st, p. 357, 723)

questions.stem: The indication for additional anti-platelet therapy in patients with transient ischemic attack (TIA) who are already receiving rivaroxaban is the presence of
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Mechanical heart valve**

The direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) include dabigatran, which inhibits thrombin, and rivaroxaban, apixaban, and Edoxaban, which inhibit factor Xa. These have a rapid onset and offset of action and have half-lives that permit once- or twice-daily administration. Designed to produce a predictable level of anticoagulation, the DOACs are more convenient to administer because they are given in fixed doses without routine coagulation monitoring.

All four DOACs are licensed for stroke prevention in patients with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, which encompasses patients without mechanical heart valves or severe rheumatic mitral valve disease, and for treatment of venous thromboembolism (VTE).

Bleeding is the most common side effect of the DOACs. The DOACS are associated with less intracranial bleeding than warfarin, but the higher dose regimens of dabigatran, rivaroxaban, and Edoxaban are associated with more gastrointestinal bleeding.

Stroke secondary to thromboembolism is one of the most serious complications of prosthetic heart valve implantation. Patients with a history of ischemic stroke or TIA before mechanical valve surgery have a higher thromboembolic risk such that additional antiplatelet therapy may outweigh the competing bleeding risk.

The other options are not usual indications for adding antiplatelet therapy in patients with TIA or ischemic stroke.

(HPIM 21st, p. 935, 3346)

questions.stem: Which of the following is an irritative symptom associated with benign prostatic hyperplasia?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Urgency and frequency**

**Mnemonic: FUN WISE**

- Irritative: FUN (frequency, urgency, nocturia)
- Obstructive: WISE (Weak stream, intermittency, straining, Emptying not full)

questions.stem: Which is NOT a cardinal feature of Parkinson's disease?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Depression and anxiety**

Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common age-related neurodegenerative disease, exceeded only by Alzheimer's disease (AD). Clinically, PD is characterized by rest tremor, rigidity (stiffness) (Choice A), bradykinesia (slowing) (Choice B), and gait dysfunction with postural instability. These are known as the classical or "cardinal" features of the disease. Patients may describe some of these symptoms as muscle weakness (Choice C).

Additional clinical features can include freezing of gait, speech difficulty, swallowing impairment, and a series of nonmotor features that include autonomic disturbances, sensory alterations, mood disorders, sleep dysfunction, cognitive impairment, and dementia. Depression and anxiety (Choice D) are mood disorders under non-motor features of Parkinson's disease, not classically associated with this condition.

**Clinical Features of Parkinson's Disease**
*(Adapted from Table 435-1. Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine. 21st ed. 2022)*

- **Cardinal motor features:** Bradykinesia, rest tremor, rigidity, postural instability
- **Other motor features:** Micrographia, masked facies (hypomimia), reduced eye blinking, drooling, soft voice (hypophonia), dysphagia, freezing, falling
- **Non-motor features:** Anosmia, sensory disturbances (e.g., pain), mood disorders (e.g., depression), sleep disturbances (e.g., fragmented sleep, RBD), autonomic disturbances (orthostatic hypotension, gastrointestinal disturbances, genitourinal disturbances, sexual dysfunction), cognitive impairment / dementia

RBS = rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder

(HPIM 21st, p. 3386-3387)

questions.stem: Hospitalization is advisable in TIA when the following conditions are present, EXCEPT
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Hypocoagulability**

Hospital admission is generally recommended in case of crescendo TIAs (Choice D), or duration of symptoms longer than 1-hour, symptomatic internal carotid stenosis greater than 50% (Choice C), a known cardiac source of embolus (Choice B) such as atrial fibrillation, a known hypercoagulable state (Choice A: NOT hypocoagulable state), or an appropriate combination of the California score or ABCD score (category 4). Crescendo TIAs are defined as disabling, recurrent transient cerebral or retinal ischemia characterized by an increased frequency, duration, or severity of events.

questions.stem: What is the MOST common cause of upper GI bleeding?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Peptic ulcer disease**

Peptic ulcers are the most common cause of upper gastrointestinal bleeding (UGIB), accounting for ~50% of UGIB hospitalizations. The three main factors in ulcer pathogenesis are Helicobacter pylori, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and acid. Furthermore, the most common complication of peptic ulcer disease is GI bleeding. The other choices are also causes of UGIB, however, they are not the most common.

(HPIM 21st, p. 311)

questions.stem: The following interventions are warranted in hypokalemia EXCEPT what?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Use of D5LR as preferred intravenous fluid**

- **A. Determine serum potassium every 3-6 hours** — During correction, frequent monitoring of plasma K+ concentration should be done to avoid transient over-repletion and transient hyperkalemia.
- **B. Use of D5LR as preferred intravenous fluid** — Intravenous K+-Cl– should always be administered in saline solutions, rather than dextrose, because the dextrose-induced increase in insulin can acutely exacerbate hypokalemia due to intracellular potassium shift.
- **C. Continuous ECG monitoring** — Patients with a prolonged QT interval and/or other risk factors for arrhythmia should be monitored by continuous cardiac telemetry during repletion.
- **D. Give intravenous potassium via central venous catheter** — Oral replacement with K+-Cl– is the mainstay of therapy in hypokalemia. The use of intravenous administration should be limited to patients unable to use the enteral route or in the setting of severe complications (e.g., paralysis, arrhythmia). If hypokalemia is severe (<2.5 mmol/L) and/or critically symptomatic, intravenous K+-Cl– can be administered through a central vein with cardiac monitoring in an intensive care setting.

(HPIM 21st, p. 350-352)

questions.stem: Patients receiving intravenous quinine should be monitored for the development of ___.
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — QR prolongation**

**Quinine**

- Minor Toxicity:
  - Common: cinchonism (tinnitus, high tone hearing loss, nausea, vomiting, dysphoria, postural hypotension); ECG QT interval prolongation (usually by <10%) (Choice A)
  - Rare: diarrhea, visual disturbance, rashes. Note: very bitter taste
- Major Toxicity
  - Common: hypoglycemia (Choice D, NOT hyperglycemia)
  - Rare: hypotension, blindness, deafness, cardiac arrhythmias, thrombocytopenia (Choice C, NOT thrombocytosis), hemolysis, hemolytic-uremic syndrome, vasculitis, cholestatic hepatitis, neuromuscular paralysis

(HPIM 21st, p. 1732)

questions.stem: Non-adherence of people infected with TB to anti-tuberculosis treatment results in the following, EXCEPT ___.
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Immediate hospitalization**

Poor adherence to treatment is one of the most important impediments to cure (Choice C) resulting in further TB transmission (Choice B). Moreover, the tubercle bacilli harbored by patients who do not fully adhere to the prescribed regimen are likely to become resistant to the drugs to which they are irregularly exposed (Choice A). Non-adherence to TB medications would not lead to immediate hospitalization (Choice D).

(HPIM 21st, p. 1373)

questions.stem: Prerenal azotemia is MOSTLY due to
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Renal hypoperfusion**

Prerenal azotemia (from "azo," meaning nitrogen, and "-emia," meaning in the blood) is the most common form of AKI. It is the designation for a rise in SCr or BUN concentration due to inadequate renal plasma flow and intraglomerular hydrostatic pressure to support normal glomerular filtration. The most common clinical conditions associated with prerenal azotemia are hypovolemia, decreased cardiac output, and medications that interfere with renal autoregulatory vascular responses such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and inhibitors of angiotensin II.

(HPIM 21st, p. 2296)

questions.stem: The medications often causing Steven-Johnson syndrome are the following, EXCEPT ___.
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Azithromycin**

The following medications may cause SJS:

**SANA's Box**

- Sulfonamides (Choice C)
- Allopurinol (Choice B)
- Nevirapine
- Anti-epileptic drugs (AEDs) (Choice D)
- Beta-lactams
- -oxicam (NSAID)

questions.stem: Your sister has been having lateralized, throbbing headache preceded by an aura. The following are known triggers of migraine attacks, EXCEPT ___.
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Coffee intake**

Migraine-prone patients are particularly sensitive and do not habituate easily to environmental and sensory stimuli. This sensitivity is amplified in women during the menstrual cycle. Headache can be initiated or amplified by various triggers, including glare, bright lights, sounds (Choice D), or other types of afferent stimulation; hunger; let-down from stress; physical exertion; stormy weather or barometric pressure changes; hormonal fluctuations during menses (Choice C); lack of or excess sleep (Choice A); and alcohol or other chemical stimulation, such as with nitrates.

On the other hand, caffeine (Choice B) has an ambiguous role in migraine as it is cited to be both a cause and cure. One possible mechanism is that it helps reduce inflammation and can bring relief. However, caffeine overuse may lead to chronic migraine, and sudden caffeine withdrawal may trigger migraine attacks.

(HPIM 21st, p. 3357)

questions.stem: Blessie has been diagnosed with ventricular septal defect (VSD). She now complains of shortness of breath and cyanosis. The probable explanation to this is the development of ___.
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Pulmonary hypertension**

Pulmonary hypertension is a complication of VSD. Such patients would likely present with shortness of breath and cyanosis.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a component of metabolic syndrome?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Insulin resistance**

**Criteria for Metabolic Syndrome:**

- Central obesity (Choice A) – Waist circumference >102cm (M) or >88cm (F)
- TG ≥ 150 mg/dL (Choice C) or use of specific medication
- HDL <40mg/dL (M) or <50mg/dL or use of specific medication
- BP ≥130 systolic or ≥85 diastolic (Choice D) or use of specific medication
- Glucose ≥100 mg/dL or use of specific medication or previously diagnosed T2DM

Hyperglycemia is part of the criteria, NOT insulin resistance (Choice B) per se. While hyperglycemia may be a sign of insulin resistance, it is the best answer given the choices.

questions.stem: Pedro is rushed to the ER after an episode of vomiting fresh blood. Systolic BP is 85 mmHg and heart rate is 120 bpm. Which intervention will NOT give additional benefit to Pepito?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Do central venous pressure monitoring**

Although central venous pressure (CVP) monitoring is generally useful to assess general volume status, its reliability as a guide to resuscitation in critically ill patients is a subject of debate. The other interventions should be done in managing patients with hemodynamic stability from GI bleeding.

questions.stem: Antibiotic therapy is NOT indicated in which condition?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Cholera**

- **A. C. difficile** — When possible, discontinuation of any ongoing antimicrobial administration is recommended as the first step in treatment of CDI. Oral administration of fidaxomicin or vancomycin was recommended as first-line treatment. Oral metronidazole is only recommended for mild or moderate CDI when fidaxomicin or vancomycin is not available.
- **B. Shigellosis** — As an enteroinvasive disease, shigellosis requires antibiotic treatment. With effective antibiotic therapy clinical improvement occurs within 48 h. The use of fluoroquinolones (first-line, preferably ciprofloxacin), and cephalosporins and β-lactams (second line) for 7–10 days is recommended for the treatment of shigellosis.
- **C. Yersinia** — A 10- to 14-day course of antimicrobial therapy (or a course continued until 2 days after fever subsides) is recommended. Streptomycin has historically been the parenteral treatment of choice for plague.
- **D. Cholera** — Although not necessary for cure in cholera, the use of an antibiotic diminishes the duration and volume of fluid loss and hastens clearance of the organism from the stool. Adjunctive antibiotics should therefore be administered to patients with moderate or severe dehydration due to cholera. In many areas, macrolides such as erythromycin (adults, 250 mg orally four times a day for 3 days; children, 12.5 mg/kg per dose four times a day for 3 days) or azithromycin (adults, a single 1-g dose; children, a single 20-mg/kg dose) are the agents of choice.

(HPIM 21st, p. 1068-1070, 1300-1301, 1308, 1324)
