questions.stem: Which of the following is INCORRECT regarding the Influenza virus?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Influenza B is more commonly associated with pandemics.**

- Choice B is the false statement because Influenza B undergoes antigenic drift, which causes seasonal epidemics (NOT pandemics). Influenza A is the strain that undergoes antigenic shift which leads to pandemics.
- All the other choices are true for Influenza virus.

questions.stem: Patient is diagnosed with Hepatitis infection. Interpret the serology findings: (+) HbsAg (-) Anti-HBs (+) Anti-HBc IgG (-) HBeAg
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Chronic carrier**

This patient is a chronic carrier. See table below for interpretation of hepatitis markers.

**Interpretation of hepatitis markers**

| Interpretation | HBsAg | Anti-HBs | Anti-HBc |
|---|---|---|---|
| Early acute HBV infection | + | − | − |
| HBV infection (acute or chronic) — differentiate with IgM anti-HBc | + | +/− | + |
| Previous HBV infection and immunity | − | + | + |
| Possible interpretations: (1) HBV infection in the remote past; (2) "low-level" HBV carrier; (3) window period between disappearance of HBsAg and appearance of anti-HBs; (4) false positive/non-specific reaction | − | − | + |
| No infection | − | − | − |
| Successful vaccine response | − | + | − |

- The only marker positive during the window period: Anti-HBc IgM.
- The only marker positive among vaccinated patients: Anti-HBs.
- What can differentiate chronic active infection from chronic carrier: HBeAg.
- Chronic infection is characterized by the persistence of HBsAg for at least 6 months.
- Persistence of HBsAg is the principal marker of risk for developing chronic liver disease and liver cancer (hepatocellular carcinoma) later in life.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a microscopic finding in a DNA virus?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Guarneri bodies**

- **A. Guarneri bodies** — Found in Variola virus (part of Poxviridae) which is an enveloped complex DNA virus known to cause smallpox.
- **B. Warthin-Finkelday bodies** — Found in Measles virus, an enveloped, helical, non-segmented negative sense RNA virus that causes measles.
- **C. Negri bodies** — Found in Rabies virus, a bullet-shaped enveloped, helical, non-segmented negative sense RNA virus that causes rabies.
- **D. Councilman bodies** — Found in Yellow fever virus, an enveloped, icosahedral, non-segmented, positive sense RNA virus.

questions.stem: 4-year-old preschooler presents with nightly pruritus ani. What is the causative agent?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Enterobius vermicularis**

- **A. Enterobius vermicularis** — The most common cause of pruritus ani among school-aged children. The female worm lays eggs around the perianal region, typically at night, which causes intense itching.
- **B. Entamoeba histolytica** — Causes amoebiasis which presents as diarrhea and abdominal pain.
- **C. Trichuris trichiuria** — Causes trichuriasis which presents as abdominal pain, diarrhea, and rectal prolapse, in severe cases.
- **D. Ascaris lumbricoides** — Causes ascariasis which also presents with gastrointestinal symptoms and is not associated with pruritus ani.

questions.stem: For the case above, what is the diagnostic method used?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Scotch tape test**

- **A. Fecal smear** — Used to detect the eggs of most nematodes such as Ascaris, Trichuris, Capillaria, etc. This is not done for Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) eggs since these eggs are not found in the feces.
- **B. Scotch tape test** — The most commonly used method for the detection of Enterobius vermicularis eggs since the eggs are seen around the perianal area.
- **C. Blood smear** — Done to detect blood-borne diseases such as malaria, babesiosis, and filariasis.
- **D. Stool antigen test** — One of the commonly used diagnostic tests for detection of H. pylori infection. It can also be used to diagnose parasitic infections such as Entamoeba histolytica and Giardia lamblia.

questions.stem: What is the first-line management for Pinworm infection?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Albendazole**

#### Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm, seatworm)
- D-shaped eggs
- Most common helminth infection in developed nations
- Most common cause of pruritus ani among school-aged children
- Increases the risk for UTI
- Can be transmitted via inhalation of eggs

**Salient features / presentation**
- Pruritus ani — due to deposition of eggs in the perianal area by the female worm
- Habitat of adult worm: cecum
- Can cause retroinfection → autoinfection — after hatching, the larvae will enter the anus and develop into adults in the cecum

**Management**
- Diagnosis: Scotch tape test at perianal fold — D-shaped eggs
- Treatment: Mebendazole or Albendazole or Pyrantel pamoate

questions.stem: Which of the following parasites would be able to cause Loeffler’s syndrome, due to larval migration to the lungs?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Ascaris lumbricoides**

- Loeffler’s syndrome is characterized by respiratory symptoms such as cough and difficulty of breathing due to the migration of larva in the lungs. Eosinophilia may also be seen due to the abundance of parasites.
- Parasites that can cause this syndrome include hookworms (Necator americanus and Ancylostoma duodenale), Strongyloides stercoralis, and **Ascaris lumbricoides** (Choice A).
- **Trichuris trichiura** (Choice B) is also known as whipworm. No heart-lung larval migration is observed. Its characteristic clinical presentation is rectal prolapse. Coconut cake rectum may also be seen in these cases.
- **Enterobius vermicularis** (Choice C) is also known as pinworm/seatworm. It may be diagnosed through the scotch tape test since it inhabits the cecum. A key symptom in its presentation is pruritus ani (itching in the perianal area).
- **Capillaria philippinensis** (Choice D) is characterized by abdominal pain and diarrhea. This is mainly due to transmission through migratory birds. Borborygmi can also be seen in these cases.

questions.stem: Excystation of Giardia lamblia occurs in which part of the gastrointestinal tract?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Duodenum**

- Excystation of Giardia lamblia occurs in the small intestine, specifically the duodenum (Choice C). This may also happen in the stomach, due to the presence of gastric acid.
- Excystation does not occur in the jejunum, cecum, or ileum (Choices A, B, and D).
- Recall the life cycle of G. lamblia.

questions.stem: Lymphogranuloma venereum is a dermatologic condition which is caused by:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Chlamydia trachomatis**

- Lymphogranuloma venereum is characterized by painless, solitary ulcer but with painful lymphadenopathy. It is caused by **Chlamydia trachomatis** (Choice A), specifically types L1-L3. A positive Frei test is also observed in these cases.
- **Klebsiella granulomatis** (Choice B) causes granuloma inguinale/donovanosis. Beefy red ulcers which are formed from small painless papules are observed.
- **Chlamydia psittaci** (Choice C) is transmitted through bird exposure, causing psittacosis. Sudden onset pneumonia, photophobia, and severe headache are seen in these cases.
- **Haemophilus ducreyi** (Choice D) is associated with chancroid, which is a painful genital ulcer. It is spread through direct contact or sexual intercourse.

choices.text: It causes a sexually transmitted disease
It will test positive on the whiff test
It is the causative agent of bacterial vaginosis

questions.stem: All of the following statements are true regarding Gardnerella vaginalis, EXCEPT:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — It causes a sexually transmitted disease**

- Gardnerella vaginalis causes bacterial vaginosis (Choice D). The following are observed in this condition (Amsel criteria – needs to fulfill 3 out of 4 to diagnose):
  - Clue cells in microscopy
  - Positive in whiff test (Choice B) – produces a fishy odor (Choice C)
  - Produces and malodorous discharge
  - pH > 4.5
- Bacterial vaginosis is NOT a sexually transmitted disease (Choice A is incorrect – meaning sexual contact is not the primary reason for its transmission), although it is associated with sexual activities such as oral sexual contact and having multiple sexual partners. It is mainly due to the imbalance of vaginal microbiota.

questions.stem: Which of the following gram-positive bacteria would not exhibit hemolysis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Streptococcus bovis**

- **Streptococcus bovis** (Choice B) is a gamma-hemolytic gram-positive bacteria, meaning it does not show hemolysis and there is no change in color when grown on culture.
- S. mutans and S. mitis are alpha-hemolytic bacteria which show incomplete hemolysis with green or brown color surrounding the colony.
- S. pyogenes is a Group A beta-hemolytic bacteria which will show complete hemolysis (clear zone).
- Recall gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, and how to differentiate through culture growth.

questions.stem: Which of the following causes of viral encephalitis can be prevented through vaccination?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Japanese encephalitis**

- Among the choices, only Japanese encephalitis (Choice C) can be prevented through vaccination.
- West Nile, CMV, and enterovirus (Choices A, B, and D) encephalitis currently have no vaccines that are effective in preventing encephalitis.
- Recall vaccinations and types of vaccines:

**Inactivated vaccines**
- Hepatitis B vaccine
- DPT vaccine
- H. influenzae b vaccine
- Pneumococcal vaccine
- Hepatitis A vaccine
- Meningococcal vaccine
- Influenza trivalent vaccine
- Human papillomavirus vaccine
- Typhoid fever vaccine (IM)
- Rabies vaccine
- Inactivated polio vaccine (IPV)

**Live vaccines**
- BCG vaccine
- Measles vaccine
- MMR vaccine
- Varicella vaccine
- Rotavirus vaccine
- Influenza attenuated vaccine (intranasal)
- Typhoid fever (oral) vaccine
- Oral polio vaccine
- Japanese Encephalitis

choices.text: Activation of G proteins leading to increase in cAMP

questions.stem: The likely mechanism of the toxin of the organism that you inoculated causing this condition in the patient is:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Inactivation of elongation factor 2 (EF-2)**

- Looking at this case, this is a probable case of Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection due to the nature of the industrial accident (gas explosion causing multiple burn wounds). Pneumonia may also be observed especially in immunocompromised individuals.
- This is a 2-step question where the causative agent, its exotoxin, and its mechanism should be known. One of the important mechanisms of P. aeruginosa infection is through exotoxin A, which causes tissue necrosis and inactivates elongation factor 2 (EF-2) (Choice C).
- Cleaving of synaptobrevin (Choice A), blockage of acetylcholine (Choice B), and activation of G proteins leading to increase in cAMP (Choice D) do not explain the mechanism of exotoxin A (correlate with the next question).

questions.stem: Which of the following organisms would have an exotoxin with the same mechanism as the causative agent in the case above?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Corynebacterium diphtheriae**

- Among the choices, only **Corynebacterium diphtheriae** (Choice A) has the same mechanism as P. aeruginosa. It also has an exotoxin which inhibits protein synthesis, thus inactivating EF-2.
- **Bordetella pertussis** (Choice B) mainly causes disease through the pertussis toxin, which causes ADP ribosylation and activates G proteins that increases cAMP.
- **Clostridium tetanii** (Choice C) prevents the release of GABA by cleaving synaptobrevin through the tetanus toxin (tetanospasmin).
- **Clostridium botulinum** (Choice D) is associated with flaccid paralysis. This is due to the botulinum toxin which blocks acetylcholine release.

questions.stem: In cases of Staphylococcus aureus infections which have been found out to be resistant to oxacillin and methicillin, which of the following drugs would be the next choice for treatment?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Vancomycin**

- For cases of methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) infections, vancomycin (Choice C) is the next-line drug of choice.
- **Nafcillin** (Choice A) is used for methicillin-sensitive S. aureus infections. If the organism is known to be resistant to oxacillin and methicillin already, it is not utilized.
- **Penicillin G** (Choice B) is the drug of choice for syphilis, not MRSA.
- **Linezolid** (Choice D) is used for vancomycin-resistant S. aureus (VRSA) infections. It is not used immediately in dealing with MRSA infections unless VRSA has been confirmed.

**Treatment summary**

| Category | Treatment |
|---|---|
| Methicillin-sensitive S. aureus (MSSA) | Penicillinase-resistant penicillins (nafcillin, oxacillin, & dicloxacillin) |
| Methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) | Contains altered PBP; DOC is vancomycin |
| Vancomycin-resistant S. aureus (VRSA) | DOC is linezolid |

questions.stem: The term “sequestrum” refers to:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Fragmented, dead necrotic tissue seen in osteomyelitis**

- Sequestrum refers to the fragmented, dead necrotic tissue seen in osteomyelitis (Choice D). Basically, due to the infection, there is disruption of the blood supply of that certain part of the bone, which would eventually necrose.
- It is not new bone formed, but part of the bone which has lost its supply, now surrounded by granulation (Choice A is incorrect).
- It does not refer to skin conditions seen in S. aureus infection. As mentioned, it is used as a term in cases of osteomyelitis (Choices B and C are incorrect).

questions.stem: Which of the following fungi is the likely causative agent in this case?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Sporothrix schenkii**

- Key points in this case include “lesions in the arms and hands”, and the occupation of the patient, a floral arranger. This likely points to a case of sporotrichosis or rose gardener disease. This is transmitted through thorn prick, and it is caused by **Sporothrix schenkii** (Choice A).
- **Phialophora richardsiae** (Choice B) causes phaeohyphomycosis, which is also a subcutaneous mycosis. It may also be transmitted through direct contact with skin.
- **Histoplasma capsulatum** (Choice C) causes histoplasmosis, which is a systemic infection. It may be spread through the inhalation of spores.
- **Trichophyton rubrum** (Choice D) causes cutaneous mycosis. It affects the skin, hair, and nails (recall comparison with Microsporum sp. and Epidermophyton sp.).

questions.stem: The drug of choice in this particular condition would be:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Itraconazole**

- As mentioned in the case, there are no systemic symptoms yet for this patient. Hence, this is considered as a local infection only. The drug of choice for local sporotrichosis infections is itraconazole (Choice C).
- **Amphotericin B** (Choice A) is utilized for cases of sporotrichosis with recorded systemic involvement meaning the fungi has disseminated already.
- **Fluconazole** (Choice B) is used for other fungal infections but is not considered as the first-line drug of choice for sporotrichosis.
- **Clotrimazole troches** (Choice D) is utilized in fungal infections in the oral cavity.

#### Sporothrix schenckii — sporotrichosis
- Dimorphic fungus that lives on vegetation
- Occurs most often in gardeners, especially those who prune roses; transmitted via thorn prick
- Diagnostic features of sporotrichosis on histopathology:
  - Cigar-shaped yeasts
  - Asteroid bodies
- Treatment:
  - Local sporotrichosis — Itraconazole
  - Disseminated, CNS sporotrichosis — Amphotericin B

questions.stem: Which of the following organisms is a trematode?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Clonorchis sinensis**

- **Clonorchis sinensis** (Choice B), also known as the liver fluke, is a trematode which is transmitted through ingestion of undercooked raw fish.
- **Diphyllobothrium latum** (Choice A) and **Taenia saginata** (Choice C) are cestodes (tapeworms).
- **Trichuris trichiura** (Choice D) is a nematode (roundworm).

questions.stem: You are examining a patient who is diagnosed with infective endocarditis. History reveals that the patient has underwent valve replacement before. Which of the following is the most likely causative agent for the patient’s condition?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Staphylococcus epidermidis**

- Recall common organisms that cause infective endocarditis. Since the case states that the patient has underwent valve replacement before, this is a case of infective endocarditis with prosthetic valve/s, which makes **Staphylococcus epidermidis** (Choice A) the most likely etiologic agent.
- **Staphylococcus aureus** (Choice B) causes infective endocarditis mostly in intravenous drug users.
- **Enterococcus faecalis** (Choice C) is usually inoculated in infective endocarditis cases after gastrointestinal surgeries.
- **Viridans streptococci** (Choice D) is encountered for those post-dental procedures (buzzword!).

**Infective endocarditis by clinical setting**

| Setting | Organism |
|---|---|
| IV drug user | Staphylococcus aureus |
| Prosthetic valve | Staphylococcus epidermidis |
| s/p GU or GI procedures | Enterococcus faecalis |
| (+) GI malignancy | Streptococcus bovis |
| Dental procedures | Viridans streptococcus |

Mitral valve is the most frequent valve involved, except in IV drug users, where it is the tricuspid valve.

questions.stem: This phase in human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection pertains to the period where there are no symptoms, but cells continue to divide.
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Latent phase**

- The **latent phase** (Choice C) of HIV occurs when patients are asymptomatic but there is still in an increase in HIV viral load while CD4 count is decreasing. The target of HIV treatment is to control the HIV viral load in this phase.
- **Acute phase** (Choice A) covers the time where a patient is first infected with HIV and there is a spike in HIV viral load. Symptoms also appear during this period.
- **Prodromal phase** (Choice B) is a general term in infections which pertains to the period between the inoculation and appearance of symptoms.
- **Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome** (AIDS, Choice D) is the end-stage of HIV infection. Opportunistic infections would occur due to the immunocompromised state of the patient.

questions.stem: Which of the following viruses would show a positive result in a monospot test?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Epstein-Barr virus**

- The monospot test, also known as the heterophile antibody test, detects if heterophile antibodies are present in a sample. Among the choices, the characteristic “heterophile-positive” description is used for **Epstein-Barr virus** (Choice A) which causes heterophile-positive mononucleosis. It is also involved in some malignancies such as Burkitt lymphoma.
- In contrast, **cytomegalovirus** (Choice D) would test negative in a monospot test. Heterophile-negative mononucleosis and congenital CMV infection are the more known manifestations of this virus.
- **Adenovirus** (Choice B) is known for causing hemorrhagic cystitis and conjunctivitis. Cowdry Type B inclusions which are intranuclear and basophilic are seen in its histopathology samples. Heterophile-negative mononucleosis may also be observed in some cases.
- **Herpes simplex virus** (Choice C) cause conditions depending on its type. HSV-1 causes gingivostomatitis/oral manifestations while HSV-2 causes genital manifestations such as ulcers. It appears as multinucleated giant cells on Tzanck smear. Heterophile-negative mononucleosis may also occur with this virus. Cowdry Type A inclusions (large, pink intranuclear inclusions) are also seen in this virus.

questions.stem: Which of the following pairs of gram-positive bacteria can be differentiated through their shape?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — L. monocytogenes & S. mitis**

- Take note of the question: it is asking for differentiation based on the shape only and not on arrangement.
- Out of all the choices, only **L. monocytogenes** which is a bacilli and **S. mitis** which comes in cocci are of different shape (Choice C).
- Other bacteria have the same shapes:
  - S. pneumoniae and S. aureus (Choice A) are both cocci.
  - S. mutans and E. faecalis (Choice B) are both cocci.
  - B. anthracis and C. diphtheriae (Choice D) are both bacilli.
- Review characteristics of gram-positive bacteria, including their shape, arrangement, and tests that would differentiate them.

questions.stem: Bipolar plugs are a characteristic of which parasite egg seen in microscopic examination?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Trichuris trichiura**

- Bipolar plugs, also termed as the “Japanese lantern-like” appearance, are seen in Trichuris trichiura eggs (Choice D).
- **Capillaria philippinensis** eggs (Choice A) are commonly confused with T. trichiura eggs, however, its eggs do not have bipolar plugs (see images below for comparison).
- **Ascaris lumbricoides** eggs (Choice B) are often round or ovoidal and may be seen in embryonated, unembryonated, or infertile forms. No bipolar plugs are seen.
- **Clonorchis sinensis** eggs (Choice C) are very small compared to other eggs. There is a characteristic abopercular knob seen in these eggs.

questions.stem: Gram-negative bacteria are given their red color by which of the following reagents during gram staining?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Safranin**

- **Safranin** (Choice C) gives the red color of gram-negative bacteria which is considered as the counterstain in gram staining.
- **Crystal violet** (Choice B) is the primary stain which gives the gram-positive bacteria their purple color. They are then reinforced by the mordant, iodine (Choice D). The primary stain is then washed off for gram-negative bacteria through applying alcohol. Gram-positive bacteria maintain the primary stain.
- **Malachite green** (Choice A) is used to visualize spores of bacteria.
- Review steps in gram staining and reagents.

questions.stem: Which of the following organisms is the likely causative agent is DG’s condition?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Campylobacter jejuni**

- History of gastrointestinal distress leading to ascending paralysis points out to a case of Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS). This is due to the autoimmune reaction in response to a previous infection.
- The common causative agents of GBS include **Campylobacter jejuni** (Choice D) and cytomegalovirus (CMV).
- **Helicobacter pylori** (Choice A) is a gram-negative bacterium which causes peptic ulcer disease. If persistent and not treated, it may lead to gastric cancer.
- **Escherichia coli** (Choice B) is a gram-negative bacterium which causes diarrhea. Its different strains cause varying manifestations (review strains of E. coli and their differences).
- **Clostridium botulinum** (Choice C) is a gram-positive bacterium associated with flaccid paralysis. It usually presents with a triad: symmetric descending paralysis (NOT ascending), absence of fever, and intact sensorium.

questions.stem: This disease is also associated with the causative agent in this case:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Reiter syndrome**

- C. jejuni may also cause Reiter syndrome (Choice A). Remember the triad of urethritis, uveitis, and arthritis — “can't pee, can't see, can't climb a tree.”
- Reiter syndrome is also associated with C. trachomatis.
- **Ritter disease** (Choice B) is also called staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, caused by S. aureus.
- **Gastric carcinoma** (Choice C) is seen in cases of chronic unaddressed H. pylori infection.
- **Hemolytic uremic syndrome** (Choice D) may occur due to E. coli strains, or in some countries, due to S. dysenteriae type 1.

questions.stem: Tsetse flies act as vectors in which of the following diseases?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — West African sleeping sickness**

- Tsetse flies act as vectors in East and West African sleeping sickness (Choice A). It is cause by Trypanosoma brucei.
- **Chagas disease** (Choice B) is transmitted through reduviid bugs carrying Trypanosoma cruzi.
- **Zika virus** (Choice C) is transmitted through mosquitoes (Aedes sp.).
- **Scrub typhus** (Choice D) is transmitted through mites (chiggers) carrying Orientia tsutsugamushi.

questions.stem: This organism is transmitted to humans as an accidental host through ingestion of eggs causing visceral and ocular larva migrans:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Toxocara canis**

- Humans are considered accidental hosts in the life cycle of **Toxocara canis** (Choice B). They will cause visceral and ocular larva migrans in humans. They are commonly encountered in domestic dogs and cats.
- **Ancylostoma caninum** (Choice A) also cause cutaneous larva migrans in humans, but not commonly ocular. Ocular and visceral larva migrans are more commonly seen in T. canis cases making it the most suitable answer. Humans are also considered accidental hosts for A. caninum.
- **Angiostrongylus cantonensis** (Choice C) is also called the cat lungworm in which humans are also accidental hosts. This causes human eosinophilic meningitis.
- **Anisakis** (Choice D) is also transmitted through accidental ingestion of humans. It manifests acutely with gastrointestinal symptoms mimicking Crohn’s disease.
- Review life cycle of Toxocara spp.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a gram-negative rod that causes meningitis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Haemophilus influenzae**

- **H. influenzae** (Choice B) is a gram-negative rod which can cause sinusitis, otitis media, epiglottitis, and meningitis.
- **N. meningitidis** (Choice A), although characteristically known for causing meningitis, is not a rod but a gram-negative diplococcus.
- **Streptococcus agalactiae** (Choice C) may also cause meningitis especially in neonates, but it is gram-positive.
- **Proteus mirabilis** (Choice D) is a gram-negative rod but it is not known to commonly cause meningitis. It usually presents with complicated urinary tract infections.

questions.stem: What is the diagnosis for the patient’s condition?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Congenital rubella syndrome**

- Key points in this case include “continuous machinery-like murmur” which indicates patent ductus arteriosus, bilateral cataracts, and maternal history indicating that there was a likely history of rubella infection. The neonate is suffering from congenital rubella syndrome (Choice C).
- **Congenital cytomegalovirus infection** (Choice A) is also common when mothers are infected in the 1st trimester. However, findings point to rubella (PDA + cataracts). CMV infection would manifest as seizures, deafness, and jaundice.
- **Congenital syphilis** (Choice B) would present as saddle nose, Hutchinson triad, mulberry molars, and sometimes pulmonary hemorrhage.
- **Congenital HIV** (Choice D) will manifest as recurrent infections in infancy, hepatomegaly, and splenomegaly.

**Congenital rubella syndrome**
- Infected during the 1st trimester
- Associated abnormalities:
  - Patent ductus arteriosus
  - Congenital cataracts
  - Sensorineural deafness
  - Mental retardation

**Memory aid — 5 B's of congenital rubella syndrome**
- Bulag (cataracts)
- Bingi (sensorineural deafness)
- Brain damage (mental retardation)
- Butas ng puso (PDA)
- Blueberry muffin baby

questions.stem: In adults, the causative agent for this condition would manifest disease as:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — German measles**

- Rubella in adults will cause German measles/three-day measles (Choice B). Maculopapular rash and posterior auricular lymphadenopathy are observed in these cases.
- Heterophil-negative mononucleosis is observed in CMV infections. Heterophil-positive mononucleosis, on the other hand, is caused by EBV (Choice A).
- Immunocompromised state is seen in a wide array of diseases (Choice C). However, this is not characteristic of rubella infection in adults which has an acute presentation.
- Hard chancres (Choice D) are seen in cases of primary syphilis caused by T. pallidum.

choices.text:
Immediate discharge of patient and mother since this is
a benign condition and may be managed conservatively

Referral to surgery for immediate management of
cardiac condition

Referral to multiple subspecialties to monitor the array
of conditions of the newborn
Medical management through loading of antibiotics

questions.stem: The appropriate step in the management of this patient is:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Referral to multiple subspecialties to monitor the array of conditions of the newborn**

- Given that congenital rubella syndrome covers a lot of fields such as cardiology for PDA, ophthalmology for cataracts, and otorhinolaryngology for sensorineural deafness, referral to multiple subspecialties and regular follow-up for monitoring are recommended steps in its management (Choice C).
- Immediate discharge (Choice A) is not recommended in this case because the newborn would still need to be monitored for possible complications and referred to proper subspecialties before discharge.
- Surgery is not immediately indicated in this case (Choice B is incorrect).
- Antibiotics are not recommended in this case because the etiologic is not bacterial and it is due to prior infection of the mother (Choice D is incorrect).

questions.stem: Which of the following is diagnosed through the scotch tape test?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Pinworm**

- **Pinworms/Seatworms** (Enterobius vermicularis, Choice C) are diagnosed through the scotch tape test wherein samples are obtained from the perianal folds.
- **Whipworm** (Choice A) is the common name for Trichuris trichiura. It can be diagnosed through direct fecal smear, kato thick, or kato katz smear.
- **Threadworm** (Choice B) is also known as Strongyloides stercoralis. Diagnosis of this parasite can be done through directly demonstrating the rhabditiform larvae, Harada-Mori culture, Koga agar, enterotest, and Baermann funnel gauze method.
- **Tapeworm** (Choice D) is the common term for cestodes. None of the cestodes are diagnosed through the scotch tape test.

questions.stem: All of the following organisms are common causative agents of the condition in this case, EXCEPT:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Streptococcus pneumoniae**

- Key points of this case include “joint pains”, “intermittent high-grade fever”, history of ToF which underwent surgery and easy fatigability which point to case of infective endocarditis.
- S. pneumoniae (Choice C) does not commonly cause infective endocarditis.
- S. aureus (Choice A), viridans Streptococci (Choice B), and E. faecalis (Choice C) are all common causes of infective endocarditis.

**Infective endocarditis**
- Causative agents are polymicrobial
  - Most common: Staphylococcus aureus, viridans Streptococcus, Enterococcus
  - HACEK: Haemophilus, Actinobacillus, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella

questions.stem: On further examination with the help of the pediatric fellow, you notice that there are hemorrhagic lesions on the palms and soles, which are painless and small. These are called:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Janeway lesions**

- **Janeway lesions** (Choice B) are described to be painless, small erythematous hemorrhagic lesions on the palms and soles.
- **Koplik spots** (Choice A) are lesions that are seen in the mucous membrane of the mouth in cases of measles (rubeola), not infective endocarditis.
- **Osler nodes** (Choice C) are also seen in infective endocarditis. These are tender, pea-sized intradermal nodules in the pads of fingers and toes.
- **Splinter hemorrhages** (Choice D) are linear lesions beneath the nails which are also signs of infective endocarditis.
- In reality, it is very hard to distinguish Janeway lesions and Osler nodes. However, since the question states that the lesions are painless (not tender), it points more towards Janeway lesions.

questions.stem: The following are diagnostic methods for identifying fungi, EXCEPT:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Harada-Mori culture**

- **Harada-Mori culture** (Choice C) is NOT utilized for identifying fungi. It is used for identifying parasites, specifically hookworms (Necator americanus, Ancylostoma duodenale) and Strongyloides stercoralis.
- All other choices are used for the diagnosis of fungi:
  - **KOH examination** (Choice A) dissolves tissue to be able to visualize the fungi clearly.
  - **India ink staining** (Choice B) is also known as negative staining and is used for identifying Cryptococcus neoformans.
  - **Gomori-methenamine silver staining** (Choice D) is used for identifying Pneumocystis carinii.

#### Laboratory diagnosis of fungi

**Staining techniques**
- **10% KOH examination** — KOH dissolves any tissue cells, making the highly refractory fungal cells more visible.
- **Calcofluor white** — Added to KOH to increase its sensitivity; stains fungal cell wall and makes it fluorescent.
- **Gomori-methenamine silver (GMS)** — Stains fungal cell wall black; used to stain Pneumocystis carinii.
- **Mucicarmine stain** — Stains fungal capsule red; used to stain Cryptococcus neoformans.
- **India ink stain** — Uses “negative staining” to highlight the heavily thickened capsule of Cryptococcus neoformans.

**Culture techniques**
- **Sabouraud’s dextrose agar (SDA)** — Standard culture for isolation of fungal agents.
- **Inhibitory mold agar (IMA)** — Enhances the recovery of fungi from clinical specimens.

**Other diagnostic tools**
- **Serology** — Helpful among immunocompetent patients. Positive antibody test may confirm the diagnosis; negative antibody test may exclude the diagnosis.
- **Molecular methods** — For rapid diagnosis of fungal organisms. Examples: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR), MALDI-TOF-MS (matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization-time of flight mass spectrometry).

questions.stem:
Hepatitis panel with the following results indicates:

| Marker | Result |
|---|---|
| HBsAg | + |
| Anti-HBs | − |
| Anti-HBc, IgM | + |
| HBeAg | + |
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Acute infection**

- This panel indicates that the individual has been acutely infected with hepatitis B (Choice A). Positive IgM anti-HBc indicates new/acute infection.
- **Chronic non-infective hepatitis B** (Choice B) would present as (+) HBsAg, (−) anti-HBs, (+) IgG anti-HBc (recall that IgG positive means infection from before), and (−) HBeAg.
- On the other hand, **infective chronic hepatitis B** (Choice C) will have a (+) HBeAg compared to non-infective chronic hepatitis B.
- **Incubation period** during infection of hepatitis B (Choice D) will show the following lab results: (+) HBsAg, (−) anti-HBs, (−) anti-HBc, and (+) HBeAg.
- Recall interpretation of hepatitis B panel below:

| Interpretation | HBsAg | Anti-HBs | Anti-HBc |
|---|---|---|---|
| Early acute HBV infection | + | − | − |
| HBV infection (acute or chronic) — differentiate with IgM anti-HBc | + | +/− | + |
| Previous HBV infection and immunity | − | + | + |
| No infection | − | − | − |
| Successful vaccine response | − | + | − |
| Interpretation unclear (see below) | − | − | + |

Four possibilities when HBsAg −, Anti-HBs −, Anti-HBc + (“Interpretation unclear”):
1. HBV infection in remote past
2. “Low-level” HBV carrier
3. “Window” period between disappearance of HBsAg and appearance of anti-HBs
4. False positive/non-specific reaction

questions.stem: Which of the following parasites do not require a vector to be transmitted?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Schistosoma japonicum**

- **Schistosoma japonicum** (Choice A) does not require a vector in its life cycle. It is transmitted through direct penetration of the skin in free water.
- **Babesia microti** (Choice B) is transmitted through the Ixodes tick.
- **Paragonimus westermani** (Choice C) is transmitted through ingestion of crustaceans containing the organism.
- **Brugia malayi** (Choice D) is transmitted through mosquitoes, commonly Mansonia spp.

questions.stem: Which gram-positive bacteria is both catalase-positive and coagulase-positive?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Staphylococcus aureus**

- **S. aureus** (Choice A) is a gram-positive cocci that is both catalase and coagulase positive.
- **S. pneumoniae** (Choice B) is catalase-negative, alpha-hemolytic, and sensitive to optochin.
- **S. epidermidis** (Choice C) is catalase-positive but coagulase-negative. It is also sensitive to novobiocin.
- **S. pyogenes** (Choice D) is catalase-negative, beta-hemolytic, and sensitive to bacitracin.
- Refer to question #17 for the summary of gram-positive bacteria characteristics.

questions.stem: Which of the following organisms is the likely cause of his condition?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Wuchereria bancrofti**

- Enlargement of the scrotum (hydrocoele) is already considered as a symptom of chronic lymphatic filariasis. Lymphatic filariasis is caused by transmission of **Wuchereria bancrofti** (Choice D) or Brugia malayi through mosquitoes. These are usually seen in provinces in Visayas, such as Sorsogon, Samar, and Leyte.
- **Loa loa** (Choice A) causes loiasis which will present as subcutaneous edema and a visible worm that is crawling across the conjunctiva.
- **Trichinella spiralis** (Choice B) causes trichinellosis which presents as severe myalgia, periorbital edema, and sometimes hemorrhagic phenomenon such as subconjunctival hemorrhage or splinters.
- **Dracunculus medinensis** (Choice C) presents as a pruritic painful papule, where there is a visible worm in a skin ulcer. This is more prevalent in African countries.
- Recall differences between causative species of lymphatic filariasis:

| Characteristic | Wuchereria bancrofti | Brugia malayi |
|---|---|---|
| Appearance | Smoothly curved | Kinky |
| Nuclei confluency | Distinct nuclei | Overlapping nuclei |
| Terminal nuclei | Absent | Present |
| Prevalence | Widespread | SEA only |
| Mosquito vectors | Culex, Aedes, Anopheles | Mansonia |
| Preference | Scrotal lymphatics | Limb lymphatics |
| Clinical picture | Hydrocoele | Elephantiasis |
| Severity | More severe | Less severe |

questions.stem: What is the first-line treatment of choice for his condition?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Diethylcarbamazine**

- For lymphatic filariasis, **diethylcarbamazine** (Choice C) is the treatment of choice. It is also the drug of choice for loiasis (eye worm disease). Its mode of action is immobilization of microfilariae.
- **Albendazole** (Choice A) is the drug of choice for hydatid disease. It inhibits microtubule assembly.
- **Pyrantel pamoate** (Choice B) is a depolarizing neuromuscular blocker which is the drug of choice for pinworms.
- **Ivermectin** (Choice D) intensifies GABA-mediated neurotransmission and is the drug of choice for strongyloidiasis.

**Diethylcarbamazine**
- MOA: immobilizes microfilariae
- Uses: filariasis (DOC), eye worm disease (DOC), onchocerciasis (backup)
- Side effects: headache, malaise, weakness, anorexia, filarial fever (fever, rashes, ocular damage, joint and muscle pain, lymphangitis)
- Notes: may cause Mazzotti reaction when used for onchocerciasis; doxycycline has also shown significant activity against W. bancrofti

questions.stem: The most common sexually transmitted infection worldwide is caused by:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Human papillomavirus**

- The most common sexually transmitted disease worldwide is **human papillomavirus** (HPV) (Choice D) which commonly causes warts (usually genital warts).
- **HIV** (Choice A) is a sexually transmitted disease which has been increasing in prevalence. It may also be transferred transplacentally and through needlesticks injuries. However, it is not the most common.
- **N. gonorrhoeae** (Choice B) is one of the most common STDs, but not the most common. It is usually in a co-infection with C. trachomatis, which is the most common bacterial sexually transmitted infection.
- Although **T. pallidum** (Choice C) is sexually transmitted, it is not the most common infection worldwide. It causes syphilis.

questions.stem: The first intermediate host in the life cycle of the causative organism is:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Snail**

- Hemoptysis and history of intake of seafood (which are most likely undercooked) are key points in this case. P. westermani will present like tuberculosis (with hemoptysis and difficulty of breathing). No exposure of tuberculosis was mentioned which make it the less likely diagnosis.
- The first intermediate host in the life cycle of P. westermani is the **snail** (Antemelania sp., Choice B).
- **Mountain crabs** (Sundathelphusa philippina, Choice C) are its second intermediate hosts.
- **Freshwater/Saltwater fishes** (Choices A/D) are not encountered in the life cycle because the second intermediate hosts are crustaceans which are ingested by humans, thus transmitting the parasite.
- Review life cycle of P. westermani.

questions.stem: What is the infective stage of this parasite?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Metacercariae**

- As seen in the life cycle of P. westermani above, transmission is through ingestion of crustaceans which contain the **metacercariae** (Choice C) of the parasite.
- After excystation of these metacercariae, they penetrate the abdominal cavity and diaphragm. They develop into **adult worms** (Choice B) in the lungs, causing the respiratory symptoms.
- **Unembryonated eggs** (Choice D) are the diagnostic stage as they are passed through the feces. In free water, these eggs become **embryonated** (Choice A).

questions.stem: The appropriate management of this case is done through:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Treatment with praziquantel**

- Paragonimiasis is treated through **praziquantel** (Choice D). This is the drug of choice and is effective in eradicating the parasite. Albendazole is not the drug of choice for this disease (Choice B is incorrect).
- Although supportive management is part of the management of paragonimiasis, observation only would not suffice in successfully treating patients with this condition (Choice A is incorrect).
- Paragonimiasis mimics pulmonary tuberculosis. However, the conditions that were stated in the case point more to paragonimiasis rather than tuberculosis. Thus, the best choice would still be D given the circumstances. Referral to TB-DOTS facility would have been the proper management if this was a confirmed case of TB (Choice C is incorrect given the case).

questions.stem: The most likely condition of the patients in this case can be caused by which of the following causative agents?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Treponema pallidum**

- The key points in this case are the findings in the baby (saddle nose deformity, difficulty of breathing) and maternal history (no screening done with history of non-tender ulcer) which point to syphilis.
- The causative agent for syphilis is **Treponema pallidum** (Choice B).
- **Leptospira interrogans** (Choice A) is the organism responsible for leptospirosis. Leptospirosis may manifest in acute (symptoms such as calf tenderness and subconjunctival suffusion are seen) or immune phases (aseptic meningitis, pulmonary symptoms, hepatic necrosis, and glomerulonephritis may be observed). The severe form of this disease is known as Weil’s syndrome.
- **Chlamydia trachomatis** (Choice C) is also spread by sexual contact and is the most common bacterial sexually transmitted disease worldwide, but the circumstances of the case point more to syphilis due to the congenital finding and ulcer on history. Diseases caused by this organism ranges from trachoma, genital tract infections, and lymphogranuloma venereum. For neonatal cases, it manifests as pneumonia which is late onset.
- **Bartonella henselae** (Choice D) causes the cat scratch fever in immunocompetent individuals. This manifests as rashes in addition to the fever. Meanwhile, for immunocompromised individuals, bacillary angiomatosis occurs which would present with neurologic symptoms.

Transmission is mainly due to sexual contact due to
inhabitation of the causative organism in the human
genital tract.

The organism is a characteristically spiral shaped
bacilli seen on gram staining, which is described as

questions.stem: All of the following statements are true regarding the condition of the patients in this case, EXCEPT:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — The organism is a characteristically spiral shaped bacilli seen on gram staining, which is described as “corkscrew shaped”.**

- Treponema pallidum is a helically coiled, spiral, or corkscrew shaped bacilli, which is NOT seen on gram staining but on darkfield microscopy (thus, Choice B is incorrect).
- Primarily, syphilis is transmitted through sexual contact (its natural habitat is the human genital tract) but it can also be transmitted through skin contact, infection in utero, blood transfusion, and transplantation (Choice A is correct).
- Tertiary syphilis occurs years after inoculation of the organism. The clinical picture of tertiary syphilis includes neurosyphilis (Choice C is correct).
- The Higoumenakis sign of the clavicle may be seen in congenital syphilis. This is described as a unilateral enlargement of the sternoclavicular portion of the clavicle, leading to detachment (Choice D is correct).

questions.stem: Which of the following is the treatment of choice for this case?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Benzathine Penicillin G**

- The drug of choice for syphilis is **Benzathine Penicillin G** (Choice D). It is bactericidal and a natural penicillin (recall categories of penicillins in pharmacology).
- **Doxycycline** (Choice A) and **Azithromycin** (Choice C) are alternatives to T. pallidum infection but are not considered first-line. Doxycycline is a tetracycline while azithromycin is a macrolide.
- **Vancomycin** (Choice B) is a glycopeptide which is usually utilized in severe cases such as methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) infections.

**Natural penicillins** (narrow-spectrum, penicillinase-susceptible) — Penicillin G (IV), Penicillin V (oral; mnemonic “oral = Vivig (bibig)”)
- DOC for syphilis
- Covers streptococci, pneumococci, meningococcal, gram-positive bacilli, spirochete, some Clostridium, Actinomyces (non β-lactamase-producing)
- Activity against enterococci enhanced with aminoglycosides
- Inactivated by beta-lactamase (penicillinase)
- Benzathine penicillin & procaine penicillin: long-acting IM preparations
- Penicillin V: oral but poor bioavailability, 4x/day, narrow spectrum

questions.stem: The following are findings under the triad of this condition during examination of the baby boy, EXCEPT:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Entropion eyelid**

- Infants with congenital syphilis may appear with the Hutchinson triad: Hutchinson teeth (more widely space teeth with notched incisors — Choice B), 8th nerve deafness (Choice D), and interstitial keratitis (Choice A).
- **Entropion eyelid** (Choice C) is not part of the Hutchinson triad and is not seen in cases of congenital syphilis.

questions.stem: Which of the following gram-positive organisms is sensitive to optochin?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Streptococcus pneumoniae**

- **S. pneumoniae** (Choice B) is alpha-hemolytic, bile soluble, and sensitive to optochin.
- **S. pyogenes** (Choice A) is beta-hemolytic and sensitive to bacitracin.
- **S. agalactiae** (Choice C) is beta-hemolytic and resistant to bacitracin.
- **S. bovis** (Choice D) is gamma-hemolytic and does not grow in 6.5% NaCl.
- Recall characteristics of gram-positive cocci in chains (Streptococcus spp.):

| Gram stain | Other features | Organism |
|---|---|---|
| Gram-positive cocci in chains | Catalase negative, alpha hemolytic, bile soluble, optochin-sensitive | Streptococcus pneumoniae |
| Gram-positive cocci in chains | Catalase negative, alpha hemolytic, bile insoluble, optochin-resistant | Viridans streptococcal sp. |
| Gram-positive cocci in chains | Catalase negative, beta hemolytic, bacitracin-sensitive | Streptococcus pyogenes |
| Gram-positive cocci in chains | Catalase negative, beta hemolytic, bacitracin-resistant | Streptococcus agalactiae |
| Gram-positive cocci in chains | Catalase negative, gamma hemolytic | Group D streptococci |

questions.stem: Walking pneumonia is under the spectrum of disease of which organism?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Mycoplasma pneumoniae**

- “Walking pneumonia” is a characteristic term (buzzword!) for pneumonia which is caused by **Mycoplasma pneumoniae** (Choice D). It is called as such since the patient would appear essentially normal but with abnormal x-ray.
- **Streptococcus pneumoniae** (Choice A) and **Staphylococcus aureus** (Choice C) are also common causes of pneumonia but there are usually pulmonary manifestations and not coined as “walking”.
- **H. influenzae** (Choice B) is a relatively common gram-negative rod which can cause sinusitis, otitis media, epiglottitis, and meningitis especially in unvaccinated children.

**Correct answer: B — All cases of varicella-zoster will reactivate and manifest as zoster.**

- Varicella-zoster (VZV) is a dsDNA virus which is transmitted through respiratory droplets (Choice A is correct).
- Rashes caused by VZV are characterized by vesicular centripetal rash which is described as “dewdrop on a rose petal” (Choice C is correct).

questions.stem: Which of the following is the vector for transmitting the child’s disease?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Aedes aegypti**

- This case points toward to a probable dengue infection given the symptoms of the child which show dehydration, rash, and fever. In addition, the country is endemic to dengue which make it a common diagnosis for these cases.
- Dengue is transmitted through mosquito bites, specifically of **Aedes aegypti** (Choice C).
- **Anopheles flavirostris** (Choice A) is the vector for transmission of malaria.
- **Simulium trifasciatum** (Choice B) is the vector for transmission of onchocerciasis or river blindness.
- **Culex tritaeniorhynchus** (Choice D) is the vector of Japanese encephalitis.

questions.stem: The appropriate management for this case is:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Ensuring proper hydration and supportive management**

- The main management for dengue cases is supportive management, achieved through proper hydration (Choice A), monitoring of platelet count and hematocrit, monitoring of complications, and anti-pyretics as needed.
- Antibiotics are of no use if the infection is solely due to dengue because it is caused by a virus (Choice B is incorrect).
- Observation only will not suffice proper management for dengue cases. Monitoring for complications should warrant proper management depending on the observed trend of laboratory results and signs/symptoms (Choice C is incorrect).
- Prophylactic transfusion of blood is not recommended in dengue cases, as this may lead to fluid overload and transfusion reactions if done hastily (Choice D is incorrect).

questions.stem: In cases of re-infection of this disease, which of the following will explain scenarios in which patients have worse outcome compared to the first infection?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Infection with a different serotype compared to the first instance**

- **A. Infection with the same serotype as the first instance** — This would lead to better outcomes because of the presence of IgG, which would persist after the initial infection.
- **B. Completed full vaccination against the disease** — This would lead to better immunity against dengue.
- **C. Infection with a different serotype compared to the first instance** — Complications that arise from dengue, such as dengue hemorrhagic fever, are common in patients infected with a different serotype after their initial infection, due to antibody-dependent enhancement of the disease.
- **D. Deficiency in antibodies** — This is not a sufficient reason to explain worse outcomes upon re-infection, since IgG antibodies persist for life after the first infection. This choice may be argued in immunocompromised states, but in general, infection with a different serotype is the better answer.

questions.stem: Which of the following viruses is a double-stranded RNA virus which can cause diarrhea?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Rotavirus**

- **A. Rotavirus** — Among the choices, only rotavirus is a double-stranded RNA virus. It is the most common cause of childhood diarrhea.
- **B. Norovirus** — A single-stranded RNA virus, which eliminates it based on the question.
- **C. Echovirus** — A single-stranded RNA virus, which eliminates it based on the question.
- **D. Astrovirus** — A single-stranded RNA virus, which eliminates it based on the question.

**Recall exceptions in RNA viruses:**
- All viruses are haploid except Retrovirus.
- All RNA viruses have single-stranded RNA EXCEPT Reovirus and Rotavirus.
- All RNA viruses replicate in the cytoplasm EXCEPT Influenza and Retrovirus.

questions.stem: The following statements are true regarding the spectrum of disease of S. aureus infection, EXCEPT:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C** — the exception (not a true statement): **"Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, or Reiter syndrome, is due to exfoliatin which results to separation of the epidermis."**

- **A. In cases of toxic shock syndrome, there is usually no site of pyogenic inflammation and blood culture will test out negative.** — Correct. Toxic shock syndrome is caused by TSST-1, usually in tampon-using women or those using nasal packing for epistaxis. No site of pyogenic inflammation is usually seen, and blood culture will turn out negative.
- **B. Osteomyelitis is a common complication of S. aureus infection, usually encountered in long bones for children and vertebrae in adults.** — Correct.
- **C. Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, or Reiter syndrome, is due to exfoliatin which results to separation of the epidermis.** — Not true. Although the description is correct for staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (it is due to exfoliatin), it is NOT synonymous with Reiter syndrome. Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is also known as Ritter disease — keep the difference between these two diseases in mind. (Refer to question #21 for a description of Reiter syndrome.)
- **D. Infective endocarditis is a known complication which is usually observed in intravenous drug users.** — Correct. For intravenous drug users who suffer from infective endocarditis, the most common causative agent is S. aureus.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings will most likely be seen if x-ray is done?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Thumb sign**

- Given the key points of the case — "drooling," "unrecalled vaccination," "difficulty of breathing" — this makes it a likely case of epiglottitis.
- Epiglottitis is caused by H. influenzae, a gram-negative rod. Spectrum of disease includes meningitis, otitis media, and pneumonia.
  - **Memory aid:** Ha**EMOP**hilus influenzae causes **E**piglottitis, **M**eningitis, **O**titis media, **P**neumonia.
- **A. Thumb sign** — Also known as the leaf sign, seen in cases of epiglottitis, characterized by a swollen epiglottis on lateral x-ray view.
- **B. Steeple sign** — Seen in cases of viral croup; a subglottic narrowing on x-ray.
- **C. Cannonball sign** — Indicative of metastasis in the lungs, as seen on chest x-ray.
- **D. Donut ring sign** — Seen in intussusception on ultrasound.

**Recall common etiologies of acute upper airway obstruction in children:**

| | Croup (LTB) | Acute epiglottitis | Acute infectious laryngitis |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Signs and symptoms** | URTI and low-grade fever 1-3 days prior to UAO presentation; "barking cough," hoarseness; fever may become high-grade; symptoms worse at night, agitation may aggravate symptoms; other family members are ill | Acute high fever, sore throat, dyspnea, and rapidly progressing obstruction (difficult swallowing, labored breathing within a few hours); drooling and hyperextended neck; no family member is ill | Sore throat, cough; generally mild; respiratory distress is unusual; hoarseness out of proportion to symptoms |
| **PE findings** | Stridor, coryza, normal to moderately inflamed pharynx, slight tachypnea | Tripod position; stridor occurs late; large, cherry-red swollen epiglottis on laryngoscopy | Unremarkable except for pharyngeal inflammation |
| **Diagnosis** | Mainly clinical; x-ray of the neck: subglottic narrowing or "steeple sign" (may be absent in patients with croup or present as a normal variant); x-rays do not correlate well with disease severity | Lateral x-ray of the upper airway: thumb sign; direct or flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy for direct visualization | Clinical and by laryngoscopy (inflammatory edema of the vocal cords and subglottic tissue); primary site of obstruction is the subglottic area |
| **Treatment** | Airway management and treatment of hypoxia; nebulized racemic epinephrine for moderate to severe croup; single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg | Medical emergency: airway management; cefotaxime, ceftriaxone, or meropenem IV | Supportive |

questions.stem: Which vaccine could have prevented this condition?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Hib vaccine**

- **A. Rotavirus vaccine** — Prevents diarrhea in children, most commonly caused by rotavirus.
- **B. Hib vaccine** — As mentioned in the previous question, the causative agent for this case is H. influenzae, whose transmission may be prevented through the H. influenzae type B (Hib) vaccine.
- **C. DPT vaccine** — Used to prevent diphtheria, polio, and tetanus, especially in children.
- **D. Oral polio vaccine** — Used to prevent transmission of poliovirus, which manifests as neurologic symptoms.

questions.stem: The following statements are correct regarding L. pneumophila, EXCEPT:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A** — the exception (not a true statement): **"It causes Pontiac fever, which management warrants azithromycin as the drug of choice."**

- **A. It causes Pontiac fever, which management warrants azithromycin as the drug of choice.** — Not true. Although azithromycin is the drug of choice for L. pneumophila infections, Pontiac fever is self-limited and does not require antibiotics.
- **B. It is a gram-negative rod which is visualized through silver staining.** — Correct. Silver staining is used to visualize L. pneumophila, a gram-negative rod.
- **C. It causes atypical pneumonia, which presents with hyponatremia and non-bloody diarrhea.** — Correct. Atypical pneumonia is part of the spectrum of disease of L. pneumophila. It presents with confusion, non-bloody diarrhea, hyponatremia, proteinuria, and hematuria.
- **D. Buffered charcoal yeast extract is the culture used for its growth.** — Correct.

| Bordet-Gengou / Regan-Lowe agar | Bordetella pertussis |
| Buffered charcoal-yeast extract | Legionella pneumophila |
| Skirrow's medium | Campylobacter |

questions.stem: You suspect that he currently has HIV. Which of the following is true regarding his condition?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Antiretroviral therapy should be started once diagnosed.**

- **A. Antiretroviral therapy should be started once diagnosed.** — Correct. For confirmed cases of HIV, antiretroviral therapy is usually started once diagnosis is made. This benefits the individual since the key to management of these cases is monitoring of HIV viral load, CD4 count, and complications that can possibly arise.
- **B. Observation is only warranted during this time.** — Not true. Observation only will not be effective against HIV; there should be proper monitoring of laboratory parameters and complications.
- **C. It is caused by a virus that is single-stranded, with negative-polarity RNA genome.** — Not true. HIV is a single-stranded, positive-sense RNA virus, not negative-sense.
- **D. HIV2 has a higher viral load compared to HIV1.** — Not true. HIV1 has a higher viral load than HIV2; thus those infected with HIV1 will have a shorter time before AIDS develops if treatment is not initiated.

**Recall HIV strains:**

| | HIV1 | HIV2 |
|---|---|---|
| Distribution | Worldwide | West Africa |
| Time before AIDS | 7-10 years | 10-25 years |
| Drug resistance | Limited resistance | Resistant to NNRTI, fusion inhibitor |

**When is HIV2 suspected?**
1. If positive on 4th-generation HIV testing (HIV Ag/Ab), which detects p24 of HIV1 and HIV2 — this does not differentiate between them.
2. If negative for HIV1 on western blot of plasma HIV RNA testing.
3. Confirmed through HIV1/HIV2 differentiation immunoassay.

questions.stem: Which of the following laboratory tests will clinch the diagnosis in this case?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Western blot analysis**

- **A. Culture in agar** — Not effective for isolating HIV; this is used more for bacterial microorganisms.
- **B. Viral load** — Not used for diagnosis of HIV, but for monitoring the condition of known HIV-positive individuals, correlated with CD4 count.
- **C. ELISA** — Also used as a laboratory test for HIV, but only for presumptive diagnosis, due to a high false-positive rate.
- **D. Western blot analysis** — As the question asks for the definitive diagnosis of HIV, the correct answer is Western blot analysis.

**Recall HIV diagnostics:**

| ELISA | Western blot |
|---|---|
| Presumptive diagnosis | Definitive diagnosis |
| Sensitive | Specific |
| High false-positive rate | Low false-positive rate |
| Low threshold | High threshold |
| Rule-out test | Rule-in test |

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most common AIDS-defining illness encountered in this condition?
questions.rationale:

- **D. Coccidioidomycosis** — An AIDS-defining illness, but not as common as PJP.

- **C. Erythrogenic toxin** — The virulence factor responsible for the development of scarlet fever, with characteristic strawberry tongue and Pastia lines.
- **D. Pyrogenic exotoxin A** — Among the virulence factors of S. pyogenes, it is pyrogenic exotoxin A that causes toxic shock syndrome. In comparison to S. aureus, this would test positive on blood culture.

questions.stem: What is the most probable diagnosis for the patient’s case?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — San Joaquin Valley fever**

- **A. San Joaquin Valley fever** — The main key point for this case is travel to San Diego, California, which predisposes him to San Joaquin Valley fever, common in the Southwestern US and California. His symptoms are consistent with its disease presentation — malaise, cough, influenza-like illness with arthralgia. This is caused by Coccidioides immitis.
- **B. Histoplasmosis** — Would present as oral ulcerations and splenomegaly (in severe cases). This is globally encountered but more seen in the Mississippi and Ohio River valleys.

questions.stem: If his condition develops to meningitis, which of the following is the drug of choice for this patient?

**Coccidioides immitis**
- **Epidemiology** — Southwestern US, California

questions.stem: Which of the following inclusions are characteristic of rabies infection, seen on histopathology?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Negri bodies**

- **A. Guarnieri bodies** — Seen as intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions in smallpox infections.
- **B. Henderson-Paterson bodies** — Also intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions, but in molluscum contagiosum infections.
- **C. Negri bodies** — Rabies virus is a single-stranded, negative-sense RNA virus, transmitted through animal bites (dogs, cats, skunks, raccoons, and bats). On histopathology of the brains of patients infected with rabies, Negri bodies can be observed.
- **D. Warthin-Finkeldey bodies** — Multinucleated giant cells seen in measles infection.

questions.stem: Successful treatment of syphilis may be monitored through which diagnostic test?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Non-treponemal tests**

- **A. Non-treponemal tests** — Used for screening of syphilis, and also to test for cure in patients who have undergone syphilis treatment.
- **B. Fluorescent treponemal antibody absorbed test (FTA-ABS)** — A treponemal test, used to confirm the diagnosis of syphilis. However, this will always test positive once infected and is unaffected by treatment, so it is not used as a diagnostic for confirming cure.
- **C. Microhemagglutination T. pallidum (MHA-TP)** — A treponemal test, used to confirm the diagnosis of syphilis. However, this will always test positive once infected and is unaffected by treatment, so it is not used as a diagnostic for confirming cure.
- **D. Darkfield microscopy** — Only used for visualization of T. pallidum. Other diagnostic tests are more impactful regarding the management of syphilis cases.

questions.stem: In acute infections of hepatitis B, which of the following markers would indicate new infection?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — IgM anti-HBcAg**

- **A. HBsAg** — Indicates hepatitis B infection and will be positive whether it is acute, chronic, or asymptomatic.
- **B. IgG anti-HBcAg** — Indicates whether there has been an old infection, or if the individual is a chronic carrier.
- **C. IgM anti-HBcAg** — Among the hepatitis B panel, IgM anti-HBcAg indicates new infection and is the most specific marker for acute hepatitis B infection.
- **D. HBeAg** — Determines infectivity of an individual; testing positive means high infectivity.

questions.stem: Which method of bacterial genetic transfer is done through the presence of bacteriophages?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Transduction**

- **A. Binary fission** — The general term for asexual reproduction of bacteria.
- **B. Transformation** — Done through uptake of free DNA, not through bacteriophages.
- **C. Transduction** — The "combination of bacteria" through bacteriophages. Bacteriophages hold the packed donor DNA and infect the recipient bacteria, releasing this donor DNA and allowing for combination of genetic material.
- **D. Conjugation** — Sharing of genetic material due to cell-to-cell contact, usually through a sex pilus.

questions.stem: Which strain of Escherichia coli can possibly cause the triad of hemolytic anemia, uremia, and thrombocytopenia?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Enterohemorrhagic E. coli**

- **A. Enterotoxigenic E. coli** — Presents with watery diarrhea.
- **B. Enteroinvasive E. coli** — Presents as bloody diarrhea, like EHEC, but with a shigella-like manifestation.
- **C. Enteropathogenic E. coli** — Presents with watery diarrhea.
- **D. Enterohemorrhagic E. coli** — The triad of hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and uremia is a complication of E. coli called hemolytic uremic syndrome, caused by enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC).

| Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC) | Watery diarrhea of long duration, mostly in infants, often in developing countries | No toxin produced; flattens villi |
| Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) | Bloody diarrhea; hemorrhagic colitis and hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) | Has shiga-like toxin (a different "shigella-like manifestation") |
| Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC) | Bloody diarrhea | Shigella-like manifestation |
| Enteroaggregative E. coli (EAEC) | Persistent watery diarrhea in children and patients infected with HIV | — |

questions.stem: In cases of uncomplicated malaria which have no proven resistance, which of the following is the first-line drug of choice for treatment?
questions.rationale:

- **A. Mefloquine** — Used for prophylaxis of areas with chloroquine-resistant malaria, and is the treatment of choice for malaria in pregnant women.
- **B. Atovaquone-proguanil** — Used for prophylaxis of areas with chloroquine- and mefloquine-resistant malaria.
- **C. Artemether-lumefantrine** — Used for treatment of uncomplicated chloroquine-resistant malaria (oral) or severe cases of malaria (intravenous).
- **D. Chloroquine** — For malaria treatment without resistance, the first-line drug of choice is oral chloroquine.

**Drugs of choice**

| Mefloquine | Areas with chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum |
| Primaquine | Areas with P. vivax only; used for presumptive anti-relapse therapy for P. vivax or P. ovale |

questions.stem: Which of the following parasites may cause group infection?

questions.stem: Hand-foot-and-mouth disease is caused by which organism?

- **A. Aerobic, motile** — All of the choices are gram-positive rods. B. cereus is aerobic and motile.

questions.stem: The appropriate management for this condition is:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Supportive treatment only through anti-emetics and proper hydration**

- **A. Supportive treatment only through anti-emetics and proper hydration** — In cases of B. cereus infection presenting only as food poisoning, symptomatic treatment alone is warranted.
- **B. Immediate admission to monitor symptoms and complications** — Not all patients with this infection need admission.
- **C. Start antibiotics to address the causative agent** — Antibiotics are used only in cases of ophthalmitis; not all cases of the infection require this.
- **D. Observation only** — Not recommended, since treatment should be based on the patient's symptoms.
