| | Botulinum toxin | Clostridium botulinum | Phage | Inhibits acetylcholine release from stimulatory neurons (Ach) |

questions.stem: Which of the following manifests with a positive Nikolsky sign?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome**

- A positive Nikolsky sign is the separation of epidermis upon manual stroking of the skin. It is an important sign to elicit to differentiate intraepidermal blisters from subepidermal blisters.
- Positive Nikolsky sign is pathognomonic of staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS), a blistering disease caused by S. aureus. Exfoliatin, a toxin produced by the bacteria, cleaves desmoglein in the desmosomes resulting in separation of epidermis at the stratum granulosum.
- Bullous pemphigoid (Choice A), epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (Choice C) and dermatitis herpetiformis (Choice D) are blistering diseases that manifest as subepidermal blisters histologically. These disorders clinically present with a negative Nikolsky sign.

choices.text: Catalase positive, coagulase negative, novobiocin sensitive
Catalase positive, coagulase negative, novobiocin resistant

Catalase negative, alpha-hemolytic, optochin sensitive and
bile soluble

questions.stem: The most common causative agent of shunt infections is CORRECTLY described as:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Catalase positive, coagulase negative, novobiocin sensitive**

- Staphylococcus epidermidis is the most common cause of shunt infections, prosthetic valve endocarditis, and septic arthritis in prosthetic joints. The pathogenesis of S. epidermidis infections is due to the adherence of glycocalyx to foreign bodies and biofilm formation.
- It is correctly described as catalase positive, coagulase negative, and novobiocin sensitive.
- Choice A refers to S. aureus, Choice C refers to S. saprophyticus, while Choice D refers to Streptococcus pneumoniae.
- Review the Gram-positive lab algorithm shown below: **Gram-Positive Bacteria**

questions.stem: Which of the following will produce colorless colonies on MacConkey agar?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Proteus**

- MacConkey agar contains a pH indicator that turns pink under acidic conditions. Therefore, lactose-fermenters will form pink colonies, while non-lactose fermenters will form colorless colonies.
- Among the choices, Proteus is the only non-lactose fermenter. Enterobacter (Choice A), Klebsiella (Choice C), and Serratia (Choice D) are lactose fermenters.
- Review the Gram-negative lab algorithm shown below: **Gram-Negative Bacteria**

choices.text:
M. genitalium has the smallest genome of known
mycoplasmas

Mycoplasmas are the smallest organisms that can
be free living in nature and self-replicating on
laboratory media

Mycoplasmas lack a rigid cell wall and instead are
bounded by a triple-layered “unit membrane” that
contains a sterol

Mycoplasmas are completely resistant to
tetracycline or erythromycin and sensitive to
penicillins

questions.stem: Which of the following is FALSE regarding Mycoplasma?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Mycoplasmas are completely resistant to tetracycline or erythromycin and sensitive to penicillins**

- The smallest genome of known mycoplasmas, M. genitalium, is little more than twice the genome size of certain large viruses. (Choice A)
- Mycoplasmas are the smallest organisms that can be free living in nature and self-replicating on laboratory media. (Choice B)
- They are highly pleomorphic because they lack a rigid cell wall (Choice C) and instead are bounded by a triple-layered “unit membrane” that contains a sterol.
- Mycoplasmas are completely resistant to penicillin because they lack the cell wall structures at which penicillin acts, but they are inhibited by tetracycline or erythromycin. (Choice D is incorrect)

questions.stem: Schistosoma japonicum eggs produce a characteristic granulomatous reaction in sites of infection such as the liver. Which of the following is NOT a consequence of this inflammatory reaction?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Abdominal obstruction**

- The most significant pathology in schistosomiasis is associated with schistosome eggs, not adult worms. A granulomatous reaction surrounds the eggs and leads to fibrosis of the liver with S. mansoni and S. japonicum infection. In chronic cases blood flow to the liver is impeded, which leads to portal hypertension (Choice A), accumulation of ascites in the abdominal cavity, hepatosplenomegaly (Choice C), and esophageal varices (Choice B).
- Abdominal obstruction (Choice C) is not a consequence of the granulomatous reaction to S. japonicum eggs in the liver.

questions.stem: Papillomavirus is classified as a ______ virus..
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — DNA**

- Remember the mnemonic for DNA viruses: DNA viruses are HHAPPPPy viruses (Hepadnaviridae, Herpesviridae, Adenoviridae, Poxviridae, Parvoviridae, Polyomaviridae, Papillomaviridae).
- The rest of the virus families not included in this mnemonic are RNA viruses (Choice A is incorrect). There is no such thing as an atypical virus (Choice C is incorrect).

choices.text:
27/M healthcare worker with no medical
comorbidities
2-month-old infant born to an HBV-infected mother

questions.stem: Which of the following patients is MOST prone to chronic liver disease from HBV infection?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — 2-month-old infant born to an HBV-infected mother**

- The likelihood of chronicity after acute hepatitis B varies as a function of age. Infection at birth is associated with clinically silent acute infection but a 90% chance of chronic infection, whereas infection in young adulthood in immunocompetent persons is typically associated with clinically apparent acute hepatitis but a risk of chronicity of only 1%. Chronic carriers are at high risk of developing hepatocellular carcinoma.
- The adult patients in the choices (Choices A&D) do not have immunocompromising conditions.
- Although Choice A has an immunocompromising condition, the patient is on HAART and can be assumed to have an intact immune system. Between Choices A & B, the best answer is Choice C because of the age of the patient.

questions.stem: Which of the following respiratory diseases is NOT common among HIV patients?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Pulmonary embolism**

- Histoplasmosis (Choice A), tuberculosis (Choice C), and Pneumocystis pneumonia (Choice D) are examples of opportunistic infections in HIV that affect the respiratory system.
- Pulmonary embolism (Choice B) is not commonly associated with HIV.

questions.stem: A 21/F social worker went to a daycare center for an outreach program. Weeks later, she noted onset of fever, nausea and vomiting, malaise, and anorexia. She attributed her symptoms to the food she ate during her visit at the daycare center. Days after, she developed jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. The most likely etiologic agent is a:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — ssRNA**

- The clinical course of the patient which started with systemic prodromal symptoms followed by onset of clinical jaundice is most consistent with a diagnosis of acute viral hepatitis, likely from Hepatitis A virus (HAV). This is suggested by the history of food intake (suggesting fecal-oral transmission of the pathogen) and visit at a daycare center (overcrowding enhances person-to-person spread of HAV).
- HAV is a naked nucleocapsid virus with a positive-sense, single-stranded RNA genome. (All other choices are incorrect)
- The other hepatitis viruses contain the following genome: incomplete circular double-stranded DNA in HBV (Choice B); positive polarity, single-stranded RNA in HCV; viroid-like, negative-sense circular single-stranded RNA in HDV; and positive-sense linear single-stranded RNA in HEV.

questions.stem: What is the gold standard in diagnosing amebic colitis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Direct microscopy**

- Direct microscopy, where trophozoites and cysts in stool specimens are identified, is the gold standard in diagnosing amebic colitis.
- Pus cells on fecalysis (fecal leukocytes) provides a presumptive diagnosis of bacillary dysentery, caused by Shigella dysenteriae.
- Serologic tests (Choice B) is the gold standard in the diagnosis of amebic liver abscess (ALA), while PCR (Choice D) is useful in differentiating between Entamoeba histolytica and Entamoeba dispar.

questions.stem: What is the most serious form of leishmaniasis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Visceral leishmaniasis**

- The genus Leishmania, widely distributed in nature, has a number of species that are nearly identical morphologically. The different leishmanias present a range of clinical and epidemiologic characteristics that, for convenience only, are combined under three clinical groupings: 1) cutaneous leishmaniasis (e.g. Oriental sore, Baghdad boil, wet cutaneous sore, etc. 2) mucocutaneous leishmaniasis (espundia) and 3) visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar).
- The most serious form is visceral leishmaniasis (Choice C) because it is almost always fatal if left untreated. It is characterized by irregular bouts of fever, weight loss, enlargement of the spleen and liver, and anemia.
- Cutaneous leishmaniasis (Choice A) is the most common form and causes skin lesions, mainly ulcers, on exposed parts of the body.
- Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis (Choice B) leads to partial or total destruction of mucous membranes of the nose, mouth, and throat.

choices.text: The organism can be grown in vitro on agar

Leprosy occurs in one of two clinical presentations:
lepromatous or tuberculoid

Diagnosis is through smears of skin scrapings
stained by the Ziehl-Neelsen technique

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT true regarding infection with Mycobacterium leprae?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — The organism can be grown in vitro on agar**

- Efforts to grow M. leprae in vitro on agar and other bacteriologic media have remained unsuccessful. Instead, bacilli from human leprosy are inoculated into footpads of mice or armadillos.
- Leprosy occurs in one of two clinical presentations: lepromatous (multibacillary) leprosy or tuberculoid (paucibacillary) leprosy. (Choice B)
- A diagnosis is made through scrapings with a scalpel blade from skin or nasal mucosa or from a biopsy of earlobe skin smeared on a slide and stained by the Ziehl-Neelsen technique. (Choice C) Another method is biopsy of skin or of a thickened nerve.
- Sulfones, such as dapsone, are first-line therapy for both tuberculoid and lepromatous leprosy. (Choice D)

questions.stem: A patient was admitted at the intensive care unit for diabetic ketoacidosis. Several days later, she developed retro-orbital headache, facial pain, and blurring of vision. A necrotic eschar was found on the nasal cavity. Biopsy of the eschar revealed aseptate, broad-based hyphae that branch at right angles. What is the most likely causative agent?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Rhizopus**

- The diagnosis is mucormycosis, specifically rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis. This disease most commonly occurs in patients with diabetes. Initial symptoms include eye or facial pain and facial numbness followed by the onset of conjunctival suffusion and swelling, and blurry vision. Infected tissue ultimately progresses into a black necrotic eschar that can be appreciated upon visual inspection.
- Rhizopus infection appears as wide, thick-walled, ribbon-like, aseptate hyphal elements that branch at right angles on biopsy.
- Aspergillus (Choice A), Fusarium (Choice C), and Scedosporium (Choice D) are septate, thinner, and branch at acute angles.

questions.stem: What structure is the basis for the Lancefield classification of streptococci?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Cell wall carbohydrate**

- Group-specific substance, a carbohydrate contained in the cell wall of many streptococci, forms the basis of serologic grouping into Lancefield groups A-H and K-U. The serologic specificity of the group-specific carbohydrate is determined by an amino sugar.
- M protein (Choice A) is the major virulence factor of S. pyogenes. The thickness of peptidoglycan layer (Choice B) as a basis of classification is used in Gram staining. Due to their antigenic specificity, capsular polysaccharides (Choice C) are used to classify S. pneumoniae into more than 90 types and to type the group B streptococci (S. agalactiae).

questions.stem: Which of the following mechanisms of resistance to antimicrobials is CORRECTLY paired with the antimicrobial drug?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Macrolides: RNA methylation**

- Hydrolysis and mutant penicillin-binding proteins are mechanisms of resistance to beta-lactams (Choice A is incorrect), reprogramming of D-ala-D-ala in vancomycin resistance (Choice B is incorrect), and mutant DNA gyrase in resistance to fluoroquinolones (Choice D is incorrect).
- Memorize the table below summarizing the various mechanisms of resistance to antimicrobial drugs:

| Drug | Mechanism of Resistance |
|---|---|
| Beta-lactams | Hydrolysis, mutant penicillin-binding protein (PBP) |
| Tetracycline | Active efflux from cell |
| Aminoglycosides | Inactivation by enzymes |
| Sulfonamides | Overproduction of the target site of the drug |
| Fluoroquinolones | Mutant DNA gyrase |
| Chloramphenicol | Destruction by chloramphenicol acetyltransferase |
| Vancomycin | Reprogramming of D-ala-D-ala |
| Quinupristin | Ribosomal methylation |
| Macrolides, Erythromycin | RNA methylation, drug efflux |

questions.stem: Which bacterial gene transfer process would be inhibited by free extracellular exonucleases?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Transformation**

- In transformation, a recipient cell uptakes a naked (free) DNA released into the environment when another bacterial cell dies and undergoes lysis. The DNA is extracellular before being picked up by competent bacteria and therefore susceptible to extracellular exonucleases.
- Conjugation (Choice A) is incorrect since the DNA is never found extracellularly during cell-to-cell contact. Similarly, transposition (Choice D) is incorrect because there is no extracellular transport involved in the “jumping” process involving a transposon.
- Transduction (Choice B) is incorrect because the DNA is protected by the viral capsid of bacteriophages.

choices.text: S. aureus is a motile organism

When found in the nasal cavity, the organism is
intracellular

Methicillin is the most commonly used drug against
this organism
It does not contain antigenic polysaccharide

questions.stem: Which of the following statements regarding Staphylococcus aureus is CORRECT?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — When found in the nasal cavity, the organism is intracellular**

- S. aureus is a facultative intracellular pathogen that colonizes about 30% of the human population asymptomatically in the nares, either transiently or persistently, and can therefore be regarded as a human commensal as well, although carriage increases the risk of infection.
- Choice A is wrong because Staphylococcus is nonmotile and does not form spores.
- Choice C is wrong because methicillin was previously used up until the emergence of methicillin-resistant S. aureus strains rendered it less effective, hence cefazolin and oxacillin are examples of more widely used antibiotics.
- Choice D is wrong because most S. aureus strains of clinical importance have polysaccharide capsules, which inhibit phagocytosis by polymorphonuclear leukocytes unless specific antibodies are present.

questions.stem: Which of the following is LEAST likely to have antigenic properties?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Ribosomes**

- O, H, and K antigens are present in E. coli.
- The K antigen is seen in the capsule (Choice A)
- The H antigen is seen in the flagella (Choice B).
- The O antigen pertains to the lipopolysaccharide present in the cell wall (Choice D).
- Thus, among the choices it would be ribosomes (Choice C) which would be LEAST likely to have antigenic properties as it is less likely to possess antigens.

choices.text: Lack of access to medical care

questions.stem: All of the following are epidemiological factors that increase the risk of acute rheumatic fever, EXCEPT?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Poor oral hygiene**

- Poor oral hygiene is NOT considered as an epidemiological factor.
- Poor living conditions, lack of access to medical care and overcrowding (choices A, B, and C) are epidemiological risk factors for acute rheumatic fever.

questions.stem: Which of the following diagnostic tests for syphilis still warrants another confirmatory test?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — RPR/VDRL**

- Diagnostics tests for syphilis can be divided into microscopy, non-treponemal tests, and treponemal tests.
- Non-treponemal tests include rapid plasma reagin (RPR) and venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL) (Choice D) which is only a screening test and for monitoring of treatment. They still need confirmatory tests to be able to diagnose syphilis.
- Microscopy such as dark field microscopy (Choice B) and fluorescent microscopy (Choice C) directly observe the organisms, confirming the diagnosis.
- FTA-ABS (Choice A) is a treponemal antibody test, which is used to confirm presence of syphilis.

questions.stem: Which of the following manifestations is more commonly seen in rubella compared to CMV infection?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Cardiovascular defect**

- Among the choices, cardiovascular defect (specifically patent ductus arteriosus - Choice A) is commonly seen in congenital rubella infection but not observed in CMV.
- Deafness, blindness, and lymphadenopathy (Choices B, C, and D) are all commonly seen in both rubella and CMV infection, thus they are incorrect since the question is asking for the manifestation more commonly seen in rubella.
- RECALL:
  - Congenital Rubella Syndrome - associated abnormalities include cataracts, sensorineural deafness, mental retardation, PDA, and blueberry muffin baby (5B - Bulag, Bingi, Brain damage, Butas ang puso, Blueberry)
  - Congenital CMV infection - most common cause of congenital abnormalities; associated with microcephaly, seizures, deafness, blindness, jaundice, purpura

questions.stem: Which of the following viruses do not cause inclusions?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Norovirus**

- Norovirus (Choice C) typically do not produce cytoplasmic inclusions.
- Herpes simplex virus (Choice A) is characterized by the presence of large, pink to purple intranuclear inclusions (Cowdry Type A inclusions).
- Smallpox virus (Choice B) is an eradicated disease. In histology, intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions are observed (Guarnieri bodies).
- Rhabdovirus (Choice D) have round or oval inclusions within the cytoplasm of neurons (Negri bodies) - buzzword for rabies!

questions.stem: Which of the following organisms would show a positive Nagler reaction?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — C. perfringens**

- The Nagler reaction is characterized by the development of milky white halo around the bacterial colony when grown in a medium (see photos below).
- This is due to the alpha toxin, lecithinase, which is a toxin that cleaves cell membranes and produces gas leading to gas gangrene. It is a characteristic of C. perfringens (Choice B).
- S. aureus, H. influenzae, and S. pneumoniae (Choices A, C, and D) typically do not have lecithinase thus are incorrect since they do not exhibit this reaction.

questions.stem: Which of the following drugs should be prescribed in patients diagnosed with syphilis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Benzathine Penicillin G**

- Benzathine Penicillin G (Choice B) remains the drug of choice for treatment of all stages of syphilis. It is a natural penicillin that is administered intravenously.
- Other choices (cefotaxime, doxycycline, and azithromycin) are not the drug of choice for syphilis infection.
- Cefotaxime (Choice A) is a 3rd generation cephalosporin and is most active against penicillin resistant S. pneumoniae.
- Doxycycline (Choice C) is a tetracycline which is used for community acquired pneumonia, bronchitis, and post-exposure prophylaxis for leptospirosis.
- Azithromycin (Choice D) is a macrolide which is usually used for community acquired pneumonia.

questions.stem: Which of the following parasites is also known as whipworm?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Trichuris trichiura**

- RECALL the common names and classifications of the parasites as these are also commonly interchanged with their scientific name.
- Trichuris trichiura (Choice A) is a nematode also known as whipworm.
- Other choices have different common names thus they are incorrect.
- Schistosoma japonicum (Choice B) is a trematode also known as the blood fluke.
- Ascaris lumbricoides (Choice C) is a nematode. It is an intestinal roundworm, typically no common name is used for it.
- Necator americanus (Choice D) is also a nematode. Together with Ancylostoma duodenale, they are known as hookworms.

questions.stem: Which parasite is most likely to be spread through children in daycare centers?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Enterobius vermicularis**

- Enterobius vermicularis (Choice A), also known as pinworm or seatworm, is the most common cause of anal pruritus among school-aged children. Thus, among the choices, it is the most likely to be transmitted through children in day centers. It can also cause retroinfection and autoinfection and may be transmitted via inhalation of eggs.
- Other choices are less likely to be spread in day care centers because of their differing mode of transmissions.
  - Paragonimus westermani (Choice B) is transmitted through the ingestion of raw crabs/crayfish.
  - Strongyloides stercoralis (Choice C) is transmitted through skin penetration of filariform larvae (its parasitic, larval form). It is a soil-transmitted helminth.
  - Hymenolepis nana (Choice D), also known as the dwarf tapeworm, is the smallest tapeworm known to man and most common tapeworm infection in developed countries. Eggs can be infectious when ingested and ingestion of rice/flour beetles with cysticercoid larvae can also infect humans.

questions.stem: Osteomyelitis caused by S. aureus commonly affects which part of the long bone?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Metaphysis**

- One of the complications of S. aureus infection is osteomyelitis which can also lead to septic arthritis. This is due to the hematogenous spread or direct inoculation.
- It involves long bones in children and vertebral osteomyelitis is more common in adults.
- More commonly, a sequestered focus of osteomyelitis may be visible, called Brodie’s abscess. This arises from the metaphyseal area (Choice D) of the long bone and not the bone marrow, epiphysis, nor the diaphysis (Choices A, B, and C).

questions.stem: A man is currently complaining of diarrhea. He ate at an eat-all-you-can buffet 3 days ago. During his dinner at the buffet, he noted consuming a lot of oysters. Which of the following is the most likely causative agent for his diarrhea?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Vibrio vulnificus**

- The main keyword for this case is “consumed a lot of oysters”. There are a lot of bacteria which can cause diarrhea but this highlights the most likely causative agent which is Vibrio vulnificus (Choice C).
- V. vulnificus is transmitted via trauma to skin or ingestion of raw shellfish, commonly oysters. It may also cause necrotizing fasciitis.
- S. aureus (Choice A) can cause gastroenteritis, however it has an acute onset and has vomiting due to heat-stable enterotoxin. Typical sources are food with cream or mayonnaise.
- C. jejuni (Choice B) causes watery, foul-smelling diarrhea followed by bloody stools accompanied by fever and severe abdominal pain which may mimic ulcerative colitis.
- The manifestation of E. coli (Choice D) infection would depend on the strain of the bacteria. It may be bloody or non-bloody diarrhea.

questions.stem: Serologic testing is deemed useful for which of the following organisms?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Histoplasma capsulatum**

- Among the choices, the best answer would be H. capsulatum (Choice A). This organism utilizes serology by detection of antibodies called anti-M and anti-H (also known as M bands and H bands). Microscopy could also be used which shows the presence of macrophage filled with oval yeast cells.
- Blastomyces dermatitidis (Choice B) is mainly diagnosed through culture. It also shows broad-based budding yeasts on microscopy.
- Aspergillus fumigatus (Choice C) diagnosis is characterized by high IgE levels and it is also detected through sputum culture. Chest x-ray also aids in the diagnosis.
- Malassezia furfur (Choice D) is a superficial mycoses which is characteristic of its “spaghetti and meatballs” (buzzword!) appearance on 10% KOH preparation.

questions.stem: Which of the following specimens is the LEAST sensitive for GeneXpert testing for tuberculosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Gastric lavage sample**

- According to multiple studies, among the choices, the specimen that has the lowest sensitivity for GeneXpert testing is gastric lavage sample (Choice A). It has a sensitivity of 30%.
- Bronchial aspirate (Choice B) has a sensitivity of 87-91%.
- Induced sputum (Choice C) has a sensitivity of around 39%.
- Lung biopsy (Choice D) in the form of transbronchial lung cryobiopsy is not utilized much for GeneXpert testing because of invasiveness. However, studies show that this sample yields a sensitivity of 81%.

questions.stem: Cryptosporidiosis is most LIKELY associated with which of the following symptoms?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Diarrhea**

- Cryptosporidiosis is caused by Cryptosporidium parvum, a parasite that is acid-fast and has waterborne transmission. It is associated with severe diarrhea in the immunocompromised state (Choice C).
- Liver abscess (Choice A) is encountered more characteristically in Entamoeba histolytica infection.
- Pneumonia (Choice B) may be encountered in cryptosporidiosis also. However, the question asks the most likely manifestation. The parasite is more known to cause diarrhea, thus it is the best answer.
- Meningitis (Choice D) is used to confuse between Cryptosporidium and Cryptococcus. Meningitis is caused by Cryptosporidium in the immunocompromised, usually in HIV/AIDS patients. A usual confusion among medical students is the clinical presentation of Cryptosporidium vs Cryptococcus. Both organisms present with a distinguishable feature in the immunocompromised host: Cryptosporidium causes diarrhea in the immunocompromised, while Cryptococcus causes meningitis in the immunocompromised.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a dimorphic fungus
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Blastomyces dermatitidis**

- Fungi that are dimorphic have two forms, depending on the temperature of their environment, being mold in the cold and yeast in the heat. These include Coccidiodes immitis, Histoplasma capsulatum, Blastomyces dermatitidis (choice A), and Paracoccidioides brasiliensis.
- All other choices only exist as either yeast or mold only

questions.stem: Which of the following has a thick cell wall which would retain the primary stain during gram staining?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Corynebacterium diphtheriae**

- This question tests the concept of gram-positive vs. gram-negative organisms. Bacteria that have thick cell walls would stain purple because they would retain the primary stain which is crystal violet. (Recall: steps in gram-staining)
- Among the choices, only Corynebacterium diphtheria (Choice D) is gram-positive, making it the correct answer.
- Gram-negative organisms, on the other hand, would not retain the primary stain and will be stained with counterstain (safranin) instead. They are colored red.
- Neisseria meningitidis (Choice A), Bordetella pertussis (Choice B), and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Choice C) are all gram-negative organisms.

questions.stem: The infective stage of Ancylostoma duodenale:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Filariform larvae**

- Ancylostoma duodenale, together with Necator americanus, are known as hookworms which are soil-transmitted helminths.
- They infect humans by penetrating the skin while in the stage of filariform larvae (Choice D) which are parasitic, larval forms of the organism that need a host.
- On the other hand, rhabditiform larvae (Choice A) are non-parasitic larval forms which are free-living and eat organic matter.
- Eggs (Choice B) are passed in the feces, which are also the diagnostic stage of the organism identified through microscopy.
- Adult stage (Choice C) of hookworms are seen in the small intestine, where the larvae also develop to these forms.

questions.stem: The organism causing granuloma inguinale will exhibit which of the following?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Donovan bodies**

- Granuloma inguinale, also known as donovanosis, is caused by Klebsiella granulomatis. This is characterized by Donovan bodies (Choice A) which look like closed safety pins. Small, painless papules are seen forming a beefy red ulcer (buzzword!) with a velvety surface.
- Cowdry Type A inclusions (Choice B) are large, pink to purple intranuclear inclusions seen in HSV infection.
- Henderson-Paterson bodies (Choice C) are intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions seen in molluscum contagiosum.
- Guarnieri bodies (Choice D) are also intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions seen in smallpox, which is now eradicated.

questions.stem: Infection with which of the following viruses would show findings of koilocytes?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Human papillomavirus**

- Koilocytes are typically seen in human papillomavirus (HPV) (Choice D) infections. This is also the most common viral STD worldwide and is associated with cervical cancer.
- Herpes simplex virus (Choice A) may be due to HSV-1 which causes oral lesions or HSV-2 which causes genital lesions. They are characterized by multinucleated giant cells seen on Tzanck smear.
- Rhabdovirus (Choice B) includes rabies virus which is transmitted through animal bites. They are characterized by negri bodies on histopathology.
- Parvovirus B19 (Choice C), also known as fifth disease, would appear as a slapped cheek appearance (buzzword!) with fever, coryza and sore throat. It is transmitted through droplets and possibly transplacental.

questions.stem: A characteristic toxin seen in C. perfringens which cleaves cell membranes causing gas membrane is called:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Lecithinase**

- Lecithinase (Choice B) is an alpha toxin that cleaves cell membrane which causes the gas gangrene in C. perfringens infection.
- Hemagglutinin (Choice A) is a protein seen in viruses such as influenza virus, which binds to cell surface receptors to initiate infection of the cell.
- Tetanospasmin (Choice C) or tetanus toxin is seen in C. tetani and cleaves proteins that are involved in the release of glycine from Renshaw cells. It prevents release of GABA by cleaving synaptobrevin.
- Exotoxin B (cytotoxin) (Choice D) is seen in C. difficile infections and it inhibits GTPases leading to apoptosis and death of enterocytes leading to pseudomembranes (buzzword!)

questions.stem: The most common bacterial infection that HIV/AIDS patients worldwide suffer from is:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Mycobacterium tuberculosis**

- This question is confusing but tackles more of reading comprehension as it asks the most common bacterial infection encountered.
- Among the choices, only Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Choice C) is considered as a bacteria. It is an acid-fast organism that causes tuberculosis.
- Cryptococcus neoformans (Choice A) is a fungus which causes meningoencephalitis in HIV patients.
- Cryptosporidium parvum (Choice B) is a protozoan which causes severe diarrhea in the immunocompromised state.
- Pneumocystis jirovecii (Choice D) was previously classified as a protozoan (P. carinii) but is now considered a fungus. It is transmitted via inhalation of cysts and causes pneumonia.

questions.stem: The drug of choice for the treatment of typhoid fever for drug susceptible infection is:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Ciprofloxacin**

- The most effective drug for the treatment of typhoid fever are fluoroquinolones, including ciprofloxacin (Choice A). In the Philippines, amoxicillin, chloramphenicol, or co-trimoxazole is usually used.
- Cephalexin (Choice B) is a first generation cephalosporin. It treats infection due to gram positive cocci, UTI, and skin and soft tissue infections.
- Azithromycin (Choice C) is a macrolide which is usually used for community-acquired pneumonia.
- Methicillin (Choice D) is an anti-staphylococcal penicillin. It is not usually used due to side effects and high antibiotic resistance.

questions.stem: A 26/F was brought to the clinic due to diarrhea. According to her, last weekend, she went camping with her group of friends. Upon further investigation, it is discovered that there is also steatorrhea. Which of the following is the most LIKELY causative agent of her diarrhea?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Giardia lamblia**

- Keywords for this case are “camping” and “steatorrhea”. G. lamblia (Choice C) infections are known to be associated with campers/hiking and appear with steatorrhea with rotten egg odor (buzzword!)
- Cryptosporidium parvum (Choice A), as mentioned previously, is a protozoan which causes severe diarrhea in the immunocompromised state.
- Trichomonas vaginalis (Choice B) is the only known sexually transmitted protozoan. It would present as a greenish, foul-smelling discharge and a strawberry cervix.
- Naegleria fowleri (Choice D) is a protozoan that causes primary amebic meningoencephalitis (PAM).

questions.stem: A 28/M consulted in your clinic, complaining of difficulty urinating, swelling and reddening of the eye, and pain in the knees. Which of the following is the MOST LIKELY organism causing his symptoms?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Campylobacter jejuni**

- Keywords for this case are “difficulty urinating” (which points to urethritis), “reddening of the eyes” (conjunctivitis), and “pain in the knees” (which points to arthritis). This triad is known as Reiter’s syndrome, also known as reactive arthritis. Among the choices, Campylobacter jejuni (Choice A) is the only one causing this. Other bacteria which cause Reiter’s syndrome include Salmonella spp, Shigella spp, and some species of Chlamydia.
- Clostridium perfringens (Choice B) may cause gas gangrene (myonecrosis) and food poisoning. Transmission is from the ingestion of contaminated (and undercooked) food like poultry and meat or contact between soil and open wounds can also lead to transmission.
- Klebsiella pneumoniae (Choice C) manifests as pneumonia with currant jelly sputum (buzzword!) and is the likely etiology of pneumonia in alcoholics. It may also cause UTI.
- Staphylococcus aureus (Choice D) is associated with many manifestations such as acute endocarditis, meningitis, pneumonia, osteomyelitis, gastroenteritis, Ritter disease, and toxic shock syndrome.

questions.stem: A patient is noted to have developed rheumatic heart disease. Upon history taking, you learn that the patient had a previous throat infection 3 months ago. When probed, the patient mentioned that he did not suffer from any skin rash during the same period. Which of the following is the best diagnostic to utilize to confirm the primary diagnosis for this patient?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Anti-streptolysin O**

- A rise in the titer of antibodies to many group A streptococcal antigens can be estimated. Such antibodies include ASO, particularly in respiratory disease; anti-DNAse B (Choice C) and anti-hyaluronidase (Choice B), particularly in skin infections; anti-streptokinase; anti-M type-specific antibodies (Choice A); and others. Of these, the ASO titer is most widely used (Choice D).
- As mentioned above, Choices A, B, and C are antibodies that could also be used in the diagnosis, but the question is asking for the best one which is ASO titer (Choice D).

choices.text: Degradation of phospholipids leading to necrosis

questions.stem: Which of the following processes describe the clinical manifestations of toxic shock syndrome?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Cytokine release**

- Toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 is a superantigen which causes potent cellular disruption without needing to enter the cells. TSST-1 stimulates most T-cells by binding directly to MHC-II and T-cell receptors. The net result is the production of large amounts of the cytokines IL-2, IFN-gamma, and TNF (Choice B).
- Degradation of phospholipids leading to necrosis, change in adenylate cyclase activity, and formation of membrane pores (Choices A, C, and D) are mechanisms of other exotoxins, not TSST-1.

questions.stem: Among the following, which characteristic more likely points to lepromatous type of leprosy rather than the tuberculoid type?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Absent cell-mediated response**

- In lepromatous type, the course is progressive and malignant, with nodular skin lesions; slow, symmetric nerve involvement; abundant acid-fast bacilli in the skin lesions; continuous bacteremia; and a negative lepromin skin test result. The cell-mediated immunity is markedly deficient (Choice A), and the skin is infiltrated with suppressor T cells.
- Other choices describe the tuberculoid type. In tuberculoid type, the course is benign and nonprogressive, with a small number of macular skin lesions containing few bacilli (Choice C), severe asymmetric nerve involvement of sudden onset, and a positive lepromin skin test result (Choice D). The cell-mediated immunity is intact, and the skin is infiltrated with helper T cells. There is also a low likelihood of transmission (Choice B).
- Recall the following table summarizing tuberculoid vs. lepromatous leprosy:

| Feature | Tuberculoid leprosy | Lepromatous leprosy |
|---|---|---|
| Number of lesions | One or few | Many lesions |
| Tissue destruction | Little | Marked |
| Number of acid-fast bacilli | Few | Many |
| Likelihood of transmitting leprosy | Low | High |
| Cell-mediated response to M. leprae | Present | Reduced or absent |
| Lepromin skin test | Positive | Negative |

questions.stem: The most common bacterial sexually transmitted disease is caused by:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Chlamydia trachomatis**

- Among the choices, Chlamydia trachomatis (Choice B) is the most common bacterial STD. It is transmitted through sexual contact, transvaginal, or hand-to-eye contact.
- G. vaginalis (Choice A) is not sexually transmitted. It is transmitted due to frequent washing and has characteristic clue cells (buzzword!) present.
- N. gonorrhoeae (Choice C) is one of the most common STDs, but not the most common. It is usually in a co-infection with C. trachomatis.
- The most common sexually transmitted disease worldwide is human papilloma virus (HPV) (Choice D) which commonly causes warts (usually genital warts). However, this is viral and not bacterial.

questions.stem: Which of the following viruses is known to cause cancer?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Hepatitis C virus**

- Hepatitis C virus (Choice A) is transmitted blood-borne mainly seen in IV drug abusers. Pathogenesis of Hep C includes a higher risk of causing liver cirrhosis and cancer.
- Smallpox virus (Choice B) is an eradicated disease. In histology, intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions are observed (Guarnieri bodies).
- Adenovirus (Choice C) can cause atypical pneumonia with conjunctivitis, pharyngitis and coryza. It is transmitted through aerosol droplet, fecal-oral, or direct contact.
- Rabies virus (Choice D) is transmitted through animal bites. Symptoms include paresthesia and fasciculations around the bite site, excessive motor activity and agitation. They are characterized by negri bodies on histopathology.

questions.stem: A 27/F comes to the clinic consulting for fever, painful rash and reddish tongue which started recently. Upon taking the history of the patient, it has been known that she has a regular menstruation, no dysmenorrhea, using tampons during this period. Which of the following causative agents MOST LIKELY caused the condition of the patient?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Staphylococcus aureus**

- Keywords for this case include “painful rash, fever and reddish tongue” and “using tampons” which are symptoms of toxic shock syndrome usually seen in tampon users.
- Toxic Shock Syndrome is due to the superantigen TSST-1 and causes strawberry tongue, desquamating rash and multiorgan involvement. This is usually seen in tampon-using menstruating women or in patients with nasal packing for nosebleed. It is caused by S. aureus (Choice B).
- Streptococcus agalactiae or GBS (Choice A) causes UTI in pregnant women and is the most common cause of neonatal sepsis.
- L. monocytogenes (Choice C) is transmitted via the placenta or ingestion of unpasteurized milk products, causing granulomatosis infantiseptica or listeriosis in adults (pneumonia, bacteremia, sepsis or meningitis in pregnant, elderly and immunocompromised patients).
- S. bovis (Choice D) may cause marantic endocarditis in patients with abdominal malignancy.

questions.stem: This lesion is characterized by lytic bone lesions with sclerosing borders usually found in the metaphysis of long bones as a result of chronic infection:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Brodie’s abscess**

- The lesion being described in the case is Brodie’s abscess (Choice C) which is seen in S. aureus infections affecting the metaphysis in osteomyelitis.
- Necrotizing fasciitis (Choice A) is seen in S. pyogenes infections due to exotoxin B. This rapidly progresses and infects deep subcutaneous tissues.
- Osteogenic sarcoma (Choice B), also known as osteosarcoma, is the most common primary bone sarcoma. The etiology of its development is more genetic (TP53, RB, CDKN2A loss, MDM2 and CDK 4 overexpression) rather than infectious. However, it is also seen in the metaphysis.
- Pastia lines (Choice D) are also seen in S. pyogenes infections, specifically those with scarlet fever. They are papules found around folds in the body, such as the armpit and the antecubital fossa.

questions.stem: Infection with Legionella pneumophila would result in which of the following manifestations?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Flu-like illness**

- Legionella pneumophila usually presents as Pontiac Fever (buzzword!). This is a mild, flu-like illness (Choice D) which is self-limiting.
- Bloody diarrhea (Choice A) is not typically seen in infection with Legionella pneumophila. Atypical pneumonia (also known as Legionnaires’ disease) will present as non-bloody diarrhea.
- Hypernatremia (Choice B) is also not encountered in Legionella pneumophila infection. Rather, Legionnaires’ disease will present as pneumonia with hyponatremia.
- Epiglottitis (Choice C) is seen in Haemophilus influenzae infections and would present as high-grade fever with muffled voice and drooling.

questions.stem: The following statements pertain to Necator americanus, EXCEPT:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — It causes more bleeding compared to Ancylostoma duodenale.**

- Choice A is incorrect because Ancylostoma duodenale causes more bleeding than Necator americanus due to its 2 pairs of teeth.
- Both hookworms would have an oval egg with a thin shell (Choice B).
- 90% of infections in the Philippines are caused by N. americanus (Choice C).
- N. americanus is characterized by 1 pair of cutting plates (Choice D), that’s why it causes less bleeding than A. duodenale.
- Buccal spears of filariform larvae: Ancylostoma has teeth; Necator has semilunar cutting plates (mnemonic: “Ne-cut-tor”).
- Mnemonic: between the 2 most common causes of hookworm infection in the Philippines, Ancylostoma duodenale causes MORE BLEEDING than Necator americanus because it has 2 PAIRS OF TEETH (vs. the 1 pair of cutting plates seen in Necator americanus).

Cleaving of synaptobrevin leading to prevention of
GABA release

Inhibition of acetylcholine release in the nerve
endings
Anaerobic metabolism leading to formation of gas

questions.stem: Which of the following statements accurately describes the pathophysiology of the toxin produced by C. botulinum?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Inhibition of acetylcholine release in the nerve endings**

- Botulinum toxin acts by blocking acetylcholine release, causing flaccid paralysis (Choice C). Botox is the commercial preparation.
- Exfoliatin cleaves desmoglein in desmosomes (Choice A) which leads to staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome also known as Ritter disease.
- Tetanospasmin (tetanus toxin) cleaves proteins that are involved in the release of glycine from Renshaw cells. It prevents GABA release through cleaving of synaptobrevin (Choice B).
- Lecithinase, an alpha toxin which is characteristic of C. perfringens, is responsible for the anaerobic metabolism leading to gas gangrene (Choice D).

questions.stem: Acalculous cholecystitis can possibly result from which of the following diseases?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Leptospirosis**

- Acute leptospirosis can present as acalculous cholecystitis, although it is commonly unrecognized (Choice D). The most severe form of leptospirosis is called Weil’s disease which shows a triad of jaundice, bleeding and uremia. Some other characteristics are orange cast skin (because of jaundice) and possible respiratory failure.
- Other diseases that could cause acalculous cholecystitis include streptococcal infections, typhoid fever, rocky mountain spotted fever, ascariasis, and giardiasis.
- The spectrum of disease of malaria (Choice B) includes shivering and chills, high fever, and sweating. Some complications that may arise include hemolytic anemia, jaundice and splenomegaly. In severe cases, cerebral failure and acute renal failure are seen.
- Dengue (Choice B) is transmitted via mosquito bite by A. aegypti. Patients who have dengue usually have maculopapular rash, severe muscle pain, and saddleback fever. Findings show thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and hemoconcentration. Hemorrhagic shock may occur if not managed.
- Yellow fever (Choice C), at the abrupt onset, is characterized by fever, chills, headache, dizziness, myalgia, and backache followed by nausea, vomiting, and bradycardia. Most patients recover at this point, but in about 15% of cases, the disease progresses to a more severe form with fever, jaundice, renal failure, and hemorrhagic manifestations. It is also transmitted by A. aegypti.
- Choices A, B, and C (malaria, dengue, and yellow fever) do not commonly cause acalculous cholecystitis, thus the best answer would be choice D.

questions.stem: Which of the following organisms would present with a gradual onset?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Rickettsia typhi**

- Among the choices, only Rickettsia typhi (Choice C) will have a gradual onset. It causes endemic typhus which is transmitted via rat flea.
- Orientia tsutsugamushi (Choice A) causes scrub typhus. It has an abrupt onset.
- Rickettsia rickettsii (Choice B) causes rocky mountain spotted fever which is transmitted through ticks. It has an abrupt onset.
- Ehrlichia chaffeensis (Choice D) causes ehrlichiosis which is also transmitted through ticks and has abrupt onset.

questions.stem: A 7/F was brought to the ER because of fever and facial rash. Upon further examination, there is bright red erythema on both cheeks. No itching or pain was associated with the condition. The following can be part of the presentation of the disease of the patient, EXCEPT:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Hemorrhagic cystitis**

- Keywords for this case include “fever” and “facial rash described as bright red erythema on both cheeks” which point to Parvovirus B19 infection.
- Among the choices, only hemorrhagic cystitis (Choice C) is an unlikely manifestation of this infection. This is more characteristic of BK Polyoma virus.
- Arthritis (Choice A), aplastic crisis (Choice B) and pancytopenia in immunocompromised patients (Choice D) are encountered in parvovirus B19 infected patients.
- Recall: red rashes in childhood, as these are commonly asked in the PLE.

| Agent | Disease | Hints |
|---|---|---|
| Measles | Measles (Rubeola; 1st Disease) | Height of fever + rash; starts at the Head; + cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots |
| S. pyogenes | Scarlet Fever (2nd Disease) | Flushed cheeks + circumoral pallor + sandpaper-like rash + strawberry tongue + sore throat + PAINFUL LN (Kawasaki: PAINLESS LN) |
| Rubella | German Measles (3rd Disease, 3-Day-Measles) | MACULOPAPULAR from head downwards + post auricular LN |
| Parvo B19 | Erythema infectiosum (5th Disease) | Slapped cheek |
| HHV6 | Roseola (exanthem subitum; 6th disease, 3-Day-Fever) | Fever then rash + SEIZURE |
| Cox A | HFMD | Oval shaped VESICLES on PALMS and SOLES |
| VZV | Chickenpox | VESICULAR rash; starts at the trunk; lesions of different stages |

- Note: the “4th Disease” (Filatov-Dukes disease) is considered obsolete.

questions.stem: Among the following, which is an inclusion that is observed in a disease that has already been eradicated?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Guarnieri bodies**

- The disease/virus that has already been declared is smallpox. In histology, intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions are observed (Guarnieri bodies) (Choice A).
- Henderson-Paterson bodies (Choice B) are intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions seen in molluscum contagiosum.
- Herpes simplex virus is characterized by the presence of large, pink to purple intranuclear inclusions (Cowdry Type A inclusions) (Choice C).
- Cowdry type B inclusions (Choice D) are intranuclear, basophilic inclusions seen in adenovirus and poliovirus.

questions.stem: The following AIDS-defining illnesses are correctly matched with their etiologic agent EXCEPT:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Kaposi’s sarcoma : HHV-7**

- Kaposi’s sarcoma is an AIDS-defining illness caused by HHV-8, not HHV-7 (Choice C is incorrect).
- All other choices are correctly paired.
- Esophagitis is caused by herpes simplex virus (Choice A).
- Mycobacterium avium complex causes invasive pulmonary disease (Choice B).
- Cryptosporidium parvum causes severe diarrhea in immunocompromised patients which includes AIDS patients (Choice D).
- Recall: AIDS-defining illnesses and their causative agents.

| Etiology | Clinical syndrome |
|---|---|
| M. tuberculosis | Disseminated tuberculosis |
| HSV | HSV esophagitis |
| C. albicans | Esophageal candidiasis |
| HHV-8 | Kaposi’s sarcoma |
| P. jiroveci | PCP pneumonia |
| T. gondii | Cerebral toxoplasmosis |
| C. neoformans | Meningoencephalitis |
| C. immitis | Coccidioidomycosis |
| C. parvum | Chronic diarrhea |
| MAC | Invasive pulmonary disease |
| H. capsulatum | Histoplasmosis |
| CMV | CMV retinitis |

questions.stem: Cysticercosis is due to the ingestion of:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Taenia solium eggs**

- Cysticercosis is transmitted via accidental ingestion of Taenia solium eggs (Choice C), usually due to autoinfection by a person who already has taeniasis. The most serious complication of this disease is neurocysticercosis. Humans are accidental hosts in cysticercosis.
- Ingestion of Taenia saginata cysticercus bovis (Choice A) and Taenia solium cysticercus cellulosae (Choice B) is termed taeniasis. Humans are definitive hosts in this infection. These are the infective stages of taeniasis.
- Taenia scolex (Choice D) are composed of suckers and rostellum. They are of diagnostic importance and recovery of scolex is one of the criteria for cure of Taenia infection.

questions.stem: Which of the following tests would be most appropriate to utilize during his initial visit?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Non-treponemal antibody testing**

- The first step in the case is to identify the causative agent. Keywords include “painless genital ulcer”, “2 weeks ago with no resolution”, and “multiple sexual partners”. These point to a primary syphilis infection, characterized by hard chancre which is non-tender ulcer that develops at the site of inoculation, usually 2-10 weeks after. It is highly infectious and heals spontaneously in 3-6 weeks.
- The next to identify is the purpose of diagnostic tests used. As mentioned in #54, the purpose of the following tests are seen below. Diagnostics tests for syphilis can be divided into microscopy, non-treponemal tests, and treponemal tests.
- Non-treponemal tests (Choice B) include rapid plasma reagin (RPR) and venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL) which is only a screening test and for monitoring of treatment. They still need confirmatory tests to be able to diagnose syphilis. Since the question asks for the appropriate diagnostic to utilize during the initial visit, a screening test would be the best to perform.
- Microscopy such as dark field microscopy (Choice C) and fluorescent microscopy (Choice D) directly observe the organisms, confirming the diagnosis.
- FTA-ABS is a treponemal antibody test (Choice A), which is used to confirm the presence of syphilis.

questions.stem: The test you performed turned out to be positive. On the other hand, which of the following is the most efficient to confirm cure after treatment?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Non-treponemal antibody testing**

- Non-treponemal tests (RPR, VDRL) (Choice B) are for screening, and used to monitor treatment response. They test negative once the patient is cured of syphilis infection and are best used in confirming cure after.
- As mentioned above, treponemal antibody tests such as FTA-ABS stay positive all throughout life once a patient is infected with syphilis (thus Choice A cannot be used to confirm cure after treatment) .
- Dark field and immunofluorescence microscopy (Choices C and D) are also more utilized in confirming the diagnosis of syphilis rather than confirming cure.

questions.stem: Which of the following pairs of organisms is the most easily distinguishable through gram staining?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Listeria monocytogenes and Proteus mirabilis**

- Gram staining could distinguish gram-positive and gram-negative organisms. Although they can also distinguish through morphology, the easily differing characteristic is the stain: purple for gram-positive organisms and red for gram-negative organisms. Listeria monocytogenes is gram-positive while Proteus mirabilis is gram-negative (Choice D).
- Both Bacillus anthracis and Clostridium perfringens (Choice A) are gram-positive.
- Both Salmonella typhi and Shigella sonnei (Choice B) are gram-negative.
- Both Corynebacterium diphtheria and Lactobacillus spp. (Choice C) are Gram-positive.

questions.stem: During investigation of a patient with malaria, you discover that he is infected with the species with multiple drug resistance. Which of the following would be observed in microscopic examination of the organism?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Maurer dots**

- These are the five main species of Plasmodium that cause malaria in humans. The two most common species are P. vivax and P. falciparum.
- The most pathogenic, and the one that can cause the most severe complications, is P. falciparum. It can cause cerebral malaria and has multiple drug resistance. Maurer dots (Choice A) are coarse granulations seen in RBCs infected by P. falciparum.
- Schuffner dots (Choice B) are punctate granulations present in RBCs infected by P. ovale and P. vivax.
- Ziemann dots (Choice C) are fine dots present in RBCs infected by P. malariae.
- Schizontal dots (Choice D) is not a term used to describe malarial dots.
- Recall malarial dots and the species associated with them:
- Memory aid: Schuffner dots = P. Ovale & Vivax (“SOVrang daming dots!”); Maurer dots = coMMa-shaped = P. falciparum.

|  | Schuffner | Maurer | Ziemann |
|---|---|---|---|
| Granulation type | Punctate granulations | Coarse granulations | Fine dots |
| Species | P. vivax, P. ovale | P. falciparum | P. malariae |

questions.stem: All of the following are chronic manifestations observed in infection with Trypanosoma cruzi, EXCEPT:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Chagoma**

- Trypanosoma cruzi causes Chagas disease (American trypanosomiasis) and is transmitted by reduviid bugs. It can be in the form of acute or chronic Chagas disease.
- Manifestations of acute Chagas disease include the Romaña sign, which is unilateral palpebral swelling, and chagoma (Choice B), which is a furuncle-like nodule near the bite site.
- Chronic manifestations of the disease include megaesophagus (Choice A), arrhythmia (Choice C), and megacolon (Choice D).
- Recall manifestations of Chagas disease:
- **Acute Chagas disease:**
  - Romaña sign – unilateral palpebral swelling
  - Chagoma – furuncle-like nodule near the bite of the reduviid bug
- **Chronic Chagas disease:**
  - Arrhythmias
  - Megaesophagus
  - Megacolon
- Memory aid for Chagas disease treatment: “BENZ, WITH A FUR COAT ON” — Benznidazole, Nifurtimox.

choices.text: Chocolate agar with factor X and V

questions.stem: Gastric carcinoma is commonly caused by infection with a certain organism. Which of the following culture media would be the best option for isolating this bacteria?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Stuart’s medium**

- Gastric carcinoma is caused by a chronic infection from Helicobacter pylori, which infiltrates the gastric mucosa specifically at the G cells. It also causes peptic ulcer disease and MALT lymphomas. The agar used to isolate H. pylori is Stuart’s medium (Choice D).
- Fletcher’s medium (Choice A) is used to isolate Leptospira species
- Xylose-Lysine-Deoxycholate (XLD) agar (Choice B) is used to isolate Salmonella spp. and Shigella spp.
- Chocolate agar with factor X and V (Choice C) is used to isolate Haemophilus influenzae.
- See item #5 for media used to grow select important bacteria.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most serious form of infection with Yersinia pestis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Pneumonic plague**

- Yersinia pestis is one of the most virulent bacteria. It is a small, gram-negative rod with bipolar (safety pin) staining and is transmitted through the oriental rat flea (Xenopsylla cheopis).
- It can come in the form of bubonic, pneumonic, and septicemic plague.
- Bubonic plague (Choice A) is characterized by painful lymph nodes called buboes. There are also systemic symptoms such as fever, headache, chills and weakness.
- Black plague (Choice B) is a pandemic of bubonic plague that happened in the mid-1300s.
- Septicemic plague (Choice D) is worsening of symptoms which now includes abdominal pain and shock. The skin and tissues turn black especially on the fingers, toes, and nose.
- Pneumonic plague (Choice C) is the most serious form of plague. It is transmitted through inhaling droplets or lung spread from bubonic or septicemic plague.

choices.text:
It is transmitted through bites that contain the
organism Borrelia recurrentis.

The first stage of the disease is characterized by the
typical bull’s eye appearance of rash.

The causative agent is typically cultured via Cary-

The drug of choice for this disease is azithromycin.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements regarding Lyme Disease is TRUE?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — The first stage of the disease is characterized by the typical bull’s eye appearance of rash.**

- Lyme disease is caused by Borrelia burgdorferi, and not B. recurrentis (Choice A is incorrect). B. recurrentis causes relapsing fever.
- Borrelia burgdorferi is isolated through the Barbour-Stoenner-Kelly (BSK) medium (Choice C is incorrect). Cary-Blair is used to isolate Vibrio spp.
- The drug of choice for Lyme disease is doxycycline, not azithromycin (Choice D is incorrect).
- Lyme disease has 3 stages:
  - First stage is characterized by erythema chronicum migrans which appears as the typical Bull’s eye configuration (Choice B).
  - Second stage includes myocarditis (AV block), meningitis, and Bell’s palsy.
  - Third stage includes autoimmune migratory polyarthritis (onion skin lesions), and acrodermatitis chronica atrophicans.

questions.stem: Among the strains of Escherichia coli, which would present with shigella-like signs and symptoms?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Enteroinvasive E. coli**

- Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC) (Choice A) would present as bloody diarrhea and with shigella-like manifestation.
- Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC) (Choice B) presents as watery diarrhea mostly in children.
- Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) (Choice C) presents as bloody diarrhea and has a shiga-like toxin (this is different from shigella-like manifestation).
- Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) (Choice D) presents as watery diarrhea with cholera-like manifestation.
- Recall characteristics of E. coli strains in the table below:

| Strain | Syndrome | Unique |
|---|---|---|
| Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) | Watery diarrhea | Cholera-like manifestation |
| Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC) | Infants | No toxin produced. Flattens villi. |
| Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) | Hemorrhagic colitis and hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) | Has shiga-like toxin |
| Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC) | Bloody diarrhea | Shigella-like manifestation |
| Enteroaggregative E. coli (EAEC) | HIV/AIDS patients |  |

questions.stem: In what type of amoebiasis are flask-shaped lesions seen?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Amoebic colitis**

- **A. Pulmonary amoebiasis** — This occurs when the lungs become infected, but these do not present as flask-shaped ulcers. This is seen in severe cases, and it manifests variably, often with cough, hemoptysis, and dyspnea.
- **B. Amoebic liver abscess** — Anchovy-like aspirate is seen in amoebic liver abscess.
- **C. Amoebic colitis** — Flask-shaped colon ulcer is seen in amoebic colitis as a result of the small point of entry (forming the "neck") and lateral spread of invading trophozoites in the lamina propria (forming the expanded base).
- **D. Amoebic cutis** — Amebic cutis is characterized by painful, necrotic skin ulcers.

questions.stem: Entamoeba histolytica can be cultured in ___.
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Diamond's medium**

- **A. MacConkey agar** — Used for Enterobacteriaceae.
- **B. NNN medium** — Novy-MacNeal-Nicolle (NNN) medium is used for Leishmania.
- **C. Diamond's medium** — Used for T. vaginalis; with some modification, it can grow E. histolytica.
- **D. CLED medium** — Cystine-lactose-electrolyte-deficient (CLED) medium is used for uropathogens except Proteus.

questions.stem: What is the MOST commonly involved area in amebiasis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Cecum**

- **A. Recto-sigmoid** — The sigmoid and rectum are favored sites for later lesions.
- **B. Lung** — As mentioned in #1, pulmonary amoebiasis manifests variably, often with cough, hemoptysis, and dyspnea, and is seen in severe cases and not commonly.
- **C. Liver** — Among the extraintestinal sites of infection, amebic hepatitis or liver abscess is the most common form.
- **D. Cecum** — Amebiasis may involve any part of the bowel, but primary lesions are usually found at the cecum, appendix, and ascending colon.

questions.stem: What does this child have?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Infant botulism**

- **A. Infant botulism** — Honey is a known risk factor for infant botulism, as it can contain C. botulinum spores, especially if it is produced from pollen gathered by bees from plants that grow in soil. Infant botulism can occur when infants ingest the spores of this bacterium, which can grow and produce toxins in the intestine.
- **B. Strychnine poisoning** and **C. Inherited zinc deficiency** — Would manifest as involuntary muscle contractions, opisthotonos, hyperthermia, respiratory muscle spasms (spastic paralysis) but NOT flaccid paralysis as seen in botulism.
- **D. Tetanus** — Choice D (acrodermatitis enteropathica) would manifest as a triad of hair loss, diarrhea, and periorificial/acral inflammatory skin rash.

synapses/junctions
