questions.stem: Which patient among the following does NOT require a screening test for TB?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Healthy full-term male newborn**

- **C. Healthy full-term male newborn** — a healthy newborn without any symptoms is unlikely to have tuberculosis. BCG vaccination is given shortly after birth to prevent complications of tuberculosis.
- **A. 30-year-old man traveling from Nairobi to United Kingdom for the first time** — needs screening, since there is a high prevalence of tuberculosis in Nairobi.
- **B. 7-year-old healthy girl living together with grandmother who has pulmonary TB infection** — also needs screening, because exposure is one of the factors for high suspicion of pulmonary TB; the grandmother is noted to be living with the girl.
- **D. 45-year-old man confirmed with HIV infection** — also warrants screening, because pulmonary TB is common in immunocompromised patients, especially HIV (specifically AIDS) patients.

questions.stem: A previously healthy 5 years old, male, with no known underlying medical condition developed fever; malaise associated with increased WBC primarily lymphocytes. He was diagnosed with Acute Infectious Mononucleosis due to the Epstein-Barr Virus. What will be the most probable course of the patient's disease?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Spontaneous recovery from disease**

- **A. Spontaneous recovery from disease** — a healthy male is likely to have a good prognosis, and the infection will resolve rapidly within 1–2 weeks.
- Immunocompromised patients are more likely to develop complications. Such patients may develop associated malignancies such as **B. nasopharyngeal carcinoma**, **D. Burkitt lymphoma**, **C. Hodgkin lymphoma**, and oral hairy-cell leukoplakia.

questions.stem: What type of pericardial fluid indicates pyogenic infection and contains leukocytes as well as debris?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Suppurative**

- Pericardial effusion may be serous (secondary to heart failure or hypoalbuminemia), serosanguineous (due to trauma, malignancy, or rupture of the heart or aorta), or chylous (due to thoracic duct obstruction or injury).
- **A. Hemorrhagic** — usually rare, and contains mainly red blood cells.
- **B. Serous** — a clear, thin, and watery exudate that typically appears during the inflammatory stage of wound healing.
- **C. Suppurative** — fluid due to infection; contains white blood cells (leukocytes) and debris.
- **D. Serosanguinous** — a thin, watery discharge that contains a small amount of blood.

choices.text:
Serum antibody testing can be used to determine
result of treatment of neurosyphilis

After an effective treatment, patient is no longer
susceptible to syphilitic infection

Spontaneous healing of an untreated primary lesion
indicates cure from the disease

Penicillin remains to be the treatment of choice of
syphilis

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is TRUE about the treatment of syphilis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Penicillin remains to be the treatment of choice of syphilis**

- **D. Penicillin remains to be the treatment of choice of syphilis** — penicillin G remains the treatment in all stages of syphilis.
- **A. Serum antibody testing can be used to determine result of treatment of neurosyphilis** — incorrect. Antibody tests (FTA-ABS) are confirmatory tests and stay positive throughout life; they are not used to monitor therapy response. Non-treponemal tests (RPR, VDRL) are for screening and are used to monitor treatment response.
- **B. After an effective treatment, patient is no longer susceptible to syphilitic infection** — incorrect. Having syphilis once does not protect patients from getting the disease again. Even after successful treatment, patients might still be re-infected by unprotected sexual contact. The re-infection rate of syphilis is high, especially among high-risk populations.
- **C. Spontaneous healing of an untreated primary lesion indicates cure from the disease** — incorrect. Even without treatment, primary lesions will go away without scarring. If untreated, primary syphilis can progress to secondary syphilis, which has many clinical and histopathological findings.

questions.stem: What species of malaria affects ONLY young RBCs?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — P. vivax**

- **B. P. vivax** and P. ovale — affect young RBCs.
- **A. P. falciparum** — affects all stages of RBC.
- **C. P. malariae** — only affects old RBCs.
- **D. None of the above**

| Species | RBC preference |
|---|---|
| P. knowlesi, P. falciparum | All ages |
| P. vivax, P. ovale | Young RBCs |
| P. malariae | Old RBCs |

questions.stem: Which of the following bacteria produces streptokinase?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Streptococcus pyogenes**

- **D. Streptococcus pyogenes** — Streptokinase (fibrinolysin) is produced by many strains of group A beta-hemolytic streptococci. It is one of the virulence factors of S. pyogenes but recall that M protein (responsible for the molecular mimicry in rheumatic fever) is the major virulence factor for the group. Additionally, streptokinase transforms the plasminogen of human plasma into plasmin, an active proteolytic enzyme that digests fibrin and other proteins, allowing the bacteria to escape from blood clots.
- **A. Staphylococcus aureus** — polysaccharide capsule (prevents phagocytosis), penicillinase (inactivates penicillin derivatives).
- **B. Enterococcus faecalis** — most common etiologic agent of infective endocarditis in patients following GU/GI procedures.
- **C. Streptococcus pneumoniae** — capsule (prevents phagocytosis).

questions.stem: Which of the following CNS diseases can be prevented with an available vaccine for humans?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Japanese B encephalitis**

- **B. Japanese B encephalitis** — Both killed-virus and attenuated live-virus Japanese B encephalitis vaccines for humans are in use in several Asian countries. Japanese encephalitis live attenuated recombinant vaccine is part of the PPS recommended vaccines given at a minimum age 9 months subcutaneously.
- **A, C, D. Eastern equine, Western equine, and West Nile encephalitis** — have no vaccine available.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an ECG finding that may be indicative of pericarditis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — ST segment elevation**

- **B. ST segment elevation** — Typical ECG findings of acute pericarditis include diffuse concave-upward ST-segment elevation, and occasionally, PR-segment depression. Coxsackie B virus is the most common enterovirus causing myocarditis pericarditis in adults and children.
- **A. ST depression** — not observed in pericarditis. This happens due to hypokalemia and cardiac ischemia.
- **C. Prolonged PR interval** — seen as a minor manifestation of acute rheumatic fever. This is mainly caused by delayed conduction in the AV node.
- **D. T elevation** — not usually seen generally when it comes to ECG findings. T waves may either be commonly inverted, flat, or tall.

questions.stem: Which organism is MOST commonly involved in pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Neisseria gonorrhoeae**

- **C. Neisseria gonorrhoeae** — PID is the inflammation of the uterus, uterine tubes, and adnexal tissues that is not associated with surgery or pregnancy. It is the major consequence of endocervical N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis infections.
- **A. Candida albicans** — etiologic agent of Candida vulvovaginitis.
- **B. Gardnerella vaginalis** — involved in bacterial vaginosis.
- **D. Treponema pallidum** — etiologic agent of syphilis.

choices.text: Toxin causes blocking of gamma-aminobutyric acid
Toxin causes blocking of the motor neurons
Toxin causes the release of inhibitory glycine
Toxin digests protein required by neurotransmitters

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is FALSE regarding the effects of the neurotoxin produced by Clostridium tetani?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Toxin causes the release of inhibitory glycine**

- **A. Toxin causes blocking of gamma-aminobutyric acid** — The neurotoxin tetanospasmin blocks the release of the inhibitory glycine and GABA.
- **B. Toxin causes blocking of the motor neurons** — The tetanus toxin also acts by blocking neurotransmitter release at the neuromuscular junction resulting in weakness or paralysis.
- **C. Toxin causes the release of inhibitory glycine** — The toxin does NOT cause the release of glycine, in fact it blocks its release.
- **D. Toxin digests protein required by neurotransmitters** — The toxin degrades synaptobrevin, a protein required for docking of neurotransmitter vesicles on the presynaptic membrane. These result in rigidity.

choices.text: Fluoroquinolones are the drug of choice

Hepatorenal syndrome may occur in up to 50% of
patients
Person to person transmission is common

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about leptospirosis is CORRECT?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Rats are prime reservoir**

- **D. Rats are prime reservoir** — Leptospirosis are essentially animal infections; human infection is only accidental, occurring after contact with water or other materials contaminated with the excreta of animal hosts. Rats, mice, wild rodents, dogs, swine, and cattle are the principal sources of human infection.
- **A. Fluoroquinolones are the drug of choice** — incorrect since the drugs of choice for mild leptospirosis include doxycycline, ampicillin, or amoxicillin, while the treatment for severe leptospirosis includes penicillin G, ampicillin, ceftriaxone, or cefotaxime.
- **B. Hepatorenal syndrome may occur in up to 50% of patients** — in 10% of cases (NOT 50%), the presentation is more severe, presenting with Weil syndrome characterized by jaundice, bleeding, and kidney dysfunction.
- **C. Person to person transmission is common** — transmission is through animal urine, usually in the setting of wading in floodwaters. Leptospires penetrate intact mucous membranes or skin through small cuts or abrasions.

questions.stem: Which of the following characterizes the infective stage of Entamoeba histolytica to humans?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Cigar-shaped chromatoidal body**

- **B. Cigar-shaped chromatoidal body** — Infection with E. histolytica occurs via ingestion of mature cysts from fecally contaminated food, water, or hands. Cigar-shaped chromatoidal body is characteristic of E. histolytica mature cysts.
- **A, C, D. Bull’s eye karyosome, Ingested RBC, and Pseudopodia** — all characteristics of the trophozoite stage of E. histolytica.

vaccines

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is CORRECT regarding the diphtheria vaccine?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — It is only available in combination with other vaccines**

- **A. It is only available in combination with other vaccines** — There is no longer a single diphtheria vaccine. Diphtheria toxoids are commonly combined with tetanus toxoid (Td) and with acellular pertussis vaccine (DaPT) as a single injection to be used in initial immunization of children.
- DTP (Diphtheria, Tetanus, Pertussis) vaccine is given at the minimum age of 6 weeks intramuscularly, with primary series consisting of 3 doses with a minimum of 4 weeks interval.
- Booster series consists of 3 doses until adolescence with the following schedule: 12-23 months (DTP), 4-7 years (DTP), and 9-15 years intervals (Td/Tdap).
- **B. If it has been given as a part of a vaccination following a tetanus prone wound, the routine booster is always necessary** — if a patient has already completed the vaccination for DTaP or DTP, there is no need for a routine booster shot for a tetanus prone wound.
- **C. The first booster dose of diphtheria should be given at least 24 months after the last in the primary course** — as stated above, the first booster dose should be given at 12-23 months, not after 24 months.
- **D. There should be 3 years between the first and second booster doses** — the minimum interval between booster doses should be at least 4 years, not 3 years.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old child was taken to a clinic in rural South Cotabato appearing listless and inattentive but with normal hearing and visual testing findings. The child is thin with potbelly of malnutrition. CBC reveals microcytic, hypochromic anemia, and the fecal exam detects too numerous to count brown, oval nematode eggs. What was the most likely means by which the child was infected?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Skin penetration by larvae**

- For this case, keywords include “microcytic, hypochromic anemia”, “malnutrition”, and “brown, oval nematode eggs”. These indicate hookworm infection.
- **D. Skin penetration by larvae** — Hookworm (intestinal nematode) eggs appear as oval or ellipsoidal thin-shelled bodies. Hookworm filariform larvae (infective stage) penetrate host skin and migrate throughout the host. Chronic or heavy hookworm infection results in a progressive, microcytic, hypochromic anemia of the iron-deficient type due to the continuous loss of blood.
- **A. Ingestion of larvae** — not a common mode of transmission since most helminths are transmitted through ingestion of eggs.
- **B. Ingestion of cysts in muscle** — most likely pertains to Trichinella spiralis, which is transmitted through ingestion of undercooked meat. The parasite then infects the muscles of the host.
- **C. Mosquito transmission of sporozoites** — pertains to Plasmodium infection, which is transmitted by Anopheles flavirostris minimus.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old college student presented with lower abdominal pain with dysuria and frequent urination. Upon palpation, there was suprapubic tenderness. No noted fever and the vital signs are unremarkable. Which of the following is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Cystitis**

- **B. Cystitis** — the term used to describe infection of the bladder with signs and symptoms including lower abdominal pain, suprapubic tenderness, dysuria, urgency, and frequency.
- **A. Appendicitis** — presents with anorexia, vomiting, periumbilical pain gradually migrating to the RLQ, and signs of peritonitis.
- **C. Pelvic inflammatory disease** — lower abdominal or pelvic pain, vaginal discharge, dyspareunia, and abnormal vaginal bleeding.
- **D. Pyelonephritis** — presents with dysuria and flank pain with systemic symptoms (i.e., fever).

choices.text: Second bout of skin rashes manifests

questions.stem: Which of the following findings would determine if there was an active ongoing dengue infection?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Significant rise in antibody titer**

- **C. Significant rise in antibody titer** — Analysis of paired acute and convalescent sera to show a significant rise in antibody titer is the most reliable evidence of an active dengue infection. Diagnosed using dengue IgM.
- **A. Platelet count decreasing** — laboratory finding of thrombocytopenia is not specific for dengue and may occur in other diseases.
- **B. Patient develops recurrence of fever** — fever lasts from 2-7 days corresponding to peak viral load. The temperature may subside on the third day and rise again about 5-8 days after onset.
- **D. Second bout of skin rashes manifests** — a rash may appear on the 3rd or 4th day and last for 1-5 days. These are both clinical findings and are not reliable in the diagnosis of active dengue infection.

choices.text:
Immunity to the virus is permanent after a single
infection

Involvement of the parotid gland is an obligatory
step in the infectious process

Infection is always followed by clinical
manifestation
The virus infects human and other animal hosts

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about mumps virus is CORRECT?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Immunity to the virus is permanent after a single infection**

- **A. Immunity to the virus is permanent after a single infection** — There is only one antigenic type of mumps virus, and it does not exhibit significant antigenic variation. Infection confers lifelong immunity. This is prevented by live-attenuated vaccine.
- **B. Involvement of the parotid gland is an obligatory step in the infectious process** — Parotitis is not an obligatory step in the infectious process; it can involve the testes, ovaries, meninges, and pancreas as well.
- **C. Infection is always followed by clinical manifestation** — most common manifestation is asymptomatic and does not necessarily translate to clinical manifestations.
- **D. The virus infects human and other animal hosts** — Humans are the only host. No other animals are host to mumps.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man, with smoker’s cough, complained of body malaise, low grade fever of 2 days duration, and productive cough. The patient continues to smoke despite experiencing shortness of breath on exertion. What is the most appropriate initial investigation for him?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Chest x-ray**

- **B. Chest x-ray** — This patient presents with symptoms of pneumonia. Chest radiography is often needed as an initial diagnostic test to differentiate pneumonia from other conditions that present similarly, such as acute bronchitis, exacerbations of chronic bronchitis, and heart failure.
- **A. C-reactive protein** — a biomarker of inflammatory response but has low sensitivity for detecting bacterial pathogens.
- **C. Spirometry** — primarily used in the diagnosis of asthma and COPD.
- **D. Sputum culture** — used to confirm the etiology of a pulmonary infection and is thus not an appropriate initial test to do for this patient.

questions.stem: Which of the following microorganisms is the causative agent of the relapsing fever?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Borrelia**

- **A. Borrelia** — Relapsing fever in epidemic form is caused by Borrelia recurrentis, which is transmitted by the human body louse.
- **B. Leptospira** — causative agent of leptospirosis.
- **C. Spirillum** — causative agent of rat-bite fever.
- **D. Treponema** — causative agent of syphilis.

questions.stem: Which of the following microorganisms can cause endocarditis infecting normal heart valves?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Staphylococcus aureus**

- **C. Staphylococcus aureus** — Massive bacteremia or particularly virulent microorganisms (e.g., S. aureus) cause endocarditis on normal valves. Mitral valve is the most frequent valve involved, except in IV drug users, in which it is the tricuspid valve, also caused by S. aureus.
- **A. Candida albicans** — can cause endocarditis in immunocompromised individuals or those with risk factors.
- **B. Enterococcus faecalis** — more commonly associated with s/p GU/GI procedures.
- **D. Viridans Streptococcus** — associated with recent dental procedures.
- Streptococcus bovis — associated with GI malignancy.
- Staphylococcus epidermidis — associated with prosthetic valves.

questions.stem: What carries the genetic code for the diphtheria toxin that is found in pathogenic Corynebacterium diphtheriae but not in non-pathogenic normal flora diphtheroid?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Integrated temperate phage**

- **D. Integrated temperate phage** — Integration of this temperate phage results in a stable prophage, which directs the production of the diphtheria toxin. Toxins that are produced by prophage-coded bacteria include shigA-like toxin, Botulinum, Cholera, Diphtheria, and Erythrogenic toxin (remember: ABCDE).
- **A. An episome** — a subset of plasmids that could integrate into the bacterial chromosome.
- **B. Diphthamide** — a post-translational histidine that is found in the elongation factor 2 of eukaryotes and archaea.
- **C. Highly repetitive bacterial DNA** — may be encountered in other bacteria but is not observed in pathogenic C. diphtheriae.

questions.stem: What is the major cause of morbidity and mortality among patients with late-stage HIV infection?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Opportunistic infections**

- **C. Opportunistic infections** — The predominant causes of morbidity and mortality among patients with late-stage HIV infection are opportunistic infections (severe infections induced by agents that rarely cause serious disease in immunocompetent individuals). Opportunistic infections usually occur when the CD4 T-cell counts of HIV-infected patients have dropped from normal levels of about 1000 cells/uL to less than 200 cells/uL.
- **A, B, D. AIDS-associated cancer, neurologic diseases, pulmonary complications** — may possibly be encountered in HIV/AIDS but they are part of the sequelae by opportunistic infections also.

questions.stem: Which of the following tests is the most widely used technique in detecting viral RNA in a clinical specimen?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction**

- **C. Reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction** — Reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) is the most commonly used technique for detection of viruses in clinical specimens (feces, vomitus) and environmental samples (contaminated food, water). I.e., in COVID-19 infection.
- **B. Particle agglutination test** — TPPA (Treponema pallidum particle agglutination assay) for syphilis.
- **A. Enzyme-linked immunoassay** — detecting past exposures with HIV, Lyme disease, and Hepatitis infections.
- **D. Viral culture** — not routinely used in clinical practice.

questions.stem: Which of the following tests is the most helpful diagnostic test to confirm the diagnosis of gonococcal arthritis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Nucleic acid amplification test**

- **B. Nucleic acid amplification test** — NAAT has greater sensitivity than culture and the question is only asking for the confirmation of the diagnosis. NAAT is the diagnostic of choice whenever available/feasible for patients with suspicion of gonorrhea.
- **A. Culture of the aspirate** — scenarios that culture would be more appropriate include treatment failure and for N. gonorrhoeae antimicrobial susceptibility studies. Culture would also take longer results compared to NAAT.
- **C. Serologic detection of the antibody** — a titer rise occurs during and after acute chlamydia infection. However, serologic tests are generally not useful in the diagnosis of chlamydial infections, particularly in populations with high prevalence of chlamydial genital tract infections.
- **D. Smear of the aspirate** — urethral swab or sampling smears may be used for males manifesting with genitourinary symptoms.

choices.text:
ACE-inhibitors are contraindicated in all patients
with renal failure

Hemolytic uremic syndrome occurs after infection
with E. coli 0157

Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis should be
treated with corticosteroids
Viral infections are most commonly implicated

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding infection-related acute glomerulonephritis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Hemolytic uremic syndrome occurs after infection with E. coli 0157**

- **B. Hemolytic uremic syndrome occurs after infection with E. coli 0157** — Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) has been associated with mild non-bloody diarrhea, hemorrhagic colitis, a severe form of diarrhea, and with hemolytic uremic syndrome, a disease resulting in acute renal failure, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, and thrombocytopenia.
- **A. ACE-inhibitors are contraindicated in all patients with renal failure** — incorrect. ACE-inhibitors are not given to patients with bilateral renal artery stenosis since ACE-i can decrease the GFR of the stenotic kidneys due to the removal of angiotensin II-induced renal vasoconstriction. It is not contraindicated in all patients with renal failure.
- **C. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis should be treated with corticosteroids** — incorrect. The role of steroids and immunosuppression in patients with PSGN is not established. The drug of choice is Penicillin G, but antibiotic therapy does not affect the natural history of PSGN.
- **D. Viral infections are most commonly implicated** — incorrect because it should be bacterial. The most common cause of infectious acute glomerulonephritis are certain nephritogenic strains of group A beta-hemolytic streptococci.

choices.text:
It is clinically and pathologically distinct from
chickenpox

It is a second episode of infection with chickenpox
virus
It is a mutated form of chickenpox

It is a reactivation of latent chickenpox virus in
sensory ganglia

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding herpes zoster?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — It is a reactivation of latent chickenpox virus in sensory ganglia**

- **A. It is clinically and pathologically distinct from chickenpox** — incorrect because chickenpox and herpes zoster are not clinically distinct from each other.
- **B. It is a second episode of infection with chickenpox virus** — incorrect because it is NOT a second episode of infection with the virus.
- **C. It is a mutated form of chickenpox** — incorrect; herpes zoster is NOT a mutated form of chickenpox.
- **D. It is a reactivation of latent chickenpox virus in sensory ganglia** — Chickenpox (varicella) and shingles (herpes zoster) are caused by the same virus. Whereas varicella is the acute disease that follows primary contact with the virus, zoster is the response of the partially immune host to reactivation of varicella virus present in latent form in neurons in sensory ganglia.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the LEAST likely feature of the epidemiology of measles?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Multiple serotype**

- **C. Multiple serotype** — The measles virus is highly contagious; there is a single serotype (thus this is the least likely feature).
- **A. Highly contagious** — Measles is a highly contagious disease that could be spread through respiratory droplets.
- **B. Lifelong immunity conferred** — It only has a single serotype as stated. Thus, when infected, it confers lifelong immunity.
- **D. No animal reservoir** — It has no animal reservoirs, and inapparent infections are rare when encountered.

questions.stem: Which of the following microorganisms is most likely associated with gas gangrene?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Clostridium perfringens**

- Clostridia cause several important toxin-mediated diseases including tetanus (C. tetani), botulism (C. botulinum), gas gangrene (C. perfringens), and antibiotic-associated diarrhea and pseudomembranous colitis (C. difficile).
- **A. Clostridium perfringens** — Gas gangrene is caused by an alpha toxin produced by C. perfringens named lecithinase.
- **B. Neisseria gonorrhoeae** — causes gonorrhea, which is one of the most common STDs.
- **C. Pseudomonas aeruginosa** — a gram-negative bacterium commonly found in soil, water, and other moist environments. It is known to cause infections in individuals with compromised immune systems, such as burn patients, and can lead to the development of greenish pus in the affected area due to the pigment pyoverdine.
- **D. Staphylococcus aureus** — associated with many manifestations such as acute endocarditis, pneumonia, osteomyelitis, gastroenteritis, Ritter disease, and toxic shock syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following infections of the reproductive tract is caused by a protozoan?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Trichomoniasis**

- **D. Trichomoniasis** — Trichomonas vaginalis is the only sexually transmitted protozoa and is the etiologic agent of trichomoniasis.
- **A. Candidiasis** — Candida albicans (fungus).
- **B. Chlamydia** — Chlamydia trachomatis (bacteria).
- **C. Gonorrhea** — Neisseria gonorrhoeae (bacteria).

questions.stem: What is the ability of the immune system to recognize self-antigens versus non-self-antigens?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Tolerance**

- **D. Tolerance** — Self-tolerance is the prevention of an immune response against a particular antigen. The immune system is generally tolerant of self-antigens, so it does not usually attack the body’s own cells, tissues, and organs.
- **A. Antigenicity** — describes the ability of a foreign material (antigen) to bind to, to interact with, the products of the final cell-mediated response such as B-cell or T-cell receptors.
- **B. Cell-mediated immunity** — T-cell mediated and is for recognizing and eliminating infected or abnormal cells.
- **C. Humoral immunity** — antibody (B cell) mediated, mainly by producing antibodies.

questions.stem: Jack 27/M was brought to the emergency room because of progressive general weakening and symmetrical involvement of both upper and lower extremities. He also presented with doubling of vision, difficulty of swallowing, and slurring of speech. In the emergency room, he suddenly went into respiratory distress and went into cardiac arrest. Upon history taking with the relative, the patient had leftover canned sardines for breakfast several hours ago. Which is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Botulism**

- **A. Botulism** — A chief risk factor for botulism lies in home-canned foods, particularly string beans, corn, peppers, olives, peas, and smoked fish or vacuum-packed fresh fish in plastic bags. Symptoms begin 18-24 hours after ingestion of the toxic food, with visual disturbances (incoordination of eye muscles, double vision), inability to swallow, and speech difficulty. Bulbar paralysis signs are progressive, and death occurs from respiratory paralysis or cardiac arrest.
- **B. Listeriosis** — in adults may present with pneumonia, bacteremia, sepsis, or meningitis in pregnant, elderly, or immunocompromised individuals.
- **C. Neisseria meningitidis** — infection most commonly presents as meningitis (fever, headache, stiff neck, and increased level of PMNs in CSF).
- **D. Tetanus** — causes spastic paralysis.

questions.stem: What is the major complication of pelvic inflammatory disease if not treated adequately?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Infertility**

- **B. Infertility** — The major complication of PID is infertility due to uterine tubal occlusion. Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is strongly associated with infertility. The infection can lead to scarring and damage to the fallopian tubes and other reproductive organs, which can make it difficult for patients to conceive or carry pregnancy to term. Specifically, infertility risk increases with the number of PID episodes: 12% with one episode, 20% with two episodes, and 40% with three or more episodes.
- **A, C, D. Chronic pelvic pain, malignant degeneration, and miscarriage** — also symptoms/sequelae associated with PID. However, considering the most common and major complication of PID, infertility is the best answer.

questions.stem: Which of the following ova do NOT float in a saturated salt solution?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — T. solium**

- Centrifugal flotation technique effectively concentrates hookworm (Choice A), fertilized eggs of Ascaris species (Choice B), Trichuris species, Hymenolepis species (Choice C), and Enterobius vermicularis.
- **D. T. solium** — Among the choices, only T. solium eggs do not float in a saturated salt solution.

choices.text:
Absence of lymphocyte adenosine deaminase
activity

Deficiency of the late-acting component C5, C6, C7,
or C8

questions.stem: Ric 40/M is suffering from multiple episodes of disseminated gonococcal infection for the last few years. Cultures of his urethra and knee fluid yield N. gonorrhoeae. Which of the following statements describe the etiology?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Deficiency of the late-acting component C5, C6, C7, or C8**

- **B. Deficiency of the late-acting component C5, C6, C7, or C8** — Neisseria bacteremia is favored by the absence of bactericidal antibodies (IgM and IgG), inhibition of serum bactericidal action by blocking IgA antibody, or a complement component deficiency (C5b, C6-C9).
- **A. Absence of lymphocyte adenosine deaminase activity** — a major cause of severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID), which presents as recurrent viral, bacterial, fungal, and protozoal infections.
- **C. Polymorphonuclear cell chemotactic factor activity** — part of the normal response of the body when there is infection, primarily bacterial in origin.
- **D. Selective IgA deficiency** — the most common primary immunodeficiency and confers an increased susceptibility to giardiasis.

questions.stem: A 45/M cachectic male, chain smoker developed flu-like disease due to an endemic mycosis. On PE, there was splenomegaly and erythema nodosum on the shins of the patient. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Histoplasmosis**

All systemic mycoses can cause pneumonia and can disseminate. There are unique signs and symptoms that may help distinguish systemic mycoses from one another:

| Disease | Manifestations |
|---|---|
| Histoplasmosis | palatal/tongue ulcers, splenomegaly, pancytopenia, erythema nodosum |
| Blastomycosis | inflammatory lung disease, dissemination to bone/skin appear as verrucous lesions |
| Coccidiomycosis | dissemination to bone/skin, erythema nodosum or multiforme, arthralgias (desert rheumatism), can cause meningitis |
| Paracoccidioidomycosis | similar to blastomycosis but has a male predisposition (M>F) |
| Nocardiosis | caused by Nocardia sp., which is not a systemic dimorphic pathogenic fungus (aerobic, Gram-positive bacteria with branching filaments) |

questions.stem: Which of the following diagnostic tests shows the classic finding of coconut cake rectum in a patient with Trichuriasis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Colonoscopy**

- **B. Colonoscopy** — The classic finding is the coconut cake rectum from white bodies of adult worms dangling from the inflamed mucosa, which is seen with sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy.
- **A, C, D. Barium enema, CT scan of the abdomen, Plain abdominal x-ray** — Since the coconut cake rectum is seen on direct observation of the large intestine, these would not show this finding.

questions.stem: Which of the following virulence factors in Streptococcus pyogenes has an important role in the pathogenesis of rheumatic fever?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — M protein**

- **B. M protein** — helps prevent phagocytosis; sequence homology with human cardiac myosin (molecular mimicry); possibly underlies the autoimmune response seen in acute rheumatic fever.
- **A. Exotoxin B** — results in necrotizing fasciitis.
- **C. Pyrogenic exotoxin A** — results in streptococcal toxic shock syndrome.
- **D. Streptokinase** — transforms the plasminogen of human plasma into plasmin, an active proteolytic enzyme that digests fibrin and other proteins, allowing the bacteria to escape from blood clots.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most common neurologic disorder which occurs in AIDS patients as a late manifestation of the disease?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Dementia complex**

- **B. Dementia complex** — AIDS dementia complex, the most common neurologic syndrome, occurs as a late manifestation in 25-65% of AIDS patients and is characterized by poor memory, inability to concentrate, apathy, psychomotor retardation, and behavioral changes.
- **A, C, D. Peripheral neuropathy, Subacute encephalitis, Aseptic meningitis** — other distinct neurologic syndromes that occur frequently (along with vacuolar myelopathy), but they are not the most common.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of Streptococcus pyogenes?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Protein A**

- **C. Protein A** — incorrect because it’s expressed by S. aureus. It prevents opsonization and phagocytosis.
- **A. Beta hemolytic** — correct because S. pyogenes is beta-hemolytic, bacitracin sensitive, PYR (+).
- **B. Hyaluronic acid capsule** — correct because the hyaluronic acid capsule is a key virulence factor that facilitates non-invasive infections of the nasopharynx and skin and confers some protection from neutrophils.
- **D. M protein** — correct because the M protein is a major virulence factor of S. pyogenes that inhibits the activation of complement cascade and phagocytosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following is caused by eating undercooked or raw pork meat?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Taenia solium**

- **D. Taenia solium** — known as the pork tapeworm of man. Transmission is through the ingestion of larvae encysted in undercooked pork.
- **A. Diphyllobothrium latum** — ingestion of larvae in raw freshwater fish.
- **B. Hymenolepis nana** — ingestion of cysticercoid-infected arthropods like fleas.
- **C. Taenia saginata** — ingestion of infected beef/cattle.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is FALSE regarding neonatal herpes?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Infection caused by the HSV type 1 carries a worse prognosis**

- Neonatal herpes can be acquired postnatally by exposure to either HSV-1 or HSV-2.
- **A. Infection caused by the HSV type 1 carries a worse prognosis** — false; whether caused by HSV-1 or HSV-2, there is no significant difference in prognosis.
- **B. Other sources of infection include family members and hospital personnel** — true; sources of infection include family members and hospital personnel who are shedding the virus.
- **C. There is no difference in the nature and severity of diseases whether acquired by a premature infant or a full-term infant.** — true; there do not appear to be any differences between the nature and severity of neonatal herpes in premature or full-term infants.
- **D. There is no difference in the severity or disease whether acquired during delivery or post-partum.** — true; in infections caused by HSV-1 or HSV-2, or in disease when virus is acquired during delivery or postpartum, there is also no difference.

questions.stem: Which of the following diseases is NOT a sexually transmitted disease?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Bacterial vaginosis**

- **C. Bacterial vaginosis** — associated with sexual activity but not sexually transmitted. It is characterized by overgrowth of certain anaerobic bacteria in the vagina due to decrease in lactobacilli.
- **A. Chancroid** — painful genital ulcer with exudate and inguinal adenopathy caused by Haemophilus ducreyi.
- **B. Hepatitis B** — presents with jaundice caused by HBV.
- **D. Trichomoniasis** — associated with foul-smelling discharge, itching, and burning pain caused by Trichomonas vaginalis.

questions.stem: Steven, a 16-year-old student, was jogging around their subdivision when he accidentally stepped on a rusty nail. A few days later, he developed spasticity starting from his right foot and eventually resulting in trismus. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Tetanus**

- **D. Tetanus** — The incubation period may range from 4-5 days up to 3 weeks. Tetanus is characterized by tonic contraction of voluntary muscles. Muscular spasms often involve the first area of injury and infection and then the muscles of the jaw (trismus aka lockjaw), which contract so that the mouth cannot be opened.
- **A. Botulism** — diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, dyspnea, descending flaccid paralysis; floppy baby syndrome.
- **C. Strychnine poisoning** — inhibits postsynaptic glycine receptors, mostly in the spinal cord, causing painful, involuntary skeletal muscle spasms. Tx is mainly supportive with benzodiazepines and the management of complications from excessive muscle contractions.
- **B. Myonecrosis** — Clostridial myonecrosis (aka gas gangrene) is a life-threatening muscle infection that develops from an area of trauma or hematogenously from the GI tract with muscle seeding.

questions.stem: Which of the following bacteria has the lowest ID50 (50% infectious dose)?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Shigella sonnei**

- Lowest infective dose means that the bacteria is the most infectious since it needs the LEAST amount of organisms to infect other individuals. Among the choices, Shigella is the most infectious.
- **C. Shigella sonnei** — has an infective dose between 10-100 organisms.
- **A. Campylobacter jejuni** — has an infective dose <500 organisms.
- **B. Salmonella typhi** — has an infective dose between 1,000 to 1,000,000 organisms, with some sources indicating 100,000.
- **D. Vibrio cholerae** — infective dose is between 10,000 and 100,000.

questions.stem: Dom, a 40-year-old horticulturist, consulted a local clinic because of multiple subcutaneous nodules and abscesses occurring along the lymphatics of his left upper extremities. His past medical history revealed trauma while tending to his plants several months ago. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Sporotrichosis**

- Keywords for this case are “horticulturist” and presence of “multiple subcutaneous nodules and abscesses along the lymphatics of upper extremities”. These point to sporotrichosis.
- **C. Sporotrichosis** — also known as Rose gardener’s disease and is caused by the entry of the sporothrix fungi, which are generally seen in soil, rose bushes, and hay. Entry through cuts or trauma is the most common form, hence previous history of trauma while in the outdoors or involvement in gardening is important to elicit. The initial lesion develops as a granulomatous nodule that may progress to form a necrotic or ulcerative lesion. Multiple subcutaneous nodules and abscesses occur along the lymphatics.
- **A. Chromoblastomycosis** — subcutaneous mycoses with melanized sclerotic bodies (copper-penny bodies), cauliflower-like lesions.
- **B. Erythema nodosum** — symptom of coccidioidomycosis that suggests robust immune response; characterized by the sudden onset of erythematous, firm, solid, deep nodules or plaques, tender, and mainly localized at the extensor surfaces of the legs.
- **D. Tuberculosis** — will more likely result in pulmonary symptoms. Based on the history of the patient, it is unlikely since no exposure was mentioned.

choices.text: Fecal contamination of drinking water and food

questions.stem: What is the mechanism of infection of amebiasis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Fecal contamination of drinking water and food**

- **A. Fecal contamination of drinking water and food** — The mechanism of infection of amebiasis is through ingestion of cysts from fecal contamination of water or food or oral/anal behaviors. The infective stage of amebiasis is the cyst of the organism.
- **B. Contamination by flies** — could transmit other parasites such as Onchercerca volvulus, Loa loa.
- **C. Mosquito bite** — transmits parasites such as Plasmodium.
- **D. Skin penetration by larvae** — the mode of transmission of hookworms (Necator americanus and Ancylostoma duodenale).

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about Staphylococcus aureus is CORRECT?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — It can be intracellular in nasal epithelial cells**

- **C. It can be intracellular in nasal epithelial cells** — S. aureus is a facultative intracellular pathogen that colonizes about 30% of the human population asymptomatically in the nares, either transiently or persistently, and can therefore be regarded as a human commensal as well, although carriage increases the risk of infection.
- **A. Methicillin is the commonly used antibiotic against it** — wrong; methicillin was previously used up until the emergence of methicillin-resistant S. aureus strains rendered it less effective, hence cefazolin and oxacillin are examples of more widely used antibiotics.
- **B. It is a motile organism** — wrong; Staphylococcus is nonmotile and does not form spores.
- **D. It does not contain antigenic polysaccharide** — wrong; most S. aureus strains of clinical importance have polysaccharide capsules, which inhibit phagocytosis by polymorphonuclear leukocytes unless specific antibodies are present.

questions.stem: Which of the following symptoms of UTI is the most common presentation of children under 2 years of age?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Fever**

- **B. Fever** — Oftentimes, fever is the only noticeable symptom of UTI in an infant, hence it is prudent to consider urinary tract infection in a baby or child under 5 with fever.
- **A, C, D. Abdominal pain, Headache, Urinary frequency** — may also occur in UTI in children, however is not commonly directly observed because infants could not localize the pain and communicate where it is coming from.

questions.stem: Which of the following fungal infections attack macrophages in the lungs and cause bloody sputum in 5% of cases?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Histoplasmosis**

- **C. Histoplasmosis** — caused by Histoplasma capsulatum. After inhalation, the conidia develop into yeast cells and are engulfed by alveolar macrophages, where they are able to replicate and produce symptoms that mimic tuberculosis.
- **A. Tuberculosis** — caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and is bacterial in etiology.
- **B. Chromoblastomycosis** — caused by subcutaneous mycoses and presents with cauliflower-like dermatologic lesions.
- **D. Blastomycosis** — caused by Blastomyces dermatitidis and presents as ulcerations and lytic bone lesions, mimicking squamous cell carcinoma.

choices.text: An accumulation of mutations in a single virus
An outbreak of influenza A virus

2+ strains of a virus or strains of 2+ viruses combine
into 1 virus

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is CORRECT regarding antigenic drift?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — An accumulation of mutations in a single virus**

- **A. An accumulation of mutations in a single virus** — Antigenic drift is caused by slow and progressive change in the composition of microorganisms resulting in altered immunological responses and susceptibility. Minor changes based on mutations in the genome RNA.
- Antigenic shift is caused by sudden change (sometimes major) in the molecular structure of a microorganism resulting in a new strain with little or no acquired immunity to these novel strains. Major changes based on the reassortment of segments of the genome RNA. Antigenic shifts cause outbreaks and pandemics.
- **B, C, D. An outbreak of influenza A virus; Relatively major changes in pathogen; 2+ strains of a virus or strains of 2+ viruses combine into 1 virus** — pertain to antigenic SHIFT, not antigenic drift. Although Choice B is considered technically correct, an outbreak of influenza A is not automatically due to antigenic drift (meaning influenza A being categorized as antigenic drift is not correct for all instances, it can be due to antigenic shift as well). Choice A would still be the best description for antigenic drift.

questions.stem: Which of the following psychiatric disorders is the most common among adolescents who are born with HIV infection and have since been on antiviral treatment?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Anxiety disorders**

- **A. Anxiety disorders** — On top of the increased risk of neuropsychiatric disorders HIV patients face, some antiviral medications used in HIV include anxiety disorder as a side effect (e.g. acyclovir and efavirenz). This is the most commonly encountered psychiatric condition in HIV. Some contributing factors include the stigma and managing the illness.
- **B. Obsessive compulsive** — disorder is present in other HIV patients and manifests as being careful with physical intimacy with intense fear.
- **C. Paranoia** — can also manifest in HIV infection, but less encountered compared to anxiety disorder.
- **D. Suicidal tendency** — seen in severe psychiatric cases and is considered a psychiatric emergency.

choices.text: Most common cause is S. aureus

questions.stem: Which of the following characteristics is NOT present in an HIV positive patient with osteomyelitis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Necrosis absent**

- **A. Most common cause is S. aureus** — In osteomyelitis, the primary focus of S. aureus growth is typically on a terminal blood vessel of the metaphysis of a long bone, leading to necrosis of bone and chronic suppuration.
- **B. Necrosis absent** — As stated above, there is necrosis of the bone, which means necrosis is NOT absent in HIV positive patients with osteomyelitis.
- **C. Often bilateral** — Causes of systemic host compromise include immunodeficiency disease such as HIV/AIDS. This predisposes the osteomyelitis to spread hematogenously, thereby occurring bilaterally.
- **D. Periosteal new bone formation** — a non-specific response of the periosteum due to underlying “irritation” such as that in osteomyelitis.

questions.stem: Diphtheria is an example of which of the following?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Toxemia**

- **D. Toxemia** — refers to the spread of toxins in the bloodstream by toxin-producing bacteria, of which C. diphtheriae is an example.
- **A. Bacteremia** — refers to the presence of bacteria in the bloodstream, not necessarily enough to produce clinical symptoms.
- **B. Pyemia** — refers to the presence of pyogenic bacteria in the blood.
- **C. Septicemia** — the presence of a significant amount of bacteria in the blood that may spread and replicate and cause severe symptoms.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is the reason for the higher fatality rate of second dengue fever infection than the first?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Preexisting dengue antibody formed complex with the virus promoting infection to more mononuclear cells**

- **D. Preexisting dengue antibody formed complex with the virus promoting infection to more mononuclear cells** — The pathogenesis of severe syndrome involves preexisting dengue antibodies. It is postulated that virus-antibody complexes are formed within a few days of the second dengue infection and that the non-neutralizing enhancing antibodies promote infection of higher numbers of mononuclear cells, followed by the release of inflammatory mediators and procoagulants leading to the disseminated intravascular coagulation seen in the hemorrhagic fever syndrome.
- **A. More medications are being given during the second attack thus more complications** — more aggressive management is warranted during the second infection, but this does not translate to more complications since monitoring would be done for these patients.
- **B. Patient has weaker immunity during the second attack as compared to the first** — not all patients have weaker immunity during the second attack in dengue. It would depend on a case-to-case basis and based on comorbidities.
- **C. Patient refuses to consult the hospital and does self-medication experienced from the first attack** — refusal to consult in the hospital and self-medication are more situational and is not the primary cause of higher fatality rate in second dengue infection.

questions.stem: Which of the following disorders is caused by the human T lymphocyte virus (HTLV)?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Adult T-cell leukemia lymphoma**

- **B. Adult T-cell leukemia lymphoma** — HTLV-1 has been established as the causative agent of adult T-cell leukemia-lymphomas (ATL) as well as tropical spastic paraparesis (a nervous system degenerative disorder).
- **A. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia** — exposure to radiation/chemo, associated with Down syndrome, and immunosuppression.
- **C. Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma** — may be associated with autoimmune diseases and viral infections.
- **D. Multiple sclerosis** — immune factors (autoimmune), environmental factors (vitamin D deficiency), and genetic associations (EBV).

questions.stem: Rafael 45/M consulted in a clinic due to acute swelling and pain of his left knee. On palpation, the left knee was not warm to touch and non-tender but positive for ballottement. Aspiration was done for 30cc of clear yellowish, non-purulent fluid which also relieved the patient of pain. What is the most useful diagnostic test to identify the organism involved?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Culture and sensitivity**

Suspicion of septic arthritis should be pursued with arthrocentesis and synovial fluid analysis, including WBC count and crystal analysis.

- **A. Culture and sensitivity** — Most important, as it plays a pivotal role in identifying the organism involved and hastens its eradication via targeted therapy.
- **B. Gram staining** — Can be done to identify the organism, but culture would yield more accurate results and growth of the organism.
- **C. Polymerase chain reaction** — Although PCR is utilized in other infections, culture remains the most sensitive diagnostic test.
- **D. Tuberculin test** — The PPD test is a skin test used to determine if an individual has been infected with TB, but it is not a reliable indicator of the infectiousness of the individual.

questions.stem: Zad presents at the clinic with “the worst sore throat he ever had”. He also complains of fatigue and anorexia. He is not immunocompromised and has not been hospitalized recently. He is febrile at 38°C and the tonsils are inflamed. There are few tender cervical lymph nodes bilaterally. No noted white lesions on the tongue or pharynx. A throat culture grows beta-hemolytic colonies on blood agar that are optochin-resistant. Which of the following is the most likely etiology?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Streptococcus pyogenes**

The most common infection caused by S. pyogenes is streptococcal sore throat or pharyngitis. In older children and adults, the disease is more acute and is characterized by intense nasopharyngitis, tonsillitis, and intense redness and edema of the mucous membranes, with purulent exudate; enlarged, tender cervical lymph nodes, and usually fever.

- **A. Parvovirus B19** — A virus that doesn't fulfill the culture findings; findings like this are more soon in bacteria, not viruses.
- **B. Epstein-Barr virus** — A virus that doesn't fulfill the culture findings; findings like this are more soon in bacteria, not viruses.
- **C. Streptococcus pneumoniae** — Wrong because it is optochin-sensitive.

questions.stem: Which of the following parasites is an example of a nematode?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Enterobius vermicularis**

- **A. Echinostoma ilocanum** — Trematode (fluke).
- **B. Enterobius vermicularis** — An intestinal nematode.
- **C. Metagonimus yokogawai** — Trematode (fluke).
- **D. Taenia solium** — Cestode (tapeworm).

questions.stem: How is dengue hemorrhagic fever treated?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Fluid replacement therapy**

- **A. Antiviral drug treatment** — Shows no benefit in the treatment of dengue.
- **B. Elimination of breeding places** — This is control, not treatment; control depends on anti-mosquito measures including elimination of breeding places and the use of insecticides.
- **C. Fluid replacement therapy** — One of the cornerstones of dengue management.
- **D. Vaccines** — Dengvaxia, the only approved dengue vaccine in the Philippines as of now, is more preventive than therapeutic.

questions.stem: What are the pathological hallmarks of dengue hemorrhagic fever?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Increased vascular permeability → plasma leakage into interstitial spaces → increased vasoactive cytokines → shock**

- The key pathological feature of dengue hemorrhagic fever is increased vascular permeability with plasma leakage into the interstitial spaces, associated with increased levels of vasoactive cytokines.
- **A. Saddle-back form of fever subsiding on 3rd day and rising again before 5-8 days**, **B. Enlarged lymph nodes and appearance of rashes on 3rd-4th day**, and **D. Myalgia and deep bone pain, back, joints, and eyeball** — These can be characteristic of dengue; however, the question asks which describes dengue HEMORRHAGIC fever specifically, so the best answer is C.

questions.stem: Ramji went drinking with raw mackerel soaked in salted vinegar as his pulutan. After 3 hours of drinking, he experienced severe pain on both legs. At the ER, the attending doctors noted bullous eruptions on his legs which progressed into necrosis of the surrounding skin. Laboratory data showed normal WBC but with elevated SGOT, SGPT, and creatinine phosphokinase. Which of the following is the most probable etiology of the patient’s condition?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Vibrio vulnificus**

Among the various non-cholera vibrios, V. vulnificus is a particularly virulent species and is primarily known to cause severe wound and soft tissue infections, as well as bacteremia/sepsis, rather than gastroenteritis. It is a free-living bacterium and part of the normal marine microbiota in association with bivalves and crustaceans.

- **A. Clostridium perfringens** — May cause gas gangrene (myonecrosis) and food poisoning. Transmission is from ingestion of contaminated (and undercooked) food like poultry and meat, or contact between soil and open wounds.
- **B. Salmonella typhi** — May cause typhoid fever and is transmitted via the oral-fecal route.
- **C. Streptococcus pyogenes** — May cause skin and soft tissue infections and pharyngitis. It is the most common cause of bacterial sore throat.

questions.stem: What is the most reliable diagnostic tool to be done on the biopsy material or exudates from an ulcerated lesion of sporotrichosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Fungal culture**

- The most reliable method of diagnosis for sporotrichosis is culture. Specimens are streaked on IMA or SDA containing antibacterial antibiotics and incubated at 25-30°C. The identification is confirmed by growth at 35°C and conversion to the yeast form.
- **A. Fluorescent antibody staining**, **B. Fungal cell wall stain**, and **D. Potassium hydroxide smear** — Other methods that are also utilized in identification of other fungi; however, culture is still the most reliable for sporotrichosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following CANNOT differentiate between pathogenic and non-pathogenic strains of Entamoeba?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Microscopy**

- **A. PCR analysis** — The gold standard in differentiating pathogenic E. histolytica from commensal E. dispar.
- **B. Microscopy** — In the context of amebiasis, microscopy is unable to distinguish the pathogenic E. histolytica from the commensal E. dispar.
- **C. Use of genetic markers** — The use of genetic markers and identification of DNA in stool is also diagnostic.
- **D. Enzyme immunoassay** — Detects the presence of the specific viral antigen of the different species.

questions.stem: Which of the following viruses can be vertically transmitted and is most commonly associated with deafness, cataracts, and patent ductus arteriosus?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Rubella**

- **A. Cytomegalovirus** — Hearing loss, seizure, petechial rash, chorioretinitis, and periventricular calcifications.
- **B. Herpes simplex virus** — Vesicular lesions are typically present, with more severe complications including encephalitis.
- **C. Rubella** — Congenital rubella findings include the classic triad of sensorineural deafness, cataracts, and patent ductus arteriosus.
- **D. Varicella-zoster virus** — Associated with limb hypoplasia, microcephaly, and ocular abnormalities like cataracts and chorioretinitis.

questions.stem: Which of the following clinical manifestations of anthrax disease has the highest mortality rate?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Inhalational anthrax**

- **A. Cutaneous anthrax** — Mortality ~20%; direct epidermal contact with spores causes formation of a malignant pustule with subsequent eschar and central necrosis.
- **B. Inhalational anthrax** — Mortality 80% or higher; inhaled spores from animals (woolsorter's disease) or from weaponized preparations (bioterrorism).
- **C. Gastrointestinal anthrax** — Mortality 25-75%; ingestion of live spores leads to UGI ulceration, edema, and sepsis in a rapidly-progressive course.
- **D. Injection anthrax** — Seen in heroin-injecting drug users; symptoms are likely similar to cutaneous anthrax. Mortality rate is around 35%.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is FALSE regarding rheumatic fever?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C** — the exception (not a true statement): **"Rheumatic fever may be associated with cutaneous streptococcal infections"**

- **A. Rheumatic fever is the most important cause of heart disease in children in developing countries** — Correct; rheumatic fever is the major cause of cardiovascular death in children and young adults in countries that have poor medical attention.
- **B. Rheumatic fever has tendency to be reactivated by recurrent streptococcal infections** — Correct; Group A, beta-hemolytic streptococcal pharyngitis in a child who has recovered from rheumatic fever is likely to reactivate the disease, and the second attack is likely to mimic the first in its manifestations.
- **C. Rheumatic fever may be associated with cutaneous streptococcal infections** — Not true; it is not associated with cutaneous streptococcal infections.
- **D. The more severe streptococcal sore throat is, the greater chance of developing rheumatic fever** — Correct; in general, patients with more severe streptococcal sore throats have a greater chance of developing rheumatic fever.

questions.stem: Which of the following microorganisms is the most common etiology of urinary tract infection (UTI)?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Escherichia coli**

- **A. Citrobacter** — Not as common, but associated with hospital-acquired UTI.
- **B. Escherichia coli** — The most common cause of urinary tract infection; accounts for approximately 90% of first urinary tract infections in young women.
- **C. Proteus mirabilis** — Most common cause of catheter-associated UTI.
- **D. Providencia rettgeri** — Seen in elderly patients with prolonged indwelling catheter use.

questions.stem: How long does the clinical illness of a primary HSV-1 infection last? This typically presents with fever, sore throat, vesicular, and ulcerative lesions involving buccal and gingival mucosa as gingivitis, pharyngitis, tonsillitis, and localized lymphadenopathy.
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — 2-3 weeks**

- Primary HSV-1 infections are usually asymptomatic. The incubation period is short (3-5 days, with a range of 2-12 days), and clinical illness lasts 2-3 weeks. Symptoms include fever, sore throat, vesicular and ulcerative lesions, gingivostomatitis, and malaise.
- **A. Less than 1 week** — Too short for the clinical illness.
- **C. 4-5 weeks** and **D. 6-8 weeks** — Too long for the illness.

questions.stem: Gio 58/M, a known chain smoker, suffered a sharp chest pain, low to moderate grade fever of almost 2 weeks associated with night sweats and fatigue. On PE, an audible friction rub was heard. Which of the following diseases is the MOST probable cause?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Tuberculous pericarditis**

- **A. Constrictive pericarditis** — Results from chronic pericardial inflammation secondary to trauma or surgery, autoimmune disease, and infection such as tuberculosis in developing countries.
- **B. Restrictive cardiomyopathy** — Leading causes include cardiac amyloidosis, cardiac sarcoidosis, and cardiac hemochromatosis.
- **C. Tuberculous pericarditis** — Clinical features of tuberculous pericardial effusion include fever, dyspnea, precordial pain, and pericardial rub. It usually develops insidiously (2-week history in the case), presenting with non-specific systemic symptoms such as fever, night sweats, fatigue, and weight loss. An audible friction rub is highly specific for acute pericarditis.
- **D. Viral myocarditis** — Presents with a 7-14-day history of flu-like illness. Adults typically present with dyspnea, chest pain, and arrhythmias.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the cardinal pathogenic feature of an HIV infection?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Depletion of T lymphocytes**

The cardinal feature of HIV infection is the depletion of T helper-inducer lymphocytes — the result of HIV replication in this population of lymphocytes, as well as the death of uninfected T cells by indirect mechanism. This is why obtaining a CD4 cell count is critical in HIV patients for prognostication and to determine immune function.

- **A. Cytolysis of monocytes**, **C. Inactivation of macrophage**, and **D. Loss of neutrophils** — All lead to opportunistic infections. They may be observed in other conditions, but are not the cardinal pathogenic features of HIV infection.

questions.stem: What bacterial species are differentiated by the coagulase test?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Staphylococcus aureus from Staphylococcus epidermidis**

- Coagulase test is used to further differentiate catalase-positive staphylococci. S. aureus is coagulase-positive while S. epidermidis is coagulase-negative.
- **B. Staphylococcus epidermidis from Neisseria meningitidis** — S. epidermidis is gram-positive while N. meningitidis is gram-negative.
- **C. Streptococcus pyogenes from Staphylococcus aureus** — S. pyogenes is catalase-negative while S. aureus is catalase-positive.
- **D. Streptococcus pyogenes from Enterococcus faecalis** — S. pyogenes is beta-hemolytic while E. faecalis is gamma-hemolytic.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is CORRECT about the treatment of syphilis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Penicillin remains to be the treatment of choice for syphilis**

- **A. After an effective treatment, patient is no longer susceptible to syphilitic infection** — Incorrect; having syphilis once does not protect patients from getting the disease again. Even after successful treatment, patients might still be re-infected by unprotected sexual contact. The re-infection rate of syphilis is high, especially among high-risk populations.
- **B. Serum antibody testing can be used to determine result of treatment of neurosyphilis** — Incorrect; antibody tests (FTA-ABS) are confirmatory tests and stay positive throughout life — they are not used to monitor therapy response. Non-treponemal tests (RPR, VDRL) are for screening and are used to monitor treatment response.
- **C. Penicillin remains to be the treatment of choice for syphilis** — Correct; penicillin G remains the treatment in all stages of syphilis.
- **D. Spontaneous healing of an untreated primary lesion indicates cure from the disease** — Incorrect; even without treatment, primary lesions will go away without scarring. If untreated, primary syphilis can progress to secondary syphilis, which has many clinical and histopathological findings.

questions.stem: Which of the following diagnostic tests can be done for tetanus infection?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Anaerobic culture of contaminated tissue**

- **A. Anaerobic culture of contaminated tissue** — Anaerobic culture of tissues from contaminated wounds may yield C. tetani, but neither preventive nor therapeutic use of antitoxin should ever be withheld pending such demonstration; this is done to isolate and correlate with clinical findings.
- **B. Blood culture** — Not an accurate diagnostic test for tetanus infection; anaerobic culture of the wound is preferred.
- **C. Serology** — Can detect antibodies in tetanus infection, but does not confirm active infection.
- **D. Toxin production and neutralization test** — Confirms exposure to tetanus toxin but is not routinely performed and does not confirm active infection.

questions.stem: Which of the following species of Plasmodium is the most pathogenic and can cause malaria?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — P. falciparum**

There are five main species of Plasmodium that cause malaria in humans. The two most common species are P. vivax and P. falciparum.

- **A. P. falciparum** — The most pathogenic, and can cause the most severe complications; it can cause cerebral malaria and has multiple drug resistance.
- **B. P. malariae** — Affects old RBCs and has the lowest parasitemia among Plasmodium species. It does not cause relapse and has few drug resistance.
- **C. P. ovale** and **D. P. vivax** — Affect young RBCs. They cause relapse but have few drug resistance.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best prognosticating factor of the long-term clinical outcome of an HIV infection?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Plasma viral load**

- **A. CD4 lymphocyte count** — The best predictor of short-term risk of developing an opportunistic disease.
- **B. Level of antibody** — Not that useful in prognosticating the long-term outcome of an HIV infection.
- **C. Plasma viral load** — Appears to be the best predictor of long-term clinical outcome.
- **D. Timing of antiviral therapy** — Especially when done early, will lead to a better prognosis for the disease, but is not the most important factor for long-term outcome.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the carrier state of Neisseria meningitidis is CORRECT?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Nasopharyngeal swab cultures are suitable for surveys**

The typical specimens for isolation of N. meningitidis include blood for culture and CSF for smear and culture. Puncture material or biopsies from petechiae may be taken for smear and culture. NPS cultures are suitable for carrier surveys.

- **A. Carriers exhibit symptoms of upper respiratory tract infection** — Not always true, because carriers may form part of the transient microbiota without producing symptoms and/or disease.
- **B. More often than not, they progress to meningitis** — Incorrect; invasive meningococcal disease occurs in only a small number of individuals who acquired the organism and are transient carriers.
- **D. Penicillin is effective in eradicating the carrier states** — Incorrect; penicillin G is the drug of choice for treating patients with meningococcal disease, not used in carrier states.

S. stercoralis undergoes free-living life cycle in soil

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about Strongyloides stercoralis is INCORRECT?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B** — the exception (not a true statement): **"S. stercoralis is acquired by ingestion of eggs"**

- **A. Migrating larvae of S. stercoralis induce marked eosinophilia** — Correct; eosinophilia may be detected during migration of larvae through perianal skin or intestinal mucosa.
- **B. S. stercoralis is acquired by ingestion of eggs** — Not true; Strongyloides stercoralis infection is acquired through penetration of intact skin by infective filariform larvae.
- **C. S. stercoralis produces filariform larvae** — Correct; S. stercoralis produces filariform larvae, which penetrate through the skin.
- **D. S. stercoralis undergoes free-living life cycle in soil** — Correct; the larvae of these free-living forms, under certain environmental conditions such as temperature, can develop into parasitic forms.

Strongyloides can produce autoinfection if newly hatched larvae never exit the host but, instead, undergo their molts within the intestine.

questions.stem: What is the incubation period of the enteric fever illness caused by Salmonella Typhi?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — 10-14 days**

- After an incubation period of 10-14 days (5-21 days according to HPIM), typhoid or enteric fever presents with fever, malaise, headache, constipation, bradycardia, and myalgia.
- On the other hand, the incubation period of enterocolitis from Salmonella typhimurium or Salmonella enteritidis is 8-48 hours (up to 7 days according to Jawetz) after ingestion of contaminated food or water, presenting with nausea, headache, vomiting, and profuse diarrhea.
- **A. 3-5 days**, **C. 20-24 days**, and **D. 24-28 days** — Do not coincide with enteric fever's correct incubation period of 5-21 days.

questions.stem: How is the clinical diagnosis of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) confirmed?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Laparoscopic visualization**

Definitive criteria for the diagnosis of PID include histopathologic evidence of endometritis on endometrial biopsy, transvaginal sonography or MRI showing thickened fluid-filled tubes (with or without free pelvic fluid or tubo-ovarian complex), and laparoscopic abnormalities consistent with PID.

- **A. Culture of discharge** and **B. Gram stain of discharge** — Can also be utilized for diagnosis of PID through identification of the organism; however, laparoscopy remains the most definitive method of diagnosing PID.
- **D. Regular pelvic examination** — Aids in suspicion of PID, but would still need confirmatory diagnostic tests to clinch the diagnosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following parasites can cause stools described as steatorrheic?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Giardia lamblia**

- **A. Balantidium coli** — Persistent diarrhea, abdominal pain.
- **B. Chilomastix mesnili** — Non-pathogenic; presence of cysts or trophozoites may be an indicator of fecal contamination.
- **C. Entamoeba histolytica** — Amebic colitis, amebic liver abscess.
- **D. Giardia lamblia** — Chronic infection is characterized by steatorrhea, or the passage of greasy stools.

Choices A, B, and C are incorrect because they do not typically present with greasy stools.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the etiologic agent of yellow fever?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Flavivirus**

- **A. Borrelia recurrentis** — Causative agent of relapsing fever.
- **B. Flavivirus** — Yellow fever virus is the prototype member of the Flaviviridae family.
- **C. Leptospira interrogans** — Causative agent of leptospirosis.
- **D. Plasmodium falciparum** — Causative agent of malaria.

questions.stem: What is the treatment for subcutaneous mycosis caused by sporotrichosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Oral itraconazole**

Treatment of sporotrichosis depends on whether it is only subcutaneous or already systemic. The treatment of choice for subcutaneous sporotrichosis is oral itraconazole or another azole.

- **A. Amphotericin B** — Given for systemic sporotrichosis.
- **B. Infection is self-limited** — Incorrect; sporotrichosis infection is not self-limited and should be treated with antifungal drugs.
- **D. Potassium iodide saturated solution** — Mentioned in some studies for the treatment of sporotrichosis, but antifungal drugs are the mainstay of treatment.

questions.stem: Which of the following complications is the LEAST likely to occur if Staphylococcus aureus disseminates and bacteremia ensues?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D** — the least likely complication: **"Pyelonephritis"**

Staphylococcus aureus is associated with many manifestations such as acute endocarditis, meningitis, pneumonia, osteomyelitis, gastroenteritis, Ritter disease, and toxic shock syndrome.

- **A. Endocarditis**, **B. Meningitis**, and **C. Osteomyelitis** — All are recognized complications of S. aureus bacteremia.
- **D. Pyelonephritis** — Since the question asks for the LEAST likely complication, the answer is pyelonephritis.

questions.stem: Which of the following groups of streptococci is the etiologic agent in acute and subacute endocarditis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Viridans Streptococcus**

- In the course of bacteremia, viridans streptococci (or enterococci, and rarely pneumococci) may settle on normal or previously deformed heart valves, producing acute endocarditis. More frequently, the viridans streptococci are associated with a subacute course. Streptococcus bovis may also cause infective endocarditis in patients with gastrointestinal malignancy. Enterococcus faecalis may cause infective endocarditis in patients post-genitourinary or gastrointestinal surgery. Among the choices, only viridans streptococci is commonly encountered in infective endocarditis.
- **A. Streptococcus agalactiae** — Causes UTI in pregnant women, and neonatal pneumonia, sepsis, and meningitis.
- **B. Streptococcus pneumoniae** — A common causative agent of pneumonia; does not commonly cause endocarditis.
- **C. Streptococcus pyogenes** — May cause skin and soft tissue infections such as impetigo, erysipelas, and cellulitis. It can also cause pharyngitis (most common bacterial cause).

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is FALSE about Corynebacterium diphtheriae?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A** — the exception (not a true statement): **"C. diphtheriae are spore-forming Gram-positive bacilli"**

- **A. C. diphtheriae are spore-forming Gram-positive bacilli** — Not true; C. diphtheriae are non-spore-forming Gram-positive bacilli.
- **B. It is Gram-positive club-shaped rods with metachromatic granules with aniline dyes** — Correct; Corynebacterium diphtheriae are Gram-positive club-shaped rods (metachromatic granules on Löffler media).
- **C. It is spread by droplets or by contact to susceptible individuals** — Correct; transmitted via respiratory droplets.
- **D. One type of colony, var gravis, of C. diphtheriae is more severe form of the disease** — Correct; in general, var gravis tends to produce more severe disease than var mitis, but similar illness can be produced by all types.

questions.stem: What is the preferred test for detecting Trichomonas vaginalis because of its high sensitivity?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Nucleic acid amplification test**

Trichomonas culture, DNA probes, and NAATs are much more sensitive in diagnosing trichomoniasis.

- **B. Wet mount** — Can also be done and is more convenient; however, the question asks which has high sensitivity, so NAAT is the better answer.
- **C. Gram staining** — Not routinely used for diagnosis of Trichomonas vaginalis, as this is more utilized for bacterial infections.
- **D. Pap smear** — Used for screening of cervical cancer, not Trichomonas infection.

choices.text: A host immune response to viral antigens
