questions.stem: A 34 year old G1P0 patient came in for BPS screening. Which among the following DOES NOT constitute a score of 2?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — 2 discrete body or limb movements within 40 minutes**

#### Biophysical Profile (BPP)

| Component | Score 2 | Score 0 |
|---|---|---|
| Nonstress test (a) | ≥ 2 accelerations of ≥ 15 beats/min for ≥ 15 sec within 20-40 min | 0 or 1 acceleration within 20-40 min |
| Fetal breathing | ≥ 1 episode of rhythmic breathing lasting ≥ 30 sec within 30 min | < 30 sec of breathing within 30 min |
| Fetal movement | ≥ 3 discrete body or limb movements within 40 min | < 3 discrete movements |
| Fetal tone | ≥ 1 episode of extremity extension and subsequent return to flexion | 0 extension/flexion events |
| Amniotic fluid volume (b) | A pocket of amniotic fluid that measures at least 2 cm in two planes perpendicular to each other (2 x 2 cm pocket) | Largest single vertical pocket ≤ 2 cm |

(a) May be omitted if all four sonographic components are normal.
(b) Further evaluation warranted, regardless of biophysical composite score, if largest vertical amniotic fluid pocket ≤ 2 cm.

- **A, B, D** — Correct.
- **C** — Incorrect. Should be ≥3 discrete body or limb movements within 30 minutes.

questions.stem: What is the most common site of implantation in ectopic pregnancy?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Ampulla**

- **A. Interstitial** — This site comprises only 2-3%.
- **B. Isthmus** — This site comprises only 12%.
- **C. Ampulla** — This is the most common site of tubal pregnancies at 70%. Tubal pregnancies comprise 95% of cases of ectopic pregnancy.
- **D. Fimbriae** — This site only comprises 11%.

choices.text: Advise patient for possible exploratory laparotomy

questions.stem: Bea 22/F consulted at your clinic due to missed menses. She notes that she just started experiencing right sided pelvic pain and some vaginal bleeding. Her vitals were stable and further work-up was done. On ultrasound, there was an empty uterine cavity and the presence of a gestational sac in the fallopian tube. What is the best management of her case?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Start methotrexate therapy**

This is a case of ectopic pregnancy with the classic triad of vaginal bleeding, abdominal pain, and missed menses. The choices are the different management choices for the case.

- **A. Expectant management** — May be done in cases of ectopic pregnancy when the following criteria is met:
  - Clinically and hemodynamically stable
  - Minimal abdominal pain
  - bHCG <1000 IU/L
  - No gestational sac

  Since the case shows a gestational sac on the ultrasound, this would not be the best management choice.

- **B. Start methotrexate therapy** — Medical management with methotrexate is the best choice for this patient. She is hemodynamically stable without any contraindications for methotrexate such as:
  - Sensitivity to MTX
  - Evidence of tubal rupture
  - Breast feeding
  - Intrauterine pregnancy
  - Hepatic, renal, or hematological dysfunction
  - Peptic ulcer disease
  - Active pulmonary disease
  - Immunodeficiency

- **C. Advise patient for salpingostomy** — Surgical management may be done when patient have the following indications for surgical management:
  - Hemodynamic instability
  - Impending or ongoing rupture
  - Contraindications to MTX
  - Failed medical therapy

  Since the patient does not have these indications, surgical management would not be the best management choice.

- **D. Advise patient for possible exploratory laparotomy** — Similar to the previous choice, surgical management is not indicated for this patient. An exploratory laparotomy is considered when the patient is unstable.

#### Medical Management in Ectopic Pregnancy

- Methotrexate – folic acid antagonist; binds to dihydrofolate reductase which reduces dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate (active form) → arrest de novo purine and pyrimidine production → arrests DNA, RNA, protein synthesis
  - Overall success rate with MTX: 90%
- Avoid the following while on MTX:
  - Folic-acid containing supplements
  - NSAIDs – reduces renal blood flow, delays drug excretion
  - Alcohol – may elevate liver enzymes
  - Sunlight – may provoke MTX-related dermatitis
  - Sexual activity – may rupture ectopic pregnancy
- Factors for success: small ectopic
  - ≤ 3.5 cm
  - Serum β-hCG level < 5,000 mIU/mL
  - No fetal heartbeat
  - Reliable follow-up, compliant, motivated
  - Single dose regimen (50 mg/m2) IM methotrexate vs multidose regimen (88% vs 93% effectiveness)
  - β-hCG levels rise after methotrexate therapy, then fall 10–15% after 4–7 days

questions.stem: A 23 year old G2P1(0111) mother came into the ER for sudden vaginal bleeding with meaty material. On history, she has a history of irregular menses and noted that her last menstrual period was 2 months ago. On IE, you noted a dilated cervix. What is your diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Incomplete abortion**

- **A. Complete abortion** — Expulsion of products of conception (POC, meaty material described in the case) before 20 weeks. This is wrong since her cervix was dilated. In complete abortion, the cervix is closed.
- **B. Inevitable abortion** — No expulsion of POC, but vaginal bleeding and dilation of cervix that will unlikely result in pregnancy. This is wrong since the case had the presence of passage of POC.
- **C. Incomplete abortion** — Partial expulsion before 20 weeks. This is the answer since there was passage of POC and dilated cervix on IE.
- **D. Threatened abortion** — Any vaginal bleeding before 20 weeks, without dilation of cervix or expulsion of any POC. This is wrong since the case had both dilation of cervix and expulsion of POC.

#### Types of Abortion

| Type | Cervix | POC in Utero | FHT | Plan |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Threatened | Closed | (+) | (+) | Bed rest, Tocolysis |
| Missed | Closed | (+) | (-) | Cervical ripening +/- curettage |
| Inevitable | Open | (+), with ruptured membranes | (+)/(-) | Expectant, Oxytocin, Curettage |
| Incomplete | Open | Partial expulsion of POC, with passage of meaty material | (-) | Curettage |
| Complete | Closed | Not appreciated | No signs of pregnancy | Observe |

**Mnemonic: "All I's Open"** — Those abortion types starting with the letter I all have OPEN cervix, hence the mnemonic all I's (eyes) open.

questions.stem: A 35 year old G4P1(1021) mother came in due for first prenatal checkup. On IE, you noted no bleeding and a closed cervix. Initial ultrasound scan taken 2 weeks ago showed a gestational sac with yolk sac but on your ultrasound you note no embryo with a heartbeat. What is your diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Missed abortion**

#### Types of Abortion

| Type | Cervix | POC in Utero | FHT | Plan |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Threatened | Closed | (+) | (+) | Bed rest, Tocolysis |
| Missed | Closed | (+) | (-) | Cervical ripening +/- curettage |
| Inevitable | Open | (+), with ruptured membranes | (+)/(-) | Expectant, Oxytocin, Curettage |
| Incomplete | Open | Partial expulsion of POC, with passage of meaty material | (-) | Curettage |
| Complete | Closed | Not appreciated | No signs of pregnancy | Observe |

- **A. Inevitable abortion** — No expulsion of POC, but vaginal bleeding and dilation of cervix will unlikely result in pregnancy. This is wrong since the patient has no signs and symptoms of vaginal bleeding and dilation of cervix.
- **B. Induced abortion** — Termination with surgery of medication of a live fetus that has not reached viability. This is wrong since there is no mention of any substance or surgery done.
- **C. Threatened abortion** — Any vaginal bleeding before 20 weeks, without dilation of cervix or expulsion of any POC. This is wrong since there would still be FHT (see table above).
- **D. Missed abortion** — Death of embryo or fetus before 20 weeks with complete retention of POC. This is correct since the mother did not note any passage of meaty material (POC), and initial ultrasound showed a POC in utero but recent ultrasound showed no FHT. Plan in this case would be cervical ripening with or without curettage.

Three or more unexplained consecutive
spontaneous miscarriages under 20 weeks AOG

One or more unexplained fetal deaths more than 10
weeks AOG

Severe preeclampsia or placental insufficiency
necessitating delivery before 37 weeks

Two or more episodes of arterial, venous, or small-

questions.stem: Which is the correct clinical criteria of Antiphospholipid Antibody Syndrome (APAS)?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — One or more unexplained fetal deaths more than 10 weeks AOG**

- **A. Three or more unexplained consecutive spontaneous miscarriages under 20 weeks AOG** — Incorrect. Should be under 10 weeks not 20 weeks.
- **B. One or more unexplained fetal deaths more than 10 weeks AOG** — Correct. This is one of the clinical criteria of APAS.
- **C. Severe preeclampsia or placental insufficiency necessitating delivery before 37 weeks** — Incorrect. Should be before 34 weeks not 37 weeks.
- **D. Two or more episodes of arterial, venous, or small-vessel thrombosis in any tissue** — Incorrect. Should be one or more episodes. One episode is enough for this criteria.

#### Antiphospholipid Antibody Syndrome

**Clinical criteria**
- Obstetrical
  - ≥3 unexplained consecutive spontaneous miscarriages <10 weeks AOG, OR
  - ≥1 unexplained fetal death(s) ≥10 weeks AOG, OR
  - Severe preeclampsia or placental insufficiency necessitating delivery before 34 weeks
- Vascular
  - ≥1 episode(s) of arterial, venous, or small-vessel thrombosis in any tissue

**Laboratory criteria**
- Presence of lupus anticoagulant according to guidelines of the International Society on Thrombosis and Hemostasis, OR
- Medium or high serum levels of IgG or IgM anticardiolipin antibodies, OR
- Anti-β2 glycoprotein-I IgG or IgM antibody

**Notes on diagnosis**
- At least one clinical and one laboratory criteria must be present for diagnosis
- Laboratory tests must be positive on two or more occasions at least 12 weeks apart

questions.stem: A 30 year old G2P1 (1001) mother came into the ER for abdominal pain, associated with persistent vaginal bleeding. On history, you note that she has been amenorrheic for the past 6 weeks. She has also been experiencing mild shoulder pain, more evident on inspiration. Your initial diagnosis is ectopic pregnancy. What could the shoulder pain indicate?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Hemoperitoneum**

Before rupture, symptoms and signs of ectopic pregnancy are subtle or absent. The classic triad is amenorrhea that is followed by pain and vaginal bleeding.

- **A. Tubal rupture** — Usually indicated by lower abdominal pain and pelvic pain, usually severe and frequently described as sharp, stabbing or tearing.
- **B. Hemoperitoneum** — Neck or shoulder pain, especially on inspiration, develops in women with diaphragmatic irritation from a sizeable hemoperitoneum.
- **C. Hypovolemia** — Hemorrhage-related hypovolemia is usually reflected by vertigo and syncope.
- **D. Incomplete abortion** — Usually presents as profuse vaginal bleeding and is occasionally seen with tubal gestations.

choices.text:
50% higher risk of spontaneous abortion (SAB) on
succeeding pregnancies compared to normal
pregnancies

Risk of SAB depends on the genetic makeup of
abortus

Late abortions are often caused by abnormal
chromosomes

questions.stem: Which statement about pregnancy loss is true
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Risk of SAB depends on the genetic makeup of abortus**

- **A. 50% higher risk of spontaneous abortion (SAB) on succeeding pregnancies compared to normal pregnancies** — Risk of spontaneous abortion (SAB):
  - After one prior SAB, 20–25%
  - After two consecutive SABs, 25–30%
  - After three consecutive SABs, 30–35%

- **B. Risk of SAB depends on the genetic makeup of abortus** —
  - More than 80% of spontaneous abortions occur within the first 12 weeks of gestation
  - 60–80% of SABs in first trimester are associated with abnormal chromosomes, 95% are due to maternal gametogenesis errors
  - 50-60% usually due to autosomal trisomy

- **C. 5-10% of pregnancies undergo spontaneous abortion** — 15-25% of pregnancies undergo SAB, not 5-10%.

- **D. Late abortions are often caused by abnormal chromosomes** — Abnormal chromosomes do NOT often cause late abortions. First trimester abortions are the ones more associated with chromosomal abnormalities.

#### Some Causes of Midtrimester Spontaneous Pregnancy Loss

- **Fetal anomalies** — Structural, Chromosomal
- **Placental causes** — Abruption, previa; Vasculopathy; Chorioamnionitis
- **Maternal disorders** — Autoimmune, Infections, Metabolic
- **Uterine defects** — Congenital, Leiomyomas, Incompetent cervix

A partial mole has a higher malignant potential than
a complete mole

There is an extra paternal set of chromosomes in
complete moles.

The most common karyotype for complete moles is
46,XX

A uterine size that is larger than its date is usually
observed for partial moles.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements regarding molar pregnancy is true?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — The most common karyotype for complete moles is 46,XX**

- **A. A partial mole has a higher malignant potential than a complete mole** — Incorrect. A complete mole has more malignant potential than a partial mole. The rate of subsequent GTN is 15-20% compared to 1-5% respectively. Risk factors for persistent trophoblastic disease are the following:
  - Older maternal age
  - Baseline b-hCG levels >100,000 mIU/mL
  - Theca lutein cysts > 6 cm
  - Large for AOG uterine sizes (14 to 16 weeks)
  - Slow decline in b-hCG
  - May give chemoprophylaxis: methotrexate + folinic acid/dactinomycin

- **B. There is an extra paternal set of chromosomes in complete moles** — Incorrect. The extra paternal set is present in partial moles because it is the fertilization of a normal ovum by two sperms simultaneously. Meanwhile, a complete mole has all paternally derived chromosomes because it results from the fertilization of an enucleated ovum or empty egg.

- **C. The most common karyotype for complete moles is 46,XX** — This is correct. As mentioned, both these chromosomes are paternally driven. Partial moles have the karyotype 69,XXY/XXX (rarely XYY).

- **D. A uterine size that is larger than its date is usually observed for partial moles** — Incorrect. Partial moles will have a uterine that is small for dates. Complete moles would usually be larger for dates.

choices.text: Uterus is typically small for gestational age
The most common karyotype is 46 XX
Marked trophoblastic atypia can be present

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT regarding complete molar pregnancy?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Uterus is typically small for gestational age**

- **A. Uterus is typically small for gestational age** — The uterine size of patients with a complete molar pregnancy is usually 50% larger for dates. On the other hand, partial moles would have a uterus smaller than dates. The rest of the statements are CORRECT regarding complete molar pregnancy.

#### Complete vs. Partial Mole

| Category | Feature | Complete Mole (90%) | Partial Mole (10%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Genetics | Most common karyotype | 46,XX | 69,XXY/XXX (or XYY – rare) |
| Genetics | Chromosomal origin | All paternally derived (androgenesis) | Extra paternal set |
| Pathology | Coexistent fetus, amnion | Absent | Often present |
| Pathology | Fetal RBCs | Absent | Often present |
| Pathology | Chorionic villi / villous edema | Hydropic, widespread | Few hydropic, focal |
| Pathology | Trophoblastic proliferation | Slight to severe | Focal, slight to moderate |
| Pathology | Trophoblast atypia | Marked | Mild |
| Pathology | p57KIP2 | Negative | Positive |
| Clinical presentation | Associated embryo | None | Present |
| Clinical presentation | Diagnosis | Molar gestation | Missed abortion |
| Clinical presentation | Medical complications (a) | Uncommon | Rare |
| Clinical presentation | Uterine size | Large for dates | Small for dates |
| Clinical presentation | Theca lutein cysts | 25-30% | Rare |
| Clinical presentation | hCG levels | High (>100,000 mIU/mL) | Slightly elevated (<100,000 mIU/mL) |
| Malignant potential | Rate of subsequent GTN | 15-20% | 1-5% |
| Follow-up | Weeks to normal hCG | 9 weeks | 7 weeks |

(a) Hyperemesis gravidarum, early preeclampsia, hyperthyroidism, anemia, excessive uterine size, and infection.

questions.stem: The following pairs of fetal presentation and its respective reference point are true except:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Brow: orbital ridge**

- **A. Sinciput: anterior fontanel** — Correct.
- **B. Brow: orbital ridge** — Incorrect. The reference point of the brow presentation is between the orbital ridge and anterior fontanel. The head was partially extended.
- **C. Breech: sacrum** — Correct.
- **D. Face: mentum** — Correct.

questions.stem: What fetal presentation is often mistaken as face presentation?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Frank**

- **A. Brow** — Incorrect. The fetal head is extended in both face and brow presentations. Brow presentation can sometimes be mistaken for face presentation due to the fetal neck being less extended in brow presentation compared to face presentation.
- **B. Frank** — Correct. The frank breech presentation is the most common type of breech presentation where the thighs are flexed, legs are extended over the anterior surface of the baby (the feet lie in proximity to the head). The fetal buttocks are most often mistaken for a face presentation because both involve soft tissues and an orifice that can be confused during vaginal examination. These can be differentiated by palpating the hard orbital ridges and mouth in a face presentation vs the anus and ischial tuberosities in a breech presentation.
- **C. Footling** — Incorrect. In footling breech presentation, one or both feet is/are below the breech. The presenting part is the foot and easily differentiated versus the face.
- **D. Shoulder** — Incorrect. In shoulder presentation, the acromion process is palpated in the cervix with the shoulder or acromion as the usual presenting part. This is also differentiated versus the face presentation.

questions.stem: An 18 year old G1P0 mother arrived in the emergency room. After hooking her to the toco, you noted a sinusoidal pattern on the cardiotocograph. What does this indicate?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Anemia**

- **A. Head compression** — Incorrect. This results in early decelerations.
- **B. Anemia** — Correct. This causes a sinusoidal pattern. Anemia results from fetomaternal hemorrhage. The patient could have presented to the emergency room with heavy vaginal bleeding.
- **C. Placental insufficiency** — Incorrect. This results in late decelerations.
- **D. Cord compression** — Incorrect. This results in variable decelerations.

#### Mnemonic: VEAL CHOP

| Letter | CTG Pattern | Cause |
|---|---|---|
| V | Variable decelerations | Cord compression |
| E | Early decelerations | Head compression |
| A | Accelerations | Oxygenation is good |
| L | Late decelerations | Placental insufficiency |

questions.stem: After a vaginal delivery, you noted that there was a laceration involving the anal sphincter but spares the rectal mucosa. What degree of perineal laceration is present?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Third degree**

- **A. First degree** — Incorrect. Involvement is up to mucosa or skin.
- **B. Second degree** — Incorrect. This extends into perineal body, spares anal sphincter.
- **C. Third degree** — Correct. This extends through anal sphincter. It is further divided into:
  - IIIa: <50% of external anal sphincter
  - IIIb: >50% of external anal sphincter
  - IIIc: Both external and internal sphincter
- **D. Fourth degree** — Incorrect. This involves the rectal mucosa. "Buttonhole" fourth degree laceration: a laceration through the rectal mucosa into the vagina, but with sphincter still intact.

questions.stem: How is the Rubin Maneuver performed?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Pressure is placed on the anterior shoulder towards the anterior chest wall of the fetus to free the impacted shoulder**

- **A. Pressure is applied to the clavicle to the clavicle of the baby’s anterior shoulder to rotate it** — Wood corkscrew maneuver.
- **B. Pressure is placed on the anterior shoulder towards the anterior chest wall of the fetus to free the impacted shoulder** — This describes the Rubin I maneuver.
- **C. Hyperflexion of maternal hips towards the maternal abdomen to decrease the pelvic inclination** — This describes the McRoberts maneuver.
- **D. Sweeping posterior arm across the chest to rotate the bisacromial diameter to an oblique diameter resulting in freeing the anterior shoulder** — This describes the delivery of the posterior arm or shoulder.

questions.stem: Which is NOT an indication for cesarean delivery?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Prior myomectomy**

- **A. Prior myomectomy** — Correct. Only select prior surgeries such as full thickness myomectomy, trachelectomy, and pelvic reconstructive surgery are indications for CS.
- **B. Placenta accreta** — Incorrect. This is a maternal indication for CS, others include the following:
  - Prior cesarean delivery
  - Abnormal placentation (e.g. placenta accreta)
  - Prior classical hysterotomy
  - Unknown uterine scar type
  - Uterine incision dehiscence
  - Select prior surgeries (full-thickness myomectomy, trachelectomy, pelvic reconstructive surgery)
  - Genital tract obstructive mass (e.g. tumor previa)
  - Invasive cervical cancer
  - HIV or HSV infection
  - Perimortem delivery
- **C. Macrosomia** — Incorrect. This is a fetal indication for CS, others include:
  - Nonreassuring fetal status
  - Malpresentation
  - Macrosomia
  - Congenital anomaly
  - Abnormal umbilical cord Doppler study
  - Thrombocytopenia
  - Prior neonatal birth trauma
- **D. Failed operative vaginal delivery** — Incorrect. This is a maternal-fetal indication for CS, others include:
  - CPD
  - Failed OVD
  - Placenta previa or placental abruption

questions.stem: Which of the following drugs are used in the induction of labor?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Dinoprostone**

- **A. Indomethacin** — Incorrect. This is an example of an NSAID that inhibits prostaglandins. Anti-prostaglandin agents inhibit contractions and may halt labor.
- **B. Dinoprostone** — Correct, this is an example of Prostaglandin E2. This is used for induction of labor as Dinoprostone gel or insert. Oxytocin is then used 6-12 hours after gel administration or 30 minutes after insert removal.
- **C. Terbutaline** — Incorrect. This is an example of a B-mimetics that is used for preterm labor to decrease contractions. Mechanism of action involves increased cAMP levels → calcium sequestered in sarcoplasmic reticulum → decreased free calcium ions and uterine contractions.
- **D. Atosiban** — Incorrect. This is an example of an oxytocin antagonist also used as a tocolytic.

questions.stem: A 26 year old G2P1 (0101) at 22 weeks AOG presents with preterm uterine contractions, stable maternal and fetal vital signs, and an intact BOW. Her cervical length was measured to be 23mm and no other tests were done. Which of the following management steps should be considered for this patient?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Administration of tocolytics**

- **A. Group B Streptococci prophylaxis** — Not indicated yet. GBS prophylaxis is given during labor or ruptured membranes in women with positive culture or unknown status at ≥37 weeks or during preterm labor with imminent delivery. At 22 weeks (pre-viable), delivery is not anticipated.
- **B. Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection** — Not indicated yet. Magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection is administered when preterm delivery is anticipated before 32 weeks, typically within 24 hours of expected delivery — not for simple contractions at 22 weeks with intact BOW.
- **C. Corticosteroids for fetal lung maturation** — Too early. Antenatal corticosteroids are indicated between 24–34 weeks for threatened preterm birth. The fetus at 22 weeks is nonviable, and lung maturity induction is not beneficial yet.
- **D. Administration of tocolytics** — The goal is to suppress preterm uterine contractions to prolong pregnancy and allow further evaluation (e.g., infection screen, fetal viability counseling). Tocolytics such as nifedipine or indomethacin (before 32 weeks) may be considered to delay progression.

questions.stem: Which of the following medications would be given for a patient in preterm labor to prevent contractions?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Nifedipine**

- **A. Carboprost** — Incorrect. This is a prostaglandin F2a and used as a uterotonic.
- **B. Nifedipine** — Correct. This is used as a tocolytic and antihypertensive drug. As a calcium channel blocker, it decreases the calcium influx into smooth muscle cells which diminish uterine contractions. It is given as 10 mg PO Q15 then 10-30 mg q4-6 with BP precaution (up to 180 mg/day).
- **C. Betamethasone** — Incorrect. This is a corticosteroid that is used for fetal lung maturity.
- **D. Labetalol** — Incorrect. This is a beta blocker and is used as an antihypertensive.

choices.text: Fetal tachycardia with loss of variability

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a contraindication for tocolysis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Tachysystole**

- **A. Tachysystole** — Means >5 uterine contractions in 10 minutes, often caused by uterotonics like oxytocin. Tocolytics are actually used to treat tachysystole to relax the uterus and restore normal contraction frequency.
- **B. Maternal cardiopulmonary disease** — β₂-agonist tocolytics (e.g., terbutaline) can cause tachycardia, arrhythmias, pulmonary edema, and are dangerous in heart or lung disease.
- **C. Poorly controlled hyperthyroidism** — β₂-agonists may exacerbate tachycardia, palpitations, and metabolic effects in hyperthyroid patients.
- **D. Fetal tachycardia with loss of variability** — Suggests fetal distress or hypoxia — tocolysis would delay necessary delivery and worsen outcome.

Williams Obstetrics 26th ed. p. 459

questions.stem: A 27 year old G1P0 mother at 34 weeks 6 days AOG by LMP came in the ER for regular uterine contractions and vaginal bleeding. You suspect preterm labor. The attending physician then decides to administer antenatal steroids. What is the correct regimen to be given to this patient?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Dexamethasone 6mg/IM every 12 hours for 4 doses**

Antenatal steroids is recommended in patients undergoing preterm labor to enhance fetal lung maturity. The correct dosing for antenatal steroids is as follows:

- Betamethasone 12mg IM q24 for 2 doses
- Dexamethasone 6mg IM q12 for 4 doses

- **A. Betamethasone 12mg/IM every 12 hours for 2 doses** — Should be every 24 hours.
- **B. Dexamethasone 6mg/IM every 12 hours for 4 doses** — Correct.
- **C. Betamethasone 6mg/IM every 24 hours for 2 doses** — Should be 12mg instead of 6mg.
- **D. Dexamethasone 12mg/IM every 24 hours for 2 doses** — Should be every 12 hours for 4 doses.

choices.text:
A fetus is small for gestational age (SGA) if their
abdominal circumference is less than 10th
percentile for gestational age

A fetus is large for gestational age (LGA) if their
estimated fetal weight is greater than 90th
percentile for gestational age

A fetus is considered to have macrosomia if their
birth weight is more than 5,000g

In asymmetric growth restriction, the head
circumference remains appropriate for aging due to
brain sparing.

questions.stem: These statements are true regarding fetal growth disorders, except:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — A fetus is considered to have macrosomia if their birth weight is more than 5,000g**

- **A. A fetus is small for gestational age (SGA) if their abdominal circumference is less than 10th percentile for gestational age** — True. Estimated fetal weight may also be used as a measurement.
- **B. A fetus is large for gestational age (LGA) if their estimated fetal weight is greater than 90th percentile for gestational age** — True. Mothers with LGA or macrosomic fetuses: increased risk for CS delivery, perineal trauma, and postpartum hemorrhage.
- **C. A fetus is considered to have macrosomia if their birth weight is more than 5,000g** — False. Birth weight should be greater than 4,500g. Elective CS is recommended for those with EFW of greater than 5,000g if with no Diabetes Mellitus and greater than 4,500g if with Diabetes Mellitus.
- **D. In asymmetric growth restriction, the head circumference remains appropriate for aging due to brain sparing** — True. Brain sparing or the preferential shunting of oxygen and nutrients to the brain is activated. Fetal abdominal circumference is reduced instead and is shown in the liver size of the fetus.

questions.stem: Diagnostic of choice for hemolytic disease of the newborn
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Direct coombs test**

- **A. Direct coombs test** — Detects IgG antibodies or complement bound directly to the neonate’s RBCs. A positive result indicates immune-mediated hemolysis, such as that caused by maternal alloantibodies (e.g., anti-D in Rh incompatibility).
- **B. Indirect coombs test** — Detects free-floating antibodies in the serum that could bind to RBCs. Mainly used for prenatal screening of Rh incompatibility and pre-transfusion testing.
- **C. CBC** — May confirm the diagnosis of anemia and determine its severity from the levels of hemoglobin and hematocrit but it is not the gold standard.
- **D. Peripheral smear** — May be useful in confirming a hemolytic disease because it may show spherocytes or nucleated RBCs but it is not the gold standard.

questions.stem: How much cumulative blood loss is expected in a patient with postpartum hemorrhage?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — > 1000 mL**

- **A. < 500 mL** — Historically, postpartum hemorrhage has been defined as blood losses >500 mL in a vaginal delivery and >1000 mL for cesarean section. This has since been redefined to >1000 mL.
- **B. > 500 mL**
- **C. > 1000 mL** — Postpartum hemorrhage is described as a cumulative blood loss >1000 mL OR blood loss + significant symptoms of hypovolemia. These occur in 1-5% of all deliveries.
- **D. > 1500 mL** — Incorrect since the threshold to be considered PPH is a blood loss of >1000 mL.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most frequent cause of postpartum hemorrhage?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Uterine atony**

- **A. Uterine atony** — Correct. The most frequent cause of obstetrical hemorrhage is failure of the uterus after delivery to contract sufficiently and arrest bleeding from vessels at the placental implantation site.
- **B. Uterine inversion** — Incorrect. Although uterine inversion is one of the classic hemorrhagic disasters encountered in obstetrics and occurs in 1 in 2000-20 000 deliveries, it’s not the most frequent cause for PPH.
- **C. Vulvovaginal lacerations** — Incorrect. However, up to 80% of women sustain laceration at vaginal birth. Small vaginal wall tears are often superficial with little to no bleeding.
- **D. Uterine rupture** — Incorrect. Uterine rupture is another event that may lead to potentially catastrophic hemorrhage. The overall prevalence is 3 cases per 10 000 births.

questions.stem: A 26 year old G4P2 (2022) mother is currently undergoing spontaneous vaginal delivery. Shortly after rupture of membranes, she becomes dyspneic and hypotensive, and becomes unresponsive. Brisk vaginal bleeding is noted. Which of the following is the most likely cause of bleeding in this patient?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Disseminated intravascular coagulation**

- **A. Disseminated intravascular coagulation** — Amniotic fluid embolism presents with a classic triad of abrupt hemodynamic and respiratory compromise along with overt disseminated intravascular coagulopathy occurring during labor or within 30 minutes of placental delivery, as described in the case.
- **B. Uterine inversion** — Although uterine inversion is a usual cause for postpartum hemorrhage, it does not usually occur in patients with amniotic fluid embolism.
- **C, D. Placenta previa, Abruptio placenta** — Considered risk factors for amniotic fluid embolism and not a cause of bleeding.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a rare clinical manifestation of placenta percreta?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Hemoperitoneum**

- **A. Hematuria** — On rare occasions, a patient with placenta percreta may present with hematuria or rectal bleeding due to spread to the bladder or rectum.
- **B. Absence of vaginal bleeding** — Patients with placenta previa classically present with profuse painless vaginal bleeding.
- **C. Hemoperitoneum** — Hemoperitoneum is more associated with ruptured ectopic pregnancies, which may present as hypotensive, unresponsive or with peritoneal irritation.
- **D. Painless vaginal bleeding** — Patients with placenta previa classically present with sudden and profuse painless vaginal bleeding. The first episode of bleeding – the “sentinel” bleed – usually occurs after 28 weeks of gestation, when the lower uterine segment develops and thins, disrupting placental attachment.

questions.stem: A 27 year old, G1P0 at 34 weeks AOG, presents with painless, profuse vaginal bleeding and fetal bradycardia. What is the best management?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Perform emergency CS**

- **A. Admit and stabilize patient** — Vasa previa is a condition where fetal blood vessels lie over the cervix, unprotected by the umbilical cord or placenta; thus, they are prone to tearing during labor. Though it is important to stabilize the patient, this is not the best answer because the patient would require emergency CS to manage the underlying cause of the bleeding.
- **B. Administer IM betamethasone** — Antenatal corticosteroids can be provided as indicated or given prophylactically at 28 to 32 weeks gestation to cover possible urgent preterm delivery.
- **C. Expectant management** — Since the patient already presents with profuse bleeding and fetal distress, expectant management is not enough.
- **D. Perform emergency CS** — Vasa previa presents as painless vaginal bleeding with fetal distress (bradycardia). Bleeding from vasa previa is from fetal blood and the blood loss can be rapid and fatal to the fetus; thus, immediate cesarean delivery is performed to prevent fetal exsanguination.

questions.stem: A 26 year old, G2P1, delivered via low vaginal forceps delivery. 1 hour after delivery, she experienced postpartum bleeding and upon palpation, the uterus was contracted. What is the possible cause?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Vaginal tear**

- **A. Ruptured uterus** —
  - Most common sign: nonreassuring fetal HR pattern with variable deceleration that may evolve into late deceleration and bradycardia
  - Sudden intense abdominal pain or may have little appreciable pain/tenderness
  - PE: fetus may be palpable in extrauterine space, possible vaginal bleeding, and fetal presenting part is suddenly at higher station than previously (loss of station)
- **B. Uterine atony** — Uterine atony is the leading cause of PPH. Diagnosis: soft, enlarged and boggy uterus. Since the uterus is contracted, this is not the answer.
- **C. Retained placenta** — The most obvious sign of retained placenta is failure to expel the placenta within 30-60 mins after the baby’s birth. Other symptoms include heavy bleeding, fever, foul-smelling vaginal discharge, large clots coming out of the vagina, and painful cramping.
- **D. Vaginal tear** — Since it was mentioned that the mother delivered via low vaginal forceps delivery, there is an increased risk of vaginal laceration due to the assisted device.

#### Postpartum Hemorrhage (PPH)

- Early PPH: within 24 hours
- Late PPH: after 24 hrs
- 4 basic processes (4 Ts):
  1. Tone - uterine atony
  2. Tissue - retained placental tissue or blood clots
  3. Trauma - genital tract laceration or hematomas
  4. Thrombin - coagulopathy
- Complication:
  - Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
  - Sheehan syndrome (pituitary infarct)

questions.stem: For #s 42 & 43 During your duty at the emergency room, a 27 year old G1P0 at 30 weeks AOG was rushed in by her husband due to difficulty breathing. She had an allegedly unremarkable prenatal course and no known comorbidities. You noted the presence of crackles and a BP of 160/100. Upon work-up, you noted increased serum creatinine and a dipstick reading of +2. You decide to give magnesium sulfate IV infusion for seizure prophylaxis. What is the therapeutic level of magnesium sulfate for this patient?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — 4.8-8.4 mg/dL**

This is a case of preeclampsia with severe features. Patient has new onset high blood pressure after 20 weeks gestation together with signs and symptoms of pulmonary edema, renal insufficiency, and proteinuria. Magnesium sulfate is administered for seizure prophylaxis.

- Loading dose then maintenance dose is continued until 24 hours after delivery.
- Continuous IV: Loading dose of 4-6 g in 100 mL IV over 15-20min → maintenance at 1-2 g/hr in 100 mL IV.

**B. 4.8-8.4 mg/dL** — Therapeutic level of MgSO4 are 4-7 mEq/L or 4.8-8.4 mg/dL or 2.0-3.5 mmol/L. Rest of the choices do not fall into the given therapeutic level of MgSO4. Note that the units of the choices were also different per choice.

choices.text:
Inject Hydralazine 5mg IV every 15 to 20 minus for
up to 3 doses

questions.stem: While monitoring the patient, an intern referred her to you for decreased RR and inability to elicit patellar reflexes. What is the next best step in the management of your patient?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Inject 10mL of 10% Calcium chloride IV**

- **A. Inject Hydralazine 5mg IV every 15 to 20 minus for up to 3 doses** — This is the antihypertensive therapy for BP ≥ 160 mmHg/110 mmHg to bring BP out of severe range. This management may also be given for the patient given her SBP is 160 mmHg.
- **B. Inject 10mL of 10% Calcium chloride IV** — Antidote to Mg toxicity. Given the patient’s signs and symptoms that indicate magnesium toxicity, the antidote is the best next step.
- **C. Measure serum Mg levels** — Since the patient is already being given IV MgSO, serial Mg is already being done to achieve the therapeutic level and adjust the dose. Serum Mg is not the best next step since she already has signs and symptoms that indicate magnesium toxicity.
- **D. Discontinue MgSO4 and manage expectantly** — Since the patient is already unstable and showing signs and symptoms of magnesium toxicity, it is important to manage this promptly.

questions.stem:
A 30 year old G3P2 (1102) mother presents with elevated BP at 150/90 at 30 weeks AOG. She has no comorbidities but her BP was allegedly also elevated last week.

Workup was done and the results are as follows:

| Test | Result |
|---|---|
| Hemoglobin | 11 g/dL |
| Platelets | 120,000 uL |
| CXR | Unremarkable findings |
| Creatinine | 1.0 mg/dL |
| 24 hour urine protein test | 350mg/24h |

What is the diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Preeclampsia without severe features**

- **A. Gestational Hypertension** — Incorrect. This is defined by an elevated BP (SBP≥140 and/or DBP≥90 mmHg) on two occasions at least 4 h apart after 20 wks’ gestation in women with previously normal BP. Although the patient has increased BP on two separate occasions, the other laboratory findings make another diagnosis a better choice.
- **B. Preeclampsia without severe features** — Correct. This is similar to Gestational Hypertension but with the additional feature of proteinuria. Proteinuria is defined by the following laboratory measures:
  - ≥300 mg/24 h or
  - Protein/creatinine ratio ≥0.3 or
  - Dipstick reading of +1 (used only if other quantitative methods are unavailable)

  Since the patient does not have any other severe features, this choice is the best answer.
- **C. Preeclampsia with severe features** — Incorrect. This is defined by the same criteria as above with the addition of new-onset of any of the following:
  - Thrombocytopenia: Platelet count < 100,000 μL−1
  - Renal insufficiency: Serum creatinine concentrations >1.1 mg/dL or 2x baseline in the absence of other renal disease
  - Impaired liver function: >2x ALT, AST measurements
  - Pulmonary edema
  - Cerebral or visual symptoms

  Since these were not present in the case, this choice is incorrect.
- **D. Chronic Hypertension with superimposed Preeclampsia** — Incorrect. This may be eliminated because the patient did not have hypertension prior to getting pregnant or before 20 weeks gestation. This diagnosis is defined as:
  - Worsening baseline BPs + new/worsening proteinuria or other findings pointing to end-organ damage (thrombocytopenia, renal insufficiency, liver involvement, cerebral symptoms, pulmonary edema)
  - In pre-existing baseline renal disease, uric acid > 6.0–6.5 is differentiates preeclampsia from exacerbation of hypertension
  - CH with superimposed preeclampsia with severe features: if with features of end-organ damage

questions.stem: What percentage of patients develop HELLP syndrome after preeclampsia diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — 80%**

- **A. 30%** — 30% of patients develop HELLP syndrome after being diagnosed with preeclampsia WITHOUT severe features.
- **B. 50%** — 50% of patients develop HELLP syndrome after being diagnosed with preeclampsia with severe features.
- **C. 60%** — Incorrect.
- **D. 80%** — 80% of patients develop HELLP syndrome after preeclampsia diagnosis – 30% without severe features and 50% with severe features.

questions.stem: Which protein is NOT associated with preeclampsia?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Relaxin**

- **A. Relaxin** — Relaxin is a peptide expressed in human corpus luteum, decidua and placenta. Elevated levels of relaxin in early pregnancy is attributed to corpus luteum secretion and was found to act on myometrium to promote relaxation. There is no mention of its association with preeclampsia, thus, this is the correct answer.
- **B. soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase 1** — Soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 (sFLt-1), also known as vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 1 (VEGFR-1) is a soluble variant of the membrane bound receptor for VEGF. Elevated maternal sFlt-1 levels inactivate and reduce PIGF and VEGF concentrations, leading to endothelial dysfunction. Women with a trisomy 13 fetus were found to have 30-40% incidence for preeclampsia since sFlt-1 is on chromosome 13.
- **C. VEGFR-1**
- **D. sENG** — Soluble endoglin (sEng) is another angiogenic peptide that inhibits various TGF-B from binding to endothelial receptors, which then diminishes endothelial nitric oxide dependent vasodilation. Serum levels of sEng rises before preeclampsia develops. Essentially, simultaneously elevated levels of sFlt-1 and sEng are associated with more severe forms of preeclampsia.

choices.text: Normalize blood pressure to pre-pregnancy levels

questions.stem: A 33 year old G3P2 (1102) mother, 37 weeks and 2 days AOG, was brought to the emergency room due to tonic-clonic seizures. Her blood pressure was noted to be 170/110. What is the primary goal of antihypertensive therapy in this patient?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Prevent recurrent seizures**

- **A. Normalize blood pressure to pre-pregnancy levels** — For eclampsia patients, the goal BP is < 160/100mmHg.
- **B. Prevent recurrent seizures** — The primary goal of antihypertensive therapy in eclampsia is to prevent recurrent seizures. For seizure control and prophylaxis, eclamptic patients are treated with magnesium sulfate (MgSO4) to decrease hyperreflexia and prevent further seizures by increasing the seizure threshold.
- **C. Stroke prevention** — The primary goal of antihypertensive therapy in preeclamptic patient is stroke prevention.
- **D. Delay delivery until 39 weeks** — For patients with eclampsia, delivery is recommended regardless of AOG. Initiate delivery only after eclampsia is controlled.

questions.stem: In pregnant patients with chronic hypertension, ⅓ of them will develop this disease
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Acute hepatocellular necrosis**

- **A. Disseminated intravascular coagulation** — Can occur in severe preeclampsia or placental abruption, but it’s not specific to ⅓ of chronic hypertensives.
- **B. Acute hepatocellular necrosis** — Chronic hypertension in pregnancy puts patients at risk for developing preeclampsia and HELLP syndrome (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets).
  - In HELLP syndrome, acute hepatocellular necrosis may occur due to hepatic ischemia and microvascular injury from endothelial dysfunction and fibrin deposition
  - Liver damage is a key complication in ⅓ of women with chronic hypertension who develop preeclampsia/HELLP
- **C. Sheehan syndrome** — Refers to postpartum pituitary necrosis due to massive hemorrhage and hypotension, unrelated to chronic hypertension.
- **D. Simmond syndrome** — Refers to pituitary insufficiency (hypopituitarism), not associated with pregnancy.

questions.stem: A female smoker with a BMI of 28 was diagnosed with hypertension. She noted that her sister also has hypertension. Which is not a risk factor for hypertension?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Nulliparity**

- **A. Nulliparity** — Nulliparity is not a risk factor for developing hypertension.
- **B. Smoking** — Risk factors for hypertension:
  - Family history, age, gender, race, chronic kidney disease
  - Lack of physical activity, unhealthy diet, being overweight or obese, alcohol and tobacco use, diabetes, stress
- **C. BMI**
- **D. Sister having hypertension**

questions.stem: How many percent of gestational diabetes mellitus patients will likely develop overt diabetes mellitus within 20 years?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — 50%**

- **A. 40%** — The pooled gestational diabetes recurrence rate among primiparas was 40%.
- **B. 48%** — The pooled gestational diabetes recurrence rate was 48 percent.
- **C. 50%** — There is a 50 percent likelihood that women with gestational diabetes will develop overt diabetes within 20 years.
- **D. 73%** — The pooled gestational diabetes recurrence rate among multiparas was 40%.

Williams, 25th Ed, p. 1113 – 1114

questions.stem: The following threshold values for gestational diabetes mellitus are correct EXCEPT:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — 1hr OGTT: 8.5 mmol/L**

Note that the choices are in different units!

- **A. Fasting: 92 mg/dL** — Fasting glucose threshold: 5.1 mmol/L OR 92 mg/dL
- **B. Fasting: 5.1 mmol/L**
- **C. 1hr OGTT: 8.5 mmol/L** — 1hr OGTT threshold: 10.0 mmol/L OR 180 mg/dL. 8.5 mmol/L is the threshold for 2hr OGTT.
- **D. 2hr OGTT: 153 mg/dL** — 2hr OGTT threshold: 8.5 mmol/L OR 153 mg/dL

questions.stem: Which of the following fetomaternal complications is likely to occur following appendectomy?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Preterm labor**

- **A. Preterm labor** — Appendicitis increases the likelihood of preterm labor, especially once peritonitis has developed. Spontaneous labor after 23 weeks ensues with greater frequency following surgery for appendicitis compared with surgery for other indications. Risks for low birth weight and fetal loss were also found to be increased in patients who underwent appendectomy.
- **B. Hemolysis** — Hemolysis is commonly found in patients with acute fatty liver of pregnancy and is unlikely to be a fetomaternal complication from appendicitis. It is usually severe and was thought to stem from effects of hypercholesterolemia on erythrocyte membranes.
- **C. Stillbirth** — Stillbirth rate was found to be increased in women with elevated total bile acid levels associated with Intrahepatic Cholestasis of Pregnancy.
- **D. Low birth weight** — Low birth weight was also found to be associated with appendicitis, however, there is a more increased likelihood for preterm labor (see letter A).

*Williams Obstetrics, 26th ed.*

questions.stem: A 25 year old G1P0 mother at 37 weeks AOG came in the ER with a chief complaint of right upper quadrant abdominal pain, associated with bloating, nausea and food intolerance. Laboratory values are found to be normal. Which of the following is NOT considered an initial management in this case?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy**

The initial diagnosis for the case above is cholelithiasis, presenting with:

- Right upper or epigastric abdominal pain
- Bloating
- Belching
- Nausea
- Fatty food intolerance
- Normal laboratory values

Leukocytosis or elevated liver and pancreatic enzymes should warn for acute cholecystitis or pancreatitis.

- **A. Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy** — NOT indicated in pregnancy. ESWL is contraindicated due to potential fetal harm from shock waves and is never part of initial management during pregnancy.
- **B. Laparoscopy** — Safe if surgical management is required, especially for complicated gallstones (cholecystitis, biliary obstruction). Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is preferred over open surgery and can be performed in the 2nd or 3rd trimester if indicated.
- **C. Ursodeoxycholic acid therapy** — Used for symptomatic relief in biliary sludge and intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. It reduces bile acid levels and improves symptoms.
- **D. Diet modification** — Low-fat diet, small frequent meals.

*Williams Obstetrics, 26th ed.*

questions.stem: Which of the following is the diagnostic of choice for appendicitis in pregnancy?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Magnetic resonance imaging**

- **A. Graded compression sonography** — For initial evaluation, sonographic abdominal imaging is reasonable in suspected appendicitis, even to exclude an obstetrical cause of pain. However, graded compression sonography is difficult because of cecal displacement and uterine imposition. Recall that the appendix commonly moves upward and outward from the right lower quadrant during pregnancy!
- **B. Appendiceal computed tomography** — Appendiceal computed tomography is more sensitive and accurate than sonography to confirm suspected appendicitis. However, specific views should be designed to diminish fetal radiation exposure.
- **C. Magnetic resonance imaging** — When available, MRI is the preferred modality for evaluation of suspected appendicitis in pregnancy. MRI has high diagnostic yield and accuracy and it also provides alternative diagnoses.
- **D. None of the above** — Although all three can be considered for the diagnosis of appendicitis, MRI is the preferred diagnostic of choice.

questions.stem: A 33 year old G2P1 (1001) mother came in the ER for a 2 day history of vomiting and diarrhea. On history, she was noted to be restless, confused and agitated for the past hour. VS were as follows: BP 110/80 HR 125 RR 18 T 38.5. On PE, you note tremors and lid lag. What is the first step in the management of this case?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Administer PTU 1000 mg PO/NGT loading dose**

The case vignette describes someone with hyperthyroidism currently on thyroid storm. The image above shows the Parkland Hospital management for thyroid storm or thyrotoxic heart failure. While all choices are done, the first step in the management of this case is to start thionamides and consider heart rate control.

- **A. Administer PTU 1000 mg PO/NGT loading dose** — Correct dose for thinoamide loading dose.
- **B. Administer Sodium iodide 500 mg IV every 8 hours** — Iodine is given 1-2 hours of thionamide therapy.
- **C. Administer Dexamethasone 2mg IV every 6 hours** — Corticosteroid therapy is done after iodine therapy.
- **D. Administer PTU 100mg every 6hr PO/NGT** — PTU 200mg (not 100mg!) every 6hr PO/NGT is given after the loading dose of PTU.

*William's Obstetrics, 26th ed., p. 1094*

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most common fetal complication associated with congenital rubella syndrome?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Sensorineural deafness**

Rubella virus is one of the most complete teratogens. If maternal infection occurs during organogenesis, any fetal organ may be affected; most common of which are:

- **A. Cataracts** — Eye defects, such as cataracts, microphthalmia or retinopathy (10-30%)
- **B. Intellectual disability** — CNS defects - intellectual disability (10-25%)
- **C. Patent ductus arteriosus** — Cardiac malformations (10-20%)
  - Most common: patent ductus arteriosus
  - Pathognomonic: supravalvular pulmonic stenosis
- **D. Sensorineural deafness** — Sensorineural deafness (60-75%, MOST COMMON)

questions.stem: The following correctly describes hypothyroidism in pregnancy, EXCEPT:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Overt hypothyroidism is described as first trimester TSH of >5 mIU/L**

- **A. The target TSH level for pregnancy is <2.5 mIU/L for the first trimester and <3.0 mIU/L for the second and third trimesters** — Correct.
- **B. Daily iodine intake of at least 250 ug is recommended during pregnancy** — Correct.
- **C. Overt hypothyroidism is described as first trimester TSH of >5 mIU/L** — Overt hypothyroidism is described as first trimester TSH of >10 mIU/L, not 5 mIU/L!
- **D. Elevated TSH and Low FT4 levels on thyroid function tests are consistent for hypothyroidism** — Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the single most important risk factor in the development of endometritis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Route of delivery**

- **A. Route of delivery** — Route of delivery is the single most significant risk factor for the development of uterine infection. Operative vaginal delivery was found to have higher risks for metritis and perineal infections than spontaneous birth.
- **B. Prolonged labor** — Prolonged labor is a known risk, however, it is more of an indication for operative vaginal delivery than a direct risk factor for endometritis.
- **C. Prophylactic antibiotics given** — A study showed that those receiving a single dose of prophylactic antibiotics had a lower infection rate.
- **D. Multiple cervical examinations** — Multiple cervical examinations is also one of the risk factor for infection following surgery.

*Williams Obstetrics, 26th ed., p. 650*

questions.stem: Phase wherein uterine fundus rises to abdomen and goes back to its original position
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — 3rd stage of labor**

- **A. 3rd stage of labor** — Delivery of placenta occurs during the 3rd stage of labor. Signs of placental separation:
  - Sudden gush of blood
  - Uterus becomes globular (round) and firmer (Calkins sign)
  - Cord lengthening
  - Rise of uterus into the abdomen
- **B. 4th stage of labor** — The 4th stage of labor is also known as the postpartum recovery period. It lasts from the delivery of the placenta to about two hours after birth. During this time, the uterus contracts to prevent excessive bleeding, and the body begins to recover.
- **C. Puerperium** — Puerperium is the period of time following delivery until 4-6 weeks after. This is also known as the "fourth trimester" which may last up to 12 weeks post-delivery.
- **D. Recuperation** — There is no such thing as a recuperation phase.

#### Stages of Labor (reference)

**1st stage**
- Stage of cervical effacement and dilation
- Begins when spaced uterine contractions of sufficient frequency, intensity, and duration are attained to bring about effacement to full cervical dilation
- OB Normal: FHR monitoring at least every 30 min
- High-risk: FHR monitoring at least every 15 min

**2nd stage**
- Stage of fetal expulsion
- Complete cervical dilatation to fetal delivery
- Mean duration: 50 min (nulliparas), 20 min (multiparas)
- OB Normal: FHR monitoring at least every 15 min
- High-risk: FHR monitoring at least every 5 min

**3rd stage**
- Stage of placental separation and expulsion
- After delivery of fetus to placental delivery

questions.stem: Hormone that stimulates FSH release from pituitary
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Activin**

- **A. Inhibin** — Inhibin inhibits FSH and LH release (FSH > LH)
- **B. Activin** — Activin stimulates FSH release from the pituitary
- **C. Progesterone** — Progesterone inhibits the release of gonadotropins
- **D. Estradiol** — Estradiol is a potent physiologic inhibitor of GnRH and gonadotropin release

#### Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Ovarian (HPO) Axis

| Released by | Hormone Released | Effects |
|---|---|---|
| Hypothalamus | Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH) | Stimulates and regulates secretion of FSH and LH from the anterior pituitary; released in a pulsatile manner |
| Anterior pituitary (produced by Gonadotropes) | Gonadotropins: FSH and LH | FSH: acts on the granulosa cells of the maturing antral follicle to stimulate follicular growth. LH: acts on the theca cells of these follicles to induce steroidogenesis |
| Ovaries | Ovarian steroids: estradiol, progesterone and androstenedione | Estradiol-17β: potent physiologic inhibitor of GnRH and of gonadotropin secretion. Progesterone: inhibits gonadotropins. Inhibin: inhibits FSH and LH (FSH>LH). Activin: stimulates FSH release from the pituitary |

questions.stem: What will you prime the patient with prior to performing a Progestin Challenge test to yield a positive result?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Estrogen**

- **A. FSH** — FSH stimulates follicular development and promotes estrogen production. It may lead to estrogen production but it is not a practical method for priming the endometrium for a Progestin Challenge Test.
- **B. LH** — LH triggers ovulation and promotes progesterone production. It works during the luteal phase and not in the development of the endometrium.
- **C. Estrogen** — You can prime a patient with estrogen prior to a Progestin Challenge Test to help yield a positive (withdrawal bleed) result. A withdrawal bleed after progestin administration indicates that the endometrium was adequately primed by estrogen and is capable of responding. Estrogen priming is typically considered after an initial negative Progestin Challenge Test, which suggests that there was insufficient endogenous estrogen to stimulate endometrial growth. By giving exogenous estrogen first, you can assess the endometrium's ability to respond to subsequent progesterone exposure.
- **D. Androgen** — Androgens are responsible for male secondary sexual characteristics and do not promote endometrial proliferation.

*Lord et al. (2024). Secondary Amenorrhea. StatPearls. Retrieved from https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK431055/*

questions.stem: How many hours after the peak of LH surge is ovulation most likely to occur?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — 16 hours**

- **A. 12 hours** — Incorrect.
- **B. 16 hours** — Ovulation occurs about 16 hours after the peak of LH surge and 32 hours after its initial rise.
- **C. 20 hours** — Incorrect.
- **D. 32 hours** — Ovulation occurs about 32 hours after the initial rise of LH surge, not peak of LH surge.

questions.stem: When does ovulation occur?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Day 14**

- **A. Day 10** — Day 10 and 12 fall under the proliferative phase wherein there is repair and regeneration of the functional zone of the endometrium.
- **B. Day 12** — Day 10 and 12 fall under the proliferative phase wherein there is repair and regeneration of the functional zone of the endometrium.
- **C. Day 14** — Ovulation usually happens on Day 14 of a 28-day cycle. The fertile window is from 5 days before ovulation to the day of ovulation.
- **D. Day 16** — Day 16 falls under the secretory phase.

#### Menstrual Cycle Reference

| Event | Remarks |
|---|---|
| Duration of the menstrual cycle | 28 +/- 7 days |
| Follicular phase | Length is more variable |
| Luteal phase | More or less constant at 14 days (lifespan of the corpus luteum is 14 days) |
| Average age of menarche | 12 years old |
| Ovulation | 32 hours after initial rise of the LH surge and 16 hours after its peak |

questions.stem: Failure of the ovaries to respond to FSH and LH
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Savage syndrome**

- **A. Kallman syndrome** — Congenital absence of GnRH and is commonly associated with anosmia; normal height and an increase in growth of long bones, resulting in a greater wingspan-to-height ratio.
- **B. Turner syndrome** — Short stature (<60 inches in height), webbing of the neck, a short fourth metacarpal, and cubitus valgus.
  - Cardiac abnormality, renal abnormalities, and hypothyroidism
- **C. Savage syndrome** — Savage syndrome is also called ovarian resistance syndrome due to the failure of the ovaries to respond to FSH and LH due to receptor defect. Patients will present with female internal and external genitalia but without breast development due to the absence of estrogen.
- **D. Swyer syndrome** — Pure gonadal dysgenesis (46,XX and 46,XY with gonadal streaks).
  - 46XY (Swyer syndrome): result of an abnormal testis in utero

#### Primary Amenorrhea

- The absence of menses in a woman who has never menstruated by the age of 15 years in the presence of normal growth and secondary sexual characteristics
- Girls who have not menstruated within 5 years of breast development, if occurring by age 10.
- Breast development (thelarche) should occur by age 13 or otherwise requires evaluation as well.

#### Syndromes Associated with Primary Amenorrhea

| Syndrome | Phenotypic Subgroup | Area of Abnormality | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| Turner Syndrome (45X) | (-) Breasts, (+) Uterus | Gonadal failure | Short stature (<60 inches in height), webbing of the neck, a short fourth metacarpal, and cubitus valgus. Cardiac abnormality, renal abnormalities, and hypothyroidism |
| Noonan Syndrome | (-) Breasts, (+) Uterus | Gonadal failure | Isolated phenotypic features of Turner syndrome (without gonadal failure) in males |
| Swyer syndrome (46XY) | (-) Breasts, (+) Uterus | Gonadal failure | Pure gonadal dysgenesis (46XY) with gonadal streaks. With normal female reproductive organs, including a uterus, fallopian tubes, and vagina |
| Savage syndrome | (-) Breasts, (+) Uterus | Gonadal failure | Ovarian resistance syndrome. Ovary fails to respond to FSH and LH. Phenotypical picture to that of ovarian agenesis; no testicular development, MIF not released, (+) female internal and external genitalia, but without estrogen so breasts will not develop |
| Kallman syndrome | (-) Breasts, (+) Uterus | Hypothalamic failure | Congenital absence of GnRH and is commonly associated with anosmia; normal height and an increase in growth of long bones, resulting in a greater wingspan-to-height ratio |

questions.stem: What is the most common cause of secondary amenorrhea?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Pregnancy**

- **A. Pregnancy** — Pregnancy is the most common cause of secondary amenorrhea. Any woman who is of reproductive age presenting with missed menses should first be evaluated for pregnancy.
- **B. Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome** — PCOS is also known to cause irregular menstruation and sometimes secondary amenorrhea, but it is not the most common cause.
- **C. Oral contraceptive pills** — OCPs may also cause secondary amenorrhea since they inhibit ovulation, but it is not the most common cause.
- **D. Thyroid Disorder** — Both Hyperthyroidism and Hypothyroidism may cause menstrual cycle disturbances but it is a less frequent cause for secondary amenorrhea.

questions.stem: Indirect test to evaluate ovulation and normal luteal function in the workup for infertility
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Progesterone**

- **A. Progesterone** — If the woman has regular menstrual cycles, a serum progesterone level should be measured in the midluteal phase to provide indirect evidence of ovulation and normal luteal function.
  - Greater than 3 to 5 ng/mL: suggests some ovulatory function
  - Greater than 10 ng/mL: found during at least 1 day of the luteal phase of normal ovulatory cycles in which conception occurred
- **B. Estrogen** — Estradiol (E2)
  - If elevated (>70 pg/mL) on D2 or 3 may independently suggest a decreased prognosis regarding ovarian reserve
- **C. Antimullerian hormone** — Antimullerian hormone (AMH)
  - Produced by ovarian granulosa cells and decreases with age
  - At 0.05 ng/mL, menopause occurs within 4-5 years
  - May suggest decreased ovarian reserve at levels <0.5 ng/mL
  - Increased levels suggest a large cohort of follicles, such as in patients with polycystic ovarian syndrome
- **D. Antral follicle count** — Antral follicle count (AFC)
  - Measuring the number of antral follicles present on days 2 to 4 measuring 2 to 10 mm in diameter
  - Presence of 4-10 follicles is a good sign of ovarian reserve

questions.stem: Which of the following is an outdated test for infertility?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Basal Body Temperature**

- **A. Basal Body Temperature** — Basal body temperature monitoring is usually a test used to detect ovulation by tracking temperature rises post-ovulation. However, it is less reliable and outdated due to its variability and poor predictive value.
- **B. Clomiphene Citrate Challenge** — Clomiphene citrate test is used to assess ovarian reserve by measuring FSH levels before and after clomiphene administration.
- **C. Semen Analysis** — Semen analysis remains a cornerstone in evaluating male infertility. In fact, it is one of the first tests that should be done when diagnosing infertility.
- **D. Pelvic ultrasound** — Pelvic ultrasound evaluation is still part of the investigation of infertility. Through this, structural problems in the reproductive system can be identified and more importantly, an antral follicle count (AFC) count can be obtained.

choices.text: Estrogen on Day 2-3, Progesterone on Mid-luteal phase
Estrogen on Mid-luteal phase, Progesterone on Day 2-3

questions.stem: When is the best time to test for levels of estrogen and progesterone when evaluating for infertility?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Estrogen on Day 2-3, Progesterone on Mid-luteal phase**

- **A. Both on Day 2-3** — Only estrogen should be obtained on cycle day 2-3.
- **B. Both on Mid-luteal phase** — Only progesterone should be obtained during the mid-luteal phase.
- **C. Estrogen on Day 2-3, Progesterone on Mid-luteal phase** — Serum hormone assays are diagnostics tools in the evaluation of infertility. Serum estrogen should be obtained on cycle day 2-3 and it will reflect follicular development while serum progesterone should be obtained in the mid-luteal phase to confirm that ovulation has occurred.
- **D. Estrogen on Mid-luteal phase, Progesterone on Day 2-3** — See explanation above.

#### Progesterone

- If the woman has regular menstrual cycles, a serum progesterone level should be measured in the midluteal phase to provide indirect evidence of ovulation and normal luteal function
  - Greater than 3 to 5 ng/mL: suggests some ovulatory function
  - Greater than 10 ng/mL: found during at least 1 day of the luteal phase of normal ovulatory cycles in which conception occurred

#### Estradiol

- Serum FSH and estradiol (E2) should be obtained on cycle day 2 or 3

Serum FSH
- < 10 mIU/mL: normal
- >10 mIU/mL: decreased ovarian reserve
- > 20 mIU/mL: poor prognosis

Estradiol (E2)
- If elevated (>70 pg/mL) on D2 or 3 may independently suggest a decreased prognosis regarding ovarian reserve

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT typically part of the history when evaluating female infertility, but is important in the assessment of male infertility?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Reduced shaving**

- **A. Reduced shaving** — Reduced shaving is not typically part of the history when evaluating female infertility, but it is relevant when assessing male infertility because it may suggest low levels of androgen (hypogonadism) which can affect sperm production.
- **B. Pubertal development** — Pubertal development is relevant in evaluating both male and female infertility. Any delays in male puberty may lead to infertility by affecting sperm quantity and quality. Delays in female puberty such as problems in menstruation can point to certain causes of female infertility.
- **C. Drugs** — Use of recreational drugs may increase the risk of both male and female infertility.
- **D. Sexual history** — Sexual history, especially frequency and timing, is essential in the evaluation of male and female infertility.

questions.stem: What is the screening age for ovarian reserve?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — 35**

- **A. 30** — See explanation below.
- **B. 32** — See explanation below.
- **C. 35** — Ovarian reserve screening is recommended for women older than 35 who have had difficulty conceiving for at least 6 months. Ovarian reserve testing includes Serum FSH, Estradiol, Anti Mullerian Hormone (AMH), and Antral Follicle Count (AFC). Normal ovarian reserve would have these findings: FSH <10 MIU/mL, Estradiol <70 pg/mL, AMH >0.5 ng/mL, AFC 4-10 follicles. (see #74 for more information on ovarian testing)
- **D. 40** — See explanation above.

questions.stem: Ligament of the uterus that reaches the labia majora
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Round ligaments**

- **A. Broad ligament** — The broad ligament is a double layer of peritoneum that folds from each side of the uterus towards the pelvic sidewall. It serves as a mesentery, holding the uterus and other pelvic structures in place.
- **B. Round ligaments** — Round ligaments are fibrous bands that extend from the cornu of the uterus to the labia majora via the inguinal canal, helping to maintain the anteverted (forward tilted) position of the uterus.
- **C. Cardinal ligament** — Cardinal ligaments (Mackenrodt's Ligaments) are located at the base of the broad ligament, these ligaments extend from the cervix to the lateral pelvic walls, supporting the uterus. They also contain the uterine artery and vein.
- **D. Uterosacral ligament** — Uterosacral ligaments extend from the posterior cervix to the anterior sacrum, providing posterior support to the uterus.

questions.stem: Mode of contraception that causes bone loss as an adverse side effect
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — DMPA**

- **A. Oral contraceptive pills** — Contraceptive steroids prevent ovulation mainly by interfering with release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) from the hypothalamus.
  - Concerns:
    - Breakthrough bleeding
    - Weight gain
    - Return to fertility
    - Neoplastic risks and benefits
      - Breast CA: transient 20 to 25% increased risk of early breast cancer
      - Cervical CA: risk of both invasive and in situ cervical cancer increases with increasing duration of OC use
      - Colorectal CA: 15% to 20% reduction in the risk of colorectal cancer
    - Coagulation parameters due to estrogen component
- **B. LNG-IUD** — Levonorgestrel containing IUDs (Mirena and Liletta)
  - Contain a total of 52 mg of levonorgestrel, which is released at a rate of about 20 μg of LNG daily into the endometrial cavity
  - Thicken cervical mucus, impeding sperm penetration and access to the upper genital tract
  - Decreases tubal motility and also produces a thin, inactive endometrium
- **C. Subdermal implants** — Subdermal implants
  - Consist of one or more thin flexible rods containing a progestin hormone
  - Nexplanon: Contains 68 mg of Etonogestrel (ENG)
    - Does not result in a decrease of bone mineral density
    - MOA: ovulation inhibition and thickening of the cervical mucus
- **D. DMPA** — Depo-medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA)
  - Long-acting derivative of progesterone formulated as an injectable crystalline suspension
  - Given in a dose of 150 mg intramuscularly (IM) or 104 mg subcutaneously (SC) every 13 weeks
  - Inhibits ovulation, keeps endometrium thin, keeps cervical mucus thick
  - Return of Fertility: 9 to 10 months after last injection
  - Clinical side effects:
    - Irregular bleeding patterns
    - Weight changes
    - Headaches
    - Mood changes
    - Bone Loss

questions.stem: Which of the following is associated with Vitamin B12 deficiency?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Combined oral contraceptive pills**

- **A. Injectables** — Injectables are not associated with Vitamin B12 deficiency.
- **B. Progestin-only pills** — POPs are not associated with Vitamin B12 deficiency.
- **C. Implants** — Implants are not associated with Vitamin B12 deficiency.
- **D. Combined oral contraceptive pills** — COCs are associated with decreased serum vitamin B12 levels, likely due to its effect on the binding of Vitamin B12 to transport proteins in the bloodstream. However, despite lower measure levels, overall B12 reserves are still typically adequate thus, no supplementation is recommended.

*Shojania & Wylie (1979). American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology. Retrieved from https://doi.org/10.1016/S0002-9378(79)80030-7*

questions.stem: What is the most important factor associated with the risk of Pelvic Inflammatory Disease and IUD use?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Time of Insertion**

- **A. Time of Insertion** — The time of IUD insertion may be high risk for Pelvic Inflammatory Disease due to potential introduction of bacteria from the cervix or vaginal canal. Thus, if there is suspicion of infectious endocervicitis, testing for gonorrhea and chlamydia should be performed first and the IUD insertion should be delayed. *(Comprehensive Gynecology, 8th edition, p. 286)*
- **B. Duration of Use** — The risk of infection after IUD insertion is small and decreases with time. Thus, long term use of IUD is not associated with a high risk of PID.
- **C. Multiple partners** — Having multiple sexual partners is a general risk factor for sexually transmitted infections, it has no direct link to IUD use and PID.
- **D. Type of IUD** — Both copper and hormonal IUDs are low risk for PID once properly placed.
