questions.stem: The following are true of peptic ulcer disease (PUD), EXCEPT:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Malignant transformation of peptic ulcers commonly occurs**

- **A. They are most commonly seen in the proximal duodenum** — Peptic ulcers occur in the context of chronic gastritis but are most common in the proximal duodenum, where they occur within a few centimeters of the pyloric valve and involve the anterior duodenal wall. Gastric peptic ulcers are predominantly located along the lesser curvature near the interface of the body and antrum.
- **B. Peptic ulcers are solitary in more than 80% of patients**
- **C. Malignant transformation of peptic ulcers commonly occurs** — Malignant transformation of peptic ulcers occurs rarely, if ever, and reports of transformation probably represent cases in which a lesion thought to be a chronic peptic ulcer was actually an ulcerated carcinoma from the start.
- **D. Classic peptic ulcers have a sharply punched-out defect** — The classic peptic ulcer is a round to oval, sharply punched-out defect. In contrast, heaped-up margins are more characteristic of cancers.

choices.text: Can be caused by other herpes viruses

questions.stem: Which of the following is true regarding herpes zoster?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Mostly unilateral and affects dermatome**

- **A. Mostly unilateral and affects dermatome** — Herpes zoster is most often characterized by painful vesicular lesions in a unilateral, dermatomal distribution.
- **B. Can be caused by other herpes viruses** — Herpes zoster (or shingles) is caused by the reactivation of latent varicella zoster virus infection.
- **C. Motor symptoms occur very frequently** — While motor symptoms can occur, these are rare and occur in less than 10% of patients.
- **D. All of the above**

questions.stem: Exposure to which of the following leads to an increased sensitivity to tuberculosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Silica**

- **A. Coal particles** — Increased exposure to coal dust particles leads to coal workers' pneumoconiosis. This disease is classified into simple or progressive, depending on whether or not there is significant pulmonary dysfunction.
- **B. Asbestos** — Exposure to asbestos increases the risk of various conditions, including localized fibrous plaques, pleural effusions, and mesothelioma.
- **C. Silica** — Silicosis is caused by inhalation of silica. It usually presents after decades of exposure as slowly progressing, nodular, fibrosing pneumoconiosis. Silicosis is also associated with an increased susceptibility to tuberculosis and a 2-fold increased risk of lung cancer. The increased susceptibility to tuberculosis may be due to crystalline silica inhibiting the ability of pulmonary macrophages to kill phagocytosed mycobacteria.
- **D. Red cedar dust** — Red cedar dust is an organic dust that induces asthma. It is common in lumbering and carpentry.

questions.stem: The following are increased in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, EXCEPT:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Bilirubin**

Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) represents a spectrum of disorders that have in common the presence of hepatic steatosis (fatty liver) in individuals who do not consume alcohol or do so in very small quantities. It is highly associated with metabolic syndrome and its incidence has been on the rise in recent times. Definitive diagnosis is done via liver biopsy, but several serum markers may point to NAFLD.

- **A. Alanine aminotransferase** — Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) elevations are the primary abnormalities seen in patients with NAFLD, though it may be normal in some patients.
- **B. Gamma-glutamyltransferase** — Gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) is also frequently elevated, with its elevation being associated with increased mortality.
- **C. Alkaline phosphatase** — Elevations in alkaline phosphatase are rare but are present in some case studies.
- **D. Bilirubin** — Serum bilirubin levels have been shown to be inversely associated with NAFLD, suggesting it may offer some protective value. Some studies have shown that bilirubin has anti-inflammatory effects and significantly contributes to total antioxidant capacity.

questions.stem: A "snowstorm" appearance on ultrasound points to what pathology?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Complete hydatidiform mole**

A "snowstorm" appearance (as seen in the picture) is the characteristic ultrasound finding in a complete hydatidiform mole. This finding is due to the widespread distribution of hydropic villi.

questions.stem: A patient had a colonoscopy done where some polyps were extracted. Histological analysis of the polyp showed a "sawtooth" appearance. Which type of polyp was found?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Hyperplastic polyp**

- **A. Adenoma** — Adenomas are characterized by the presence of epithelial dysplasia. Consistent with their precursor lesions, the prevalence of colorectal adenomas correlates with that of colorectal adenocarcinoma.
- **B. Hyperplastic polyp** — Colonic hyperplastic polyps are benign epithelial proliferations that are typically discovered in the sixth and seventh decades of life. They are thought to result from decreased epithelial cell turnover and delayed shedding of surface epithelial cells, leading to a "piling up" of goblet cells and absorptive cells. This delayed shedding causes the characteristic "sawtooth" appearance of these polyps. Hyperplastic polyps have no malignant potential.
- **C. Juvenile polyp** — Juvenile polyps, a kind of hamartomatous polyp, are focal malformations of the epithelium and lamina propria. They most often occur in children younger than 5 years of age and are found in the rectum.
- **D. Peutz-Jeghers polyp** — Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is a rare autosomal dominant syndrome that presents at a median age of 11 years with multiple GI hamartomatous polyps (Peutz-Jeghers polyps) and mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation. These polyps are most commonly found in the small intestine.

questions.stem: Which parasite can be found in abundant amounts in sputum in cases of hyperinfection?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Strongyloides stercoralis**

- **A. Echinococcus granulosis** — Hydatid disease is caused by the ingestion of Echinococcus sp. eggs. Humans are accidental intermediate hosts, infected by ingestion of food contaminated with eggs shed by dogs or foxes, which are the definitive hosts. Eggs then hatch in the duodenum and invade the liver, lungs, or bone.
- **B. Taenia solium** — Taenia solium is transmitted to humans by ingestion of either larval cysts or eggs, each with distinct outcomes. Ingestion of larval cysts, or cysticerci, attach to the intestinal wall, where they develop into mature adult tapeworms. The parasite life cycle is completed with this mode of infection and cysticercosis does not develop. Ingestion of eggs, on the other hand, leads to the hatching of larvae that penetrate the gut wall. They then disseminate hematogenously and encyst in many organs. They can encyst in the brain and cause neurocysticercosis.
- **C. Trichinella spiralis** — Its life cycle begins in the human intestine but ends within muscle, as humans are dead-end hosts.
- **D. Strongyloides stercoralis** — Strongyloides stercoralis lives in soil and infects humans when larvae penetrate the skin; they then travel in circulation to the lungs where they travel up the trachea to be swallowed. It exhibits both autoinfection and hyperinfection. Autoinfection occurs when larvae hatched in the gut invade the colon mucosa and reinitiate infection. Uncontrolled autoinfection, especially in the case of immunocompromised hosts, leads to hyperinfection. In hyperinfection, worms of all stages may be found in other organs, including the skin and lungs, and may even be found in large numbers in sputum.

questions.stem: Which of the following refers to round, faintly basophilic, periodic acid-Schiff (PAS)-positive, concentrically lamellated structures that are located wherever there are astrocytic end processes?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Corpora amylacea**

Some types of astrocyte injury lead to the formation of cytoplasmic inclusion bodies.

- **A. Corpora amylacea** — Also called polyglucosan bodies, these are more common. They are round, faintly basophilic, periodic acid-Schiff (PAS)-positive, concentrically lamellated structures 5 to 50 micrometers in diameter that are located within astrocytic end processes.
- **B. Rosenthal fibers** — Thick, elongated, brightly eosinophilic, irregular structures that occur within astrocytic processes.
- **C. Lafora bodies** — Seen in the cytoplasm of neurons in a variant of myoclonic epilepsy. These have a similar composition to corpora amylacea.
- **D. Psammoma bodies** — Sand-like lamellated calcifications seen in papillary tumors.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most common neuronal tumor in the CNS and is most commonly found in the temporal lobe with a propensity to cause seizures?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Ganglioglioma**

Neuronal tumors, such as gangliogliomas, are those that exhibit neuronal differentiation and are far less common than glial tumors, such as astrocytomas, oligodendrogliomas, and ependymomas.

- **A. Medulloblastoma** — A malignant embryonal tumor that occurs predominantly in children and exclusively in the cerebellum.
- **B. Ependymoma** — Often arises near the fourth ventricle and may also appear in the central canal of the spinal cord.
- **C. Ganglioglioma** — Tumors composed of a mixture of mature neuronal and glial cells. They are slow-growing tumors with a propensity for the temporal lobe and are the most common neuronal tumors in the CNS. They also commonly cause seizures due to their location.
- **D. Pilocytic astrocytoma** — Relatively benign gliomas that are typically located in the cerebellum.

questions.stem: Which of the following is affected in sickle cell anemia?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — β-globin gene**

Sickle cell anemia is due to an autosomal recessive mutation that causes the 6th codon on the β-globin gene, normally glutamate, to encode valine instead. This causes red blood cells to become sickled at low intracellular pH and low oxygen tensions, changing their shape and predisposing them to clumping up. These clumped-up RBCs may then occlude vessels.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old female presents in your clinic with two painful lumps near her right armpit and one on her left breast. On questioning, she mentions that they have been there for some time now and they noticeably get more painful when she's about to have her menstruation. There is also no family history of breast cancer. On physical examination, the masses are about 1cm long, are soft, round, movable, and there is no notable discharge. What will be your initial impression?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Fibroadenoma**

- **A. Duct ectasia** — Duct ectasia typically presents as a palpable periareolar mass with thick, white nipple secretions. It is most often found in females in their 50s–60s.
- **B. Intraductal papilloma** — An intraductal papilloma would also present with nipple discharge that may be bloody.
- **C. Fibroadenoma** — Fibroadenomas are the most common benign tumors of the female breast. They are usually seen in females aged 20-30 years old. Fibroadenomas are frequently multiple and bilateral. They are usually small, round, movable, and typically do not present with nipple discharge.
- **D. Invasive breast carcinoma** — Invasive breast carcinoma is rare in young patients. Also, it typically presents with a firm, irregularly-shaped, non-movable mass which may or may not have nipple retraction and discharge depending on the stage.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the drug of choice for Campylobacter infections?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Azithromycin**

Campylobacter jejuni is a comma-shaped gram-negative rod. It is the most common cause of bacterial gastroenteritis. C. jejuni infections cause watery, foul-smelling diarrhea followed by bloody stools accompanied by fever and severe abdominal pain that mimics ulcerative colitis. It is also associated with Guillain-Barre syndrome due to antigenic cross-reactivity and reactive arthritis (also known as Reiter syndrome).

Macrolides, such as azithromycin (Choice A), are the drugs of choice for C. jejuni infections.

questions.stem: What type of hypersensitivity reaction is found in Goodpasture syndrome?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Type IIB**

Antibody-mediated (Type II) hypersensitivity relies on the use of antibodies for their effects. There are three subtypes for this, which include type IIA, type IIB, and type IIC.

- **A. Type IV** — T cell-mediated hypersensitivity involves the action of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells. CD4+ T cells produce cytokines that promote inflammation, while CD8+ T cells cause direct killing of the target cell. Examples of diseases that use type IV hypersensitivity include rheumatoid arthritis, type I diabetes mellitus, psoriasis, and tuberculin skin testing.
- **B. Type IIA** — Relies on antibodies for opsonization and phagocytosis of target cells. Examples include autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) and acute hemolytic transfusion reaction (AHTR).
- **C. Type IIB** — Uses antibodies to promote inflammation via complement activation. Examples include Goodpasture syndrome and acute rheumatic fever.
- **D. Type IIC** — Has antibodies that bind to target receptors to disrupt cellular function. Examples include myasthenia gravis and Graves' disease.

questions.stem: What causes Itai-Itai disease?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Cadmium**

- **A. Lead** — Lead toxicity causes microcytic, hypochromic anemia, basophilic stippling, and ring sideroblast formation. There is also poorly localized abdominal pain, called lead colic, as well as some neurologic and renal dysfunction.
- **B. Mercury** — Mercury toxicity causes Minamata disease, specifically when there is in utero exposure by consumption of contaminated fish. It is characterized by cerebral palsy, deafness, blindness, and mental retardation.
- **C. Arsenic** — Arsenic is known as the poison of kings and king of poisons. Its toxicity leads to arsenical keratosis, sensorimotor neuropathy, hypertension, arrhythmias, and numerous cancers, such as lung, bladder, and skin.
- **D. Cadmium** — Cadmium toxicity causes Itai-Itai disease, meaning "ouch-ouch" in Japanese. Clinically, it is characterized by osteoporosis and osteomalacia associated with renal disease seen in postmenopausal Japanese women working in rice fields.

questions.stem: All of the following are medulloblastoma-associated syndromes, EXCEPT:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Lynch syndrome**

Medulloblastomas are the most common malignant brain tumor. They are associated with a number of syndromes, notably familial cancer syndromes, such as Gorlin (Choice C), Li-Fraumeni, Turcot (Choice D), Gardner, and Cowden (Choice B) syndrome.

Lynch syndrome (Choice A) is the most common form of hereditary colorectal cancer and is not associated with medulloblastoma.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most common inherited bleeding disorder?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Von Willebrand disease**

- **A. Von Willebrand disease** — Von Willebrand disease (vWD) is the most common inherited bleeding disorder. It is caused by some degree of deficiency in von Willebrand factor (vWF), causing impaired platelet function. Because vWF and factor VIII (part of the coagulation cascade) form a complex, a decrease in vWF levels also leads to a decrease in factor VIII levels, leading to a prolonged PTT.
- **B. Hemophilia** — Hemophilia is the most common hereditary disease associated with life-threatening bleeding. It is due to an X-linked recessive inherited factor deficiency, and the specific factor that is missing is the basis for classification. Hemophilia A is due to factor VIII deficiency. Hemophilia B, or Christmas disease, is due to factor IX deficiency. Hemophilia C is due to factor XI deficiency.
- **C. Bernard-Soulier syndrome** — Bernard-Soulier syndrome (BSS), also called giant platelet syndrome, is due to an autosomal recessive mutation causing GPIb/IX deficiency. This causes decreased platelet adhesion and thrombocytopenia from increased platelet clearance.
- **D. Glanzmann thrombasthenia** — Glanzmann thrombasthenia (GTA) is due to an autosomal recessive mutation involving GPIIb/IIIa that causes its levels to decrease. This causes a decrease in platelet aggregation and an increase in bleeding time.

questions.stem: The top 2 locations for ectopic pancreas include which of the following?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Duodenum**

Pancreatic tissue that is aberrantly situated, or ectopic, is found in about 2% of postmortem examinations. The most common sites for ectopia are the stomach and duodenum (Choice D). These are followed by the jejunum (Choice C), Meckel diverticula (Choice B), and ileum (Choice A).

questions.stem: What are ovaries homologous to in males?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Testes**

- **A. Epididymis** — The epididymis, vas deferens, and ejaculatory ducts in males come from the Wolffian duct, which develops in the presence of testosterone. These structures correspond to the uterine tubes, uterus, and upper vagina in females, which come from the Mullerian duct. The Mullerian duct develops owing to a lack of anti-Mullerian hormone in females.
- **B. Prostate gland** — The prostate gland in males corresponds to the urethral and paraurethral glands in females.
- **C. Testes** — The ovaries in females correspond to the testes in males. This is due to the action of testis determining factor (TDF) encoded in the Y chromosome.
- **D. Penis** — The penis in males corresponds to the clitoris in females.

questions.stem: How many α globin genes are deleted in α-thalassemia trait?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — 2**

Alpha thalassemia is due to deletions in the α globin gene in chromosome 16, of which there are 4 copies. Different diseases occur depending on the number of deleted genes, as shown below.

| Disease | α-globin genes deleted | Phenotype |
|---|---|---|
| Silent carrier | 1 | Asymptomatic |
| Alpha-thalassemia trait | 2 | Asymptomatic, like beta-thalassemia minor; normal HbA2 |
| HbH disease | 3 | Severe, like beta-thalassemia intermedia; Hb: HbH (β4) |
| Hydrops fetalis | 4 | Fetal death in utero or shortly after birth; Hb: Hb Barts (γ4) |

questions.stem: Which type/s of aneurysm is/are associated with hypertension?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — All of the above**

- **A. Saccular** — Saccular aneurysms, also known as "berry" aneurysms, are the most common type of intracranial aneurysm and are the most common cause of spontaneous subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). They usually occur at the junctions of large arteries, most commonly at the anterior cerebral artery (ACA) - anterior communicating artery (ACoA) junction. Hypertension is a predisposing factor for the development of saccular aneurysms, with an estimated 50% of patients having hypertension at the time of diagnosis.
- **B. Berry** — Saccular aneurysms, also known as "berry" aneurysms, are the most common type of intracranial aneurysm and are the most common cause of spontaneous subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). They usually occur at the junctions of large arteries, most commonly at the anterior cerebral artery (ACA) - anterior communicating artery (ACoA) junction. Hypertension is a predisposing factor for the development of saccular aneurysms, with an estimated 50% of patients having hypertension at the time of diagnosis.
- **C. Charcot-Bouchard** — Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms are rare aneurysms that form on small cerebral arteries. They are also associated with chronic hypertension.
- **D. All of the above**

questions.stem: In patients dying of acute severe asthma (status asthmaticus), which cell type plays a key role?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Eosinophils**

In patients dying of acute severe asthma (status asthmaticus), the lungs are overinflated and contain small areas of atelectasis. The most striking gross finding is the occlusion of bronchi and bronchioles by thick mucus plugs. There are also Curschmann spirals found in sputum, which are due to extrusion of mucus plugs from subepithelial mucous gland ducts or bronchioles.

- **A. Mast cells** — Aside from eosinophils, other inflammatory cells present include mast cells, neutrophils, and T lymphocytes.
- **B. Eosinophils** — Numerous eosinophils and Charcot-Leyden crystals, which are composed of an eosinophil-derived protein called galectin-10, are present.
- **C. Neutrophils** — Aside from eosinophils, other inflammatory cells present include mast cells, neutrophils, and T lymphocytes.
- **D. T lymphocytes** — Aside from eosinophils, other inflammatory cells present include mast cells, neutrophils, and T lymphocytes.

questions.stem: The following are all components of CREST syndrome, EXCEPT:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Cytopenia**

CREST syndrome is a form of limited scleroderma. It has limited skin involvement (mainly fingers, forearms, face) with late visceral involvement. CREST stands for calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon (Choice B), esophageal dysmotility (Choice C), sclerodactyly, and telangiectasia (Choice D) — not cytopenia (Choice A).

The autoantibody associated with this syndrome is anti-centromere.

questions.stem: Which class of lupus nephritis has diffuse capillary thickening with increased production of basement membrane-like material and subepithelial immune complex deposits?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Class V**

Class I (minimal mesangial) lupus nephritis has no structural changes. Class II (mesangial proliferative) has mesangial cell proliferation with accumulation of mesangial matrix.

- **A. Class VI** (advanced sclerosing) — Involves sclerosis of >90% of glomeruli.
- **B. Class V** (membranous) — Has diffuse capillary thickening with increased production of basement membrane-like material and subepithelial immune complex deposits.
- **C. Class IV** (diffuse) — Involves ≥50% of glomeruli and also has subendothelial immune complex deposits.
- **D. Class III** (focal) — Involves <50% of glomeruli and has subendothelial immune complex deposits.

questions.stem: What do you call the process of decreasing basophilia of chromatin in the context of cell death?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Karyolysis**

Necrosis (Choice D) is irreversible cell death. It is usually pathologic and occurs due to overwhelming cellular stress. The nuclear changes found in necrosis include pyknosis, karyorrhexis, and karyolysis.

- **A. Karyorrhexis** — Fragmentation of the pyknotic nucleus.
- **B. Karyolysis** — Decreased basophilia of chromatin as it is acted upon by nucleases released during the death of the cell.
- **C. Pyknosis** — Nuclear shrinkage with increased basophilia.
- **D. Necrosis** — Irreversible cell death; usually pathologic and occurs due to overwhelming cellular stress.

questions.stem: In which layer of the skin are fingerprints formed?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Papillary layer**

From top to bottom, the layers of the skin are the epidermis (Choice B), dermis, and hypodermis (Choice D). The dermis is further divided into a papillary layer and a reticular layer (Choice A).

The papillary layer (Choice C) gives the dermis a bumpy surface that interlocks with the epidermis above it. On the palms and soles, it creates epidermal ridges which are commonly called fingerprints.

questions.stem: The following cells are mainly found in chronic inflammation, EXCEPT:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Neutrophils**

- **A. Macrophages** — Contribute to chronic inflammation by secreting cytokines and growth factors that act on other cells. They also activate other cell types, most notably T lymphocytes.
- **B. Plasma cells** — Activated B lymphocytes and antibody-producing plasma cells are often present at sites of chronic inflammation. The antibodies they produce may be specific for persistent foreign or self-antigens in the inflammatory site.
- **C. T lymphocytes** — Specifically CD4+ T lymphocytes, secrete cytokines that help promote inflammation.
- **D. Neutrophils** — Mainly present in acute inflammation, though some forms of chronic inflammation that last for prolonged periods of time and have persistent microbes also have them in large numbers.

questions.stem: Vasculitis is present in the following diseases, EXCEPT:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Systemic sclerosis**

- **A. Systemic sclerosis** — Systemic sclerosis (or scleroderma), while involving repeated cycles of injury and repair of small blood vessels, is not associated with vasculitis.
- **B. Rheumatoid arthritis** — Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disorder that principally attacks the joints, producing a nonsuppurative proliferative and inflammatory synovitis. In severe cases, RA may be associated with leukocytoclastic vasculitis.
- **C. Sjogren syndrome** — Sjogren syndrome is a chronic disease characterized by dry eyes (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) and dry mouth (xerostomia) resulting from immunologically mediated destruction of the lacrimal and salivary glands. More often than not, however, it presents in association with other disorders, such as SLE, scleroderma, vasculitis, and others.
- **D. Systemic lupus erythematosus** — Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a multisystem disease that is highly variable in its presentation. In blood vessels, it causes an acute necrotizing vasculitis involving capillaries, small arteries, and arterioles.

questions.stem: A deficiency in which vitamin would lead to squamous metaplasia and vulnerability to measles infection?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Vitamin A**

- **A. Vitamin A** — Vitamin A deficiency leads to night blindness, xerophthalmia, squamous metaplasia of different epithelia, and vulnerability to measles.
- **B. Vitamin D** — Vitamin D deficiency leads to rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.
- **C. Vitamin C** — Vitamin C deficiency leads to scurvy.
- **D. Vitamin E** — Vitamin E deficiency leads to spinocerebellar degeneration and hemolytic anemia.

#### Vitamin deficiency reference

| Vitamin D | Rickets (children) and osteomalacia (adults) |

| Vitamin K | Bleeding diathesis |

| Vitamin B12 | Megaloblastic anemia, degeneration of posterolateral spinal cord tracts |
| Vitamin C | Scurvy |
| Folate | Megaloblastic anemia, neural tube defects |

questions.stem: Which of the following refer/s to partial hydatidiform moles?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — None of the above**

Partial hydatidiform moles have a triploid karyotype, often present embryo/fetus, and a limited distribution of hydropic villi. Complete hydatidiform moles are the ones that have a diploid karyotype (Choice A), absent embryo/fetus (Choice B), and widespread hydropic villi (Choice C).

| Feature | Partial hydatidiform mole (PHM) | Complete hydatidiform mole (CHM) |
|---|---|---|
| Karyotype | Triploid | Diploid |
| **Morphology** | | |
| Embryo/fetus, amnion, fetal RBCs | Often present | Absent |
| Hydropic villi | Focal | Widespread |
| Trophoblastic proliferation | Slight to severe | Marked |
| Trophoblastic atypia | Mild | Marked |
| **Clinical features** | | |
| Diagnosis | Missed abortion | Molar gestation |
| Uterine size | Smaller for dates | Larger for dates |
| Theca-lutein cysts | Rare | Uncommon |
| Initial hCG levels | <100,000 mIU/mL | >100,000 mIU/mL |
| Medical complications* | Rare | Uncommon |
| Rate of subsequent GTN** | 1-5% of cases | 15-20% of cases |

questions.stem: The majority of cardiac muscle cells and neurons fall under which category below?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Permanent tissues**

- **A. Labile tissues** — Also known as continuously dividing tissues, are continuously being lost and replaced by maturation from tissue stem cells and by proliferation from mature cells. Examples include hematopoietic cells in the bone marrow and the majority of surface epithelium.
- **B. Permanent tissues** — Considered to be terminally differentiated and nonproliferative in postnatal life. The majority of neurons and cardiac muscle cells belong to this category. Thus, injury to the brain or heart is irreversible and results in a scar, because neurons and cardiac myocytes cannot regenerate.
- **C. Stable tissues** — Made up of cells that are quiescent, meaning they are in the G0 stage of the cell cycle. They have minimal proliferative activity in their normal state. However, these cells are capable of dividing in response to injury or loss of tissue mass. Examples include the parenchyma of most tissues, such as liver, kidney, and pancreas. They also include endothelial cells, fibroblasts, and smooth muscle cells.
- **D. Quiescent tissues**

questions.stem: A patient presents with frequent fractures, "blue" sclera, hearing loss, and dental problems. Several close family members are also known to a similar set of symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Osteogenesis imperfecta**

- **A. Achondroplasia** — The most common skeletal dysplasia. It is caused by a gain-of-function mutation of the FGFR3 gene, which leads to dwarfism, but without any effects on longevity, intelligence, and reproductive status.
- **B. Thanatophoric dysplasia** — The most common cause of lethal dwarfism. It is also caused by a gain-of-function mutation in the FGFR3 gene, but the mutation causes a larger increase in activity of said gene compared to that found in achondroplasia. Patients usually die young, mainly due to respiratory insufficiency from an underdeveloped chest cavity.
- **C. Osteopetrosis** — Due to mutations that cause decreased osteoclast activity leading to decreased bone resorption and skeletal sclerosis.
- **D. Osteogenesis imperfecta** — Also known as brittle bone disease, is the most common inherited disorder of connective tissue. It is due to deficient type I collagen synthesis, leading to too little bone being made and frequent fractures. Its most noticeable symptom is the presence of translucent "blue" sclera, due to thinning out of the sclera allowing the underlying uvea to be seen.

questions.stem: Which of the following is FALSE with regards to duodenal atresia?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — It invariably leads to bilious vomiting**

- **A. It is caused by a congenital absence of a portion of the duodenum** — Duodenal atresia is the congenital absence of a portion of the duodenum causing discontinuity and obstruction.
- **B. It is characterized by maternal polyhydramnios** — It is characterized by maternal polyhydramnios, as the fetus cannot swallow the amniotic fluid.
- **C. It invariably leads to bilious vomiting** — Vomiting occurs, which may either be bilious or non-bilious depending on the site of atresia.
- **D. The "double bubble" sign is seen in imaging** — On imaging, the double bubble sign is seen, which corresponds to the distended stomach and distended proximal portion of the duodenum separated by the pyloric valve.

questions.stem: The following statements are true of pneumoconioses, EXCEPT:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Choices A and B only**

- **A. The most dangerous particles are those that are >8 micrometers in diameter** — In terms of particle size, the most dangerous ones are those that are 1-5 micrometers in diameter (not >8 micrometers), because they can reach the terminal small airways and air sacs and deposit in their linings.
- **B. They refer to neoplastic lung reactions to inhalation of mineral dusts** — The term "pneumoconiosis" was originally coined to describe the non-neoplastic (not neoplastic) lung reaction to inhalation of mineral dusts encountered in the workplace.
- **C. Examples of particles that cause pneumoconioses are asbestos, silica, and beryllium** — There are numerous agents that can cause pneumoconioses; many of them are mineral dust, such as coal dust, silica, asbestos, and beryllium.
- **D. Choices A and B only**

questions.stem: Which of the following mutations is/are almost universally inactivated in small cell carcinoma of the lung?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — TP53**

Small cell carcinoma is virtually always smoking-related and has the highest mutational burden among lung cancers. There is almost universal inactivation of both TP53 (Choice A) and RB.

- **A. TP53** — Almost universally inactivated in small cell carcinoma, along with RB.
- **B. EGFR** — Most commonly mutated in cases of lung adenocarcinoma in never-smokers.
- **C. KRAS** — KRAS mutations are almost never found in these patients.
- **D. FGFR1** — FGFR1 mutations are found in many cases of squamous cell carcinomas.

questions.stem: The following statements are true regarding Marfan syndrome, EXCEPT:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — All clinical manifestations of Marfan syndrome can be explained by a loss of structural support in microfibril-rich connective tissue**

- **A. The fibrillin-1 protein is encoded by the FBN1 gene located on chromosomes 15q21.1** — Marfan syndrome is due to a defect in the fibrillin-1 protein. Fibrillin-1 is encoded by FBN1, which is located on chromosome 15q21.1.
- **B. All clinical manifestations of Marfan syndrome can be explained by a loss of structural support in microfibril-rich connective tissue** — While many clinical manifestations of Marfan syndrome can be explained by changes in the mechanical properties of the extracellular matrix resulting from abnormalities of fibrillin, several others, such as bone overgrowth and myxoid changes in mitral valves, cannot be attributed to changes in tissue elasticity. For these, it is thought that abnormal and excessive activation of transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) may play a role.
- **C. The skeleton, eyes, and cardiovascular system are most affected in Marfan syndrome** — Marfan syndrome is a disorder of connective tissue manifested principally by changes in the skeleton, eyes, and cardiovascular system.
- **D. None of the above**

questions.stem:
A patient comes in with the following laboratory results:

| Test | Value |
|---|---|
| Hgb (g/L) | 250 |
| WBC (×10⁹/L) | 8.00 |
| Platelets (×10⁹/L) | 250 |
| MCV (fL) | 90 |
| MCHC (g/dL) | 34 |
| EPO levels | Decreased |

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Polycythemia vera**

In the patient's laboratory results, only hemoglobin and erythropoietin (EPO) levels are abnormal, with hemoglobin being elevated and EPO levels being decreased. This is consistent with polycythemia vera.

- **A. Hereditary spherocytosis** — Presents with an increase in MCHC on CBC.
- **B. Polycythemia vera** — Characteristically presents with erythrocytosis and decreased EPO levels but may also present with leukocytosis and/or thrombocytosis.
- **C. Essential thrombocythemia** — Presents with thrombocytosis.
- **D. Chronic myeloid leukemia** — Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) presents with leukocytosis (mainly neutrophils and myelocytes), basophilia, and thrombocytosis.

questions.stem: According to the WHO, what will give the best possible protection to populations against polio?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — A combination of both oral and inactivated polio vaccines**

While there is no cure for polio, it can be prevented. Polio vaccine, given multiple times, can protect a child for life. There are two vaccines available: oral polio vaccine (by Sabin) and inactivated polio vaccine (by Salk). Both are effective and safe, and both are used in different combinations worldwide, depending on local epidemiological and programmatic circumstances, to ensure the best possible protection to populations can be provided.

questions.stem: Which of the following tumors typically arise near the fourth ventricle or, in adults, in the spinal cord?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Ependymoma**

- **A. Pilocytic astrocytoma** — Occurs more commonly in the cerebellum and has relatively benign behavior.
- **B. Medulloblastoma** — A malignant embryonal tumor that occurs predominantly in children and exclusively in the cerebellum.
- **C. Ependymoma** — Ependymomas are glial tumors that most often arise in proximity to the ependyma-lined ventricular system, including the central canal of the spinal cord. In the first two decades of life, they typically occur near the fourth ventricle. In adults, the spinal cord is the most common location.
- **D. Meningioma** — Predominantly benign tumors of adults that arise from the meningothelial cells of the arachnoid and are usually attached to the dura.

questions.stem: What can be a cause of dark, pigmented gallbladder stones?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Both B and C**

Cholelithiasis (gallstones) afflicts 10%-20% of adult populations. There are two general classes of gallstones: cholesterol stones and pigment stones.

- **A. Dyslipidemia** — Cholesterol stones are composed of >50% crystalline cholesterol monohydrate and are mostly due to cholesterol supersaturation in the context of dyslipidemia and metabolic syndrome.
- **B. Escherichia coli infection** — Pigment stones are mainly due to increases in unconjugated bilirubin in bile. Causes include bacterial contamination of the biliary tree, such as with Escherichia coli.
- **C. Sickle cell disease** — Pigment stones are mainly due to increases in unconjugated bilirubin in bile. Causes include chronic hemolytic anemias (such as sickle cell disease), and severe ileal dysfunction or bypass.
- **D. Both B and C**

questions.stem: Which of the following refers to small erythematous or hemorrhagic, macular, nontender lesions on the palms and soles?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Janeway lesions**

The presence of Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, and Roth spots are part of the minor criteria for infective endocarditis.

- **A. Osler nodes** — Small, tender subcutaneous nodules that develop in the pulp of the digits and persist for hours to several days.
- **B. Janeway lesions** — Small erythematous or hemorrhagic, macular, nontender lesions on the palms and soles, which are the consequence of septic embolic events.
- **C. Roth spots** — Oval retinal hemorrhages with pale centers.
- **D. Elschnig spots** — Infarcts from choroidal vessel damage in the setting of malignant hypertensive retinopathy.

questions.stem: Which of the following is/are causes of hepatocellular adenoma that may lead to progression to malignancy?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease**

Hepatocellular adenomas are benign neoplasms developing from hepatocytes. There are three large subtypes that differ on the basis of molecular analysis and associated clinical and pathological findings.

- HNF1-α inactivated hepatocellular adenomas. HNF1-α encodes a transcription factor, and mutations are responsible for autosomal dominant MODY-3 (maturity-onset diabetes of the young, type 3).
- β-catenin activated hepatocellular adenomas. Activating mutations of β-catenin are associated with neoplasia and malignancy in many organs. Hepatocellular adenomas that arise from these mutations have a high chance of developing into malignancy and should be removed even when asymptomatic.
- Inflammatory hepatocellular adenomas. These are associated with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (Choice B) and have a small, but definite, risk of malignant transformation.

questions.stem: The following are true regarding the effects of OCPs in the menstrual cycle, EXCEPT:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Both A and B**

In individuals using oral contraceptives, progestogen-negative feedback decreases the pulse frequency of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) released by the hypothalamus.

- **A. There is decreased secretion of FSH and LH by the hypothalamus** — This decreases the secretion of FSH and LH by the anterior pituitary, not the hypothalamus.
- **B. Decreased levels of LH inhibit follicular development, preventing an increase in estradiol levels** — Decreased FSH levels, not LH, stop follicular development, preventing an increase in estradiol levels.
- **C. A lack of estrogen positive feedback on LH secretion prevents a mid-cycle LH surge, and stops ovulation** — Progestogen-negative feedback and the lack of estrogen-positive feedback on LH secretion prevent a mid-cycle LH surge. The inhibition of follicular development and the absence of an LH surge prevent ovulation.

questions.stem: In a patient that died of drowning in saltwater, which of the following ions would be found in different concentrations between the left and right chambers of the heart?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Chloride**

Drowning in saltwater can leave different concentrations of sodium and chloride ions in the left and right chambers of the heart, but they will dissipate if the person survived for some time after aspiration, or if CPR was attempted.

questions.stem: The following statements about cardiac biomarkers are true, EXCEPT:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Troponin T levels are more associated with myocardial infarction and coronary heart disease compared to Troponin I**

- **A. Troponin I is more sensitive than CK-MB** — In general, cardiac troponins, troponin I (cTnI) and troponin T (cTnT), are more sensitive and specific compared to the MB fraction of creatine kinase (CK-MB).
- **B. Troponin I levels peak at 24 hours** — CK-MB and cTnI peak at 24 hours.
- **C. Troponin T levels return to normal in 5 to 14 days** — CK-MB levels return to normal in 48-72 hours, cTnI in 5-10 days, and cTnT in 5-14 days.
- **D. Troponin T levels are more associated with myocardial infarction and coronary heart disease compared to Troponin I** — Troponin I (not troponin T) levels are associated more with myocardial infarction and coronary heart disease compared to troponin T, which is associated more with the risk of non-CVD death.

questions.stem: Generalized hypoxic injury leads to which of the following?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Cytotoxic edema**

- **A. Vasogenic edema** — May originate from inflammation or tumors, leading to increased vascular permeability and disruption of the blood-brain barrier. This leads to an increase in extracellular fluid.
- **B. Cytotoxic edema** — Caused by generalized hypoxic injury leading to the cells of the brain being unable to maintain ionic balance. This type of edema then occurs from the increase in intracellular fluid.
- **C. Osmotic edema** — Caused by derangements affecting osmolarity, such as hyponatremia, diabetic ketoacidosis, or other metabolic pathologies.
- **D. Both A and C**

questions.stem: Which collagen type is defective in vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Type III**

Note that the type of collagen that is defective is different from the type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS). For example, the vascular type of EDS is type IV, but it is collagen type III that is defective in this condition.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old male presents to the emergency department with fever, jaundice, severe muscle pain, and altered sensorium. He reports recent recreational exposure to rivers and lakes. On examination, he has conjunctival suffusion and hepatomegaly. Laboratory tests reveal a platelet count of 40,000/mm³ and elevated liver enzymes (ALT 400 U/L, AST 350 U/L). What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Weil’s disease**

Fever, jaundice, severe muscle pain, conjunctival suffusion, altered sensorium, exposure to possibly contaminated water, thrombocytopenia, and elevated liver enzymes suggest Weil's syndrome (the severe, icteric form of leptospirosis).

#### Case classification

**Suspected leptospirosis** — an individual presenting with:
- Acute febrile illness of at least 2 days
- AND residing in a flooded area or with a high-risk exposure (wading in flood water, contact with animal fluid, ingestion of dirty water, etc.)
- AND at least 2 of the following:
  - Myalgia
  - Calf tenderness
  - Conjunctival suffusion
  - Chills
  - Abdominal pain
  - Headache
  - Jaundice
  - Oliguria

**Mild, anicteric leptospirosis** — any suspected case with acute febrile illness presenting with varied symptoms but with:
- Stable vital signs
- Anicteric sclerae
- Good urine output
- No evidence of meningismus, sepsis, or difficulty of breathing
- Other findings: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, rash, nonproductive cough, maculopapular rash

**Moderate to severe leptospirosis (Weil's syndrome)** — any suspected case with acute febrile illness with:
- Unstable vital signs
- Icteric sclerae
- Abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea
- Oliguria, anuria
- Meningismus
- Sepsis, septic shock
- Altered sensorium
- Difficulty of breathing, hemoptysis

questions.stem: A 55-year-old smoker presents with persistent cough, unintentional weight loss, and hemoptysis. Chest X-ray reveals a centrally located mass in the right upper lobe. questions.stem: What is the most common cause of cancer?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Environmental**

- **A. Idiopathic** — While the cause of cancer may be unknown in some cases, knowledge in cancer has greatly advanced.
- **B. Environmental** — According to Robbins, although both genetic and environmental factors contribute, environmental influences are the dominant risk factors for most cancers. Among the best-established environmental factors affecting cancer risk are infectious agents, smoking, alcohol consumption, diet, obesity, reproductive history, and environmental carcinogens.
- **C. Age** — Age has an important influence on the risk of cancer, but it is not the most common cause.
- **D. Genetic** — Interactions between environmental and genetic factors may be important determinants of cancer risk. However, genetic factors are not the most common cause of cancer.

*Source: Kumar, V., Abbas, A. and Aster, J. (2020) Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases. 10th Edition, Elsevier, Amsterdam.*

questions.stem: Which of the following diseases is associated with a mutation that results in a deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme, arylsulfatase A?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Metachromatic leukodystrophy**

- **A. Adrenoleukodystrophy** — Deficiency: peroxisomal acyl-coenzyme A oxidase/ALD protein/ALDP.
- **B. Metachromatic leukodystrophy** — Deficiency: arylsulfatase A.
- **C. Krabbe disease** — Deficiency: β-galactosidase.
- **D. Farber’s Disease** — Deficiency: ceramidase.

questions.stem: Which of the following subtypes of Hodgkin lymphoma is NOT typically associated with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection, and is characterized by a generally good prognosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Nodular sclerosis**

- **A. Nodular sclerosis** — Most common subtype of Hodgkin lymphoma. Uncommonly associated with EBV. Good prognosis.
- **B. Lymphocyte-rich** — Associated with EBV in about 40% of cases. Has a very good to excellent prognosis.
- **C. Lymphocyte-depleted** — Least common form of Hodgkin lymphoma. The Reed-Sternberg cells are infected with EBV in over 90% of cases. Occurs predominantly in older adults, in HIV-positive individuals of any age, and in individuals living in lower-income countries. The overall outcome is less favorable than in the other subtypes.
- **D. Mixed cellularity** — The Reed-Sternberg cells are infected with EBV in about 70% of cases. More likely to be associated with older age, systemic symptoms such as night sweats and weight loss, and advanced tumor stage. The overall prognosis is very good.

#### Hodgkin lymphoma subtypes

| Subtype | Morphology and immunophenotype | Typical clinical features |
|---|---|---|
| Nodular sclerosis | Frequent lacunar cells and occasional diagnostic RS cells; background infiltrate composed of T lymphocytes, eosinophils, macrophages, and plasma cells; fibrous bands dividing cellular areas into nodules. RS cells CD15+, CD30+; usually EBV− | Most common subtype; usually stage I or II disease; frequent mediastinal involvement; equal occurrence in males and females, most patients young adults |
| Mixed cellularity | Frequent mononuclear and diagnostic RS cells; background infiltrate rich in T lymphocytes, eosinophils, macrophages, plasma cells; RS cells CD15+, CD30+; 70% EBV+ | More than 50% present as stage III or IV disease; occurrence greater in males than females; biphasic incidence, peaking in young adults and again in adults older than 55 |
| Lymphocyte-rich | Frequent mononuclear and diagnostic RS cells; background infiltrate rich in T lymphocytes; RS cells CD15+, CD30+; 40% EBV+ | Uncommon; occurrence greater in males than females; tends to be seen in older adults |
| Lymphocyte depletion | Reticular variant: frequent diagnostic RS cells and variants and a paucity of background reactive cells; RS cells CD15+, CD30+; most EBV+ | Uncommon; more common in older men, HIV-infected individuals, and people in low-income countries; often presents with advanced disease |
| Nodular lymphocyte predominant | Frequent L&H (popcorn cell) variants in a background of follicular dendritic cells and reactive B cells; RS cells CD20+, CD15−, CD30−; EBV− | Uncommon; young males with cervical or axillary lymphadenopathy; mediastinal involvement is uncommon |

*Source: Kumar, V., Abbas, A. and Aster, J. (2020) Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases. 10th Edition, Elsevier, Amsterdam.*

questions.stem: Which of the following diseases is most strongly associated with ulcerative colitis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Primary sclerosing cholangitis**

- **A. Membranous nephropathy** — Association (secondary membranous nephropathy):
  - Drugs: penicillamine, captopril, gold, NSAIDs
  - Tumors: lung and colon carcinomas, melanomas
  - Autoimmune diseases: SLE, thyroiditis
  - Infections: chronic HBV, HCV, syphilis, schistosomiasis, malaria
- **B. Burkitt lymphoma** — Association: EBV.
- **C. Primary sclerosing cholangitis** — Association: inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis).
- **D. Primary biliary cholangitis** — Associations: Sjögren syndrome (70%), Hashimoto thyroiditis, scleroderma.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old male with a history of alcohol abuse presents to the emergency department with sudden onset fever, cough, and blood-tinged sputum. Chest X-ray reveals a lobar opacification with a cavity containing a gas-fluid level in the right lung. Which of the following pathogens is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Klebsiella pneumoniae**

- **A. Streptococcus pneumoniae** — Most common cause of community-acquired acute pneumonia. Associated with numerous neutrophils containing the typical gram-positive, lancet-shaped diplococci. Associated with lobar consolidation.
- **B. Haemophilus influenzae** — May follow a viral respiratory infection. Most common bacterial cause of acute exacerbations of COPD. Pulmonary consolidation is usually lobular and patchy but may be confluent and involve the entire lung lobe.
- **C. Klebsiella pneumoniae** — Most frequent cause of gram-negative bacterial pneumonia. Commonly afflicts debilitated and malnourished people, particularly chronic alcoholics. Thick, mucoid (often blood-tinged) sputum is characteristic because the organism produces an abundant viscid capsular polysaccharide. Tissue destruction and necrosis, causing abscess formation (appearing as a cavity containing a gas-fluid level), are common with pneumococcal or Klebsiella infections.
- **D. Mycoplasma pneumoniae** — Common among children and young adults. Occurs sporadically or as local epidemics in closed communities (schools, military camps, and prisons). Early in the course, the patient appears only moderately ill, and physical signs of pulmonary consolidation are often negligible compared with the striking consolidation seen on radiographs. Later, when the infiltration is at a peak, the illness may be severe.

*Sources: Kumar, V., Abbas, A. and Aster, J. (2020) Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases. 10th Edition, Elsevier, Amsterdam. Riedel, S., Morse, S.A., Mietzner, T.A., Miller, S. (2019). Jawetz, Melnick & Adelberg's Medical Microbiology (28th ed.). New York: McGraw-Hill Education.*

questions.stem: Which of the following pathogens commonly presents as otitis media in children but can cause pneumonia in the elderly?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Haemophilus influenzae**

- **A. Pseudomonas aeruginosa** — Produces infection of wounds and burns. Causes meningitis when introduced by lumbar puncture or during a neurosurgical procedure. Causes UTI when introduced by catheters and instruments or in irrigating solutions. Causes necrotizing pneumonia from contaminated respirators. Causes chronic pneumonia in CF patients. Causes mild otitis externa in swimmers. Causes infection of the eye, sepsis, ecthyma gangrenosum, and hot tub folliculitis.
- **B. Haemophilus influenzae** — H. influenzae and pneumococci are two of the most common etiologic agents of bacterial otitis media and acute sinusitis. Bronchitis and pneumonia may be seen in smoking, chronic obstructive lung disease, and cystic fibrosis. May cause meningitis and septic arthritis. Pneumonitis and epiglottitis may follow URTI.
- **C. Legionella pneumophila** — Causes Legionnaire's disease, the form of pneumonia caused by this organism. Causes Pontiac fever, a related self-limited upper respiratory tract infection.
- **D. Staphylococcus aureus** — If localized, infection appears as a “pimple,” hair follicle infection, or abscess. If disseminated, it causes endocarditis, acute hematogenous osteomyelitis, meningitis, or pulmonary infection. Also associated with food poisoning and toxic shock syndrome.

#### Community-acquired bacterial pneumonia — organism reference table

| Organism | Significance |
|---|---|
| Streptococcus pneumoniae | Most common cause of community-acquired acute pneumonia; most common cause of lobar pneumonia; otitis media in children |
| Haemophilus influenzae | Most common bacterial cause of acute exacerbations of COPD; otitis media and acute, purulent conjunctivitis (pink eye) in children |
| Moraxella catarrhalis | 2nd most common bacterial cause of acute exacerbations of COPD; otitis media in children; pneumonia in the elderly |
| Staphylococcus aureus | Secondary bacterial pneumonia post-viral respiratory illnesses (measles and influenza); lung abscess and empyema; pneumonia and endocarditis in IV drug users; hospital-acquired pneumonia |
| Klebsiella pneumoniae | Most common cause of Gram-negative bacterial pneumonia; debilitated, malnourished people and chronic alcoholics; currant jelly sputum |
| Pseudomonas aeruginosa | Hospital-acquired infections; cystic fibrosis and neutropenic patients |
| Legionella pneumophila (flourishes in artificial aquatic environments) | Pontiac fever: self-limited upper respiratory tract infection; pneumonia in patients with comorbidities and organ transplant patients; X-ray: focal infiltrates or consolidations, with pleural effusions and lymphadenopathy less commonly seen |
| Mycoplasma pneumoniae | Atypical pneumonia in children and young adults; local epidemics in closed communities (schools, military camps, prisons); X-ray: interstitial pneumonitis |

*Sources: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, Chapter 159, 21st edition, 2022. Riedel, S., Morse, S.A., Mietzner, T.A., Miller, S. (2019). Jawetz, Melnick & Adelberg's Medical Microbiology (28th ed.). New York: McGraw-Hill Education.*

questions.stem: A 77-year-old female presents with a recent intertrochanteric fracture. Which of the following systemic complications is most likely to occur in this patient?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Pulmonary embolism**

- **A. Hematoma** — Hematoma is common after fractures. It is usually localized. It does not result in significant systemic complications.
- **B. Gangrene of the foot** — Gangrene is not a common complication of intertrochanteric fracture. It is commonly associated with infections or ischemia.
- **C. Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)** — DIC is not a common complication of intertrochanteric fracture. DIC is commonly associated with a recent history of severe infections, hepatic failure, obstetric complications, and malignancy.
- **D. Pulmonary embolism** — DVT is a common complication in patients with intertrochanteric fractures that can lead to a potentially fatal pulmonary embolism (PE).

*Sources: Buttolph A, Sapra A. Gangrene. [Updated 2023 Aug 7]. In: StatPearls [Internet]. Treasure Island (FL): StatPearls Publishing; 2023 Jan-. Costello RA, Nehring SM. Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation. [Updated 2023 Jan 20]. In: StatPearls [Internet]. Treasure Island (FL): StatPearls Publishing; 2023 Jan-. Fei, C. et al. (2020). Deep Vein Thrombosis in Patients with Intertrochanteric Fracture: A Retrospective Study. Indian Journal of Orthopaedics, 54(Suppl 1), 101–108.*

questions.stem: A 65-year-old male with a history of COPD is admitted to the hospital with worsening dyspnea. His initial ABG reveals a PaO2 of 55 mmHg and a PaCO2 of 60 mmHg. The patient is started on oxygen therapy. Which intervention is most appropriate?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Improve V/Q to prevent atelectasis**

- **A. Increase tidal volume** — May lead to air trapping and hyperinflation.
- **B. Increase negative pressure** — Not included in the intervention.
- **C. Improve V/Q to prevent atelectasis** — Improves gas exchange and prevents atelectasis.
- **D. Administer 99% oxygen** — High O2 levels can result in hypoventilation, which can cause respiratory depression and CO2 retention.

*Source: Brill, S.E., & Wedzicha, J.A. (2014). Oxygen therapy in acute exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. International Journal of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease, 9, 1241–1252.*
