questions.stem: A newborn was found to have extrusion of abdominal viscera upon delivery. Which of the following describes an omphalocele?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — The abdominal viscera is covered with peritoneum without overlying skin.**

- An omphalocele is a herniation or protrusion of the abdominal contents into the base of the umbilical cord. The sac is covered by peritoneum without overlying skin (choice A), and the insertion of the distal umbilical cord into the sac itself distinguishes it from gastroschisis.
- Choices B–D all describe gastroschisis (see table below).

| | Omphalocele | Gastroschisis |
|---|---|---|
| Sac | + | - |
| Location | Below the umbilicus | Lateral to the umbilicus, right |
| Umbilical cord | Center of membrane | Left of the defect |
| Associated defects | 60% | 10% |
| Bowel | Normal | Inflamed |
| Alimentation | Normal | Delayed |
| Management | Surgical, TPN, hydration | Surgical, TPN, hydration |

questions.stem: An asthmatic patient with an acute exacerbation has been on low-dose inhaled steroids for the past four weeks. He has daytime asthma symptoms more than thrice a week, thus needing a reliever SABA thrice a week. He has been having nighttime awakening due to his symptoms, resulting in difficulty concentrating in school and playing with friends. Based on the GINA assessment of symptom control, under what level of symptom control does the patient belong?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Uncontrolled**

The patient has had daytime symptoms more than twice/week, night waking, reliever use more than twice/week, and activity limitation due to asthma. This classifies them under uncontrolled asthma, per the GINA Pocket Guide for Asthma Management and Prevention (2023) assessment of symptom control and future risk.

questions.stem: A baby boy was brought to the ER for progressive weakness and lethargy. On history, he was found to have intermittent crying spells accompanied by knee flexion when straining. He had one episode of vomiting with severe abdominal pain. Which of the following has been found to be correlated with the disease?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Adenovirus**

- The patient above appears to be a case of intussusception, which occurs when a portion of the alimentary tract is telescoped into an adjacent segment. Usually there is sudden onset of severe paroxysmal colicky pain in a previously well child. It is accompanied by straining efforts with legs and knees flexed. If not reduced, the infant becomes progressively weaker and lethargic.
- While 90% of intussusception cases are idiopathic, there is a correlation with prior or concurrent respiratory adenovirus (type C) (choice B) infection. The disease has also been correlated with the rotavirus vaccine, but this is a rare side effect.

questions.stem: Which of the following parameters decreases upon a baby’s first breath?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Pulmonary vascular resistance**

- At birth, there is a shift of blood flow for gas exchange from the placenta to the lungs. Lung expansion results in reduction of pulmonary vascular resistance (making choice C the correct answer), causing an increase in pulmonary blood flow. There is also an increase in systemic vascular resistance (making choice B incorrect) due to removal of the low-resistance placenta.
- Air entry into the lungs displaces fluid, decreases hydrostatic pressure in the pulmonary vasculature, and increases pulmonary blood flow (choice D is incorrect). The greater blood flow in turn increases the blood volume of the lung and the effective vascular surface area available for fluid uptake (choice A is incorrect).

**Transitions of the cardio-respiratory system at birth**

- Pulmonary vascular resistance decreases
- SVR (systemic vascular resistance) increases
  - Removal of the placenta
- Closure of PDA
  - Patency dependent on low O2 and high prostaglandins
    - High prostaglandins because of decreased pulmonary circulation (metabolized in lungs) and increased production in the placenta
- Functional closure of PDA (15h)
  - ↑ PO2, preferential blood flow from RV to lungs (↓ pulmonary vascular resistance)
- Anatomic closure
  - 2-3 weeks, fibrous proliferation of the intima

questions.stem: Which of the following supplements is strongly recommended for the prevention of community-acquired pneumonia?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Zinc**

- The following strategies are recommended to prevent PCAP:
  - Vaccination against Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus), Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), Bordetella pertussis (pertussis), Rubeola virus (measles) and Influenza virus
  - Breastfeeding
  - Avoidance of environmental tobacco smoke or indoor biomass fuel exposure
  - Zinc supplementation (choice C)
- There is insufficient evidence to recommend Vitamin A, C or D supplementation for the prevention of PCAP.

Source: De Ocampo, C.C.J., & Padua, J.R.O. (2021). 2021 Clinical practice guidelines in the evaluation and management of
pediatric community-acquired pneumonia. In Philippine Pediatric Society, Inc. Retrieved from https://pps.org.ph/wp-
content/uploads/2024/01/1.-2021-PCAP-CPG-PAPP-PIDSP.pdf

questions.stem: Calculate the APGAR score for the following case: A newborn baby girl was born with good cry and activity upon stimulation. Physical examination showed acrocyanosis with some flexion of extremities. Her heart rate on the first minute was found to be 133 bpm.
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — 8**

| Sign | 0 Points | 1 Point | 2 Points |
|---|---|---|---|
| Activity | Absent | Arms and legs flexed | Active movement |
| Pulse | Absent | Below 100 bpm | Over 100 bpm |
| Grimace (reflex irritability) | Flaccid | Some flexion of extremities | Active motion (sneeze, cough, pull away) |
| Appearance (skin color) | Blue, pale | Body pink, extremities blue | Completely pink |
| Respiration | Absent | Slow, irregular | Vigorous cry |

Total score interpretation:

- 0–3: Severely depressed
- 4–6: Moderately depressed
- 7–10: Excellent condition

questions.stem: The earliest age to give rotavirus vaccine is at:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — 6 weeks**

The rotavirus vaccine is given at a minimum age of 6 weeks (choice A), with a minimum interval of 4 weeks between doses. The last dose should be administered not later than 24 weeks of age.

questions.stem: Which of the following SMR stages is correctly matched?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Stage 4: the areola forms a secondary mound above the contour of the breast**

Only choice D shows the correct pairing. For the other choices:

- Choice A is incorrect because this refers to stage 2 (enlargement of the testes and scrotum, with reddening and thinning of the scrotum, but no enlargement of the penis).
- Choice B is incorrect because this refers to stage 3 (penis begins to enlarge, first in length then in diameter).
- Choice C is incorrect because this refers to stage 2 (breast bud forms below the areola).

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy presents with low-grade fever and rashes that started from the head and progressed to include the trunk. Further PE shows posterior auricular lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the associated enanthem of his likely condition?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Forchheimer spots**

- The case above most likely describes Rubella (German Measles or 3-day measles), characterized by low-grade fever, cephalo-caudal rash, and posterior auricular lymphadenopathy.
- About the time of onset of the rash, examination of the oropharynx may reveal tiny, rose-colored lesions called Forchheimer spots (choice B). The rash fades from the face as it extends to the rest of the body so that the whole body may not be involved at any one time. The duration of the rash is generally 3 days, and it usually resolves without desquamation.
- Koplik spots (choice A) are seen in measles or rubeola. Nagayama spots (choice C) are seen in roseola. A strawberry tongue (choice D) may be seen in Kawasaki disease or scarlet fever.

questions.stem: This refers to a patient with a positive TST or IGRA result, but with no signs or symptoms, with normal physical examination, and normal chest radiograph findings.
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — TB infection**

- Tuberculosis infection (TBI, choice C) occurs when the individual inhales a droplet of nuclei containing M. tuberculosis, which survive intracellularly within the lung and associated lymphoid tissue. The hallmark of TBI is a positive TST or IGRA result. In this stage the child has no signs or symptoms, a normal physical examination, and the chest radiograph is either normal or reveals a granuloma or calcifications in the lung parenchyma.
- TB exposure (choice A) means a child has significant contact with a TB patient but lacks proof of infection. TST or IGRA is negative at this stage.
- TB disease (choice B) occurs when signs or symptoms or radiographic manifestations become apparent.
- Disseminated TB (choice D) occurs when the mycobacterial infection has spread from the lungs to other parts of the body.

questions.stem: A mother who has been undergoing TB treatment for 4 months consults her pediatrician regarding breastfeeding for her newborn baby. What should be advised?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Continue breastfeeding**

- After two weeks of treatment, the mother may continue breastfeeding since she will no longer be considered infectious, hence choice A is correct. Prior to this, expressed milk or donated human breast milk (choice D) may be given.
- Discontinuation of breastfeeding (choice B) is not necessary since the mother is already on 4 months of treatment. Choice C is a false statement.

**Absolute and relative contraindications to breastfeeding due to maternal health conditions** (Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics, 21st Ed, 2020)

| Maternal Health Condition | Degree of Risk |
|---|---|
| HIV and HTLV infection | In the United States, breastfeeding is contraindicated. In other settings, health risks of not breastfeeding must be weighed against the risk of transmitting virus to the infant. |
| Tuberculosis infection | Breastfeeding is contraindicated until completion of approximately 2 wk of appropriate maternal therapy. |
| Varicella-zoster infection | Infant should not have direct contact to active lesions. Infant should receive immune globulin. |
| Herpes simplex infection | Breastfeeding is contraindicated with active herpetic lesions of the breast. |
| CMV infection | May be found in milk of mothers who are CMV seropositive. Transmission through human milk causing symptomatic illness in term infants is uncommon. |
| Hepatitis B infection | Infants routinely receive hepatitis B immune globulin and hepatitis B vaccine if mother is HBsAg positive. No delay in initiation of breastfeeding is required. |
| Hepatitis C infection | Breastfeeding is not contraindicated. |

choices.text: Fever persisting for at least 5 days

questions.stem: An essential criteria for clinical diagnosis of classic Kawasaki disease is:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Fever persisting for at least 5 days**

Only choice B (fever persisting for at least 5 days) is considered essential criteria for classic Kawasaki disease. The rest of the choices may or may not be present.

**Kawasaki disease (mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome) — quick sheet**

- Fever for at least 5 days + 4 of the following features:
  - Conjunctivitis
    - Bilateral, bulbar injection without exudate
  - Rash
    - Any form of rash
  - Adenopathy
    - Cervical adenopathy, non-suppurative
  - Strawberry tongue and other oropharyngeal changes
    - Red, cracked, swollen lips
  - Hand changes
    - Brawny edema, induration
    - Peeling around the nail beds

questions.stem: A 7-month-old infant was brought for consult due to white, curdish material on his tongue and palate. He has been increasingly fussy with poor appetite. Management of this condition involves which agent?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Nystatin**

- Oral thrush is a superficial mucous membrane infection that affects approximately 2-5% of normal neonates. It is characterized by pearly white, curdish material visible on the tongue, palate, and buccal mucosa. C. albicans is the most commonly isolated species.
- Oral thrush may be asymptomatic or can cause pain, fussiness, and decreased feeding, leading to inadequate nutritional intake and dehydration.
- Treatment of mild cases might not be necessary. When treatment is warranted, the most commonly prescribed antifungal agent is topical nystatin (choice B).

questions.stem: Children on strict vegetarian diets may suffer from a deficiency of which vitamin?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — B12**

- Deficiency of vitamin B12 (choice D) caused by inadequate dietary intake occurs primarily in persons consuming strict vegetarian or vegan diets. Prevalence of vitamin B12 deficiency is high in predominantly vegetarian populations. Breastfeeding infants of B12-deficient mothers are also at risk for significant deficiency. This may lead to severe and persisting neurological damage.

**Buzzwords for B vitamins**

| B Vitamin | Name | Clue |
|---|---|---|
| B1 | Thiamine | Beri-beri |
| B2 | Riboflavin | Nonspecific (cheilosis, glossitis) |
| B3 | Niacin | Pellagra |
| B5 | Pantothenic Acid | Nonspecific |
| B6 | Pyridoxine | Microcytic anemia + estrogen pills |
| B7 | Biotin | Alopecia + neurologic changes |
| B9 | Folic Acid | Megaloblastic anemia |
| B12 | Cobalamin | Megaloblastic anemia + neurologic deficit |

questions.stem: A 25-year-old male presents with prolonged PTT and a normal bleeding time. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Hemophilia**

- Hemophilia (A or B) is caused by deficiencies in factors VIII or IX, which are part of the intrinsic pathway, leading to prolonged PTT but not affecting bleeding time.
- Von Willebrand Disease (choice B) causes both prolonged PTT (due to low Factor VIII stabilization) and increased bleeding time (due to platelet adhesion defects).
- Vitamin K deficiency (choice C) affects factors II, VII, IX, and X, typically prolonging both PT and PTT.
- Platelet disorders (choice D) increase bleeding time but do not affect PTT.

questions.stem: A young child presents with an abdominal mass. Imaging shows a mass located near the adrenal glands. The child has a history of irritability and unexplained weight loss. Given the common causes of abdominal masses in pediatric patients, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Neuroblastoma**

- Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid tumor in children and often arises from the adrenal medulla or sympathetic ganglia.
  - It presents with symptoms such as an abdominal mass, irritability, and unexplained weight loss, as seen in this child.
  - Imaging typically reveals a mass near the adrenal glands. Neuroblastoma is also associated with systemic symptoms (e.g., fever, bone pain, or opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome).

questions.stem: A 25-year-old patient presents with fatigue, pallor, and frequent infections. Laboratory tests show pancytopenia with low levels of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. A bone marrow biopsy reveals hypocellularity with a fatty marrow replacement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Aplastic anemia**

- Pancytopenia (low RBCs, WBCs, and platelets) combined with a hypocellular bone marrow replaced by fatty tissue is characteristic of aplastic anemia.
- Leukemia can also present with pancytopenia, but the bone marrow biopsy typically shows hypercellularity with malignant (leukemic) cells.
- Myelodysplastic syndrome often shows dysplastic (abnormal) bone marrow cells with ineffective hematopoiesis, but not the severe hypocellularity seen in aplastic anemia.
- Iron deficiency anemia causes isolated anemia with low red blood cell counts, not pancytopenia or hypocellular bone marrow.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child presents with symptoms of fatigue, frequent infections, and easy bruising. Blood tests reveal leukocytosis with a predominance of immature white blood cells. What is the most common type of leukemia in pediatric patients?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — ALL**

Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) is the most common type of leukemia in children, accounting for approximately 75-80% of pediatric leukemia cases.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child presents with a persistent dry cough, fever, and fatigue for the past week. On examination, the child appears generally well but has mild respiratory distress. A chest X-ray shows patchy infiltrates suggestive of atypical pneumonia. What is the most likely causative agent?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Mycoplasma pneumoniae**

- Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a common cause of atypical pneumonia in school-aged children and adolescents.
- Streptococcus pneumoniae is a leading cause of typical pneumonia, presenting with high fever, productive cough, and lobar consolidation on X-ray.
- Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) — typically causes bronchiolitis in infants and young children, rather than atypical pneumonia.
- Haemophilus influenzae can cause pneumonia but is less common in vaccinated children and usually presents with typical pneumonia features.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old child presents with fever, rash, and muscle pain. On the third day of illness, the child begins to develop signs of shock, including hypotension and edema. Laboratory results show a low platelet count. Based on the progression of symptoms, what is the correct sequence of events in dengue fever?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Low platelet count → plasma leakage → hemorrhage**

In dengue fever, the progression of symptoms typically follows this sequence:

1. **Low platelet count** — Thrombocytopenia develops early due to bone marrow suppression and immune-mediated platelet destruction.
2. **Plasma leakage** — Occurs during the critical phase (around days 3-7 of illness) due to increased capillary permeability, leading to edema, ascites, and potentially shock (Dengue Shock Syndrome).
3. **Hemorrhage** — Severe thrombocytopenia and plasma leakage increase the risk of bleeding, which may range from minor mucosal bleeds to life-threatening hemorrhages.

This sequence reflects the clinical phases of dengue: febrile → critical (with plasma leakage and thrombocytopenia) → recovery.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old child with severe dengue fever has been receiving IV fluids and monitoring for signs of shock. The child's fever subsides, and signs of fluid retention, such as edema, begin to resolve. Which of the following is the best indicator of improving dengue?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Rising platelet count**

- In severe dengue, thrombocytopenia (low platelet count) is a hallmark finding. A rising platelet count indicates recovery from the critical phase and improvement in the bone marrow's ability to produce platelets. As the patient transitions from the critical phase to the recovery phase, platelet counts are one of the earliest laboratory markers of improvement.
- Increased white blood cell count may occur during recovery but is less specific than platelet count as an indicator of improvement.
- Fluid reabsorption marks the end of capillary leakage but does not necessarily indicate overall recovery.
- Improved liver function may occur later and is not the primary marker for improving dengue.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child presents with an abdominal mass, weight loss, and intermittent fever. After imaging and further investigation, a diagnosis of neuroblastoma is suspected. Which of the following is the most commonly elevated tumor marker associated with neuroblastoma?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — VMA (Vanillylmandelic acid)**

Neuroblastoma is a tumor of neural crest origin that often produces catecholamines. The breakdown products of catecholamines, including vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) and homovanillic acid (HVA), are frequently elevated in the urine of patients with neuroblastoma. These metabolites serve as key diagnostic tumor markers for the disease.

questions.stem: A 2-month-old infant presents with jaundice, pale stools, and dark urine. After further investigation, biliary atresia is diagnosed. What is the primary surgical treatment for this condition?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Kasai procedure**

- Biliary atresia is a congenital condition in which the bile ducts are either absent or damaged, leading to obstruction of bile flow and resulting in jaundice, pale stools, and dark urine.
- The Kasai procedure (also known as hepatoportoenterostomy) is the primary surgical treatment. It involves creating a direct connection between the liver and the small intestine to allow bile to flow, bypassing the obstructed or absent bile ducts.
- Early intervention with the Kasai procedure is crucial to prevent progressive liver damage and the need for liver transplantation.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child presents with a swollen, tender neck mass and a history of prolonged cough. Upon further investigation, tuberculosis (TB) is suspected. What is the most common extrapulmonary manifestation of tuberculosis in children?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Scrofula**

Scrofula refers to tuberculous lymphadenitis, which is the most common extrapulmonary manifestation of tuberculosis (TB) in children.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child is diagnosed with a kidney condition that has resulted in significant renal dysfunction, pain, and recurrent infections. The condition is severely affecting the kidney's function, and nephrectomy is considered as the next step in management. Which of the following kidney conditions is most likely to warrant nephrectomy in a pediatric patient?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Fibrous kidney**

- Fibrous kidney (or chronic obstructive uropathy due to fibrosis) is a condition where extensive scarring and fibrosis lead to significant renal dysfunction, often resulting in recurrent infections, pain, and deterioration of kidney function. In such cases, nephrectomy (surgical removal of the kidney) may be required when the kidney becomes nonfunctional and a source of infection or pain.
- Polycystic kidney disease (choice A): While it can lead to renal dysfunction, it is usually managed conservatively, and nephrectomy is not commonly performed unless complications such as recurrent infections or massive enlargement occur.
- Minimal change disease (choice C): This condition is primarily managed with steroids, and nephrectomy is not a typical treatment.
- Glomerulonephritis (choice D): Nephrectomy is not indicated for glomerulonephritis unless it progresses to end-stage renal disease with other complications.

questions.stem: Which of the following congenital heart defects requires a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) to maintain systemic or pulmonary circulation?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Transposition of the great arteries (TGA)**

In TGA, the systemic and pulmonary circuits run in parallel, and a PDA is crucial for mixing oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child presents with fever, flank pain, and irritability. On examination, the child is febrile, and the urine dipstick shows leukocytes and blood. Which of the following is the most likely site of obstruction in this patient?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Ureteropelvic junction**

- Fever, flank pain, irritability, and urine dipstick showing leukocytes and blood suggest a urinary tract infection (UTI), possibly with obstruction. The most likely site of obstruction causing these symptoms in a young child is at the ureteropelvic junction (UPJ).
- UPJ obstruction is a common congenital condition where there is a blockage between the renal pelvis and the ureter, causing urine to back up into the kidney, leading to pain, infection, and fever.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant is brought in for a routine check-up. The parents report that the baby has been drooling more than usual and seems irritable. Upon examination, the first tooth is starting to emerge. At what age does the first tooth typically erupt in infants?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — 6 months**

The first tooth (usually a lower central incisor) typically erupts around 6 months of age. However, there can be some variation, with some infants getting their first tooth a little earlier or later.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old child presents with localized bone pain, especially at night, and some swelling over the affected area. X-rays reveal a mass in the bone. What is the most likely cause of the bone pain in this pediatric patient?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Osteosarcoma**

Osteosarcoma is the most common malignant bone tumor in children and adolescents, typically affecting the long bones such as the femur or tibia. It often presents with localized bone pain, especially at night, and swelling over the affected area. X-rays may show a mass or "sunburst" appearance due to the tumor's aggressive growth.

questions.stem: A mother presents at 20 weeks of pregnancy with oligohydramnios. Which of the following syndromes is most commonly associated with oligohydramnios and may present similarly with other characteristic features such as limb deformities and pulmonary hypoplasia?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Potter syndrome**

Potter syndrome is a condition caused by renal agenesis or severe renal dysfunction, leading to oligohydramnios (low amniotic fluid). The lack of sufficient amniotic fluid causes compression of the fetus, resulting in characteristic features such as limb deformities, facial anomalies (e.g., flattened face, low-set ears), and pulmonary hypoplasia (underdeveloped lungs).

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child presents with diarrhea for the past 2 days. The child appears dehydrated and irritable. What is the most appropriate treatment to give to help reduce the duration and severity of diarrhea in this patient?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Oral rehydration salts (ORS)**

- Zinc supplementation is recommended to reduce the duration and severity of the illness. However, the most appropriate first-line treatment for a dehydrated child with diarrhea is oral rehydration salts (ORS).
- Antidiarrheal medications are generally not recommended for young children, as they can have adverse effects and may interfere with the body's ability to expel the infection.
- Antibiotics are not routinely used for most cases of diarrhea, as the majority of childhood diarrhea is viral in origin. Antibiotics are only indicated if a bacterial infection is confirmed or highly suspected.

questions.stem: A preterm infant is diagnosed with bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) after prolonged mechanical ventilation and oxygen therapy. Which of the following vitamins is commonly deficient in patients with bronchopulmonary dysplasia?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Vitamin A**

Vitamin A is commonly deficient in infants with bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD). BPD is a chronic lung disease that often develops in preterm infants who have undergone prolonged mechanical ventilation and oxygen therapy. Vitamin A plays a crucial role in lung development and repair, and its deficiency has been associated with worsened outcomes in infants with BPD.

questions.stem: A newborn presents with ambiguous genitalia and salt-wasting crisis. After further investigation, congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) is suspected. What is the most common enzyme deficiency in congenital adrenal hyperplasia?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — 21-hydroxylase**

- The most common enzyme deficiency in congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) is 21-hydroxylase deficiency. This enzyme is involved in the production of cortisol and aldosterone in the adrenal glands. A deficiency in 21-hydroxylase leads to a build-up of precursors (e.g., 17-hydroxyprogesterone), which are diverted into androgen production, causing virilization (ambiguous genitalia in females) and salt-wasting (due to low aldosterone levels).
- 11β-hydroxylase (choice A): This enzyme deficiency also causes CAH but is less common. It can lead to hypertension due to the accumulation of deoxycorticosterone, a mineralocorticoid, and androgen excess.
- 17α-hydroxylase (choice C): This deficiency leads to sexual infantilism and hypertension due to impaired cortisol and sex steroid synthesis.
- 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (choice D): This deficiency results in a lack of cortisol, aldosterone, and sex steroids, but it is rare and less commonly seen in CAH.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child is diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). What is the most common presenting symptom of this condition in children?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Bone pain**

Bone pain occurs in about 50-75% of children with ALL and is due to the infiltration of leukemic cells in the bone marrow, causing pressure on the bone and surrounding structures. This often manifests as tenderness or aching in the long bones, especially the legs.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl presents with multiple episodes of abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. She has a history of constipation. X-ray shows air-fluid levels and dilated bowel loops. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Volvulus**

Volvulus occurs when a portion of the intestine twists on itself, leading to bowel obstruction. The patient's history of abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and constipation, along with the X-ray findings of air-fluid levels and dilated bowel loops, suggests an obstruction, which is common in volvulus. Volvulus can cause ischemia if not treated promptly and often presents with a sudden onset of abdominal distension and pain.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child is diagnosed with talipes equinovarus. What is the treatment for this condition?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Serial casting followed by foot abduction bracing**

Talipes equinovarus is typically treated using the Ponseti method, which involves a series of weekly casting to correct the foot's position, followed by the use of a foot abduction brace to maintain the correction. Surgery is only required if the deformity does not respond to casting. This approach is effective in most cases and helps avoid the need for more invasive treatments like surgery or amputation.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child presents with fever, sore throat, and painful ulcers in the mouth, particularly on the soft palate and tonsils. The child also has difficulty swallowing and is drooling. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Herpangina**

Herpangina is characterized by the sudden onset of fever, sore throat, and the presence of small, painful ulcers or vesicles, typically on the soft palate, tonsils, or uvula. The difficulty swallowing and drooling are common due to the pain from the lesions. It is most commonly caused by Coxsackievirus A. The lesions in herpangina are usually confined to the back of the mouth, which distinguishes it from other conditions like hand, foot, and mouth disease (which also involves the hands and feet).

choices.text: Use of antibiotics for all respiratory infections

Integrated management of multiple conditions
in one visit
Only focusing on one illness at a time
Admission to the hospital for every sick child

questions.stem: Which of the following is a key principle in the IMCI approach to the management of childhood illnesses?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Integrated management of multiple conditions in one visit**

- **B. Integrated management of multiple conditions in one visit** — The IMCI (Integrated Management of Childhood Illness) approach emphasizes a comprehensive strategy where multiple conditions affecting a child can be assessed and managed in one visit. This method promotes efficient care and focuses on both prevention and treatment.
- **A. Use of antibiotics for all respiratory infections** — IMCI does not recommend the routine use of antibiotics for all respiratory infections.
- **C. Only focusing on one illness at a time** — IMCI does not prioritize focusing on only one illness at a time.
- **D. Admission to the hospital for every sick child** — Not every sick child requires admission to the hospital; care can often be managed at the outpatient level.

questions.stem: A term neonate presents with jaundice on day 3 of life. Total bilirubin is 15 mg/dL, and direct bilirubin is 1.9 mg/dL. What is the next best step in management?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Start phototherapy**

- Phototherapy is indicated for unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with levels above 15 mg/dL (depending on the neonate's age and other factors).
- A Coombs test would be indicated if there were higher levels of direct bilirubin (above 2 mg/dL) or signs of hemolysis, but in this case, further testing is not urgently required.
- Wait and observe is not appropriate given the bilirubin levels and the potential risk of worsening jaundice.
- Exchange transfusion is typically only considered if the bilirubin exceeds 20 mg/dL or if there is evidence of severe hemolysis or kernicterus.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant presents with a history of periorificial dermatitis, alopecia, and diarrhea. The infant was recently weaned off breastfeeding. Physical examination reveals erythematous patches with crusting around the mouth and anus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Acrodermatitis enteropathica**

- Acrodermatitis enteropathica is a rare genetic disorder characterized by zinc deficiency, which can result in symptoms like periorificial dermatitis, alopecia, diarrhea, and erythematous patches with crusting around the mouth and anus. It often occurs after the weaning off of breast milk, as breast milk provides zinc, and the child may not be getting adequate zinc through solid foods.
- This condition is most common in infants and can be treated with zinc supplementation. The presentation in this case—along with the timing of weaning—supports the diagnosis of acrodermatitis enteropathica.

choices.text: Rabies vaccine only, on days 0, 3, 7, and 14
Rabies vaccine only, on days 0 and 3

questions.stem: A 25-year-old male is bitten by a stray dog on his right hand while jogging. The wound is superficial but bleeding. The dog cannot be captured for observation. The patient has no prior rabies vaccination. What is the appropriate post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) regimen for this patient?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Rabies vaccine and rabies immunoglobulin (RIG)**

- The patient has a Category III exposure (deep wound, bleeding) and the biting animal is a stray dog, which cannot be observed.
- This categorization requires rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) for passive immunity and rabies vaccine for active immunity.

questions.stem: A 9-month-old infant is brought to the clinic for a well-baby checkup. Which of the following gross motor skills is expected at this age?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Crawling**

By 9 months, most infants can crawl. Sitting without support develops around 6 months, while standing and walking independently occur later, typically at 12 months or beyond.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings is characteristic of secretory diarrhea?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Stool output persists despite fasting**

Secretory diarrhea results from active secretion of electrolytes and water into the intestinal lumen and typically persists even with fasting. In contrast, osmotic diarrhea decreases with fasting.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child is brought to the emergency department after experiencing a generalized tonic-clonic seizure that lasted 3 minutes. The parents report the child has had a fever of 39°C (102.2°F) for the past day but no prior history of seizures. Physical examination reveals no focal neurological deficits. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Febrile seizure**

Febrile seizures are common in children aged 6 months to 5 years. Key features:

- Associated with fever ≥38°C (100.4°F).
- No prior afebrile seizures or neurological conditions.
- Generalized tonic-clonic seizures are typical and last <15 minutes.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child presents with 5 days of fever, conjunctival injection, erythematous and cracked lips, a strawberry tongue, cervical lymphadenopathy, and a polymorphous rash. Laboratory studies show elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). What is the most important initial treatment to reduce the risk of coronary artery aneurysms?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG)**

- The presentation of fever, conjunctival injection, erythematous and cracked lips, strawberry tongue, cervical lymphadenopathy, and polymorphous rash, along with elevated CRP and ESR, is consistent with Kawasaki disease. This is an inflammatory vasculitis that primarily affects children and can lead to complications such as coronary artery aneurysms if not treated appropriately.
- The most important initial treatment for Kawasaki disease to reduce the risk of coronary artery aneurysms is intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG). IVIG is most effective when administered early, ideally within the first 10 days of illness, and has been shown to significantly reduce the risk of cardiovascular complications.

questions.stem: Pruritus ani spread throughout pre-schools and day care centers can be observed in infection with which of the following organisms?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Enterobius vermicularis**

- Pruritus ani is a symptom which is seen in pinworm infections caused by E. vermicularis (choice B). This is commonly seen in school-age children.
- The other organisms are not associated with pruritus ani but present with other symptoms:
  - A. lumbricoides (choice A) presents with gastrointestinal symptoms and malnutrition.
  - T. trichiura (choice C) may also present with diarrhea and, in severe cases, rectal prolapse.
  - S. japonicum (choice D) infects the mesenteric or bladder veins, which leads to gastrointestinal and urinary symptoms.

choices.text: Presence of eggs in stool sample
Presence of eggs in perianal folds
All are possible diagnostic stages of the parasite

questions.stem: Diagnosis of the infection above can be done through observing:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Presence of eggs in perianal folds**

- For diagnosis of pinworm infections, the scotch tape test is utilized, wherein tape is used to obtain samples from the perianal folds (choice C).
- Other parasites are diagnosed through presence of eggs in stool sample (choice A), but pinworm infections are not diagnosed through this. They also do not have visible cutaneous worms (choice B), which are seen in other infections such as those of hookworm.

choices.text: All diagnostic tests are beneficial to this patient

questions.stem: The primary impression of the medical team is nephroblastoma. Which of the following diagnostic tests would not be beneficial in this case?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — All diagnostic tests are beneficial to this patient**

- As mentioned in the question, the most likely diagnosis for this case is Wilms tumor. It presents as a painless abdominal mass and may present with hematuria and hypertension.
- For cases of Wilms tumor, imaging of the abdomen to locate and check the size of the mass is beneficial. This includes abdominal ultrasound and x-ray (Choices B and C).
- Additionally, since this is a case that may possibly metastasize, adding a chest x-ray (Choice A) to check for pulmonary metastasis is also beneficial.

questions.stem: All of the following conditions are associated with the disease of the child, except:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Mesothelioma**

- Mesothelioma (Choice C) is not associated with Wilms tumor.
- Neurofibromatosis (Choice A), WAGR syndrome (Choice B), and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome are all associated with this condition.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is true regarding this condition?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Diagnostic tests will show that the mass does not cross midline.**

- In cases of Wilms tumor, masses will present in the flank and do not cross midline (Choice B). It is located in the kidneys and will usually metastasize to the lungs (correlating with the benefit of chest x-ray mentioned earlier).
- All other choices pertain to neuroblastoma:
  - It occurs within the neuroaxis, most commonly the adrenals (Choice A).
  - Metastasis is commonly observed in bones (Choice C).
  - Cord compression is a possible complication given its location (Choice D).
- Recall Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) vs. neuroblastoma.

questions.stem: Bitot spots are observed in children with deficiency of which vitamin?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Vitamin A**

- Bitot spots are keratinized epithelium in the conjunctiva observed in cases of Vitamin A deficiency (Choice B). Nyctalopia and other eye symptoms may be observed in this condition.
- Vitamin D deficiency (Choice A) would present as rickets and other conditions affecting the bones.
- Vitamin E deficiency (Choice C) mainly manifests with neurologic symptoms.
- Vitamin K deficiency (Choice D) will present as bleeding problems leading to hemorrhagic conditions.
- Recall vitamin deficiencies and toxicities.

questions.stem: Which of the following conditions is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Intussusception**

- The symptoms presented in this case are consistent with findings of intussusception (Choice B). Remember, currant jelly stools are indicative of this condition (buzzword!). Flexing of the legs and knees is also observed in these cases.
- Duodenal atresia (Choice A) will present as bilious vomiting that is seen early after birth.
- Pyloric stenosis (Choice C) would present as non-bilious vomiting, with noted loss of appetite and dehydration.
- Meckel's diverticulum (Choice D) is characterized by painless rectal bleeding, although in severe cases, such as those with perforation already present, abdominal crampy pain is noted.

questions.stem: Ultrasound results of this case will show this finding:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Target sign**

- In ultrasound imaging of intussusception, the "target sign" (Choice B) is seen.
- Coiled spring sign (Choice A) is also seen in cases of intussusception but not on ultrasound — this is observed on barium enema.
- Double bubble sign (Choice C) is encountered in cases of duodenal atresia on abdominal x-ray, indicating obstruction.
- Volvulus will show the coffee bean or omega sign (Choice D) on abdominal x-ray due to the multiple obstruction sites.

questions.stem: This condition is associated with which of the following viruses?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Adenovirus**

- Among these viruses, adenovirus (Choice A) has an association with intussusception. Part of its pathophysiology includes hyperplasia of the lymphoid tissue in the intestines, which can lead to the condition.
- Coxsackie virus (Choice B), EBV (Choice C), and Ebola virus (Choice D) are not known to predispose children to intussusception.

questions.stem: The most common congenital heart disease worldwide is:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Ventricular septal defect**

- According to recent studies regarding congenital heart diseases, the most common condition seen is ventricular septal defect (Choice A), which accounts for 20–30% of these conditions.
- Atrial septal defect (Choice B) and patent ductus arteriosus (Choice D) are seen in around 5–10% of children born with congenital heart disease.
- Transposition of great arteries (Choice C) is observed in around 5% of this population.

*Reference: Van der Linde D, Konings EE, Slager MA, et al. "Birth prevalence of congenital heart disease worldwide: a systematic review and meta-analysis." J Am Coll Cardiol. 2011;58(21):2241-2247.*

questions.stem: Urinary tract infections in children are commonly diagnosed with a colony count showing a bacterial concentration of:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — ≥105 CFU/ml**

- Urinary tract infections are diagnosed when an organism is detected in a sample with a colony count of ≥105 CFU/ml (Choice B).
- Although it can be argued that some laboratory standards consider ≥106 CFU/ml (Choice C) as diagnostic for UTI, there are only some exceptions, and ≥105 CFU/ml is still most accepted in general.

*Reference: Hay, A. D., Birnie, K., Busby, J., Delaney, B., Downing, H., Dudley, J., ... & Butler, C. C. (2016). The Diagnosis of Urinary Tract infection in Young children (DUTY): a diagnostic prospective observational study to derive and validate a clinical algorithm for the diagnosis of urinary tract infection in children presenting to primary care with an acute illness. Health technology assessment, 20(51).*

questions.stem: Which of the following conditions is characterized by an onion skin appearance of bone on imaging?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Ewing sarcoma**

- Onion skin or moth-eaten appearance on x-ray imaging is seen in cases of Ewing sarcoma (Choice A). This is the 2nd most common bone sarcoma encountered in the pediatric age group.
- Osteosarcoma (Choice B) appears with a sunburst pattern on imaging. This is the most common primary bone sarcoma.
- Osteochondroma (Choice C) is the most common benign bone tumor. It usually occurs in adolescents or young adults. There is no atypia or invasion of the bone seen.
- Fibrous dysplasia (Choice D) is characterized by a "Chinese character"-like appearance with no osteoblastic rimming.

*Image reference: Moth-eaten/onion-skin appearance seen in Ewing sarcoma, left femur — Radiopedia.*

questions.stem: Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis can be caused by which of the following organisms?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Group A Streptococcus**

- Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis can be caused by Group A Streptococcus, specifically *Streptococcus pyogenes* (Choice A).
- Group B Streptococcus (Choice B), or *S. agalactiae*, is more commonly known to cause UTI in pregnant women and neonatal pneumonia.
- Viridans streptococci (Choice C) are known to cause infective endocarditis (recall causative agents of infective endocarditis).
- *Peptostreptococcus* sp. (Choice D) is present in the normal flora. Its spectrum of disease includes wound infections and endometritis.

choices.text: None since this is seen in cases of bronchial asthma

questions.stem: “Staccato” pattern cough is observed in infection of which of the following organisms?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Chlamydia pneumoniae**

- Cough due to *Chlamydia pneumoniae* (Choice C) has a staccato pattern and is classified as atypical pneumonia. It is described as having a sharp quality with sudden bursts.
- Cough caused by *Staphylococcus aureus* (Choice A) is described as "brassy." This is seen in cases of bacterial tracheitis. However, brassy/metallic cough can also describe croup, tracheomalacia, tracheitis, and epiglottitis.
- Parainfluenza virus (Choice B) is characterized by a "barking" cough. It causes croup/laryngotracheobronchitis and can also present with a brassy/metallic cough as mentioned.
- Bronchial asthma (Choice D) presents with a tight-sounding cough with wheezing due to narrowing of the bronchi.

questions.stem: Endocardial cushion defect is seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Trisomy 21**

- Endocardial cushion defect, also known as atrioventricular septal defect, is seen in cases of trisomy 21 (Choice C, also known as Down syndrome).
- Congenital rubella syndrome (Choice A) is associated with patent ductus arteriosus.
- Turner syndrome (Choice B) causes primary amenorrhea due to a lack of, or an incomplete, X chromosome.
- Marfan syndrome (Choice D) mainly affects the musculoskeletal system and the eyes (outward and upward lens subluxation). It is associated with mitral valve prolapse.
- Recall the diseases associated with Down syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the appropriate management for this child?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — No treatment is warranted at this point, symptomatic screening should be observed.**

- Given that the child has no definitive diagnosis of tuberculosis yet, the proper step in management is symptomatic screening (Choice D), as recommended by the DOH for those under 5 years of age. Treatment is only warranted for proven tuberculosis cases.
- Contact with the father should not be stopped entirely (Choice A is incorrect). Building rapport and guidance with the parents is a must during childhood, and abrupt changes may affect the child's development. The father should make sure he completes treatment and practices precautions such as wearing a mask around his child to prevent spread of infection.
- Although PPD testing and chest x-ray are beneficial in tuberculosis cases, they are not enough to clinch the diagnosis (Choice B is incorrect). PPD may test positive even in cases of exposure, and chest x-ray should always be correlated clinically.
- Antibiotic regimen is not warranted at this point, since there is no proven diagnosis of tuberculosis in the child (Choice C is incorrect).

*Reference: NTP Manual of Procedures, 6th Edition, Department of Health.*

questions.stem: Which diagnostic test will test positive in individuals which have been previously exposed to the disease?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Protein derivative skin test**

- PPD testing, or protein derivative skin test (Choice B), will test positive in cases of tuberculosis exposure.
- MTB GeneXpert (Choice A) indicates active TB disease.
- Chest x-ray (Choice C) may point to TB disease but must be correlated clinically or with other TB diagnostic tests.
- Sputum microscopy (Choice D) is an alternative to MTB GeneXpert for checking for active TB disease.

questions.stem: Hartnup disease is a defect in the absorption in mainly which of the following amino acids?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Tryptophan**

- Hartnup disease is an autosomal recessive condition due to a defect in the SLC6A19 gene, causing poor absorption of amino acids, particularly tryptophan (Choice C).
- This leads to niacin/vitamin B3 deficiency.

questions.stem: Which vitamin deficiency is seen in a newborn with problems in bleeding and clotting?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Vitamin K**

- As mentioned in question #6, Vitamin K deficiency (Choice D) presents with bleeding problems. This is due to its crucial role in the synthesis of clotting factors.
- The following were mentioned above regarding the other choices:
  - Bitot spots are keratinized epithelium in the conjunctiva observed in cases of Vitamin A deficiency (Choice B). Nyctalopia and other eye symptoms may be observed in this condition.
  - Vitamin D deficiency (Choice A) would present as rickets and other conditions affecting the bones.
  - Vitamin E deficiency (Choice C) manifests mainly with neurologic symptoms.

questions.stem: The most commonly encountered type of hernia in infants is:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Indirect inguinal**

- Indirect inguinal hernia (Choice A) is the most common type of hernia encountered in infants, with a prevalence of 1–5% of all full-term births.
- Diaphragmatic hernia (Choice C) has a prevalence of 1 in every 2,500 live births.
- Direct inguinal and femoral hernias (Choices B and D) are considered rare in infants.

*Reference: Journal of Pediatric Surgery.*

questions.stem: A 4th dose of Hepatitis B vaccine is warranted to be given if the 3rd dose was given before __ weeks of age.
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — 24 weeks**

- If the 3rd dose is given at an age less than 24 weeks (Choice B), or 6 months, then a 4th dose of Hepatitis B vaccine is warranted.

questions.stem: All of the following are bacterial organisms causing diarrhea in children, except:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Giardia lamblia**

- Although all organisms in the question will cause diarrhea in children, only *C. jejuni* (Choice A), *Salmonella* sp. (Choice B), and *Shigella* sp. (Choice C) are bacteria.
- *G. lamblia* (Choice D) is a protozoan.
- Always digest the questions, since there are simple questions like this that are answerable only by technicalities, such as correctly categorizing the organisms.

questions.stem: Which of the following vaccines is not included in the Expanded Program on Immunization (EPI)?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Varicella**

- The Expanded Program on Immunization (EPI) was established in 1976 with the goal of reducing the morbidity and mortality of children affected by vaccine-preventable diseases prevalent in the country. This program is under the Department of Health (DOH).
- Tuberculosis (Choice A), tetanus (Choice B), and measles (Choice D) vaccines are included in the EPI.
- Varicella (Choice C) is not included in the EPI.
- Recall the vaccines included in this DOH program.

questions.stem: The primary impression of the child in this case is most likely caused by which organism?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Neisseria meningitidis**

- Key points for this case include the high-grade fever and fast-spreading rash with noted decrease in sensorium, which are symptoms indicative of meningococcemia.
- Meningococcemia is the dissemination of meningococci resulting in multiorgan symptoms and purpuric rash, caused by *N. meningitidis* (Choice C).
- *H. influenzae* (Choice A) causes epiglottitis, meningitis, otitis media, and pneumonia. Rash is not that common during infection with this organism, and when present, it presents as a petechial rash.
- Measles virus (Choice B) presents with maculopapular rash, cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis (recall the 3 C's of measles). Koplik spots (buzzword!) are also present in infection with this virus.
- *C. jejuni* (Choice D) manifests with watery, foul-smelling stools which will eventually present as bloody stools with abdominal pain. It may mimic ulcerative colitis and cause Guillain-Barré syndrome.

questions.stem: The drug of choice for treatment of this child is:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Penicillin G**

- The drug of choice for treatment of meningococcemia in children may be penicillin G (Choice A), ceftriaxone IM or IV, or cefotaxime IM or IV.
- Rifampicin (Choice B) and ciprofloxacin (Choice D) are used for prophylaxis at times of exposure to infected individuals.
- Some countries use chloramphenicol (Choice C) in cases resistant to first-line drugs, but this is not usually observed locally.

questions.stem: Prophylaxis of the classmates of the child in school should be done by administering:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Rifampicin**

- Given that the child is 4 years old in the case, the classmates are assumed to fall under the category of children younger than 15 years but older than 1 month.
- **A. Chloramphenicol** — utilized for meningococcemia in other countries only.
- **B. Rifampicin** — for children in this age category, rifampicin 10 mg/kg per orem every 12 hours for 2 days is one of the antibiotics that can be administered.
- **C. Ceftriaxone**
- **D. Penicillin G** — the drug of choice for treatment of known (active) cases.
- Recall antibiotic prophylaxis for exposed individuals in *N. meningitidis* infection.

questions.stem: The triad of the choledochal cyst which may be seen in children includes the following, except:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Fever**

- Choledochal cysts usually present in childhood with a triad of jaundice, right upper quadrant mass, and abdominal pain (Choices A, C, and D).
- Fever (Choice B) is more commonly observed in the adult population with this condition.
- This condition can be diagnosed through ultrasound, CT scan, or magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP).

questions.stem: For a child who tested positive with HBsAg, which of the following laboratory parameters will indicate acute infection?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Anti-HBc IgM**

- Watch out for crossover questions like this in the PLE — this was asked in both the microbiology and pediatrics exams.
- Recalling the rationale from microbiology and parasitology practice test 6:
  - Among the hepatitis B panel, it is IgM anti-HBc (Choice C) that indicates new infection and is the most specific marker for acute hepatitis B infection.
  - Anti-HBs (Choice A) indicates the presence of antibodies but no active disease. This tests positive in vaccinated individuals and in complete recovery.
  - Anti-HBc IgG (Choice B) is a marker that tells whether there has been an old infection, or if the individual is a chronic carrier.
  - HBeAg (Choice D) determines the infectivity of an individual. Testing positive means high infectivity.

questions.stem: Overload in which vitamin will lead to pseudotumor cerebri?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Vitamin A**

- Pseudotumor cerebri includes symptoms such as headache, blurred vision, and stupor (thus called pseudotumor since it can be confused with a brain tumor). This is caused by vitamin A toxicity (Choice A).
- Vitamin D toxicity (Choice B) results in hypertension and metastatic calcification.
- Vitamin E toxicity (Choice C) manifests as reduced platelet aggregation.
- Vitamin K toxicity (Choice D) results in hemolysis.
- Recall the toxicities of fat-soluble vitamins as listed in question #6.

questions.stem: All of the following are true regarding breastmilk, except:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Whey-to-casein ratio increases from early to late lactation.**

- Be careful whether the question asks about the whey-to-casein or casein-to-whey ratio. Whey is increased during early milk and decreases eventually — thus, the whey-to-casein ratio *decreases* (Choice C is incorrect).
- The following vitamins and minerals have higher concentrations in formula milk than in breast milk (note these exceptions, which include iron — Choice A):

  **Mnemonic — "KID":** Vitamin **K**, **I**ron, Vitamin **D**

- The whey-to-casein ratio in mature milk is 60:40, or 3:2 (Choice B).
- Colostrum is >80% watery, protein-rich, and low in fat and carbohydrates (Choice D).

choices.text:
Monkey-like appearance is observed in children
with this condition.

Fatty infiltration of the liver is not seen in these
cases.
Children with this condition have a poor appetite.
Edema is absent in these cases.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements correctly describes kwashiorkor?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Children with this condition have a poor appetite.**

- For children affected by kwashiorkor, poor appetite is observed (Choice C).
- The other descriptions are indicative of marasmus:
  - Monkey-like facial features (Choice A)
  - No fatty infiltration of the liver (Choice B)
  - No edema seen (Choice D)
- Kwashiorkor is generally due to protein deficiency in the diet, while marasmus is due to general caloric deficiency. Thus, kwashiorkor presents with edema due to the protein deficiency leading to an imbalance in oncotic pressure (review the physiology of fluids).
- Recall kwashiorkor vs. marasmus.
