questions.stem: Which of the following CORRECTLY describes Higoumenakis sign of congenital syphilis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Unilateral or bilateral thickening of the sternoclavicular third of the clavicle**

All of the findings below are signs associated with congenital syphilis.

- **A. Unilateral or bilateral thickening of the sternoclavicular third of the clavicle** — this is Higoumenakis' sign (correct answer).
- **B. Anterior bowing of the midportion of the tibia** — this describes saber shin, not Higoumenakis' sign.
- **C. Peg-shaped upper central incisors with a notch along the biting surface** — this describes Hutchinson teeth, not Higoumenakis' sign.
- **D. Linear scars that extend in a spoke-like pattern from previous mucocutaneous fissures of the mouth, anus, and genitalia** — this describes rhagades, not Higoumenakis' sign.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy had a 3-day history of fever followed by inflammation of the parotid gland. He was eventually diagnosed to have mumps. A few days later, the mother noted the onset of seizures and altered sensorium. On PE, there was note of nuchal rigidity and positive Kernig sign. Which of the following findings is consistent with his clinical picture?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Clear CSF, WBC 200/hpf, all lymphocytes, protein 60 mg/dL, normal glucose**

Mumps is a viral infection caused by paramyxovirus; one of its complications is the development of meningitis.

- **A. Clear CSF, WBC 200/hpf, all lymphocytes, protein 60 mg/dL, normal glucose** — the typical finding in viral meningitis (correct answer).
- **B. Clear CSF, WBC 3/hpf, all lymphocytes, protein 25 mg/dL, normal glucose** — a normal CSF analysis.
- **C. Slightly turbid CSF, WBC 100/hpf, all PMNs, protein 100 mg/dL, glucose 30% of plasma glucose** — indicates a bacterial etiology.
- **D. Clear CSF, WBC 100/hpf, mostly lymphocytes, protein 100 mg/dL, decreased glucose** — characteristic of tuberculous meningitis.

#### CSF findings in CNS disorders
*Adapted from Table 603-1, Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics, 20th ed.*

**Normal**

| Pressure (mm H2O) | Leukocytes (mm3) | Protein (mg/dL) | Glucose (mg/dL) | Comments |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 50-80 | <5, ≥75% lymphocytes | 20-45 | >50 (or 75% serum glucose) | -- |

**Common forms of meningitis**

| Condition | Pressure (mm H2O) | Leukocytes (mm3) | Protein (mg/dL) | Glucose (mg/dL) | Comments |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Acute bacterial meningitis | Usually elevated (100-300) | 100-10,000 or more; usually 300-2,000; PMNs predominate | Usually 100-500 | Decreased, usually <40 (or <50% serum glucose) | Organisms usually seen on Gram stain and recovered by culture |
| Partially treated bacterial meningitis | Normal or elevated | 5-10,000; PMNs usual but mononuclear cells may predominate if pretreated for extended period of time | Usually 100-500 | Normal or decreased | Organisms may be seen on Gram stain |
| Viral meningitis or meningoencephalitis | Normal or slightly elevated (80-150) | Rarely >1,000 cells. Eastern equine encephalitis and lymphocytic choriomeningitis may have cell counts of several thousand. PMNs early but mononuclear cells predominate through most of the course | Usually 50-200 | Generally normal; may be decreased to <40 in some viral diseases, particularly mumps (15-20% of cases) | HSV encephalitis is suggested by focal seizures or by focal findings on CT or MRI scans or EEG. Enteroviruses and HSV infrequently recovered from CSF. HSV and enteroviruses may be detected by PCR of CSF |

**Uncommon forms of meningitis**

| Condition | Pressure (mm H2O) | Leukocytes (mm3) | Protein (mg/dL) | Glucose (mg/dL) | Comments |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tuberculous meningitis | Usually elevated | 10-500; PMNs early, but lymphocytes predominate through most of the course | 100-3,000; may be higher in the presence of block | <50 in most cases; decreases with time if treatment is not provided | Acid-fast organisms almost never seen on smear. Organisms may be recovered in culture of large volumes of CSF. Mycobacterium tuberculosis may be detected by PCR of CSF |

**Brain abscesses and parameningeal focus**

| Condition | Pressure (mm H2O) | Leukocytes (mm3) | Protein (mg/dL) | Glucose (mg/dL) | Comments |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Brain abscess | Usually elevated (100-300) | 5-200; CSF rarely acellular; lymphocytes predominate; if abscess ruptures into ventricle, PMNs predominate, and cell count may reach >100,000 | 75-500 | Normal unless abscess ruptures into ventricular system | No organisms on smear or culture unless abscess ruptures into ventricular system |
| Subdural empyema | Usually elevated (100-300) | 100-5,000; PMNs predominate | 100-500 | Normal | No organisms on smear or culture of CSF unless meningitis is also present; organisms found on tap of subdural fluid |

questions.stem: Immunizations against disease are under which type of immunity?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Active artificial immunity**

- **A. Active natural immunity** — this describes immunity from infection.
- **B. Active artificial immunity** — antibody production after immunizations is classified under active artificial immunity (correct answer).
- **C. Passive natural immunity** — this describes antibodies passed down by the mother to the fetus.
- **D. Passive artificial immunity** — this describes administration of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg).

questions.stem: Hydrocephalus and intracerebral calcifications can be a presentation of a neonate with which of the following ToRCHeS infections?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Toxoplasmosis**

- **A. Cytomegalovirus** — congenital CMV infection is characterized by hearing loss, seizures, petechial rash, blueberry muffin rash, and periventricular calcifications (as opposed to intracerebral calcifications in toxoplasmosis).
- **B. Congenital syphilis** — often results in stillbirth or hydrops fetalis; if the child survives, it presents with cutaneous lesions on the hands/feet, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, anemia, and rhinorrhea.
- **C. Congenital rubella** — presents with patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), cataracts, and deafness, with or without blueberry muffin rash.
- **D. Toxoplasmosis** — usually presents with chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and intracerebral calcifications, with or without blueberry muffin rash (correct answer).

questions.stem: A 6-year-old male has a history of recurrent gross hematuria, especially a few days after URTI. Urinalysis is positive for RBCs (too many to count) with urinary protein +2. C3 is normal. Kidney biopsy revealed mesangial proliferation and IgA deposits in the mesangium. What is the diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Berger’s nephropathy**

- **A. Post-infectious glomerulonephritis** — develops 1-2 weeks after an episode of URTI and has low serum C3. Biopsy findings include diffuse proliferation on light microscopy and subepithelial humps on electron microscopy.
- **B. Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis** — may show a positive ANCA in some patients and has normal serum complement. There is crescentic glomerulonephritis on light microscopy, with no deposits seen on electron microscopy.
- **C. Berger’s (IgA) nephropathy** — the most common cause of acute glomerulonephritis, characterized by mesangial proliferation and IgA deposits in the mesangium. It is often preceded by URTI and develops within days after infection (correct answer).
- **D. Lupus nephritis** — also presents with low serum C3. Immune complexes in the tubular or peritubular capillary basement membrane are characteristic findings.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old male presented with disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) at the ER. Past medical history is remarkable for a diagnosis of leukemia. Which of the following mutations is expected on further work-up?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — t(15;17)**

- Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is a buzzword for acute promyelocytic anemia (APML). The mutation t(15;17) is most commonly associated with APML.

- **A. t(9;22)** — the Philadelphia chromosome; associated with chronic myelogenous leukemia, and less commonly, acute lymphoblastic leukemia.
- **B. t(8;14)** — associated with Burkitt lymphoma.
- **C. t(15;17)** — most commonly associated with APML (correct answer).
- **D. t(11;22)** — associated with Ewing sarcoma.

questions.stem: Robert, 8/M, is an aspiring professional basketball player. His mother’s height is 158 cm and his father’s height is 174 cm. Calculate his midparental height.
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — 172.5 cm**

Using the standard midparental height formula, with a maternal height of 158 cm and a paternal height of 174 cm, the calculated midparental height is 172.5 cm (Choice D).

questions.stem: What is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Lipoid nephrosis**

Most children with nephrotic syndrome have a form of primary or idiopathic nephrotic syndrome.

- **A. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis** — the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome among adults; also a cause of idiopathic nephrotic syndrome in children, but less common than minimal change disease.
- **B. Membranous nephropathy** — a cause of idiopathic nephrotic syndrome in children, but less common than minimal change disease.
- **C. Lipoid nephrosis** — also known as minimal change disease; the most common cause of idiopathic nephrotic syndrome in children (correct answer).
- **D. Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis** — a cause of idiopathic nephrotic syndrome in children, but less common than minimal change disease.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child at the ER presented with high-grade fever, respiratory distress, and brassy cough. Chest X-ray was done showing subglottic narrowing and a ragged tracheal air column. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Bacterial tracheitis**

- **A. Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis)** — the most common form of acute upper respiratory obstruction; caused by viral infection of the glottic and subglottic regions. Clues to diagnosis include the characteristic barking cough, hoarseness, inspiratory stridor, and the typical subglottic narrowing or "steeple sign" on neck radiographs.
- **B. Foreign body aspiration** — presents with sudden-onset respiratory obstruction, manifesting as choking and coughing, usually without prodromal signs of infection. Chest X-ray findings include air trapping on the right lung with mediastinal shift toward the right lung.
- **C. Epiglottitis** — a potentially lethal condition characterized by an acute, rapidly progressive and potentially fulminating course of high fever, sore throat, dyspnea, and rapidly progressing respiratory obstruction. Drooling is usually present, and the neck is hyperextended in an attempt to maintain the airway. Classic upper airway radiographs of a child with epiglottitis show the "thumb sign."
- **D. Bacterial tracheitis** — an acute bacterial infection of the upper airway that is potentially life-threatening. S. aureus is the most commonly isolated pathogen. It often follows a viral respiratory infection (especially laryngotracheitis). Typically, the child has a brassy cough, high fever, purulent airway secretions, and absence of drooling and dysphagia (as seen with epiglottitis). Chest radiographs often show patchy infiltrates and may show focal densities as well as subglottic narrowing and a rough, ragged tracheal air column (correct answer).

questions.stem: Rhabdomyosarcoma occurs most frequently at which anatomic site?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Head and neck**

Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common pediatric soft tissue sarcoma, accounting for ~3.5% of childhood cancers. These tumors may occur at virtually any anatomic site.

- **A. Head and neck** — accounts for ~25% of cases (correct answer, the most frequent site).
- **B. Orbit** — accounts for ~9% of cases.
- **C. Genitourinary tract** — accounts for ~24% of cases.
- **D. Extremities** — accounts for ~19% of cases.

These tumors are thought to arise from the same embryonic mesenchyme as striated skeletal muscle. Rhabdomyosarcoma belongs to the general category of small, round, blue cell tumors, which includes neuroblastoma, non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, and Ewing sarcoma. Definitive diagnosis is established by biopsy, microscopic appearance, and immunohistochemistry.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding the management of biliary atresia?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — the short-term benefit of the Kasai procedure is decompression and drainage sufficient to forestall the onset of cirrhosis**

- **A. Only select patients with suspected biliary atresia should undergo exploratory laparotomy and direct cholangiography to determine the presence and site of obstruction** — incorrect; all patients with suspected biliary atresia should undergo exploratory laparotomy and direct cholangiography.
- **B. Higher success rate for establishing good bile flow after Kasai procedure is observed if performed after 8 weeks of life** — incorrect; the success rate for establishing good bile flow after the Kasai operation is much higher (90%) if performed before 8 weeks of life.
- **C. The definitive management of biliary atresia is surgical correction through Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy** — incorrect; liver transplantation is the definitive management for biliary atresia.
- **D. The short-term benefit of Kasai procedure is decompression and drainage sufficient to forestall the onset of cirrhosis** — correct; the short-term benefit of hepatoportoenterostomy is decompression and drainage sufficient to forestall the onset of cirrhosis and sustain growth until a successful liver transplantation can be done (correct answer).

questions.stem: What is the most common causative agent in spontaneous bacterial peritonitis among patients with nephrotic syndrome?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Streptococcus pneumoniae**

Children with nephrotic syndrome are especially susceptible to infections such as cellulitis, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, and bacteremia due to: (1) hypoglobulinemia because of urinary losses of immunoglobulin, and (2) defects in the complement cascade from urinary loss of complement factors (mainly C3 and C5) and alternative pathway factors, leading to impaired opsonization of microorganisms. This puts these patients at significantly increased risk for infection with encapsulated bacteria and pneumococcal disease. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis presents with fever, abdominal pain, and peritoneal signs.

- **A. Enterococcus faecalis** — may cause peritonitis but is not the most common cause in this setting.
- **B. Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus)** — the most frequent cause of peritonitis in these patients (correct answer). Gram-negative bacteria are also associated with a significant number of cases.
- **C. Klebsiella pneumoniae** — may cause peritonitis but is not the most common cause in this setting.
- **D. Escherichia coli** — may cause peritonitis but is not the most common cause in this setting.

questions.stem: An 10-month-old baby presents for evaluation of fever and rash. There was a noted onset of high-grade fever (40°C) three days ago. He appeared well and was eating and playing normally. After the fever lysed, he developed a red rash on his trunk that progressed rapidly over the past 24 hours. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Exanthem subitum**

- **A. Rubella** — the rash appears during the course of fever and progresses in a cephalocaudal manner; rubella does not cause high-spiking fevers unlike roseola infantum.
- **B. Rubeola** — the rash appears during the course of fever and progresses in a cephalocaudal manner.
- **C. Varicella** — the rash appears after the fever, first on the trunk (similar to roseola), but this is a morphologically distinct rash described as maculopapular, vesicular, and pustular lesions.
- **D. Exanthem subitum (roseola infantum)** — caused by human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6); characterized by high-grade fever lasting 3-5 days, with rashes appearing after the fever abates. Seizures may be seen due to the high-grade fever (correct answer).

#### Differential diagnosis of maculopapular rashes

| Condition | Etiology | Characteristics | Incubation | Communicability |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Measles (Rubeola) | RNA virus, Paramyxoviridae | Coryza, cough, conjunctivitis; high-grade fever; maculopapular rash appears at peak of fever; photophobia; cephalocaudal progression; branny desquamation when rash reaches soles; Koplik spots | 8-12 | 4 days before and 4 days after onset of rash |
| Rubella (German measles or 3-day measles) | Togaviridae, RNA | Low-grade fever; no photophobia; cephalocaudal rash; posterior auricular lymphadenopathy; Forchheimer spots | 14-21 | 7 days before, 7 days after rash |
| Roseola (Exanthem Subitum, Sixth Disease) | HHV 6 | Fever 3-5 days; high-grade fever; fussiness; seizures; rash appears when fever abates; Nagayama spots | 9-10 days | Unknown |
| Erythema Infectiosum (5th disease) | Parvovirus B19 | Slapped-cheek appearance; lacy pattern; spreads to trunk; spares palms and soles; complication: aplastic crisis | 4-14 | Before onset of the rash until after onset of rash |
| Dengue Fever | Dengue virus, with Aedes aegypti mosquito as the primary vector | Fever with headache, myalgia, retro-orbital pain, nausea/vomiting, rash, mucosal bleeding (if with warning signs) | 4-10 days | Not communicable |

choices.text:

increases the response to simple ferrous salts

The maximum dose is 300 mg of elemental iron
daily

A daily dose of 3-6 mg/kg of elemental iron in 1 or
2 doses is adequate

If the anemia is mild, repeat the complete blood

questions.stem: Which of the following is TRUE regarding the treatment of iron-deficiency anemia?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — A daily dose of 3-6 mg/kg of elemental iron in 1 or 2 doses is adequate**

- **A. Addition of hematinic substances significantly increases the response to simple ferrous salts** — incorrect; there is no evidence that adding any trace metal, vitamin, or other hematinic substance significantly increases the response to simple ferrous salts.
- **B. The maximum dose is 300 mg of elemental iron daily** — incorrect; the maximum dose is 150-200 mg of elemental iron daily.
- **C. A daily dose of 3-6 mg/kg of elemental iron in 1 or 2 doses is adequate** — correct; in the treatment of iron-deficiency anemia, elemental iron is taken daily at an adequate dose of 3-6 mg/kg in 1 or 2 doses per day (correct answer).
- **D. If the anemia is mild, repeat the complete blood count 1 week after initiating therapy** — incorrect; if the anemia is mild, a repeat blood count is done approximately 1 month after initiating therapy.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl presented with a 2-month history of progressive difficulty in ambulation, particularly in climbing up and down the stairs. After going on a hike, she came home with an erythematous rash in the malar area crossing the nasolabial fold and violaceous discoloration with swelling over the periorbital area. On the day of consultation, she was noted to have papules over the elbows and interphalangeal joints. Which of the following is an expected laboratory finding?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Elevated ALT**

This is a case of juvenile dermatomyositis, as signified by the presence of symmetric, proximal weakness manifesting as difficulty climbing up and down stairs, associated with the classic heliotrope rash (violaceous discoloration with swelling over the periorbital area), malar rash crossing the nasolabial fold, and the presence of classic Gottron papules (bright-pink or pale, shiny, thickened, or atrophic plaques over the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints).

- **A. Elevated ALT** — elevated serum levels of muscle-derived enzymes, such as creatine kinase, aldolase, aspartate transaminase, alanine transaminase (ALT), and lactate dehydrogenase, reflect muscle inflammation in juvenile dermatomyositis. ALT is usually elevated at initial presentation (correct answer).
- **B. Elevated ESR** — incorrect; ESR is often normal in juvenile dermatomyositis.
- **C. Positive rheumatoid factor (RF)** — incorrect; the rheumatoid factor test result is typically negative.
- **D. Polycythemia** — incorrect; there may be anemia (not polycythemia) consistent with chronic disease.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a component of clubfoot deformity?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Cavus deformity**

Clubfoot, or congenital talipes equinovarus (CTEV), is the term used to describe a deformity involving malalignment of the calcaneotalar-navicular complex. The components of clubfoot deformity are remembered as CAVE: **C**avus deformity, forefoot **A**dductus, **V**arus heel, and hindfoot **E**quinus.

- **A. Cavus deformity** — a component of clubfoot deformity (correct answer).
- **B. Hindfoot adduction** — not a component; forefoot adductus (not hindfoot adduction) is the actual component.
- **C. Midfoot equinus** — not a component; hindfoot equinus (not midfoot equinus) is the actual component.
- **D. Valgus heel** — not a component; varus heel (not valgus heel) is the actual component.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy presented at the ER with a 3-day history of fever, headache, and myalgia. He had a history of wading in floodwaters 1 week prior to the onset of symptoms. He had conjunctival suffusion, lymphadenopathy, and jaundice. Which of the following is the patient most at risk for?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Acute kidney injury**

Conjunctival suffusion, lymphadenopathy, and jaundice are all symptoms characteristic of leptospirosis, and the history of exposure to floodwater also makes the diagnosis more likely.

- **A. Pulmonary hemorrhage** — a hemorrhagic manifestation that occurs rarely in Weil syndrome.
- **B. Acute kidney injury** — jaundice is usually seen in the immune phase of Weil syndrome, where acute kidney injury is known to occur in 16-40% of cases (correct answer).
- **C. Adrenal hemorrhage** — a hemorrhagic manifestation that occurs rarely in Weil syndrome.
- **D. Congestive heart failure** — abnormal electrocardiograms are present in 90% of cases, but congestive heart failure is uncommon.

questions.stem: What is the term for an error in morphogenesis wherein there is destruction of a normally-developing tissue?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Disruption**

- **A. Malformation** — a structural defect arising from a localized error in morphogenesis that results in the abnormal formation of a tissue or organ.
- **B. Deformation** — an alteration in the shape or structure of a structure or organ that has developed, or differentiated, normally.
- **C. Disruption** — an error of morphogenesis in which there is breakdown of normal tissue due to a vascular or infectious event (correct answer).
- **D. Dysplasia** — refers to the abnormal organization of cells into tissues.

choices.text:
It is the most common neurobehavioral disorder of
childhood

Diagnosis is made primarily in clinical settings after
a thorough evaluation
It is often diagnosed in preschoolers
Psychostimulants are used to treat ADHD

questions.stem: Which of the following is FALSE regarding ADHD?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — It is often diagnosed in preschoolers**

- **A. It is the most common neurobehavioral disorder of childhood** — true; ADHD is the most common neurobehavioral disorder of childhood, among the most prevalent chronic health conditions affecting school-aged children, and one of the most extensively studied neurodevelopmental disorders of childhood.
- **B. Diagnosis is made primarily in clinical settings after a thorough evaluation** — true; this includes a careful history and clinical interview to rule in or identify other causes or contributing factors; completion of behavior rating scales by different observers from at least 2 settings (e.g., teacher and parent); a physical examination; and any necessary or indicated laboratory tests arising from conditions suspected based on history and/or physical examination.
- **C. It is often diagnosed in preschoolers** — false (this is the answer); ADHD is often difficult to diagnose in preschoolers because distractibility and inattention are often considered developmental norms during this period.
- **D. Psychostimulants are used to treat ADHD** — true; the most widely used medications for ADHD are the presynaptic dopaminergic agonists, commonly called psychostimulant medications, including methylphenidate, dexmethylphenidate, amphetamine, and various amphetamine and dextroamphetamine preparations.

questions.stem: Which of the following characterizes the conjunctival injection in Kawasaki disease?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Bilateral without purulence**

The conjunctival injection in Kawasaki disease is described as bilateral and nonexudative, with limbal sparing. It is one of the 5 principal clinical criteria of Kawasaki disease. The other criteria are: (2) erythema of the oral and pharyngeal mucosa with strawberry tongue and red, cracked lips; (3) edema (induration) and erythema of the hands and feet; (4) rash of various forms (maculopapular, erythema multiforme, scarlatiniform, or less often psoriasis-like, urticarial, or micropustular); and (5) nonsuppurative cervical lymphadenopathy, usually unilateral, with node size >1.5 cm.

- **A. Unilateral with purulence** — incorrect; the conjunctival injection is bilateral and nonexudative.
- **B. Unilateral without purulence** — incorrect; the conjunctival injection is bilateral.
- **C. Bilateral without purulence** — correct; the conjunctival injection is bilateral and nonexudative, with limbal sparing (correct answer).
- **D. Bilateral with purulence** — incorrect; the conjunctival injection is nonexudative (without purulence).

questions.stem: At the delivery room, a newborn was noted to have hypertelorism, low nasal bridge, midface hypoplasia, and hypoplasia of distal phalanges and nails. He was born to a mother with a known seizure disorder maintained on an unrecalled anti-epileptic drug. What is the most likely culprit drug?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Phenytoin**

The distinctive features of hypertelorism, low nasal bridge, midface hypoplasia, hypoplasia of the distal phalanges and nails, and eventually growth impairment and intellectual disability characterize fetal hydantoin syndrome, most commonly associated with maternal intake of phenytoin during pregnancy.

- **A. Valproate** — confers the highest risk for fetal malformations among the anti-epileptic drugs. Together with carbamazepine, these drugs cause various major malformations, including neural tube defects and poor cognitive development.
- **B. Carbamazepine** — together with valproate, causes various major malformations, including neural tube defects and poor cognitive development.
- **C. Phenytoin** — the drug most commonly associated with fetal hydantoin syndrome, the diagnosis in this case (correct answer).
- **D. Lamotrigine** — evidence to date suggests that the teratogenic risks associated with older anti-epileptic drugs do not appear to hold for the newer agents levetiracetam and lamotrigine; there is no evidence of teratogenicity for these drugs, and they are thus considered safe to use in pregnancy.

choices.text:
Administration of empiric antibiotics to cover for a
possible infection

Correct attendant hypokalemia with IV potassium
drip

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best initial step in the management of this case?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Fluid resuscitation with 0.9% NaCl**

This is a case of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), given the history of polyuria and weight loss, and classic symptoms of abdominal pain, altered sensorium, and Kussmaul breathing (rapid, deep, non-dyspneic breathing), further supported by hyperglycemia and acidosis on laboratory analysis. The immediate problems to address in DKA are hyperglycemia, dehydration due to osmotic diuresis, various electrolyte derangements, and metabolic acidosis from accumulation of ketoacids.

- **A. Administration of empiric antibiotics to cover for a possible infection** — may be done if the patient presents clinically with infection, especially as a trigger for ketoacidosis; however, this is done on a case-by-case basis and is not the initial step in DKA management.
- **B. Start insulin therapy** — important to promote movement of glucose into cells, to suppress hepatic glucose production, and to halt the movement of fatty acids from the periphery to the liver; usually started after initial fluid resuscitation.
- **C. Fluid resuscitation with 0.9% NaCl** — fluid resuscitation with a glucose-free isotonic solution is done first, to restore peripheral circulation and lower glucose levels by improving renal perfusion and enhancing renal excretion (correct answer).
- **D. Correct attendant hypokalemia with IV potassium drip** — incorrect as an initial step; although patients with DKA have a total body potassium deficit, the initial serum level is often normal or elevated (hyperkalemia) due to potassium shifts from ketoacid buffering and catabolic losses. This hyperkalemic state is often reversed with improved hydration, which increases the renal excretion of potassium.

questions.stem: In relation to the question above, which is a potential disastrous consequence of this step in the management of the case?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Cerebral edema**

Repair of fluid deficits must be tempered by the potential risk of cerebral edema; hence, it is prudent to approach any child in a hyperosmotic state with cautious rehydration. Patients should not be allowed oral fluids until rehydration is well underway and significant electrolyte shifts are no longer likely. All fluid intake and output should be closely monitored.

- **A. Nephrotoxicity from antibiotic therapy** — a consequence of a different intervention (empiric antibiotic therapy) from the management of this case, not of fluid resuscitation.
- **B. Hypoglycemia and hypokalemia** — a consequence of a different intervention (insulin therapy) from the management of this case, not of fluid resuscitation.
- **C. Cerebral edema** — a potential disastrous consequence of fluid resuscitation/rehydration in DKA (correct answer).
- **D. Hyperkalemia** — a consequence of a different intervention from the management of this case, not of fluid resuscitation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the mainstay of therapy in diphtheria?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Antitoxin**

- **A. Antimicrobial therapy** — its role is to halt toxin production, treat localized infection, and prevent transmission of the organism to contacts; antibiotic therapy is not a substitute for antitoxin therapy.
- **B. Antitoxin** — specific antitoxin is the mainstay of therapy and should be administered on the basis of clinical diagnosis. Because it neutralizes only free toxin, antitoxin efficacy diminishes with elapsed time after the onset of mucocutaneous symptoms (correct answer).
- **C. Vaccine** — the only effective control measure for diphtheria.
- **D. Supportive care** — includes droplet and contact precautions, cutaneous wound care, and bed rest; a component of diphtheria management, but not the mainstay treatment.

questions.stem: Based on the history given by the parents of the infant and your physical examination, what is your most likely primary working impression?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Pyloric stenosis**

Keywords for this case include "non-bilious vomiting" and "olive-shaped mass," which point to pyloric stenosis.

- **A. Tracheoesophageal fistula** — associated with esophageal atresia. Symptoms include frothing and bubbling at the mouth and nose, cough, cyanosis, and respiratory distress; there is also an inability to pass an NGT or OGT.
- **B. Intussusception** — would present as colicky pain recurring at frequent intervals; most cases have the characteristic "currant jelly" stools.
- **C. Pyloric stenosis** — also presents with abdominal distension; ultrasound or barium studies can be used to confirm the diagnosis, showing a bulge of the pyloric muscle in the antrum (shoulder sign) or streaks of barium in the narrowed channel (double-tract sign) (correct answer).
- **D. Duodenal atresia** — characterized by bilious vomiting without abdominal distension; a plain abdominal X-ray shows a "double bubble" sign, due to a distended, gas-filled stomach and proximal duodenum.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings is LEAST likely to be seen in his case?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Hyperventilation**

Pyloric stenosis leads to hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis due to vomiting of gastric contents.

- **A. Hypokalemia** — frequently occurs in cases of pyloric stenosis.
- **B. Metabolic alkalosis** — frequently occurs in cases of pyloric stenosis.
- **C. Hypochloremia** — frequently occurs in cases of pyloric stenosis.
- **D. Hyperventilation** — occurs in cases of metabolic acidosis, to "blow off" excess acid, not metabolic alkalosis; least likely to be seen in this case (correct answer).

questions.stem: Immunity against which disease is primarily acquired through an inactivated vaccine?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Hepatitis B**

- Among the choices, only Hepatitis B (Choice C) vaccine is an inactivated vaccine.
- Vaccination for mumps (Choice A – MMR), Japanese encephalitis (Choice B), and chickenpox (Choice D – varicella) all involve use of live, attenuated vaccines.
- Recall classification of vaccines:

| Inactivated vaccines | Live vaccines |
|---|---|
| Hepatitis B vaccine | BCG vaccine |
| DPT vaccine | Measles vaccine |
| H. influenzae b vaccine | MMR vaccine |
| Pneumococcal vaccine | Varicella vaccine |
| Hepatitis A vaccine | Rotavirus vaccine |
| Meningococcal vaccine | Influenza attenuated vaccine (intranasal) |
| Influenza trivalent vaccine | Typhoid fever (oral) vaccine |
| Human papillomavirus vaccine | Oral polio vaccine |
| Typhoid fever vaccine (IM) | Japanese Encephalitis |
| Rabies vaccine | |
| Inactivated polio vaccine (IPV) | |

questions.stem: During a child’s wellness check-up, the parents note that he is already able to draw a square. What is the estimated developmental age of the child?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — 60 months old**

- Children who can draw a square have a developmental age of 5 years old or 60 months old (Choice C).
- 12-month-old children (Choice A) can turn pages of a book.
- 3-year-old or 36-month-old children (Choice B) can draw a circle.
- 6-year-old or 72-month-old children (Choice D) can draw a triangle.

questions.stem: The following are disorders which would exhibit right to left shunts, EXCEPT:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Patent ductus arteriosus**

- Right to left shunts mean that there is shunting of deoxygenated blood to the left side of the heart that is pumping oxygenated blood to the body. This will lead to cyanosis. Among the choices, only patent ductus arteriosus (Choice B) would not appear as cyanotic. It is a non-cyanotic congenital heart defect that would present as a continuous machinery-like murmur (buzzword!).
- Total anomalous pulmonary venous return (TAPVR) (Choice A) is characterized by all 4 pulmonary veins draining to the right atrium, causing right ventricular volume overload. There is total mixing of systemic and pulmonary venous blood.
- Tetralogy of Fallot (Choice C) is the most common cyanotic heart defect beyond infancy. It consists of right ventricular outflow tract obstruction, right ventricular hypertrophy, large ventricular septal defect, and overriding aorta.
- Ebstein’s anomaly (Choice D) is a cyanotic heart defect wherein the tricuspid valve is displaced toward the apex. This can be caused by maternal exposure to lithium during pregnancy.

questions.stem: Due to the mother’s severe pre-eclampsia with pending eclampsia, the obstetrician had to hasten the delivery of Jamie’s baby. After delivery, she asked you the condition of the baby and how well the baby is. You respond by saying that you have to get the _______ first.
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — APGAR score**

- The APGAR score (Choice C) is used to rapidly assess the condition of the baby and assess the need to resuscitate. However, it must not be used to guide the steps of resuscitation.
- Ballard score (Choice A) determines the pediatric age in AOG; physical and neurologic maturity are scored in this scale.
- Bishop’s score (Choice B) aids in determining if the cervix of the mother is already suitable for labor. Recall the components of the Bishop’s score in the obstetrics module.
- Glasgow Coma Scale (Choice D) is used to assess the responsiveness of a patient. Eye, movement, and speech are used as parameters.

questions.stem: In children who have kwashiorkor, deficiency of which is most apparent?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Protein**

- Kwashiorkor is characterized by protein malnutrition (Choice A). Deficiency in proteins would lead to other complications such as edema, mental changes, dermatosis, and fatty liver infiltration.
- Overall deficiency in calories (Choice B) is known as marasmus. Compared to kwashiorkor, these patients have marked wasting all over the body (kwashiorkor would present as abdominal distension due to edema).
- Carbohydrates, other vitamins and minerals (Choices C and D) may also be deficient in both situations; however, for kwashiorkor, protein deficiency is the main etiology and is characteristic of the disease.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a physiologic response to dehydration?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Increased urine osmolality**

- During dehydration, the body’s natural response would be to retain water as much as possible. Thus, if water is retained and not excreted, the urine osmolality is increased (Choice B).
- Serum creatinine rises during dehydration, while the glomerular filtration rate will decrease, meaning there is also a decrease in urine creatinine (Choice A is incorrect).
- As mentioned, there is an increase in osmolality of urine in this situation, thus there will be no decrease in urine sodium and chloride (Choices C and D are incorrect).

questions.stem: This is the most common form of leukemia in children:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia**

- The most common cancer in children is acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) (Choice A). Manifestations include bone marrow failure in children and thymic masses in adolescent males. CNS and testicular metastases are common.
- Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APML) (Choice B) is a hematologic emergency. It is characterized by translocation (15;17) and PML:RARA fusion, which have Auer rods and Faggot cells (take note of these buzzwords!). Disseminated intravascular coagulation is seen in these cases, and all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) is used for its treatment.
- Chronic myeloid leukemia (Choice C) has translocation (9;22), which is usually asymptomatic. However, it can transform to a blast phase in around 3 years if left untreated.
- Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (Choice D) is the most common leukemia of adults. Clinical features include autoimmune phenomenon, hepatosplenomegaly, and lymphadenopathy.

questions.stem: The following conditions would exhibit suboptimal blood oxygen saturation, EXCEPT ______.
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Left to right shunt**

- Left to right shunts (Choice D) would NOT present with cyanosis because oxygenated blood is shunted towards the right side that has deoxygenated blood. Suboptimal oxygen is not seen in these cases since there is no mixing of blood in the left side of the heart that distributes it throughout the body.
- Underlying pulmonary disease (Choice A), such as pneumonia, would present with lower oxygen saturation than normal due to the inability to fully utilize the lungs in oxygenation.
- Underventilation (Choice B) happens when there is reduced ability of the lungs to supply optimal levels of oxygen in the blood, leading also to hypoxia.
- Right to left shunts (Choice C), as mentioned earlier, cause shunting of deoxygenated blood to the left side of the heart that is pumping oxygenated blood. This will lead to mixing of blood and cyanosis. Because of mixing of blood, the supplied blood is not fully oxygenated, which will cause a decrease in oxygen saturation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a component of Tetralogy of Fallot?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Patent ductus arteriosus**

- Components of the Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) are the following:
  - Right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) obstruction (Choice A)
  - Right ventricular hypertrophy (Choice C)
  - Overriding aorta (Choice D)
  - Ventricular septal defect
- It does NOT include patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) (Choice B).

questions.stem: Conn syndrome is characterized by the following, EXCEPT ______.
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Hypotension**

- Conn syndrome is also known as primary hyperaldosteronism and is usually due to tumors in the adrenal glands. This results in high levels of aldosterone, which can cause hypokalemia (Choice A) due to excessive excretion of potassium, hypernatremia (Choice B) because of excessive retention of sodium, and metabolic alkalosis (Choice C) due to the excretion of H+ ions.
- It also causes HYPERtension because of sodium retention and subsequent fluid retention leading to elevated blood volume, not hypotension (Choice D is incorrect).

questions.stem: In order to sweeten some beverages with zero calories, aspartame is used in the processing of these drinks. Intake of these beverages is contraindicated in which of the following conditions?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Phenylketonuria**

- Aspartame is a commonly used artificial sweetener. It contains phenylalanine. Among the choices, phenylketonuria (Choice A) will have contraindications for aspartame because there is accumulation of phenylalanine in the body due to decreased phenylalanine hydroxylase or decreased tetrahydrobiopterin. Symptoms include musty body odor, severe mental retardation, and seizures.
- Alkaptonuria (Choice B) is a congenital deficiency of homogentisate oxidase. Symptoms include urine turning black while left standing and dark connective tissues (ochronosis). Phenylalanine and tyrosine are recommended to be reduced in the diet of patients with this disease.
- Cystinuria (Choice C) is an inherited defect of transporting cystine, ornithine, lysine, and arginine (mnemonic: COLA) in the PCT. Symptoms include possible cystine kidney stones and staghorn calculi.
- Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) (Choice D) is due to a deficiency in alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, resulting in accumulation of alpha-ketoacids. Symptoms include vomiting, seizures, mental retardation, and the characteristic “maple syrup” or “burnt sugar” odor. Treatment involves limiting intake of valine, isoleucine, and leucine.

questions.stem: Which of the following is least likely seen in patients with biliary atresia?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Kernicterus**

- Biliary atresia is due to obstruction of bile flow in the liver and bile ducts. This manifests as an increase in direct bilirubin.
- Tea-colored urine (Choice A) is caused by the obstruction of bile flow, which leads to accumulation of bilirubin in the blood and filtration by the kidneys. This is seen in biliary atresia.
- Acholic stools (Choice B) are a result of the lack of bilirubin in stools. Since there is obstruction of bile flow, bile is not able to flow into the intestines, causing clay-colored stools.
- Jaundice (Choice C) is a hallmark sign of bilirubinemia. This can be seen in both indirect and direct hyperbilirubinemia because of the buildup of bilirubin in the blood.
- Kernicterus (Choice D) is a dreaded complication of unaddressed hyperbilirubinemia. It is indirect bilirubinemia that leads to buildup of bilirubin in the brain, causing neurological damage. Since it is indirect (unlike biliary atresia, which is direct hyperbilirubinemia), this is the least likely finding in the condition, although it may still be encountered in severe cases.

questions.stem: An infant was delivered via CS to a 36-year old primigravid mother, 37 weeks AOG. It was noted that upon delivery, she was vigorously crying, had active movement, a heart rate of 135 beats/min, with grimace, and noted to be cyanotic in the extremities. What is the APGAR score at 1 minute?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — 8**

- Recall the APGAR scoring system, as this is usually asked in the PLE.
- Scores in this case are the following:
  - Activity – active movement = 2
  - Pulse – 135/min = 2
  - Grimace – with grimace = 1
  - Appearance – cyanotic in the extremities = 1
  - Respiration – vigorous cry = 2
- Total APGAR score: 2+2+1+1+2 = 8 (Choice B).
- Based on the score of 8, this baby is also in excellent condition.

questions.stem: In a patient presenting with bleeding due to deficiency in Vitamin K, all of the following diagnostics are indicated EXCEPT _______.
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Lumbar tap**

- In Vitamin K deficiency, it is important to investigate through blood tests and checking blood parameters to know how to assess the bleeding and manage the patient. Among the choices, lumbar tap (Choice C) would yield the least information for Vitamin K deficiency-associated bleeding. It is mostly used for neurologic conditions such as CNS infections.
- Complete blood count (CBC) (Choice A) would be helpful in this condition since it would monitor and check for anemia in the patient. It would also give details regarding other blood levels and could detect other conditions related to Vitamin K deficiency.
- Prothrombin time (PT) (Choice B) is important to request for this condition since Vitamin K is needed for synthesis of clotting factors. This could indicate if there is impaired blood clotting.
- Liver function tests (Choice D) are used to monitor the condition of the liver. Clotting factors are synthesized in the liver, and requesting these tests may detect liver dysfunction, which can be contributory to Vitamin K deficiency bleeding.

choices.text:
Separate the mother and the baby then give
chemoprophylaxis for tuberculosis to the child.

Do not separate the mother and the baby. Continue
regular breastfeeding while observing safety
precautions.

Feed the baby through formula milk while the
mother is wearing a mask to avoid transmission of
the disease.

Start treatment for tuberculosis for both mother
and the baby.

questions.stem: A mother recently gave birth to an infant 2 weeks ago. Upon visiting the clinic and having her check-up, she tested positive for PPD. Which of the following is the appropriate step for managing the mother and her baby?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Do not separate the mother and the baby. Continue regular breastfeeding while observing safety precautions.**

- The best option for this case would be not separating the mother and the baby while continuing breastfeeding, while observing safety precautions (Choice B). This would provide quality time between mother and baby, while also fulfilling the feeding needs. Safety precautions include wearing a mask to reduce transmission of possible TB. However, it would be recommended that the mother has a work-up for the disease.
- Separation of the mother and baby with immediate chemoprophylaxis (Choice A) is not recommended. This would take away quality time between the two. Isoniazid preventive therapy is only initiated in children <5 years old without signs and symptoms of TB nor radiologic findings who are contacts of bacteriologically confirmed TB or clinically diagnosed TB cases. Only PPD was mentioned, which means the mother is not yet categorized as such.
- Use of formula milk (Choice C) is not recommended for newborns. It is suggested that exclusive breastfeeding be practiced until 6 months of age.
- Starting treatment for both the mother and baby (Choice D) is not yet recommended at this point in time because no additional diagnostics have been done yet except for PPD. Treatment would be warranted once there is proven TB infection through diagnostics such as GeneXpert and chest x-ray, and a more thorough physical examination.

questions.stem: Cryptorchidism is associated with the following manifestations, EXCEPT ________.
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Urethritis**

- Among the choices, only urethritis (Choice D) is not directly associated with undescended testis/cryptorchidism. It is more related to inflammation of the urinary tract and is separate from the problem with the testes.
- Testicular tumors (Choice A), inguinal hernia (Choice B), and infertility (Choice C) are all associated with cryptorchidism.

questions.stem: A child is suffering from a traumatic head injury. On your physical examination, you note that the Glasgow Coma Scale for this patient is 10. Which category would this fall into?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Moderate**

- For traumatic brain injury, the Glasgow Coma Scale score can be classified into the following:
  - Mild (Choice C) – GCS 13 to 15
  - Moderate (Choice B) – GCS 9 to 12
  - Severe (Choice A) – GCS 3 to 8
- The term “complicated” (Choice D) is not used in classifying the GCS score.

questions.stem: Physiologic anemia in the newborn happens when the infant is around ______.
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — 2 months old**

- Physiologic anemia of the newborn happens due to decrease in bone marrow activity, blood volume expansion leading to hemodilution, and increased rate of hemolysis. This happens at around 6-8 weeks of age / 2 months (Choice C).
- 2 weeks old (Choice A) and 1 month old (Choice B) are too early to have physiologic anemia.
- If the child has extended anemia until 3 months old (Choice D), this may warrant further investigation.

questions.stem: A 12/M was brought into the clinic due to bouts of high-grade fever, weight loss, and night sweats. Upon further investigation on imaging, X-ray showed anterior mediastinal mass. Which of the following is the most likely condition of this patient?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Hodgkin’s lymphoma**

- Keywords for this case include “high-grade fever, weight loss, and night sweats” and “anterior mediastinal mass,” which point to Hodgkin’s lymphoma (Choice D). It is a neoplasm of lymphoid cells and presents as such.
- For reference, Hodgkin lymphoma histologically shows Reed-Sternberg cells (arising from germinal-center B cells) and spreads contiguously between lymph node regions, with variants including nodular sclerosis, mixed cellularity, lymphocyte-predominant (best prognosis), and lymphocyte-depleted subtypes. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, in contrast, spreads non-contiguously and is graded as low-, intermediate-, or high-grade.
- Pulmonary tuberculosis (Choice A) could also present with weight loss and night sweats; however, it would not explain the anterior mediastinal mass seen in this case. Pulmonary symptoms would also likely be seen in these patients.
- COPD (Choice B) can be due to emphysema or chronic bronchitis, which present with pulmonary symptoms. Emphysema would be described as alveolar wall destruction and irreversible enlargement of airspaces. Chronic bronchitis would present as persistent cough with sputum production for at least 3 months in at least 2 consecutive years.
- Thymoma (Choice C) is the most common thymic epithelial tumor, commonly seen at around the 5th decade of life. Symptoms include anterior mediastinal mass, autoimmune phenomenon, and immunodeficiency.

questions.stem: Which of the following parameters would distinguish iron deficiency anemia from thalassemia?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Red cell distribution width**

- Both IDA and thalassemia present as microcytic, hypochromic anemia. Thus, mean corpuscular volume (MCV, which measures the size and volume of the RBC — Choice A) and mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC, which measures the average concentration of hemoglobin inside RBCs — Choice D) would be the same in both conditions.
- Reticulocyte count (Choice B) would also not differentiate the two diseases, since they would both show low levels.
- Red cell distribution width (RDW — Choice C) would differentiate between iron deficiency anemia and thalassemia, since IDA has high RDW and thalassemia has normal levels.

questions.stem: Children who are able to hop on one foot have an estimated developmental age of:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — 4 years old**

- Recall the developmental milestones, since these are more often asked in the PLE.
- For gross motor milestones, the following are observed:
  - 3 years old (Choice A) – walks with alternating feet
  - 4 years old (Choice B) – hops on one foot
  - 5 years old (Choice C) – heel-to-toe walks
  - 6 years old (Choice D) – balances on each foot for 6 seconds

| Age | Milestone | Milestone |
|---|---|---|
| 3 yr | Walks up steps, alternating feet | Broad jump |
| 4 yr | Balances well on each foot | Hops on one foot |
| 5 yr | Skips | Heel-to-toe walks |
| 6 yr | Balances on each foot for 6 sec | — |

*(Nelson’s 21st Edition)*

questions.stem: Negative red-orange reflex would be observed in the following conditions EXCEPT ______.
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Congenital glaucoma**

- Among the choices, only congenital glaucoma (Choice D) would NOT have a negative red-orange reflex. It consists of a triad of epiphora (teary eyes), photophobia (eyes hurt with exposure to bright lights), and blepharospasm (uncontrollable eye movements such as blinking).
- In leukocoria (Choice A), there is abnormal blockage of light, which presents as a white or absent red reflex (negative red-orange reflex). It is the general term for a white pupil.
- Congenital cataract (Choice B) is characterized by having an opacified lens at birth. This would also have a negative red-orange reflex because of the cloudy lens.
- Retinoblastoma (Choice C) is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in children. Leukocoria and strabismus are symptoms of this condition.

questions.stem: Which of the following conditions affect purine and pyrimidine synthesis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Lesch-Nyhan syndrome**

- Lesch-Nyhan syndrome (Choice A) is a deficiency in HGPRT, which is included in the purine salvage pathway. It is an X-linked recessive disease that results in mental retardation, self-mutilation, and gout.
- Fabry disease (Choice B) is a deficiency in alpha-galactosidase, which results in rash and renal failure (remember the 3 R’s: Recessive X-linked, Rash, and Renal failure).
- Danon disease (Choice C) is a deficiency in the LAMP2 gene, which causes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. It is an X-linked dominant disease, and other symptoms include heart failure, developmental delay, and possible visual and hepatic abnormalities.
- Hunter syndrome (Choice D) is a lipid accumulation disorder due to a deficiency of iduronate sulfatase. It is the only lipid accumulation disorder without corneal clouding (buzzword — Hunter needs sharp vision to target X). Symptoms include hyperactivity and mental retardation. It is X-linked recessive.

questions.stem: A 4/M is presenting with polyuria and polydipsia. Serum osmolality is noted to be increased while urine osmolality is decreased. Which of the following diseases is likely to be present in this patient?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Diabetes insipidus**

- Cardinal features of diabetes insipidus (Choice B) are polyuria and polydipsia (which are encountered in this case). In this condition, the serum osmolality is increased (>300 mOsm/kg) and the urine osmolality is decreased (<300 mOsm/kg). It may be central (vasopressin deficiency) or nephrogenic (vasopressin insensitivity). Management depends on the type of DI.
- Diabetes mellitus (Choice A) would present with polyphagia, polydipsia, and polyuria. In this condition, there is elevated blood glucose level, which leads to the symptoms. However, given the age of the patient, this makes it a less likely diagnosis, since Type 2 DM is more commonly associated with other comorbidities and increasing age.
- Hyperthyroidism (Choice C) may be due to multiple etiologies such as Graves’ disease. Symptoms include hyperactivity, irritability, fatigue, and possible enlarged anterior neck mass. Studies show that it rarely manifests with polydipsia and polyuria.
- Hypocalcemia (Choice D) is the least likely to present with polyuria and polydipsia. Its symptoms include neuromuscular irritability and seizures (more neurological).

questions.stem: What is the most common class of congenital anomalies?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Cardiac**

- 3–4% of newborns have a congenital defect, of which the most common is cardiac etiology (Choice C). Common congenital heart defects include VSD, endocardial cushion defect, and pulmonary atresia/stenosis. It has an incidence of 1 in 100 per year.
- Musculoskeletal defects (Choice A), such as clubfoot and other limb defects, have an incidence of 14 per 1000 per year.
- Spinal congenital defects (Choice B), which are composed mainly of spina bifida, have an incidence of around 1 in 2,500 per year.
- Gastrointestinal defects (Choice D), such as pyloric stenosis, have an incidence of 4–5 per 1000 per year.

questions.stem: Hemophilia B is a deficiency in which of the following clotting factors?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Factor IX**

- Hemophilia B is an X-linked recessive disease that is a deficiency in Factor IX (Choice B). It is also known as Christmas disease, since Factor IX is also known as the Christmas factor.
- Hemophilia A is the most common and most serious congenital coagulation factor deficiency, which is a deficiency in Factor VIII (Choice A). Both hemophilia types will present with prolonged bleeding depending on factor levels.
- Factor X deficiency (Choice C) is also known as Stuart-Prower factor deficiency. It is not as common as Factor VIII or IX deficiency but will also cause prolonged bleeding.
- Von Willebrand factor deficiency (Choice D) is called von Willebrand disease. This is the most common hereditary hypercoagulable disorder.

choices.text:
Always standing up in the classroom and not
staying at the assigned seat
Inability to focus on tasks given by parents
Socially at par with classmates in school

questions.stem: Upon consultation, the parents of the patient were informed that their child is diagnosed with Attention-Deficit / Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). Which of the following is least likely to occur with the patient?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Socially at par with classmates in school**

- Children with ADHD have impairing levels of inattention, disorganization, and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity. Because of their condition, they are NOT socially at par with classmates in school (Choice D is least likely to occur), because they have manifestations that are excessive for their age and developmental level.
- Inattention is one of the hallmarks of ADHD. This includes losing toys and personal objects (Choice A) and inability to focus and organize tasks (Choice C).
- Hyperactivity and impulsivity are the other hallmarks of ADHD. Symptoms include often leaving the seat in the classroom (Choice B).

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most important risk factor for the development of insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — HLA mutation**

- Diabetes mellitus may be categorized into Type 1 and Type 2. Among the two, Type 1 DM comprises more of the insulin-dependent cases. The most important contributing factor to development of this disease is a genetically susceptible host through HLA mutation (Choice C). T1DM has a sudden onset and mostly develops in young patients. This is due to destruction of pancreatic beta cells, leading to no insulin production. Thus, patients who have this disease have to be insulin dependent.
- Old age (Choice A), presence of other comorbidities (Choice B), and environmental/risk factors (Choice D) more commonly contribute to the development of Type 2 diabetes mellitus. Compared to T1DM, it develops slowly over time, and the body has insulin insensitivity leading to high blood sugar levels and multiple complications.

questions.stem: The body temperature target for newborns is:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — 36.5-37.5°C**

- Thermoregulation is important for newborns because they are prone to heat loss and hypothermia. There is a recommended room temperature and temperature target for newborns.
- 36.5-37.5°C (Choice B) is the target temperature for newborns.
- 35.5-36.5°C (Choice A) already indicates low temperature and may lead to hypothermia. Heat-producing mechanisms are recommended at this point to prevent complications.
- 37.5-38.5°C (Choice C) already indicates low-grade fever.
- 38.5-39.5°C (Choice D) is already considered fever and may indicate infection if it does not subside.

questions.stem: These lesions are characterized by neutrophilic predominance, appearing as vesiculopustular eruptions around the chin, neck, back and soles.
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Pustular melanosis**

- Findings in pustular melanosis (Choice D) include vesiculopustular eruption over a dark macular base around the chin, neck, back, and soles, and it contains neutrophils.
- Erythema toxicum (Choice A) contains eosinophils and appears as small, white, occasionally vesiculopustular papules on an erythematous base.
- Cutis marmorata (Choice B) is a mottling of skin with venous prominence and a cobblestone, lacy appearance.
- Epstein pearls (Choice C) are cysts on the hard palate composed of epithelial cells.

Recall common dermatologic physical findings in newborns:

| Physical findings | Diagnosis |
|---|---|
| Slate blue, well-demarcated areas of pigmentation over the buttocks and back | Mongolian spots |
| Small, white, occasionally vesiculopustular papules on an erythematous base, developing after 1–3 days. Contains eosinophils. | Erythema toxicum |
| Vesiculopustular eruption over a dark macular base around the chin, neck, back, and soles. Contains neutrophils. | Pustular melanosis |
| Cysts appearing on the hard palate, composed of accumulations of epithelial cells. | Epstein pearls |
| Pearly white papules seen mostly on the chin and around the cheeks | Milia |
| Open and closed comedones, or inflammatory pustules and papules on the cheeks of the baby, usually after a week from delivery | Neonatal acne |
| Pink macular lesions on the nape, glabella, upper eyelids, or nasolabial region | Nevus simplex |
| Hair that covers the skin of preterm infants; seen on term infants around the shoulders | Lanugo |
| Thick, white, creamy material usually absent in post-term infants | Vernix caseosa |
| Mottling of the skin with venous prominence; cobblestone, lacy appearance | Cutis marmorata |

questions.stem: Testes that have not descended by what age will remain undescended?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — 4 months old**

- Cryptorchidism will remain undescended if the testes have not descended by 4 months (Choice A). Thus, if the testes are still undescended by this time, consultation is warranted.
- Pediatric surgery is done through orchiopexy, where the affected testes are moved into place and stitched.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis of the patient in the case above?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Transient tachypnea of the newborn**

- Keywords in this case include “38 weeks AOG via CS,” “respiratory distress,” and “prominent vascular markings with hyper-aerated lungs.” These point to a case of transient tachypnea of the newborn (TTN) (Choice A). This is usually seen in pre-term or term CS patients and has an early onset.
- Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) (Choice B), or hyaline membrane disease, is due to the lack of surfactant, leading to under-aerated lungs.
- Persistent pulmonary hypertension (PPHN) (Choice C) is persistence of right-to-left shunting through the patent ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale. This leads to cyanosis and has an unpredictable course.
- Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) (Choice D) develops in neonates who are treated with oxygen and PPV for respiratory failure. It may be classified as mild, moderate, or severe depending on the patient’s oxygen supplementation.

Recall differentials for respiratory distress in neonates:

| | RDS | TTN | PPHN |
|---|---|---|---|
| Demographic | Pre-term | Pre-term or term, CS | Term or post-term, MAS |
| X-ray | Ground glass opacities, underaerated, atelectasis | Hyper-aerated, prominent vascular markings | May be normal, or depends on comorbid condition |
| Onset of signs and symptoms | Within minutes of birth; grunting | Early onset but relieved with minimal oxygen supplementation | Within first 12 hours of birth; cyanosis; oxygen gradient |
| Natural course | Progressive worsening of cyanosis and dyspnea; symptoms peak within 3 days then improve | Recovers rapidly within 3 days | Unpredictable course |
| Treatment | Prevent with antenatal steroids; surfactant replacement; PEEP; supplemental O2 | Supportive | Treat underlying cause |

choices.text:
Performing real-time echocardiography with
doppler flow

questions.stem: The patient in the case above should be managed by:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Giving supplemental oxygen**

- Patients with transient tachypnea of the newborn are managed with minimal oxygen supplementation (Choice B). Rapid recovery is usually observed within 3 days.
- Replacing surfactant (Choice A) is done for RDS patients due to the lack of surfactant naturally produced by type II pneumocytes.
- Performing real-time echocardiography with doppler flow (Choice C) is done for patients with PPHN.
- Referral to pediatric surgery (Choice D) is not indicated in this case. This is usually done for patients who have congenital defects such as esophageal atresia.

questions.stem: The baby is most likely having the symptoms due to what condition?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Breast milk jaundice**

- Keywords for this case include “2-week-old,” “jaundice,” and “purely breastfed.” These point to a case of breast milk jaundice (Choice C). The onset of breast milk jaundice is >1 week after birth, and it is due to glucuronidase encountered in breast milk.
- Physiologic jaundice (Choice A) would present as jaundice visible only at the 2nd–3rd day of life. It is a diagnosis of exclusion.
- Breastfeeding jaundice (Choice B) appears 3–4 days after birth. This is due to decreased caloric intake, and clues include supplementing feeding with sugar water.
- Biliary atresia (Choice D) is due to obstruction of bile flow in the liver and bile ducts. This manifests as an increase in direct bilirubin. Most neonates are normal at birth and progressively develop symptoms due to obliteration of the bile ducts.

Recall clues in the diagnosis of jaundice in newborns:

**Jaundice within 24 hours**

| Key clue | Most likely etiology |
|---|---|
| First-born child | ABO incompatibility |
| Second-born child | Rh incompatibility |
| History of prolonged second stage of labor; no prenatal check-up | Sepsis neonatorum |
| History of maternal infection during pregnancy | TORCH infection |

**Jaundice after 24 hours**

| Onset of jaundice | Key clue | Most likely etiology |
|---|---|---|
| 2–3 days | Baby otherwise normal | Physiologic |
| 3–4 days | Mother supplements feeding with sugar water | Breastfeeding |
| >1 week | Baby is purely breastfed | Breast milk |

questions.stem: Which of the following is TRUE regarding his condition?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Management for the cause is stopping breastfeeding for around 2 days.**

- Breast milk jaundice management includes stopping breastfeeding for 2 days (Choice B) while monitoring for progression or improvement of symptoms.
- Decreased caloric intake is one of the main factors for the development of breastfeeding jaundice, not breast milk jaundice (Choice A is incorrect).
- The etiology, as mentioned above, is due to glucuronidase and not obstructive causes (Choice C is incorrect).
- The duration of breast milk jaundice is around 3 weeks to 3 months, not a few days only (Choice D is incorrect).

Recall breastfeeding vs. breast milk jaundice:

| | Breastfeeding jaundice | Breast milk jaundice |
|---|---|---|
| Onset | 3–4 DOL | End of the 1st week |
| Factors | Inadequate nursing, decreased caloric intake | Substance in breast milk: glucuronidase |
| Duration | Few days | 3 weeks – 3 months |
| Treatment | Continue breastfeeding, 10h/day | Stop for 2 days |

questions.stem: Which nutrient is seen more in breast milk compared to formula milk?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Zinc**

- Breast milk has more nutrients in general compared to formula milk. However, there are three exceptions (mnemonic: KID):
  - Vitamin K (Choice C)
  - Iron (Choice D)
  - Vitamin D (Choice B)
- Out of the four choices, only zinc (Choice A) is not seen more in formula milk.

questions.stem: Vaccine for which of the following diseases is given at the age of 9 months?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Measles**

- Measles (Choice A) and Japanese encephalitis vaccines are given at the age of 9 months.
- MMR, which contains measles, mumps (Choice B), and rubella (Choice C), is given at the age of 12 months or 1 year old.
- Influenza vaccine (Choice D) is given initially starting at the age of 6 months and yearly thereafter.
- Recall the vaccines and the age they are given, since this is always asked in the PLE:

**Vaccines given at birth**
- BCG (within 1st 2 months)
- Hep B (within 12 hrs)

**Vaccines given at 6-10-14 weeks**
- Hep B
- DPT
- Hib
- Polio
- Pneumococcal
- Rotavirus

**Vaccines given with minimum age of 9 months**
- Measles
- Japanese encephalitis

*(Mnemonic: “Michael Jordan 9”)*

**Vaccines given at minimum age of 12 months** *(mnemonic: 1+2 = 3; A’s)*
- MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) – 2nd dose usually at 4-6 years old
- Varicella – 2nd dose after 6 months
- Hep A

questions.stem: A 7/M was brought to your clinic due to vomiting. On inspection, the child had sunken eyes, lethargic, but was still eager to drink. His dehydration according to the IMCI is classified as:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Severe**

- Keywords for this case include “sunken eyes” and “lethargic.” Eagerness to drink is stated to likely confuse you into answering “some” dehydration. However, since two criteria have already been fulfilled, this child is already considered to have severe dehydration (Choice D).
- Some dehydration (Choice C) would have two of the following signs: restless/irritable, sunken eyes, drinks eagerly or thirsty.
- Classification of dehydration in the Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) includes severe, some, and no dehydration. There is no “moderate” (Choice A) or “mild” (Choice B) classification.

Recall classifications of dehydration and their management:

| Signs | Classification | Treatment |
|---|---|---|
| Two of the following signs: abnormally sleep or difficult to awaken; sunken eyes; not able to drink or drinks poorly; skin pinch goes back slowly | Severe dehydration | Plan C; refer urgently to the hospital; if child is 2 years old and there is cholera in the area, give Tetracycline |
| Two of the following signs: restless/irritable; sunken eyes; drinks eagerly, thirsty | Some dehydration | Plan B; continue feeding; follow up in 5 days |
| Not enough signs to classify as some or severe dehydration | No dehydration | Give fluid and food; Plan A; follow up in 5 days if not improving |
| Blood in stool | Dysentery | Treat for 5 days with co-trimoxazole and return after 2 days |

questions.stem: While taking care of your 4 month old nephew, you notice that turning his head to one side would lead to the extension of the arm of that side, while the arm on the other side would bend at the elbow level. As a medical doctor, you assess that this reflex would disappear at what age?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — 6 months old**

- The reflex being described in the case is the tonic neck reflex, also known as the “fencing” reflex.
- The tonic neck reflex appears at 35 weeks age of gestation and disappears at around 6-7 months of age (Choice A).
- At 4 months after birth, the reflex should still be present (Choice D is incorrect).
- Presence of the tonic neck reflex at 9 months old (Choice B) or 1 year old (Choice C) may indicate a possible delay or underlying condition in the child.

choices.text: Immediately after the condition has resolved

questions.stem: How long does it take before the C3 level normalizes after post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — 6-8 weeks**

- Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is a sporadic infection following a prior strep infection.
- After infection, symptoms and blood levels subside over different durations. C3 levels would normalize 6-8 weeks (Choice D) after the infection.

choices.text: Metastasis more commonly seen in bones

questions.stem: Which of the following distinguishes Wilms Tumor from Neuroblastoma?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Does not cross midline**

- Among the choices, the only description that suits Wilms tumor is that it does not cross midline (Choice C).
- Bone metastasis is more commonly seen in neuroblastoma. Metastasis in the lungs is more associated with Wilms tumor (Choice B is incorrect).
- Wilms tumor is seen in the kidneys, while neuroblastoma is commonly located in the adrenals (Choice D is incorrect).
- Hypertension is seen in both conditions and does not distinguish the two (Choice A is incorrect).

questions.stem: In the pediatric emergency room, you were obtaining the details of a neurology patient. According to the parents, their 2/F child suddenly showed shaking movements on all 4 extremities, lasting around 3 minutes. They note that while trying to control the shaking, the patient was hot to touch. No recurrence was observed for 2 days already. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Simple febrile seizure**

- Keywords for this case are “lasting around 3 minutes,” “hot to touch” (which probably indicates fever), and “no recurrence for 2 days.” These point to a diagnosis of simple febrile seizure (Choice A). Simple febrile seizures last less than 15 minutes and have no recurrence in the first 24 hours.
- In contrast, complex febrile seizures (Choice B) last more than 15 minutes and commonly recur. They also have focal signs in the post-ictal period.
- Structural causes (Choice C) can be ruled out using imaging; however, the case does not state such findings, and the presentation points more toward simple febrile seizure.
- Absence seizures (Choice D) are characterized by brief staring spells lasting less than 15 seconds and do not have a post-ictal period. There is also immediate resumption of what the patient was doing before.

questions.stem: For children exposed to patients with meningococcemia, which of the following drugs is given for prophylaxis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Rifampicin**

- For children who have been exposed to meningococcemia cases, the drug of choice for prophylaxis would be rifampicin (Choice B) or ceftriaxone.
- Ciprofloxacin (Choice C) is a 2nd-generation fluoroquinolone used for prophylaxis in adults (>18 years old) exposed to meningococcemia.
- Azithromycin (Choice A) is a macrolide usually used for community-acquired pneumonia.
- Chloramphenicol (Choice D) is used for meningitis and is a backup for Salmonella, Rickettsia, and Bacteroides infections. It can also possibly cause gray baby syndrome.

**What do you give to exposed persons?**
- Children: Rifampicin 10 mg/kg PO every 12 hrs for a total of 4 doses (max 600 mg); 5 mg/kg/dose for <1 month old every 12 hours for 2 days
- Or ceftriaxone 125 mg single dose IM for <12 yrs old
- >18 yrs old: Ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO as a single dose

Antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent *Neisseria meningitidis* infection *(adapted from Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics, 20th ed.)*:

| Drug | Age group | Dose | Duration |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rifampin | Infants <1 mo | 5 mg/kg PO every 12 hours | 2 days (4 doses) |
| Rifampin | Children ≥1 mo | 10 mg/kg PO every 12 hours (max 600mg) | 2 days (4 doses) |
| Rifampin | Adults | 600 mg PO every 12 hours | 2 days (4 doses) |
| Ceftriaxone | Children <15 yrs | 125 mg IM | 1 dose |
| Ceftriaxone | Children ≥15 yrs | 250 mg IM | 1 dose |
| Ciprofloxacin | Children ≥1 mo | 20 mg/kg (max 500 mg) PO | 1 dose |

Present of bilateral vestibulocochlear nerve
masses
Café au lait macules with sparing of the face
