questions.stem: A pharmaceutical company is conducting a clinical trial to test the effectiveness of a new drug for treating hypertension. In this study, the participants do not know whether they are receiving the new drug or a placebo. Additionally, the healthcare providers administering the treatment and the researchers analyzing the data also do not know which participants received the drug or the placebo. What type of blinding is used?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Triple-blind trial**

Blinding refers to keeping participants and/or study personnel unaware of the true nature of the treatment given.

| Single-blind trial | Double-blind trial | Triple-blind trial |
|---|---|---|
| Either the subject or the investigator is unaware of the nature of the treatment given | Neither the subject nor the person assessing treatment efficacy is aware | The subject, data collector, and data analyst are all unaware |

- **A. Single-blind trial** — Incorrect; see table above.
- **B. Double-blind trial** — Incorrect; see table above.
- **C. Triple-blind trial** — In a triple-blind trial, the subject, the data collector, and the data analyst are all unaware of the nature of the treatment given. This matches the scenario where participants, healthcare providers, and researchers analyzing the data are all blinded.
- **D. Open-label trial** — In an open-label trial, both the participants and the researchers know which treatment is being administered.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a parametric test?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA)**

| Parametric test | Nonparametric test |
|---|---|
| Two-sample (unpaired) t test | Mann-Whitney U test |
| One-sample (paired) t test | Wilcoxon matched pairs test |
| One-way analysis of variance (F test) using total sum of squares (ANOVA) | Kruskal-Wallis analysis of variance by ranks |
| One-way ANOVA with repeated measures | Friedman test (Choice A) |
| Two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) (Choice D) | Two-way analysis of variance by ranks |
| χ² (chi-square) test | Fisher exact test (Choice B) |
| Product moment correlation coefficient (Pearson r) | Spearman rank correlation coefficient (rσ) (Choice C) |
| Regression by least squares method | Nonparametric regression (various tests) |
| Multiple regression by least squares method | Nonparametric regression (various tests) |

Choice D, two-way ANOVA, is the parametric test among the options; Choices A (Friedman test), B (Fisher exact test), and C (Spearman rank correlation coefficient) are all nonparametric tests.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes the formula for the F-statistic in both one-way and two-way ANOVA?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — F = (between group variability)/(within group variability)**

The F-statistic is a ratio used in ANOVA to determine whether there are significant differences between the means of different groups:

- F = (between group variability) / (within group variability)

A higher F-statistic indicates a greater probability that the observed differences between group means are not due to random chance.

questions.stem: Which of the following signs and symptoms are not commonly seen in COVID-19?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Blurring of vision**

| Most common | Less common | Serious / warning symptoms |
|---|---|---|
| Fever | Headache | Shortness of breath |
| Cough (dry) | GI symptoms including diarrhea | Chest pain / pressure |
| Fatigue | Conjunctivitis | Confusion |
| Myalgia | Loss of taste or smell | Lethargy |
| Pharyngitis (or other respiratory symptoms) | Rash (chilblains, discoloring on fingers/toes) | Cyanosis |

Note that symptoms of Omicron infection may be milder, resembling a URTI, in both immunized and unimmunized individuals, but the infection is still capable of being severe.

- **A. Fatigue**, **B. Fever**, and **C. Anosmia** are all common symptoms of COVID-19.
- **D. Blurring of vision** is not a typical symptom of COVID-19 (correct answer).

questions.stem: In COVID Alert Level 3, what activities are allowed?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Government offices with 30% indoor occupancy**

Under Alert Level 3, establishments or activities are allowed to operate at a maximum of 30 percent indoor venue capacity (for fully vaccinated individuals only) and 50 percent outdoor venue capacity, provided that all workers of the establishment are fully vaccinated against COVID-19.

Prohibited activities include:

- **A.** Face-to-face or in-person classes for basic education, except those earlier permitted by the IATF and Office of the President.
- **C.** Contact sports, except those conducted under a bubble-type setup, as provided for under relevant guidelines adopted by the IATF, Games and Amusement Board, and Philippine Sports Commission, and approved by the LGU where such games shall be held.
- Funfairs/carnivals and kid amusement industries like playgrounds, playrooms, and kiddie rides.
- Venues with live voice or wind-instrument performers and audiences, such as karaoke bars, clubs, concert halls, and theaters.
- Casinos, horse racing, cockfighting and operation of cockpits, lottery and betting shops, and other gaming establishments, except those that will be allowed by the IATF or Office of the President.
- **D.** Gatherings in residences with individuals not belonging to the same household.

**B** (government offices at 30% indoor occupancy) is not on this prohibited list, making it the allowed activity and the correct answer.

questions.stem: The following are best practices whenever doing nasopharyngeal swabs for COVID-19 testing, except:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Divide the length into half in order to know into what extent will be inserted into the nostril (usually 5–6 cm in adults) to ensure that it reaches the anterior pharynx.**

Steps for nasopharyngeal swabs (Bureau of Quarantine):

- Using the swab, measure from the base of the nostril towards the auditory pit. Divide the length in half to know the extent to be inserted into the nostril (usually 5–6 cm in adults) to ensure it reaches the posterior pharynx. (Choice A is incorrect — it states "anterior" pharynx.)
- With the patient seated, tilt the head slightly backwards. Insert the swab into the nostril parallel to the palate. (Choice B)
- Insert the swab into the nasal cavity until a slight resistance is met. Rotate the swab and apply a little force to take large quantities of mucosa. (Choice C) Repeat in the other nostril using the same swab. Swab direction is therefore **straight and posterior**.
- Place the NPS immediately in the Universal Transport Medium tube to avoid drying of the swab. Break/cut the end of the shaft that sticks out of the tube (break point) and close the tube tightly. (Choice D) Secure the cap with Parafilm to prevent leakage during transport.
- Transport the specimen to the laboratory and store immediately inside a refrigerator (2–8°C). If the site is far from a refrigerator, use a thermo bag/box with 4–6 ice packs.

questions.stem: A patient has tested positive for COVID-19 and has developed symptoms, while another individual was in close contact with a confirmed COVID-19 case but has not shown any symptoms. Health authorities need to decide on the appropriate measures to prevent further spread of the virus. Which of the following statements is correct regarding the management of these two individuals?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — The symptomatic COVID-19 patient should be isolated for the period of communicability of the illness.**

| Isolation | Quarantine |
|---|---|
| Separates sick people with a contagious disease from people who are not sick | Separates and restricts the movement of people who were exposed to a contagious disease, to see if they become sick |
| Lasts for the period of communicability of the illness, which varies by disease and the availability of specific treatment | Lasts only as long as necessary to protect the public by: (1) providing public health care (such as immunization or drug treatment/prophylaxis); (2) ensuring that quarantined persons do not infect others — corresponds to the known incubation period |

- **B.** The symptomatic COVID-19 patient should be isolated for the period of communicability of the illness. *(Correct.)*
- **A** and **C** are incorrect: quarantine is used for individuals who have been exposed to a contagious disease but are not yet symptomatic, while isolation is the appropriate measure for symptomatic individuals to prevent them from spreading the disease.
- **D** is incorrect: only the symptomatic individual should be isolated; the asymptomatic close contact should be placed in quarantine.

questions.stem: Which part of the COVID-19 virus is most known for undergoing mutations, which has significant implications for vaccine development?

- Other parts of the virus are less important for vaccine development:
  - The nucleocapsid protein is involved in the packaging of the viral RNA and is less exposed to the host immune system. **(Choice A)**

questions.stem: Which aspect of a COVID test is most important if COVID is curable?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — More specific**

- **A. More specific** — Specificity refers to the ability of a test to correctly identify those without the disease (true negative rate). High specificity means fewer false positives, which is crucial in a curable-disease scenario, to avoid unnecessary treatment and focus on those truly infected.
- **B. More sensitive** — Sensitivity is vital to catch true positive cases, but in the context of the question, specificity more directly addresses the accuracy of identifying non-infected individuals.
- **C. Increased predictive value** — Predictive value is also important but is influenced by both the sensitivity and specificity of the test.
- **D. Increased negative predictive value** — Negative predictive value is also important but is influenced by both the sensitivity and specificity of the test.

questions.stem: What is the basis for risk stratification in the administration of COVID vaccines?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Prioritizing high-risk populations**

- **A. Studies of effectiveness of vaccines** — While important for understanding vaccine performance, this does not directly inform which groups should receive the vaccine first.
- **B. Based on the origin of the virus** — Not important in risk stratification for vaccine administration.
- **C. Prioritizing high-risk populations** — Ensuring that those most vulnerable to severe illness from COVID-19, such as the elderly and those with underlying health conditions, receive the vaccine first. *(Correct answer.)*
- **D. Geographic location of patients** — Not important in risk stratification for vaccine administration.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes artificial acquired immunity in the context of COVID vaccination?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Immunity developed through the administration of a COVID vaccine**

- **A. Immunity gained through natural infection with the COVID-19 virus** — This is natural immunity, which occurs when a person is exposed to the actual pathogen and their immune system responds to it.
- **B. Immunity provided by antibodies transferred from mother to child** — This is passive immunity, referring to antibodies transferred naturally from mother to child, usually through the placenta or breast milk. It does not involve an active immune response from the individual's own immune system.
- **C. Immunity developed through the administration of a COVID vaccine** — Artificial acquired immunity occurs when a person is given a vaccine that stimulates their immune system to produce a response to a specific pathogen, without the person having to be exposed to the disease itself.
- **D. Immunity resulting from exposure to COVID-19 in the environment** — This is natural immunity, which occurs when a person is exposed to the actual pathogen and their immune system responds to it.

questions.stem: What is considered the best COVID-19 treatment for patients on oxygen support?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Dexamethasone**

- **A. Vitamin C** — Supports overall immune function but is not a proven treatment for severe COVID-19.
- **B. Remdesivir** — Typically used in the early stages of severe disease to help reduce the duration of symptoms.
- **C. Dexamethasone** — Used in the later stages of severe disease, especially for patients with severe respiratory symptoms and those on mechanical ventilation. Dexamethasone has been specifically shown to improve survival rates in patients requiring oxygen support, making it the best treatment option for this group.
- **D. Hydroxychloroquine** — Was initially considered for COVID-19 treatment, but studies have shown it is not effective and may cause harmful side effects.

questions.stem: Understanding how specific populations comprehend their disease and cope with it is essential in ________?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Public health**

Public health focuses on the health and well-being of populations, emphasizing prevention, education, and interventions that help people understand their health conditions and manage them effectively. This understanding helps in designing and implementing programs that support individuals in coping with diseases and improving their overall health outcomes.

Note: there are some "common sense" questions on the board exams — remember your training as a medical doctor, and these kinds of questions should be easy points.

questions.stem: A family wellness plan typically includes the following components except ________?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Tertiary prevention**

- **D. Tertiary prevention** — Involves managing and mitigating the effects of an established disease to prevent further deterioration and improve quality of life. This is typically beyond the scope of a general family wellness plan, which focuses more on risk assessment (Choice A) and primary prevention (health education, protective measures) and secondary prevention (screening, vaccinations).

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man has been diagnosed with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). His healthcare provider designs a comprehensive treatment plan that includes medication management, pulmonary rehabilitation, and lifestyle modifications to help manage his symptoms and improve his quality of life. This new treatment plan is an example of what level of prevention?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Tertiary prevention**

Launching a new treatment plan typically falls under tertiary prevention rather than secondary prevention because:

- **Secondary prevention** focuses on early diagnosis and prompt treatment to halt the progression of a disease during its latent stage. Examples include screening programs like self-breast examinations or Pap smears.
- **Tertiary prevention** involves managing an ongoing symptomatic disease to limit its impact, prevent complications, and improve the patient's quality of life. This includes rehabilitation and treatment plans for established diseases.

#### Levels of Prevention

- **Primordial prevention** — Predisease stage. Addresses broad health determinants rather than personal exposure to risk factors; minimizes future hazards to health. *Examples:* outlawing alcohol in certain countries (note: the campaign against drinking itself is primary prevention), pictures on cigarette boxes under the Tobacco Regulation Act, Seatbelt Use Acts.
- **Primary prevention** — Predisease stage. Inhibits the establishment of risk factors (environmental, economic, social, behavioral, cultural); prevents onset and reduces the incidence of disease via health education & promotion, protective measures, and environmental sanitation. *Examples:* vaccination, malaria prophylaxis, nutritional supplements, health campaigns, occupational and automobile safety measures.
- **Secondary prevention** — Latent disease stage. Early diagnosis and prompt treatment via screening programs. *Examples:* self-breast examination, medication compliance to prevent heart attacks or strokes, Pap smear, PSA.
- **Tertiary prevention** — Symptomatic disease stage. Disability limitation and rehabilitation; "softens" the impact of an ongoing illness/injury. *Examples:* PT and psychological rehabilitation for deformities, cardiac or stroke rehab programs, post-op chemotherapy.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis reports difficulty performing daily activities such as dressing and cooking due to joint pain and stiffness. This limitation in her functional ability reflects which concept?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Disability**

Per the WHO International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF), the consequences of disease can be classified as follows:

- **C. Impairment** — Micro level (organ): a problem with a structure or organ of the body (psychological, physiological, or anatomical structure or function).
- **A. Disability** — Individual level (person): a functional limitation of activity.
- **D. Handicap** — Macro level (societal): an environmental factor preventing the fulfillment of a normal life role.
- **B. Illness** — Encompasses a person's perception and experience of disease.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with a history of smoking and hypertension is found to have atherosclerotic changes in his coronary vessels during a routine check-up, but he has no symptoms yet. At which stage of disease is he currently?
questions.rationale: **Correct answer: B — Stage of Pre-symptomatic Disease**

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has been diagnosed with diabetes and is now experiencing difficulty in managing her daily activities due to complications from the disease. At which stage of disease is she?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Stage of Disability**

#### Stages in the Natural History of Disease

- **Stage of Susceptibility** (Choice A)
  - Disease has not developed, but the groundwork has been laid by the presence of factors that favor its occurrence.
  - Portal of entry; risk factors.
- **Stage of Pre-symptomatic Disease** (Choice B)
  - No manifestation of disease yet, but pathogenic changes have started to occur.
  - Incubation period.
  - Example: atherosclerotic changes in coronary vessels prior to any signs and symptoms.
- **Stage of Clinical Disease** (Choice C)
  - End-organ damage has occurred, so there are recognizable signs or symptoms of the disease.
  - The clinical horizon.
- **Stage of Disability** (Choice D)
  - Any limitation in a person's activities, including psychosocial role.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman attends a health promotion workshop where she learns about the importance of regular exercise and a balanced diet for maintaining cardiovascular health. The workshop includes interactive activities to teach proper exercise techniques and role-playing to help participants plan healthy meals. This approach targets which domains of learning according to Tannahill’s Model of Health Promotion?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Cognitive, Psychomotor, and Affective**

- The workshop provides information and knowledge about health (**Cognitive**), teaches skill acquisition for exercise techniques (**Psychomotor**), and encourages habit formation and behavioral change through planning healthy meals (**Affective**).

#### Tannahill's Descriptive Model

- Widely accepted model among healthcare workers.
- Three overlapping spheres of activity: health education, prevention, and health protection.

#### Learning Domains

1. **Cognitive** — information & knowledge about an aspect of health (~ Knowledge)
2. **Psychomotor** — skill acquisition and reinforcement (~ Skills)
3. **Affective** — habit formation, new practice, behavioural change (~ Attitude)

questions.stem: A public health team is tasked with controlling the spread of dengue in a community. According to the principles of Integrated Vector Management (IVM) promoted by WHO, what is the best form of vector control?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Implementing a multi-faceted approach that includes advocacy, collaboration, disease control, evidence-based decision-making, and capacity-building**

#### Integrated Vector Management (IVM)

- Strategic approach to vector control promoted by WHO.
- Rational decision-making process for optimal resource use.
- Key elements of IVM:
  - Advocacy, social mobilization, and legislation
  - Collaboration within the health sector and other sectors
  - Integrated approach to disease control
  - Evidence-based decision-making
  - Capacity-building

- **A. Solely using chemical insecticides to eliminate vectors** — Only focusing on chemical controls does not address the broader, multi-faceted nature of effective vector management.
- **B. Promoting community awareness and legislative action to strengthen public health policies** — While community awareness and legislative action are crucial components of IVM, relying solely on this aspect does not encompass the entire strategy needed for effective vector control; it lacks integration with other essential elements such as evidence-based decision-making and capacity-building.
- **C. Focusing exclusively on biological control methods** — Only focusing on biological controls does not address the broader, multi-faceted nature of effective vector management.
- **D. Implementing a multi-faceted approach that includes advocacy, collaboration, disease control, evidence-based decision-making, and capacity-building** — Correct; this comprehensive strategy aligns with WHO's IVM approach described above.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the primary vector for the transmission of toxoplasmosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Cats**

- **D. Cats** — Toxoplasmosis is primarily transmitted through cats, the definitive hosts of the parasite *Toxoplasma gondii*. The parasite can be spread through cat feces, contaminating soil, water, and food, and subsequently infecting humans and other animals.
- **A. Mosquitoes** — Vectors for diseases such as malaria, dengue, and Zika.
- **B. Fleas** — Can transmit diseases like plague and typhus.
- **C. Ticks** — Vectors for Lyme disease and Rocky Mountain spotted fever.

questions.stem: A pediatrician in the Philippines is reviewing the vaccination records of a 1-year-old child. Which of the following vaccines is NOT included in the Expanded Program on Immunization (EPI) in the Philippines?

#### Expanded Program on Immunization (EPI), Philippines

- Mandated by Republic Act No. 10152, "Mandatory Infants and Children Health Immunization Act of 2011," signed by President Benigno Aquino III on July 26, 2010.
- Coverage — the mandatory basic immunization for all infants and children under 5 provided under this Act covers the following vaccine-preventable diseases:

questions.stem: Which of the following is the recommended prophylactic measure for preventing diphtheria in children?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Diphtheria toxoid-containing vaccine**

- **C. Diphtheria toxoid-containing vaccine** — This is the primary prophylactic measure for preventing diphtheria. Vaccination with diphtheria toxoid is highly effective in inducing immunity and preventing infection.
- **D. Live attenuated vaccine** — There is no live attenuated vaccine for diphtheria; the vaccine used is an inactivated toxoid.
- **A. Oral antibiotics** — Used for treatment and post-exposure prophylaxis but not the primary method for routine prevention.
- **B. Intramuscular immunoglobulins** — Used in certain post-exposure scenarios but not a standard prophylactic measure.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old factory worker has been diagnosed with diphtheria and has completed treatment. According to the criteria for a return-to-work examination, which of the following is NOT a focus of this evaluation?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Assessing whether the worker is physically fit for any type of work**

#### Return-to-Work Examination

Per the classification of health examinations for workers, the return-to-work exam has three aims:

1. Detect if still contagious (**Choice A**)
2. Determine whether the worker is fit to return to his previous job (**Choice C**)
3. After prolonged absence for health reasons, identify possible occupational causes (**Choice D**)

"Assessing whether the worker is physically fit for **any type of work**" (**Choice B**) is not part of the return-to-work exam — it instead reflects the *entrance/pre-employment examination* classification, where:

- **Class A** — physically fit for any work
- **Class B** — physically underdeveloped or with correctible defects but otherwise fit for work
- **Class C** — employable but, owing to certain impairments or conditions, requires special placement or limited duty in a specified assignment with follow-up treatment/periodic evaluation
- **Class D** — unfit or unsafe for any type of employment

questions.stem: A child in a rural community is diagnosed with diphtheria. According to the first level of health care, which of the following actions should be prioritized?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Administering antibiotics and diphtheria antitoxin at the primary health center**

- **C. Administering antibiotics and diphtheria antitoxin at the primary health center** — This is the appropriate first-level health care action. Primary health care is the first contact between the individual and the health system, where essential health care is provided.
- **A. Contacting the leaders of the community to organize a health campaign** — A valuable public health measure, but not the immediate action needed at the first level of health care.
- **B. Referring the child to a district hospital for more complex care** — Part of secondary health care.
- **D. Providing specialist care at a regional hospital** — Falls under tertiary health care.

#### Levels of Health Care

1. **Primary health care**
   - The first contact between the individual and the health system; closest to the people.
   - Essential health care (PHC) is provided.

2. **Secondary health care** — First Referral Level
   - More complex problems are dealt with.

3. **Tertiary health care**

questions.stem: A local health department is investigating an outbreak of diphtheria in a community. The cases have been steadily increasing over several weeks, and person-to-person transmission is suspected. Which type of epidemic pattern does this outbreak most likely represent?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Propagated**

- **D. Propagated** — Propagated epidemics are characterized by person-to-person transmission, leading to a gradual rise in cases over time as the infection spreads through the population.
- **A. Point common source** — Point common-source epidemics occur when exposure to the source happens at a single point in time, leading to a sharp rise in cases followed by a decline.
- **B. Continuous common source** — Continuous common-source epidemics result from prolonged exposure to the source, leading to cases occurring over an extended period.
- **C. Mixed** — Mixed epidemics have features of both common-source and propagated spread but are not the best match for the described situation of steady, person-to-person transmission.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child with diphtheria is admitted to the hospital with severe respiratory distress. Blood oxygen saturation (SpO2) is measured at 85% on room air. According to the classification of hypoxemia, which category does this child's condition fall into?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Moderate hypoxemia**

The classification of hypoxemia can be found in various guidelines and medical literature, such as those from the American Thoracic Society (ATS) and the British Thoracic Society (BTS). These guidelines generally classify hypoxemia based on oxygen saturation (SpO2) levels:

- **Mild hypoxemia** — SpO2 of 90–94%
- **Moderate hypoxemia** — SpO2 of 85–89%
- **Severe hypoxemia** — SpO2 less than 85%

questions.stem: A 78-year-old patient with severe diphtheria is on a ventilator in the ICU. Despite aggressive treatment, the patient's condition continues to deteriorate, and the medical team determines that further intervention is futile and only prolongs suffering. The family, however, hopes for a miraculous recovery and wishes to continue all life-sustaining treatments. What do you call this scenario?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Medical futility**

- **C. Medical futility** — Correct. Medical futility describes a situation where medical interventions are unlikely to produce any significant benefit for the patient, especially in attempts to prolong life in end-stage illness, as seen in this scenario.
- **A. Informed consent** — Incorrect. Informed consent refers to the process of understanding the risks and benefits of a treatment before agreeing to it, which is not the primary issue in this scenario.
- **B. Advanced directive** — Incorrect. An advanced directive is a legal document that outlines a patient's wishes for medical treatment if they become unable to communicate, which is not the focus of this situation.
- **D. Palliative care** — Incorrect. Palliative care focuses on providing relief from the symptoms and stress of a serious illness, but the scenario described is specifically about the concept of futility in medical interventions.

questions.stem: The hospital's Public Health Unit is calculating the case fatality rate for diphtheria in their recent outbreak. Which of the following best defines the case fatality rate?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — The number of deaths from diphtheria divided by the number of cases of diphtheria, multiplied by 100**

- **C. The number of deaths from diphtheria divided by the number of cases of diphtheria, multiplied by 100** — Correct. The case fatality rate (CFR) measures the killing power of a disease and is calculated by dividing the number of deaths from a specified cause (numerator) by the number of cases of the same disease (denominator), then multiplying by 100.
- **A. The number of new cases of diphtheria in a population over a specific period** — Incorrect. This defines the incidence rate.
- **B. The number of deaths from diphtheria divided by the total population, multiplied by 100** — Incorrect. This defines the mortality rate.
- **D. The number of hospitalizations for diphtheria divided by the total population, multiplied by 100** — Incorrect. This does not accurately represent the case fatality rate or any standard epidemiological measure related to disease fatality.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman from a rural area is pregnant and has not received any prior vaccinations. According to WHO guidelines, what is the most important measure to control tetanus?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Vaccination with tetanus toxoid-containing vaccines**

- **C. Vaccination with tetanus toxoid-containing vaccines** — Correct. According to WHO guidelines, the most important measure to control tetanus is vaccination with tetanus toxoid-containing vaccines.
- **A. Regular wound care and hygiene** — Incorrect. While regular wound care and hygiene are important in preventing infections, they are not the most effective measure to control tetanus.
- **B. Administration of tetanus immunoglobulin** — Incorrect. Tetanus immunoglobulin is used for post-exposure prophylaxis and treatment, not as a primary measure for controlling tetanus in the population.
- **D. Antibiotic treatment for tetanus-prone wounds** — Incorrect. Antibiotic treatment can help in managing tetanus-prone wounds, but it is not the primary control measure.

questions.stem: A researcher is conducting a study on the practices for donning PPE among healthcare workers in a TB- DOTS clinic. Which method of data collection is most appropriate for this study?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Observation**

- **A. Observation** — Correct. This is the most appropriate method for this scenario, as it allows the researcher to directly observe and record the practices of healthcare workers as they don PPE. This method provides real-time, first-hand information about the accuracy and consistency of PPE usage, which is crucial for understanding compliance and identifying areas for improvement.
- **B. Structured interview** — While structured interviews can provide valuable information, they rely on self-reported data, which may not always accurately reflect actual practices.
- **C. Review of documents** — Reviewing documents can provide background information and existing protocols, but it does not capture current practices and real-time adherence to procedures.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old patient with pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) is being evaluated for medication side effects. During the assessment, the patient reports difficulty distinguishing between red and green colors. Which anti-TB medication is most likely responsible for this symptom?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Ethambutol**

- **C. Ethambutol** — Correct. Ethambutol is known to cause optic neuritis, which can result in red-green color blindness. This side effect is dose-dependent and can be reversible if the medication is discontinued promptly.
- **A. Isoniazid** — Incorrect. Isoniazid can cause peripheral neuropathy but is not typically associated with red-green color blindness.
- **B. Rifampicin** — Incorrect. Rifampicin can cause orange discoloration of bodily fluids but does not affect color vision.
- **D. Pyrazinamide** — Incorrect. Pyrazinamide can cause hepatotoxicity and hyperuricemia but is not associated with red-green color blindness.

#### Managing Adverse Drug Reactions During PTB Treatment

**Minor reactions**

| Adverse Reaction | Drug(s) Probably Responsible | Management |
|---|---|---|
| Gastro-intestinal intolerance | Rifampicin / Isoniazid / Pyrazinamide | Give drugs at bedtime or with small meals. |
| Mild or localized skin reactions | Any kind of drugs | Give antihistamines. |
| Orange/red colored urine | Rifampicin | Reassure the patient. |
| Pain at the injection site | Streptomycin | Apply warm compress; rotate sites of injection. |
| Burning sensation in the feet due to peripheral neuropathy | Isoniazid | Give Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6): 50–100 mg daily for treatment, 10 mg daily for prevention. |
| Arthralgia due to hyperuricemia | Pyrazinamide | Give aspirin or NSAID. If symptoms persist, consider gout and request blood chemistry (uric acid determination) and manage accordingly. |
| Flu-like symptoms (fever, muscle pains, inflammation of the respiratory tract) | Rifampicin | Give antipyretics. |

**Major reactions**

| Adverse Reaction | Drug(s) Probably Responsible | Management |
|---|---|---|
| Severe skin rash due to hypersensitivity | Any kind of drugs (especially Streptomycin) | Discontinue anti-TB drugs and refer to appropriate specialist. |
| Jaundice due to hepatitis | Any kind of drugs (especially Isoniazid, Rifampicin, and Pyrazinamide) | Discontinue anti-TB drugs and refer to appropriate specialist. If symptoms subside, resume treatment and monitor clinically. |
| Impairment of visual acuity and color vision due to optic neuritis | Ethambutol | Discontinue Ethambutol and refer to an ophthalmologist. |
| Hearing impairment, ringing of the ear, and dizziness due to damage of the eighth cranial nerve | Streptomycin | Discontinue Streptomycin and refer to appropriate specialist. |
| Oliguria or albuminuria due to renal disorder | Streptomycin / Rifampicin | Discontinue anti-TB drugs and refer to appropriate specialist. |
| Psychosis and convulsion | Isoniazid | Discontinue Isoniazid and refer to appropriate specialist. |
| Thrombocytopenia, anemia, shock | Rifampicin | Discontinue anti-TB drugs and refer to appropriate specialist. |

*Source: Table No. 15, National Tuberculosis Control Program Manual of Procedures, 5th ed.*

questions.stem: A researcher is conducting a study on the efficacy of a new treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) using a sample of patients from a local clinic. The goal is to make generalizations about the effectiveness of the treatment for the broader population of PTB patients. Which aspect of inferential statistics is the researcher primarily utilizing?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Hypothesis testing**

- **B. Hypothesis testing** — Correct. Hypothesis testing is a key component of inferential statistics. It allows the researcher to make conclusions about the broader population based on the sample data, testing whether the observed effects in the sample can be generalized to the population.
- **A. Descriptive statistics** — Incorrect. Descriptive statistics involve summarizing and organizing data from a sample, but they do not involve making generalizations or inferences about a larger population.
- **C. Data collection** — Incorrect. Data collection is the process of gathering information but does not involve making inferences or testing hypotheses.
- **D. Descriptive epidemiology** — Incorrect. Descriptive epidemiology focuses on describing the distribution of diseases within a population but does not involve the inferential aspect of drawing conclusions from a sample to a population.

questions.stem: A patient presents with difficulty seeing in low light conditions, commonly referred to as night blindness. Which vitamin deficiency is most likely responsible for this condition?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Vitamin A**

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child is found to have white foamy patches on the conjunctiva of their eyes. This finding is indicative of a deficiency in which vitamin?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Vitamin A**

questions.stem: A patient complains of painful cracks and fissures at the corners of their mouth, a condition known as cheilosis. This condition is most likely caused by a deficiency in which vitamin?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Vitamin B2**

questions.stem: In response to an outbreak of swine flu, the government implemented several public health measures. Which of the following actions is also likely to help in lowering the cases of Trichinella infection?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Prohibition of feeding carcasses to pigs**

- **D. Prohibition of feeding carcasses to pigs** — Correct. This can prevent the spread of *Trichinella*, as pigs can become infected by consuming meat contaminated with the parasite. This practice also supports overall biosecurity and disease control in swine populations.
- **A. Implementing widespread use of face masks among the population** — Incorrect. This is effective in controlling the spread of respiratory infections like swine flu, but it does not impact the transmission of *Trichinella*.

questions.stem: A 2-month-old infant is brought to the pediatric clinic for a routine check-up. The mother reports that the infant has been irritable and is not feeding well. questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Phenylalanine hydroxylase**

- **B. Phenylalanine hydroxylase** — Correct. Phenylketonuria (PKU) is caused by a deficiency in the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase, which is necessary for converting phenylalanine to tyrosine. Without this enzyme, phenylalanine accumulates in the blood, leading to toxic effects on the brain and other organs.
- **A. Tyrosinase** — Incorrect. A deficiency in this enzyme causes albinism.
- **C. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase** — Incorrect. A deficiency in this enzyme causes G6PD deficiency, not PKU.
- **D. Lactase** — Incorrect. A deficiency in this enzyme causes lactose intolerance.

questions.stem: A public health team is working to address an outbreak of gonorrhea in a rural community. In which phase of COPAR will the team integrate with the community and gather the relevant information necessary for conceptualizing a community diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Entry phase**

#### Community Organizing Participatory Action Research (COPAR)

- An integral tool in community development that follows a systematic and cyclical process.
- Facilitates the education of the people alongside capability-enhancement activities.
- Nurtures the ability of society to organize itself and emphasizes people's involvement in resolving issues and concerns in the community.

#### Phases of COPAR

1. **Pre-entry phase** (Choice A)
   - Involves selection of the target community.
   - Should include at least 50 families; criteria are used to determine their need for community organizing.
   - Preliminary investigation is conducted using secondary records, and ocular inspection is done prior to immersion.
2. **Entry phase** (Choice B)
   - Involves the integration process and the acquisition of relevant information necessary for conceptualizing the community diagnosis.
   - Potential leaders are also identified during this phase.
3. **Formation phase** (Choice C)
   - A core group is created and then trained to develop their capabilities in leading their community.
4. **Organization-building phase** (Choice D)
   - The most crucial stage, since it is during this time that the people are mobilized through the creation of the community health organization.
5. **Sustenance and strengthening phase**
   - The end portion of COPAR but the most important phase — the community and its people are developed to become self-reliant.

questions.stem: When is secondary prevention justifiable?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Initial contact of agent and host**

- **B. Initial contact of agent and host** — Correct. Secondary prevention is justifiable at the initial contact of the agent and host. It involves early detection and prompt intervention to halt the progression of a disease, typically through screening and early treatment.
- **A. Before contact of agent and host** — Incorrect. This is the stage for primary prevention.
- **C. During convalescence** and **D. After convalescence** — Incorrect. These refer to the recovery phase after acute illness, where tertiary prevention is more applicable, focusing on reducing complications and aiding rehabilitation.

questions.stem: In the communication process between a doctor and a patient, which of the following is the stage where the patient interprets the information provided by the doctor?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Decoding**

#### Shannon–Weaver Model of Communication

This model outlines a framework for understanding how communication occurs and can be broken down into several key components:

- **Sender (Encoder)** — The person who initiates the communication. In healthcare, this could be a doctor or nurse who conveys information to the patient.
- **Encoding** (Choice A) — The process of converting thoughts or information into a communicable form, such as spoken words, written text, or non-verbal signals.
- **Message** (Choice B) — The actual content of the communication, including the information, ideas, or instructions being sent.
- **Channel** — The medium through which the message is sent (e.g., verbal communication, written documents, electronic media).
- **Receiver (Decoder)** — The person for whom the message is intended. In healthcare, this is often the patient who receives and interprets the information.
- **Decoding** (Choice D) — The process by which the receiver interprets or makes sense of the message.
- **Feedback** (Choice C) — The response from the receiver back to the sender, indicating whether the message has been understood or if further clarification is needed.
- **Noise** — Any interference that may distort or hinder the communication process, such as physical noise, language barriers, or misunderstandings.

According to guidelines on privacy in research, such as those from the Office for Human Research Protections (OHRP) and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the immediate action should be to report the data breach to the IRB or ethics committee. This body will provide guidance on how to handle the breach, including notifying participants and taking steps to prevent future breaches.

- **B. Conduct a new round of data collection** — Conducting a new round of data collection does not address the breach of existing data.
- **D. Delete all data from the laptop remotely** — While deleting data remotely might be part of the response, it should be done according to the guidance of the IRB or ethics committee after the breach is reported.

- **B. Give hope and change the course of treatment** — Giving hope and changing the treatment course might not be effective, as the patient's decision may not be based on the treatment's effectiveness.
- **D. Offer financial assistance to cover treatment costs** — Offering financial assistance is beneficial but does not directly address the emotional and psychological state of resignation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the recommended post- exposure prophylaxis for close contacts of a patient diagnosed with meningococcemia?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Rifampin**

- Rifampin is one of the recommended antibiotics for post-exposure prophylaxis to prevent meningococcal disease in close contacts of an infected person.
- Other recommended antibiotics include ciprofloxacin and ceftriaxone.

questions.stem: A researcher is analyzing a dataset of patient recovery times following a new surgical procedure. The data is positively skewed. Which of the following conclusions can be appropriately drawn about the dataset, considering the characteristics of a positively skewed distribution?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — The majority of patients have recovery times shorter than the mean**

| | Skewed Right (Positively Skewed) | Skewed Left (Negatively Skewed) |
|---|---|---|
| Outlying values | Large | Small |
| Mean vs. median | Mean is larger than the median | Mean is smaller than the median |
| Order | Mean > Median > Mode | Mean < Median < Mode |

- **B. The majority of patients have recovery times shorter than the mean** — Correct. In a positively skewed distribution, most data points (in this case, recovery times) cluster toward the lower end, making the mean higher due to the influence of a few longer recovery times.

questions.stem: An infectious disease outbreak in a hospital has a high case fatality rate (CFR). How does this high CFR impact healthcare workers?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Healthcare workers experience greater stress and anxiety due to the potential for severe outcomes**

- **A.** — Correct. A high CFR indicates that the disease is particularly lethal, which can cause increased stress and anxiety among healthcare workers due to the potential for severe outcomes if they contract the disease. This can also impact their mental health and job performance.
- **B. The exposure to the disease remains unchanged regardless of the CFR** — Incorrect. Exposure to the disease is determined by the level of contact with infected individuals and protective measures, not directly by the CFR.
- **C. There is no impact on healthcare worker protocols and protective measures** — Incorrect. A high CFR usually necessitates stricter protocols and more rigorous protective measures to prevent infection among healthcare workers.
- **D. Healthcare workers' exposure to the disease decreases because of the high CFR** — Incorrect. A high CFR does not decrease exposure risk; it highlights the severity of outcomes if exposed. Exposure risk is managed through infection control practices.

questions.stem: Based on the latest COVID-19 isolation guidelines from the Department of Health (DOH) in the Philippines, how many days should a confirmed COVID-19 positive case with mild symptoms isolate?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — 5 days**

Per DOH Department Memorandum 2022-0324 (July 23, 2023), masking, quarantine, and isolation protocols:

| Category | Protocol |
|---|---|
| Asymptomatic close contact exposed to a confirmed COVID-19 positive individual | No need to quarantine. Wear a well-fitted face mask for 10 days. |
| Asymptomatic but confirmed COVID-19 positive case; **or** confirmed COVID-19 positive case with mild symptoms / acute respiratory symptoms | Home isolation for 5 days, OR until afebrile/fever-free for at least 24 hours without antipyretics and with improvement of respiratory symptoms — whichever is earlier. Wear a well-fitted face mask for 10 days. *(Isolation may be shortened on the advice of a healthcare provider.)* |
| Confirmed COVID-19 positive case with moderate to severe symptoms, or immunocompromised* | Isolation for at least 10 days from onset of signs and symptoms, per the advice of the attending physician (including whether to admit to a health care facility). Wear a well-fitted face mask for 10 days. *(For severe disease or immunocompromised patients, discontinue isolation only on the advice of a healthcare provider.)* |

\* **Immunocompromised** includes: (1) individuals receiving active chemotherapy for cancer; (2) within one year of receiving a hematopoietic stem cell or solid organ transplant; (3) untreated HIV infection with CD4 <200; (4) primary immunodeficiency; (5) taking immunosuppressive medications (e.g., drugs to suppress rejection of transplanted organs or to treat rheumatologic conditions such as mycophenolate and rituximab); (6) taking more than 20 mg/day of prednisone for more than 14 days; (7) the degree of immunocompromise is determined by the health care provider, with preventive actions adapted to each individual and situation. Repeat RT-PCR testing is recommended for this group upon completion of the isolation period — if negative, the patient may be discharged from isolation; if positive, refer to an Infectious Disease Specialist, who may issue clearance and discharge if warranted.

questions.stem: Based on the SCREEM-RES system, how would a family with a score of 8 be classified?
questions.rationale:

- Scoring:

  - 7–12: Moderately inadequate family resources
  - 13–18: Adequate family resources

questions.stem: Which of the following principles is included in the traditional Hippocratic Oath?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Commitment to patient confidentiality**

The traditional Hippocratic Oath includes the following:

> I swear to fulfill, to the best of my ability and judgment, this covenant:
>
> I will respect the hard-won scientific gains of those physicians in whose steps I walk, and gladly share such knowledge as is mine with those who are to follow.
>
> I will apply, for the benefit of the sick, all measures [that] are required, avoiding those twin traps of overtreatment and therapeutic nihilism.
>
> I will remember that there is art to medicine as well as science, and that warmth, sympathy, and understanding may outweigh the surgeon's knife or the chemist's drug.
>
> I will not be ashamed to say "I know not," nor will I fail to call in my colleagues when the skills of another are needed for a patient's recovery.
>
> I will respect the privacy of my patients, for their problems are not disclosed to me that the world may know. Most especially must I tread with care in matters of life and death. If it is given me to save a life, all thanks. But it may also be within my power to take a life; this awesome responsibility must be faced with great humbleness and awareness of my own frailty. Above all, I must not play at God.
>
> I will remember that I do not treat a fever chart, a cancerous growth, but a sick human being, whose illness may affect the person's family and economic stability. My responsibility includes these related problems, if I am to care adequately for the sick.
>
> I will prevent disease whenever I can, for prevention is preferable to cure.
>
> I will remember that I remain a member of society, with special obligations to all my fellow human beings, those sound of mind and body as well as the infirm.
>
> If I do not violate this oath, may I enjoy life and art, respected while I live and remembered with affection thereafter. May I always act so as to preserve the finest traditions of my calling and may I long experience the joy of healing those who seek my help.

questions.stem: Which term is analogous to statistical power?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Sensitivity**

- **A. Positive predictive value** — assesses the likelihood of a positive result being correct among all positive results.
- **B. Negative predictive value** — gauges the probability of a negative result being accurate among all negative results.
- **C. Sensitivity** — Sensitivity is akin to statistical power because both measures are concerned with the ability to detect true positives. Sensitivity evaluates the proportion of actual positives that are correctly identified by a test or model. Similarly, statistical power gauges the ability of a study to identify an effect or difference when it exists (i.e., true positives) and helps to minimize false negatives.
- **D. Specificity** — measures the proportion of actual negatives that are correctly identified.

questions.stem: The following are included in the five stages of grief EXCEPT:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Recovery**

- **A. Anger** — included in the five stages of grief. The five stages of grief can be recalled using the mnemonic "DABDA" — Denial, Anger, Bargaining, Depression, and Acceptance.
- **B. Denial** — included in the five stages of grief. The five stages of grief can be recalled using the mnemonic "DABDA" — Denial, Anger, Bargaining, Depression, and Acceptance.
- **C. Depression** — included in the five stages of grief. The five stages of grief can be recalled using the mnemonic "DABDA" — Denial, Anger, Bargaining, Depression, and Acceptance.
- **D. Recovery** — not part of the stages of grief.

questions.stem: A co-worker of yours recently started experiencing intractable abdominal pain usually lasting 30 minutes. She began researching about her condition on the internet, and shared that she was scared that it might be a serious illness since results showed possible colon cancer. Currently, she is in what stage of the illness trajectory?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Onset of illness to diagnosis**

The patient is yet to consult a physician, meaning she is currently in the stage of "onset of illness to diagnosis" (Choice A). The results that are stated are results of her internet search, not diagnostic results, since it wasn't mentioned that she already consulted with a physician.

Brief description of the illness trajectory stages:

| Stage | Description |
|---|---|
| Stage I: Onset of Illness to Diagnosis (Choice A) | Experienced prior to contact with physician. Starts from physical symptoms of the patient, health beliefs, and previous experiences of others. |
| Stage II: Impact Phase / Reaction to Diagnosis (Choice B) | Initial contact with MD. Curable or non-debilitating diseases lead to acceptance, while chronic or terminal illness leads to protracted reaction (DABDA). |
| Stage III: Major Therapeutic Efforts (Choice C) | Includes mobilization, therapeutic plans, the economic impact, and possible hospitalizations. |
| Stage IV: Early Adjustment to Outcome / Recovery Phase (Choice D) | Disappearance of symptoms (acute) / return to home with some degree of functionality (chronic). |
| Stage V: Adjustment to the Permanency of Outcome | The family's adjustment to crisis when they must accept the condition and state. |

questions.stem: A hospital reported 80 new cases of monkeypox in a community of 10,000 individuals over the past year. What is the incidence rate of this disease?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — 8 per 1,000**

Incidence rate measures the rate of occurrence of new cases within a specified time frame in a defined population. It is calculated by dividing the number of new cases by the total population and multiplying by a constant (here, 1,000) for ease of interpretation.

Incidence rate = (80 / 10,000) × 1,000 = 8 per 1,000 individuals (Choice B)

questions.stem: Mark was scratched by a stray cat wherein he sustained superficial wounds at the arms with bleeding when induced. What category of rabies exposure is described?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Category II**

- **A. Category I** — exposure includes licking and/or nibbling of intact skin.
- **B. Category II** — exposure includes superficial wounds or abrasions without bleeding; or those with bleeding only when induced. It also includes nibbling of uncovered skin with or without bruising or hematoma.
- **C. Category III** — exposure is characterized by transdermal bites or abrasions with spontaneous bleeding. Any Category II exposures to the head and neck area are automatically considered Category III.
- **D. Category IV** — there is no Category IV.

questions.stem: The following are included in the Four Pillars of primary health care EXCEPT:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Specialized medical interventions**

- **B. Specialized medical interventions** — not part of the Four Pillars of primary health care.

The four pillars of primary health care include:

- **A. Active community participation**
- **C. Intersectoral coordination**
- **D. Use of appropriate technologies**
- Support mechanisms made available

questions.stem: What kind of family structure based on authority is characterized as having the power and authority equally shared between husband and wife?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Egalitarian**

- **A. Patriarchal** — structures allocate power to the father or male figure.
- **B. Matriarchal** — families emphasize the authority of the mother or eldest female.
- **C. Egalitarian** — families prioritize equal distribution of authority and decision-making power between spouses. Both assume joint responsibility for decisions in the household.
- **D. Matricentric** — families give the mother power because of the father's prolonged absence.

questions.stem: A couple adopts a parenting style where they indulge their children's desires and avoid setting strict rules or boundaries. They allow their children to make decisions about bedtime, meal choices, and recreational activities without much guidance or structure. This refers to what kind of parenting style?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Permissive**

- **A. Authoritarian** — parenting style is characterized by high demands and low responsiveness, emphasizing strict rules and control over children's behavior. It contrasts with the scenario's emphasis on freedom and minimal rules.
- **B. Permissive** — The scenario aligns with the characteristics of permissive parenting, emphasizing low demands and high responsiveness. In this style, parents tend to avoid strict rules and instead grant their children significant freedom to make their choices.
- **C. Democratic** — parenting involves parents who set clear rules and guidelines while being responsive to their children's needs. They encourage independence, provide reasoning behind rules, and foster open communication, allowing children to express their opinions within a structured environment.
- **D. Rejecting** — parenting is when parents do not pay attention to their children's needs and seldom have expectations regarding how they should behave.

questions.stem: Which strain of hepatitis is most commonly associated with intravenous drug users?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Hepatitis C**

- **A. Hepatitis A** — usually transmitted through the consumption of contaminated water, making it less linked to intravenous drug use.
- **B. Hepatitis B** — can also be transmitted through blood, but it is less commonly associated with intravenous drug use compared to Hepatitis C.
- **C. Hepatitis C** — Intravenous drug use, particularly sharing needles, significantly increases the risk of contracting Hepatitis C due to blood-to-blood transmission.
- **D. Hepatitis E** — usually transmitted through the consumption of contaminated water, making it less linked to intravenous drug use.

questions.stem: A couple in their early 30s just had their first child. They are adjusting their routines, dealing with sleepless nights, and adapting to the responsibilities of caring for an infant. In which stage of the family life cycle are the couple most likely situated?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Family with young children**

- **A. Newly married couple** — refers to the stage where there is a transition towards realigning one's relationships to include the spouse.
- **B. Family with young children** — aligns with the scenario, where the couple is experiencing the initial phase of parenthood, marked by the arrival of their first child. This stage involves adapting to the needs of an infant and adjusting to the new roles of being parents.
- **C. Launching family** — is when children leave home to establish their own lives.
- **D. Family with adolescent** — describes the stage wherein older children and teenagers become more independent.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old male was diagnosed with stage III colon cancer. The oncologist recommended a treatment plan involving multiple therapeutic modalities. Which treatment is most suitable for targeting actively dividing cancer cells in this scenario?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Chemotherapy**

- **A. Biologic agents** — are medications that specifically target certain molecules or pathways involved in cancer growth. While effective, they may not exclusively target actively dividing cells and often have specific molecular targets that might not encompass all actively dividing cancer cells in the body.
- **B. Chemotherapy** — is a systemic treatment that works by targeting actively dividing cells, including cancer cells. It involves the administration of drugs that disrupt the cell cycle, inhibit cell growth, and induce cancer cell death. Its ability to target rapidly dividing cells, a hallmark of cancer, makes it a crucial component of the treatment plan in such cases.
- **C. Radiotherapy** — uses high-energy radiation to damage the DNA of cancer cells, but it's more location-specific and may not be employed for systemic cancer treatment like chemotherapy.
- **D. Surgery** — aims to physically remove the tumor but does not specifically address actively dividing cells present elsewhere in the body, as chemotherapy does.

questions.stem: In a certain population, 50% have error of refraction while 10% have glaucoma, which are not mutually exclusive. What percent of the population has either glaucoma or error of refraction?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — 55%**

To calculate the probability of overlapping (non-mutually-exclusive) events, the following formula is used:

P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B)

Where P is the probability, A is having error of refraction, and B is having glaucoma. P(A and B) is the probability of having both error of refraction and glaucoma at the same time.

Using the formula above, the probability of having either glaucoma or error of refraction is computed:

P(EOR or Glaucoma) = 0.5 + 0.1 − (0.5 × 0.1) = 0.5 + 0.1 − 0.05 = 0.55 = 55% (Choice B)

questions.stem: Gerry, a former employee, underwent a re-employment health examination as part of the company's standard policy. The examination revealed that he is fit for re-employment, but there were minor health concerns noted that required further attention or follow-ups, such as borderline blood pressure readings, a slight iron deficiency, or mild musculoskeletal concerns that do not hinder his ability to perform the job. What is his patient classification?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Class B**

- **A. Class A** — physically fit to work.
- **B. Class B** — The scenario describes a Class B patient wherein he is physically fit for work but with minor interventions/follow-ups needed. It is a cautious classification, ensuring that any potential health issues are addressed or monitored, albeit they do not significantly impact his overall ability to work.
- **C. Class C** — fit for work but with specific restrictions based on the health assessment findings.
- **D. Class D** — not fit or unsafe for any type of employment.

questions.stem: In a manufacturing facility, workers are routinely exposed to loud machinery noise exceeding safe decibel levels, leading to potential hearing damage. To mitigate this risk, the management team decides to install noise-canceling barriers around the machinery area. What kind of hazard control measure is employed?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Engineering**

- **A. Elimination** — involves completely removing the hazard from the workplace.
- **B. Substitution** — involves replacing the hazard with a less hazardous option.
- **C. Administrative** — controls involve changing work practices or policies to reduce exposure to hazards. This could include scheduling breaks away from the noisy area or rotating workers, but it does not directly eliminate or isolate the hazard itself.
- **D. Engineering** — The installation of noise-canceling barriers around the machinery area exemplifies the engineering control of hazard mitigation, specifically isolation. This approach aims to isolate workers from the hazardous noise by creating physical barriers to reduce their exposure, thereby directly addressing the hazard at its source.

questions.stem: In an office setting, employees frequently complain of discomfort due to prolonged sitting, resulting in backaches and muscle strain. To address this issue, the company conducts ergonomic assessments and introduces adjustable chairs, standing desks, and encourages regular breaks and stretching exercises. What type of hazard was being addressed?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Ergonomic**

- **A. Physical** — hazards involve factors like noise, temperature, or radiation that directly impact physical well-being.
- **B. Chemical** — hazards involve exposure to harmful substances.
- **C. Ergonomic** — The measures introduced, such as adjustable chairs, standing desks, and promoting breaks and exercises, directly target the ergonomic hazard. Ergonomic hazards arise from uncomfortable postures or repetitive movements in the workplace, leading to physical strains or musculoskeletal disorders. These interventions aim to improve posture and reduce physical strain caused by prolonged sitting, aligning with ergonomic hazard control.
- **D. Psychosocial** — hazards pertain to factors like stress, workload, and interpersonal relationships impacting mental health.

choices.text: Treatment after lost to follow up

questions.stem: A 32-year-old individual, previously treated for drug-sensitive pulmonary tuberculosis, completed a full course of anti-tuberculosis treatment six months ago. The individual now presents with a persistent cough, fever, and weight loss. Sputum smear microscopy reveals acid-fast bacilli. What type of tuberculosis patient classification does this scenario represent?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Relapse**

- **A. Relapse** — The scenario describes a previously treated tuberculosis patient who completed treatment but now exhibits symptoms and positive sputum smear microscopy, indicating the reappearance of the disease. This aligns with the classification of relapse, which refers to the recurrence of tuberculosis after completing a previous treatment successfully.
- **B. Treatment after failure** — refers to patients whose initial treatment failed due to continued positive bacteriological results or clinical deterioration despite treatment.
- **C. Treatment after lost to follow up** — pertains to patients who interrupted treatment for two or more consecutive months and are returning for re-initiation of treatment.
- **D. Previous treatment outcome unknown** — applies to patients for whom the treatment outcome of a previous episode of tuberculosis is unknown or undocumented.

questions.stem: You have a 19 year old female patient who is currently suffering from obesity. Management of this patient includes which of the following principles?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Involving the patient in decision making and discussing possible steps to manage the condition**

- **A. Allowing the patient to do anything freely as she wants** — is not suitable for cases of lifestyle-related diseases, because management banks mainly on changing diet and behavior.
- **B. Talking to the parents of the patient about the management and introducing your plan to them** — is not entirely incorrect; however, this would be more suitable for patients in the pediatric age group. The patient is already a 19-year-old female and can already give consent and discuss the plan, so this is not entirely applicable.
- **C. Imposing your plan and telling the patient to change her lifestyle as soon as possible** — means disregarding the patient's opinion on the matter, which is important when it comes to disease management.
- **D. Involving the patient in decision making and discussing possible steps to manage the condition** — In management of disease, a valued principle is involving the patient in decision making and discussing his/her condition and management. This gives voice to both the patient and the physician to explain each other's point of view and come to a mutual plan.

questions.stem: In a small town, several cases of a rare infection suddenly emerged within a short period. The infection, primarily affecting the respiratory system, displayed a rapid onset of symptoms such as high fever, cough, and shortness of breath. Medical authorities conducted investigations and identified a common exposure among the affected individuals—attendance at a local community event held indoors, which was crowded and poorly ventilated. What occurrence is being depicted?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Epidemic**

- **A. Endemic** — occurrence refers to the consistent presence of a disease or infection within a particular area or population.
- **B. Pandemic** — occurrence involves the widespread and global dissemination of a disease, not limited to a specific region or country. However, in this scenario, the most appropriate description is an epidemic, due to the sudden surge of cases tied to a common exposure event in a localized area.
- **C. Sporadic** — occurrence involves occasional and isolated cases, lacking a specific pattern.
- **D. Epidemic** — In this scenario, the sudden rise in the number of cases of the rare infection within a specific geographic area and a short time frame aligns with the definition of an epidemic occurrence.

questions.stem: In the humoral theory of disease transmission, the four humors include the following EXCEPT:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Lymph**

The humoral theory of disease transmission was a medical concept dating back to ancient times. It posited that bodily health was governed by the balance of bodily fluids, or humors. Illness or disease was believed to arise from an imbalance or alteration in these humors.

- **A. Phlegm** — one of the four humors: blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile.
- **B. Yellow bile** — one of the four humors: blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile.
- **C. Blood** — one of the four humors: blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile.
- **D. Lymph** — NOT part of the four humors.

questions.stem: Jane had recently recovered from a respiratory infection caused by a specific pathogen. Despite her recovery, she continued to carry the virus in her respiratory tract, which didn't cause any symptoms but posed a risk of transmission to others. Jane is what kind of carrier?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Convalescent carrier**

- **A. Incubatory carrier** — those who can transmit the agent during the incubation period before clinical illness begins.
- **B. Healthy carrier** — those who never experience symptoms despite being infected.
- **C. Convalescent carrier** — In this scenario, Jane is no longer symptomatic but carries the pathogen after her recovery from the infection. A carrier state following convalescence, where the individual harbors and potentially transmits the pathogen, defines a convalescent carrier.
- **D. Chronic carrier** — those who experience persistent infection and can transmit the pathogen for an extended period.

questions.stem: A rapid antigen test has a sensitivity of 90% and a specificity of 98%. If consecutive tests are known to be independent of each other, what is the probability that a person suspected to have COVID-19 will have a negative screening test for two consecutive times?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — 1/100**

The likelihood of contracting a disease is reflected by the sensitivity of the test. Since the sensitivity of the given test is 90%, the likelihood of not catching the disease (a negative test) is 10%.

If consecutive tests are independent of each other, the probability that a person suspected to have COVID-19 will have a negative screening test for two consecutive times is the product of the individual probabilities of a negative test, i.e., 10% multiplied by 10%:

Probability = 0.1 × 0.1 = 0.01 = 1/100 (Choice C)

questions.stem: A 50/F came to your clinic complaining of gastrointestinal distress and diarrhea. She was noted to be taking large amounts of multivitamins. Intake of which of the following caused her symptoms?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Ferrous sulfate**

- **A. Thiamine** — there are no known toxicities with the intake of thiamine (Vitamin B1).
- **B. Riboflavin** — there are no known toxicities with the intake of riboflavin (Vitamin B2).
- **C. Ferrous sulfate** — GI distress is the most common adverse effect of iron supplementation. Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or epigastric distress.
- **D. Tocopherol** — Vitamin E is the most powerful naturally occurring antioxidant. Toxicity with Vitamin E manifests with bleeding due to reduced platelet aggregation and disturbance in the effects of Vitamin K.

questions.stem: Pain scale is considered what type of numerical data?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Ratio**

In a ratio scale, the zero is fixed or absolute. Zero on the pain scale means the absence of pain, and is hence considered absolute.

questions.stem: What non-parametric test is used when three or more sets of observations made on a single sample are compared?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Kruskal-Wallis test**

- **A. One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA)** — the parametric test used when three or more sets of observations made on a single sample are compared; the analogous non-parametric test is the Kruskal-Wallis test.
- **B. Mann-Whitney U test** — the non-parametric test used when two independent samples are compared.
- **C. Wilcoxon matched pairs test** — used when two sets of observations are compared on a single sample.
- **D. Kruskal-Wallis test** — the non-parametric test used when three or more sets of observations made on a single sample are compared.

questions.stem: A female neonate was noted to have a stormy course at the delivery room and was admitted to the neonatal ICU for sepsis. She eventually succumbed to death six days after birth. Her death is classified as a/an:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Perinatal mortality**

- **A. Neonatal mortality** — includes deaths among those under 28 days of age in a calendar year.
- **B. Perinatal mortality** — Deaths from 28 weeks AOG to infants <7 days old are classified as perinatal mortality. In this case, the neonate died at 6 days old.
- **C. Infant mortality** — deaths under 1 year of age in a calendar year are classified as infant mortality.
- **D. Child mortality** — deaths at 1–4 years old are considered child mortality.

questions.stem: At least how many doses of tetanus toxoid vaccine should a pregnant woman receive?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — 2**

Pregnant women should receive at least two (2) doses of tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine, with an interval of at least 4 weeks between doses and the second dose at least 2 weeks before birth.

It is given during 27–36 weeks AOG to maximize passive antibody transfer and protection at birth.

questions.stem: The test for HIV screening tests for the presence of:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Antigen and/or antibody**

The standard blood screening tests for HIV infection are based on the detection of antibodies to HIV and/or the p24 antigen of HIV. The diagnosis of HIV infection depends on the demonstration of antibodies to HIV (Choice B) and/or the direct detection of HIV or one of its components (the antigen itself, Choice A). The best answer is Choice C, since both are possible to detect.

- **D. Toxin** — toxins are not detected in HIV tests; these are more characteristic of bacterial infections.
