questions.stem: Which of the following is TRUE about the phases of wound healing?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A**

- **A.** — The maturation and remodeling phase of wound healing begins during the fibroblastic phase and is characterized by a reorganization of previously synthesized collagen.
- **B.** — The proliferative phase (not the inflammation phase) is the second phase of wound healing and roughly spans days 4 through 12.
- **C.** — PMNs (not macrophages) are the first infiltrating cells to enter the wound site, peaking at 24 to 48 hours.
- **D.** — Epithelialization (not the proliferative phase) is characterized primarily by proliferation and migration of epithelial cells adjacent to the wound.

#### Phases of wound healing (reference)

**Hemostasis → Inflammation (Day 0–6)**
- Hemostasis precedes inflammation.
- PMNs (peak at 24–48 hours post-injury) — first cells to infiltrate the wound.
- Macrophages (peak at 48–96 hours post-injury).
- T cells (peak at 1 week post-injury) — bridge the transition from inflammation to the proliferative phase.

**Proliferation (Day 4–12)**
- Establishes tissue continuity.
- Involves invasion of fibroblasts and endothelial cells (participate in angiogenesis).
- PDGF — strongest chemotactic factor for fibroblasts.
- Deposition of type III collagen fibers.

**Maturation and Remodeling (Day 8 – months)**
- Shift of type III collagen fibers → type I collagen fibers.
- Mediated by matrix metalloproteinases.
- Scar strength achieves only 75–80% of normal tissue.

**Epithelialization**
- Final step in establishing tissue integrity.
- Characterized by proliferation and migration of epithelial cells.
- Once epithelial layering is re-established, the surface will keratinize.

**Wound contraction**
- Caused by myofibroblasts, due to the presence of actin filaments allowing "contraction."

Source: Schwartz Principles of Surgery, 11th ed., p. 272.

questions.stem: What is the target glucose level to best prevent surgical site infections?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — <200 mg/dL**

Perioperative glycemic control targets a glucose level <200 mg/dL in patients with and without diabetes.

Perioperative recommendations for the prevention of surgical site infection (SSI):

**Parenteral antimicrobial prophylaxis**
- Give preoperative antibiotics only when indicated based on clinical practice guidelines, timed so that a bactericidal concentration of the agent is established in the serum and tissues when the incision is made.
- For clean and clean-contaminated procedures: no need to administer additional prophylactic antimicrobial doses after the surgical incision is closed in the operating room, even in the presence of a drain.

**Non-parenteral antimicrobial prophylaxis**
- Do not apply antimicrobial agents (e.g., ointments, solutions, or powders) to the surgical incision for the prevention of SSI.
- Consider the use of triclosan-coated sutures for the prevention of SSI.

**Glycemic control**
- Perioperative glycemic control: target glucose level <200 mg/dL in patients with and without diabetes.

**Antiseptic prophylaxis**
- Advise patients to shower or bathe (full body) with soap or an antiseptic agent on at least the night before the operative day.
- Perform intraoperative skin preparation with an alcohol-based antiseptic agent unless contraindicated.
- The use of plastic adhesive drapes (e.g., sterile incise drapes), with or without antimicrobial properties, is not necessary for the prevention of SSI.

Source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Guideline for the Prevention of Surgical Site Infection; 2017.

rationaleMeta.sources: Source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Guideline for the Prevention of Surgical Site Infection; 2017

questions.stem: A 25-year-old male presents with an infected laceration of his leg. He then underwent debridement. What surgical wound class does this belong to?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Dirty**

Debridement of a soft tissue infection falls under Class IV – Dirty.

Operative wound classes, with infection rates, descriptions, and example cases:

**Class I – Clean** (infection rate 1–2%)
- Atraumatic, uninfected
- No entry of the GU, GI, or respiratory tract
- Primarily closed; if necessary, drained with closed drainage (e.g., JP drain)
- Example cases: breast surgery (MRM), thyroid surgery, inguinal hernia, operative incisional wounds following non-penetrating (blunt) trauma

**Class II – Clean-Contaminated** (infection rate 2.1–9.5% for elective GI surgery; 4–14% for colorectal surgery)
- Wound involving normal but colonized tissue
- Minor breaks in sterile technique
- Entry of the GU, GI, or respiratory tract without significant change
- Example cases: operations involving the biliary tract, appendix, vagina, and oropharynx (provided no evidence of infection or major break in technique is encountered)

**Class III – Contaminated** (infection rate 3.4–13.2%)
- Wound containing foreign or infected material
- Traumatic wounds
- Open, fresh, accidental wounds
- Gross spillage from the GI tract
- Entry into infected tissue, bone, urine, or bile
- Example cases: operations with major breaks in sterile technique (e.g., open cardiac massage); incisions in which acute, non-purulent inflammation is encountered, including necrotic tissue without evidence of purulent drainage (e.g., dry gangrene)

**Class IV – Dirty** (infection rate 3.1–12.8%)
- Old traumatic wounds with retained devitalized tissue, and those involving existing clinical infection or perforated viscera
- Organisms causing postoperative infection were present in the operative field before the operation
- Example cases: drainage of abscess, debridement of soft tissue infection, resection of infarcted bowel

questions.stem: Which of the following is most characteristic of Class III Hemorrhagic shock?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Low blood pressure**

- **A. Patient is confused and lethargic** — This finding is considered under Class IV hemorrhagic shock.
- **B. Low blood pressure** — Blood pressure in Class III and Class IV hemorrhagic shock is usually decreased, making this the correct answer.
- **C. Blood loss of 750–1000 mL** — This describes Class II hemorrhagic shock.
- **D. Urine output of >30 mL/h** — This describes Class I hemorrhagic shock.

Estimated fluid and blood losses based on the patient's presentation (adapted from American College of Surgeons' Committee on Trauma, 20024):

| Parameter | Class I | Class II | Class III | Class IV |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Blood loss (mL) | Up to 750 | 750–1500 | 1500–2000 | >2000 |
| Blood loss (% BV) | Up to 15% | 15–30% | 30–40% | >40% |
| Pulse rate | <100 | >100 | >120 | >140 |
| Blood pressure | Normal | Normal | Decreased | Decreased |
| Pulse pressure (mmHg) | Normal or increased | Decreased | Decreased | Decreased |
| Respiratory rate | 14–20 | >20–30 | 30–40 | >35 |
| Urine output (mL/h) | >30 | >20–30 | 5–15 | Negligible |
| CNS/mental status | Slightly anxious | Mildly anxious | Anxious and confused | Confused and lethargic |

BV = blood volume; CNS = central nervous system.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old male is brought to the emergency department after a motorcycle crash. He is pale, restless, and confused. His blood pressure is 80/50 mmHg, heart rate is 134 bpm, and his skin is cool and clammy. There is no obvious external bleeding, but his abdomen is distended and tender to palpation. He has no significant medical history. What is the most likely type of shock this patient is experiencing?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Hypovolemic shock**

- **A. Cardiogenic shock** — Usually presents with signs of heart failure, often after a myocardial infarction.
- **B. Neurogenic shock** — Usually seen in spinal cord injury, and typically presents with hypotension and bradycardia, and warm skin due to vasodilation.
- **C. Hypovolemic shock** — The patient has signs of Class III–IV hypovolemic shock: tachycardia, hypotension, altered mental status, and cool extremities, a classic presentation for hypovolemic shock. The abdominal distention suggests internal bleeding, likely intra-abdominal hemorrhage from blunt trauma.
- **D. Septic shock** — Typically presents with fever or known infection, often with warm skin, but this patient has no signs of infection and the case is traumatic in nature.

**Hemodynamic characteristics of the major types of shock** (adapted from Table 296-2, Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed., 2022)

| Type of shock | CVP | PCWP | Cardiac output | Systemic vascular resistance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Distributive | ⬇ | ⬇ | ⬆ | ⬇ |
| Cardiogenic | ⬆ | ⬆ | ⬇ | ⬆ |
| Obstructive | ⬆ | ⬇/⬆ | ⬇ | ⬆ |
| Hypovolemic | ⬇ | ⬇ | ⬇ | ⬆ |

- **Distributive shock** — Decrease in systemic vascular resistance (septic shock) → increase in cardiac output → "warm extremities."
- **Cardiogenic shock** — Poor contraction of the heart → damming of fluid in the LA and RA → "cold extremities."
- **Obstructive shock** — Flow obstruction beyond the heart (aortic dissection) → damming of fluid in the LA and RA → "cold extremities"; flow obstruction beyond the RV but before the LA (pulmonary embolism) → damming of fluid in the RA → "cold extremities."
- **Hypovolemic shock** — Low preload (massive blood loss) → decreased Frank-Starling mechanism → low cardiac output → "cold extremities."

questions.stem: A 33-year-old male was brought to the emergency room. You note that he has eye opening to pain, confused, and localizes to pain. What is his Glasgow Coma Score?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — 11**

For this patient: Eye opening (E) = 2, Verbal (V) = 4, Motor (M) = 5. Total GCS = E + V + M = 11.

**Glasgow Coma Scale**

| Eye opening | Score |
|---|---|
| Spontaneously | 4 |
| To verbal command | 3 |
| To pain | 2 |
| None | 1 |

| Verbal response | Score |
|---|---|
| Oriented | 5 |
| Confused | 4 |
| Inappropriate or incoherent words | 3 |
| Incomprehensible sounds | 2 |
| None | 1 |

| Motor response | Score |
|---|---|
| Obeys commands | 6 |
| Localizes to pain | 5 |
| Flexion and withdrawal to pain | 4 |
| Abnormal flexion | 3 |
| Abnormal extension | 2 |
| None | 1 |

The GCS-P (pupil-reactivity-adjusted GCS) further subtracts points for pupillary reactivity:

| Pupil reactivity | Subtracted points |
|---|---|
| Both normal (isocoric) | Minus 0 |
| 1 abnormal (anisocoric) | Minus 1 |
| Both dilated, unreactive | Minus 2 |

questions.stem: A patient was diagnosed to have chronic subdural hematoma. Which of the following imaging findings is most consistent with this condition?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Crescentic and hypodense hematoma**

| Feature | Epidural hematoma | Subdural hematoma |
|---|---|---|
| Shape | Lenticular or biconvex | Crescent |
| Source of bleeding | Middle meningeal artery | Dural bridging veins |
| Location | Between dura and skull | Between dura and arachnoid mater |
| Crosses suture lines? | Cannot cross suture lines (dura is anchored) | Can cross suture lines |
| Clinical course | Lucid interval | Acute (immediate), subacute (days), or chronic (weeks) |

A chronic subdural hematoma is crescentic in shape, consistent with Choice C.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old male came in the ER following a motor vehicular crash with extensive maxillofacial injuries. On imaging, the fracture was seen to extend through the nasofrontal buttress, medial orbital wall, infraorbital rim and zygomaticomaxillary articulation. What the likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Le Fort II**

- **A. Le Fort I** — Involves transverse maxillary alveolus fractures above the teeth, resulting in a mobile hard palate.
- **B. Le Fort II** — Fractures extend superiorly to include the nasofrontal buttress, medial orbital wall, and even as high as the infraorbital rim and zygomaticomaxillary articulation laterally.
- **C. Le Fort III** — Fractures involve the frontozygomaticomaxillary, frontomaxillary, and frontonasal suture lines.
- **D. Le Fort IV** — There is no Le Fort IV.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old male came in the emergency room following an MVC. His VS are as follows: BP 70/50, HR 120, RR 36, T 36.4. You note decreased breath sounds on the right lung field. On X-ray, you note tracheal deviation to the left, together with multiple broken ribs. What is the next best step for the patient?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Needle thoracostomy**

The most likely diagnosis for the case above is tension pneumothorax. Tension pneumothorax is presumed in any patient manifesting respiratory distress and hypotension, in combination with any of the following physical signs:

- Tracheal deviation away from the affected side
- Decreased breath sounds on the affected side
- Subcutaneous emphysema on the affected side
- Distended neck veins

Tension pneumothorax and simple pneumothorax have similar signs, symptoms, and examination findings, but hypotension qualifies the pneumothorax as a tension pneumothorax.

The initial management for tension pneumothorax is immediate needle thoracostomy decompression with a 14-gauge angiocatheter.

Source: Schwartz Principles of Surgery, 11th ed., p. 186.

questions.stem: Which of the following imaging findings is most associated with aortic rupture on Chest Xray?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Mediastinal widening**

Traumatic aortic rupture is a condition in which the aorta is ruptured; victims with severe injury usually die at the scene or in transport.

Usual radiologic signs:
- Widened mediastinum >8 cm
- Abnormal aortic contour
- Tracheal shift, NGT shift
- Left apical cap
- Paraspinal stripe thickening
- Depression of the main bronchus
- Obliteration of the aorticopulmonary window
- Left pulmonary hilar hematoma

questions.stem: Which of the following is not expected in a patient with abdominal compartment syndrome?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Increased urine output**

Abdominal compartment syndrome is defined as intra-abdominal hypertension sufficient to produce physiologic deterioration and manifests via end-organ sequelae.

- **A. Increased urine output** — Not expected; abdominal compartment syndrome actually causes decreased urine output, which is why this is the correct answer to this "not expected" question.
- **B. Decreased cardiac output** — Expected in abdominal compartment syndrome.
- **C. Increased pulmonary inspiratory pressure** — Expected in abdominal compartment syndrome.
- **D. Decreased cardiac preload** — Expected in abdominal compartment syndrome.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old patient came in the ER following a fall. On X-ray, you detect a fracture of the radial shaft at the junction of the middle and distal thirds without an associated fracture of the ulna. What is being described?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Piedmont fracture**

**Common fracture eponyms**

| Fracture | Description |
|---|---|
| Colles fracture | Fracture of the distal radius with the fragment displaced dorsally ("dinner-fork") |
| Smith fracture (Reverse Colles) | Fracture of the distal radius with the fragment displaced volarly |
| Hutchinson / Chauffeur fracture | Fracture of the radial styloid |
| Monteggia fracture | Fracture of the [proximal third of the] ulna with dislocation of the radial head |
| Galeazzi fracture | Fracture of the distal radius (middle-distal third) with dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ) |
| Piedmont fracture | Fracture of the radial shaft at the junction of the middle and distal thirds without an associated fracture of the ulna |
| Jones fracture | Fracture at the base of the 5th metatarsal diaphysis |
| Bennett fracture | Fracture-dislocation of the first metacarpal (thumb) with disruption of the carpometacarpal joint |
| Boxer fracture | Fracture of the metacarpal neck |
| Nightstick fracture | Ulnar fracture |
| Clay shoveler fracture | Fracture of C6–C7 spinous processes |
| Hangman fracture | Fracture of C2 pedicles |
| Jefferson fracture | Fracture of the C1 ring |
| Pott's fracture | Fracture of distal fibula |

**MUGR mnemonic:**
- MU: Monteggia — Ulnar fracture. "MonteggiA" ends with A, the first letter of the alphabet = proximal.
- GR: Galeazzi — Radial fracture. "GalleaZZi" has the letter Z, the last letter of the alphabet = distal.

choices.text: Apply a tourniquet superior to the wound
Apply deep direct pressure to the wound

questions.stem: A patient involved in a motor vehicle accident presents with a deep, actively bleeding wound on the lower extremity. What is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Apply deep direct pressure to the wound**

- **A. Initiate massive transfusion protocol** — This is done after initial hemorrhage control and once the patient is stabilized.
- **B. Apply a tourniquet superior to the wound** — This is done if direct pressure is not effective.
- **C. Apply deep direct pressure to the wound** — In a situation with severe, life-threatening external bleeding, the most appropriate initial management is to apply direct, firm pressure to the wound to slow or stop the bleeding.
- **D. Perform emergency suturing** — This is done after the bleeding has been controlled.

Source: Bleeding (life-threatening external). Red Cross. (n.d.). https://www.redcross.org/take-a-class/resources/learn-first-aid/bleeding-life-threatening-external

questions.stem: Which type of burn is characterized by blistering, pain, and partial-thickness skin loss?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Second-degree burn**

**Depth of burn wounds**

| Burn depth | Presentation |
|---|---|
| First degree | Painful and erythematous (without blisters) |
| Second degree | Painful and blistered |
| Third degree | Painless, white, and charred |

choices.text: To estimate body surface area burned

questions.stem: What is the Parkland formula used for in burn patients?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — To calculate fluid resuscitation needs**

The Parkland formula estimates fluid requirements in the first 24 hours following a burn: 3–4 mL × body weight (kg) × % TBSA burned. Half is given in the first 8 hours.

**Fluid needs for the first 24 hours post-burn**
- Parkland's (Baxter) formula = 3 to 4 mL plain LR/kg/%TBSA
- Revised Parkland's (Baxter) formula:
  - 2 mL PLR/kg/%TBSA — adult
  - 3 mL D5% LR/kg/%TBSA — child
  - 4 mL PLR/kg/%TBSA — electrical burns
- First ½ given in the first 8 hours
- Next ½ given over the next 16 hours

choices.text: Lower angle of mandible to above clavicle
Base of skull to angle of mandible
Cricoid cartilage to angle of mandible

questions.stem: Penetrating neck trauma involving Zone II affects which anatomic region?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A**

Zone II of the neck is described as:
1. Schwartz: from the cricoid cartilage to the angle of the mandible ("best answer")
2. Other references: use the cricoid as the landmark

It is the most accessible zone for surgical exploration.

- Choices B and C refer to Zones I and III, respectively.

In some references (Figure 7-20, Schwartz's Principles of Surgery, 11th ed., 2019):
- Zone I: thoracic inlet → "chest zone"
- Zone II: between cricoid and mandible → "surgical zone" (most accessible)
- Zone III: above the mandible → "skull base zone" (hardest to expose surgically)

questions.stem: Myringotomy with tube placement is used in the management of?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Chronic otitis media**

- **A. Acute otitis media** — If there is no clinical improvement in the first 48 to 72 hours, it is treated with oral antibiotics. First-line therapy is high-dose amoxicillin or amoxicillin-clavulanate for β-lactamase coverage.
- **B. Chronic otitis media** — Frequently treated with myringotomy and tube placement. This treatment is indicated for frequent acute episodes and aims to remove the effusion and provide a route for middle ear ventilation.
- **C. Malignant otitis externa** — Requires aggressive medical therapy, including ototopical and IV antibiotics targeting *Pseudomonas*.
- **D. Acute otitis externa** — Managed with removal of debris under otomicroscopy and application of appropriate ototopical antimicrobials, such as neomycin/polymyxin or quinolone-containing eardrops.

questions.stem: Which of the following X-ray views can best visualize the maxillary sinuses?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Waters view**

- **A. Waters view** — Best for visualization of the maxillary sinuses.
- **B. Towne view** — Also known as the fronto-occipital view; best shows the foramen magnum and both petrous pyramids.
- **C. Caldwell view** — Best for visualization of the frontal and ethmoidal sinuses.
- **D. Odontoid view** — The best imaging choice to detect Jefferson fractures.

questions.stem: Cleft palate is associated with an increased risk of?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Otitis media**

The tensor veli palatini muscles, which normally function to vent and drain the Eustachian tubes, are disrupted in cleft anatomy. Eustachian tube dysfunction predisposes patients to frequent bouts of otitis media, which can lead to permanent hearing loss if left untreated.

Source: Schwartz Principles of Surgery, 11th ed., p. 1984.

questions.stem: Bezold's abscess is a complication of which condition?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Mastoiditis**

- **A. Mastoiditis** — Bezold's abscess is a deep neck abscess that occurs as a complication of mastoiditis when infection erodes through the mastoid tip.
- **B. Otitis media** — Incorrect; while otitis media can lead to mastoiditis, it is not the direct cause of Bezold's abscess.
- **C. Cleft lip/palate** — Unrelated to the pathophysiology of this abscess.
- **D. Diabetes mellitus** — Unrelated to the pathophysiology of this abscess.

Source: Winters, R. (2023, July 4). Bezold abscess. StatPearls [Internet].

questions.stem: Which salivary gland is most commonly affected by sialolithiasis (salivary stones)?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Submandibular gland**

- Approximately 85% of sialoliths occur within the submandibular gland, making it the most common location for sialolithiasis.
- One reason is that the submandibular duct ascends toward its opening in the oral cavity, resulting in a stagnant flow of saliva.
- Additionally, the submandibular gland produces predominantly mucinous saliva, which is more viscous than the secretions produced by the parotid gland, resulting in a more stagnant flow of secretions. The submandibular gland also produces more alkaline saliva, which predisposes to the precipitation of inorganic salts, further leading to salivary stone formation.
- Approximately 15% of salivary stones occur within the parotid gland, and less than 5% occur within the sublingual and minor salivary glands.

Source: Hammett, J. (2024, September 10). Sialolithiasis. StatPearls [Internet].

questions.stem: A 70-year-old female presents with a 10-year history of neck mass with sudden enlargement associated with hoarseness, dysphagia and lymph node enlargement. What is the most likely type of thyroid cancer?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Anaplastic carcinoma**

- **A. Follicular carcinoma** — 10% of thyroid malignancies.
  - Usually solitary and encapsulated
  - More common in areas with iodine deficiency
  - F>M, mean age 50 years
  - Presentation: solitary nodule with a history of rapid size increase and long-standing goiter
  - Hematogenous spread is more common
  - Lymph node metastasis is uncommon
- **B. Papillary carcinoma** — Most common, 80% of thyroid malignancies.
  - Predominant in children, childhood radiation exposure, and iodine-sufficient areas
  - F>M, mean age 30–40 years (most important prognostic factor: age)
  - Prior history of radiation exposure
  - Commonly metastasizes to cervical lymph nodes
  - Excellent prognosis (>95% survival at 10 years)
  - Presentation: slow-growing, painless mass, palpable lymphadenopathy
- **C. Medullary carcinoma**
  - Arises from the neuroendocrine parafollicular cells (C cells), located at the superolateral lobes of the thyroid gland
  - Secondary to a germline mutation in the RET protooncogene
    - MEN2A: medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, primary hyperparathyroidism
    - MEN2B: medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, marfanoid habitus, mucocutaneous ganglioneuromas
  - Produces calcitonin, CEA, CGRP, histaminidase, serotonin
- **D. Anaplastic carcinoma** — 1% of thyroid malignancies (correct answer).
  - F>M, patients in their 60s or 70s
  - Long-standing neck mass that rapidly enlarges with symptoms of local invasion (hoarseness and dysphagia, and compressive symptoms), with lymph node and distant metastases at presentation
  - Lymph node metastases are usually present
  - Metastases may be evident at the time of diagnosis

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man, chronic smoker and drinker, presents with a non-healing ulcer on the left lateral border of the tongue. He reports progressive pain while eating and difficulty speaking over the last 2 months. On examination, the lesion measures 3.5 cm, and there is a palpable, firm, mobile, 1.5 cm ipsilateral cervical lymph node in level II. No signs of distant metastasis are found on imaging. According to the TNM classification, what is the most appropriate stage for this patient?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — T2 N1 M0**

**Head and neck staging — TNM classification**

| T | Description |
|---|---|
| T1 | 2 cm or less in diameter, confined to site of origin |
| T2 | >2 to 4 cm in diameter |
| T3 | >4 cm in diameter |
| T4 | Massive tumor with invasion of surrounding structures |

| N | Description |
|---|---|
| N0 | No regional lymph node metastasis |
| N1 | Metastasis in a single ipsilateral node < 3 cm |
| N2a | Metastasis in a single ipsilateral lymph node between 3–6 cm |
| N2b | Metastasis in multiple ipsilateral lymph nodes, node < 6 cm |
| N2c | Metastasis in bilateral or contralateral nodes < 6 cm |
| N3 | Metastasis in a lymph node > 6 cm |

| M | Description |
|---|---|
| M0 | No distant metastasis |
| M1 | With distant metastasis |

*Tip to memorize head and neck staging: the magic numbers for T are 2 and 4; for N they are 3 and 6.*

- **Tumor (T):** A lesion that is greater than 2 cm but not more than 4 cm is classified as T2. The patient's 3.5 cm lesion fits this criterion.
- **Node (N):** A single ipsilateral lymph node ≤3 cm qualifies as N1. The patient's 1.5 cm mobile lymph node matches this criterion.
- **Metastasis (M):** No distant metastases = M0.
- Thus, the TNM classification is T2 N1 M0.

- **A. T1 N1 M0** — Incorrect T; T1 is for tumors ≤2 cm, but in this case the tumor is 3.5 cm.
- **C. T2 N2a M0** — Correct T, but incorrect N; N2a requires metastasis in an ipsilateral cervical lymph node of 3–6 cm, which is not the case here.
- **D. T3 N2a M0** — Incorrect T; T3 requires a tumor >4 cm, which is not the case here. N2a is also not the proper staging for this lymph node metastasis.

questions.stem: A full-term baby boy is born via NSD with no complications during pregnancy, develops respiratory distress and excessive frothing and spitting following attempts at breastfeeding. OGT was attempted but cannot be advanced beyond a certain point. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Proximal tracheoesophageal fistula with distal esophageal atresia**

The most common type of tracheoesophageal anomaly is Type C, where the esophagus ends blindly (esophageal atresia) and the distal esophagus is connected to the trachea (distal TEF).

In this case, there is respiratory distress and frothing after feeding, suggesting aspiration. The OGT cannot be advanced, which is classic for esophageal atresia.

- **B. H-type tracheoesophageal fistula** — Incorrect; H-type has no esophageal atresia, so the OGT would pass into the stomach.
- **C. Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis** — Incorrect; it typically presents later, with projectile vomiting, not immediate respiratory distress in newborns.
- **D. Duodenal atresia** — Incorrect; presents with bilious vomiting and a "double bubble" sign on X-ray.

choices.text: More than 2 infections prior to removal
Age less than 2 years at the time of removal

questions.stem: What is the most common reason for recurrence of a thyroglossal duct cyst after surgical removal?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Incomplete resection**

**Thyroglossal duct cyst**
- Residual thyroid tissue left behind during its descent
- Presents as a midline neck mass in children
- 80% occur at or just below the hyoid bone
- Moves with deglutition or tongue protrusion
- Treatment: Sistrunk procedure

- **A. Incomplete resection** — The most common reason for recurrence of a thyroglossal duct cyst after surgery is incomplete resection of the thyroglossal tract.
- **B. More than 2 infections prior to removal** — May complicate surgery but is not the primary cause of recurrence.
- **C. Age less than 2 years at the time of removal** — Might be a factor in some studies, but age is generally not cited as the leading cause of recurrence.
- **D. Non-adherence to antibiotics** — Post-surgery, this can contribute to complications (infection) but generally does not affect recurrence after proper surgical excision.

questions.stem: Which thyroid cancer is associated with amyloid stroma and MEN 2 syndrome?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Medullary**

Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from parafollicular C-cells and is associated with MEN 2A/2B. It shows amyloid deposition from calcitonin.

**Medullary carcinoma**
- Arises from the neuroendocrine parafollicular cells (C cells), located at the superolateral lobes of the thyroid gland
  - 75% sporadic
  - 25% familial
- Secondary to a germline mutation in the RET protooncogene
  - MEN 2A: medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, primary hyperparathyroidism
  - MEN 2B: medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, marfanoid habitus, mucocutaneous ganglioneuromas
- Familial MTC: MTC gene
- More than half are bilateral
- Produces: calcitonin, CEA, CGRP, histaminidase, serotonin
- Pathology:
  - Unilateral in sporadic cases
  - Bilateral in familial cases
  - Amyloidosis (stains with Congo red)
- Diagnosis: FNAB (all patients must be screened for RET point mutations, pheochromocytoma, and primary hyperparathyroidism)
  - CT scan or MRI to exclude neck, chest, and liver metastases
- Treatment:
  - Total thyroidectomy + routine bilateral central neck dissection — operation of choice
  - MEN 2A: total thyroidectomy before age 6
  - MEN 2B: total thyroidectomy before age 1
- Postoperative follow-up: annual calcitonin and CEA
- Best survival is seen in non-MEN familial MTC
- For MEN syndromes, address pheochromocytoma and hyperparathyroidism first

questions.stem: The most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism is:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Parathyroid adenoma**

Parathyroid adenoma is the most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism, accounting for over 80% of cases.

**Primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT)**
- Increased PTH production with resultant increase in calcium level
- Etiology:
  - Parathyroid adenoma (80%)
  - Parathyroid hyperplasia (15–20%)
  - Parathyroid carcinoma (1%)
- Clinical manifestations (most patients are asymptomatic):
  - Pentad: kidney stones, painful bones, abdominal groans, psychic moans, fatigue overtones
- Physical findings: usually non-palpable

choices.text: Internal branch of superior laryngeal nerve
External branch of superior laryngeal nerve

questions.stem: What is the most commonly injured nerve during thyroid surgery?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Recurrent laryngeal nerve**

The recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) is most commonly injured in thyroidectomy, potentially causing hoarseness or airway obstruction.

- **A. Non-recurrent laryngeal nerve** — A rare anatomic finding, and thus also rarely injured.
- **C. Internal branch of superior laryngeal nerve** — Affects sensation above the vocal folds; less commonly injured.
- **D. External branch of superior laryngeal nerve** — Affects pitch; less commonly injured.

**RLN injury — clinical manifestations**

*Unilateral RLN injury*
- Vocal cord in paramedian position: normal but weak voice
- Vocal cord in abducted position: hoarse voice, weak cough

*Bilateral RLN injury*
- Airway obstruction → necessitates emergency tracheostomy

**Superior laryngeal nerve**

*Internal branch*
- Provides sensation above the vocal folds
- Injury: increases risk of aspiration

*External branch*
- Innervates the cricothyroid muscle
- Injury: inability to hit high notes

questions.stem: Milky white nipple discharge may be suggestive of?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Fibroadenoma**

Nipple discharge is a finding that can be seen in a number of clinical situations.

It is suggestive of cancer if it is:
- Spontaneous
- Unilateral
- Localized to a single duct
- Present in women ≥40 years of age
- Bloody
- Associated with a mass

It is suggestive of a benign condition if it is:
- Bilateral
- Multiductal
- Occurs in women ≤39 years of age
- Milky or blue-green

The best answer is fibroadenoma, a benign disorder of the breast presenting as a painless, round, oval, or circumscribed mass that can change with the menstrual cycle or pregnancy. The rest of the choices are types of invasive breast carcinoma and are more likely to present with bloody nipple discharge.

Source: Schwartz Principles of Surgery, 11th ed., p. 600.

questions.stem: Which BIRADS category corresponds to a 'probably benign' finding that requires a 6-month follow-up?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — BIRADS 3**

BIRADS 3 is "probably benign" (<2% risk), with recommended short-term (6-month) follow-up.

| BIRADS category | Assessment | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Incomplete | Additional imaging recommended; prior mammogram for comparison |
| 1 | Negative (normal finding) | Routine screening recommended |
| 2 | Benign finding | Routine screening recommended |
| 3 | Probably benign finding; <2% risk of malignancy; very high probability of benign finding | Short-interval follow-up recommended (6 months) to establish stability, then every 6–13 months for 1–2 years |
| 4A | Low suspicion for malignancy (3–10%) | Perform biopsy, preferably needle biopsy |
| 4B | Intermediate risk for malignancy (11–50%) | Perform biopsy, preferably needle biopsy |
| 4C | Moderate risk for malignancy (51–94%) | Perform biopsy, preferably needle biopsy |
| 5 | Highly suggestive of malignancy (>95%) | Appropriate action should be taken |
| 6 | Biopsy-proven malignancy | Assure that treatment is completed |

Additional imaging for BIRADS 0 is usually breast ultrasonography.

questions.stem: Which of the following breast lesions is most likely to present as a painless, firm, mobile mass in a young woman?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Fibroadenoma**

Fibroadenoma is a common benign tumor in young women, typically painless, firm, and mobile. Phyllodes tumors are similar but less common.

**Benign disorders of the breast — Fibroadenoma**
- Painless, round, oval, or circumscribed mass
- Firm and freely mobile
- May change with the menstrual cycle or pregnancy
- Some regress in size, but most are stable
  - Predominates in younger women
  - Grows to 1–2 cm
  - Most are self-limiting (growth ceases at 2–3 cm)
- Diagnostic:
  - Ultrasound: oval, circumscribed, homogeneous solid mass with low internal echoes
  - Mammography: circumscribed round, oval, or lobular, low- or equal-density radiopaque mass indistinguishable from cysts
- Treatment:
  - Women <25–30 years with typical imaging appearance: close clinical follow-up
  - Women >30 years without a prior mammogram: needle aspiration; mammography to assess borders of the lesion (controversy exists regarding the size threshold for follow-up mammography vs. immediate biopsy)

questions.stem: Which is the most common location for breast cancer development?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Upper outer quadrant**

The upper outer quadrant has the greatest volume of glandular tissue, making it the most common site for breast cancer.

**Functional anatomy**
- Composed of 15 to 20 lobes
- Cooper's suspensory ligament provides structural support
- Extends from the 2nd or 3rd rib superiorly to the 6th or 7th rib inferiorly at the inframammary fold, and from the lateral border of the sternum to the anterior axillary line (axillary tail of Spence)
- The upper outer quadrant contains a greater volume of tissue compared to the other quadrants (most common location of malignant mass)

questions.stem: A 44/F patient diagnosed with breast cancer came into your clinic for staging. On examination, you note a 4cm mass with matted ipsilateral axillary lymph nodes. There is no evidence of distant metastasis. What is the staging for this patient?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — IIIA**

The staging for the case given above is T2N2M0 – Stage IIIA:
- 4 cm breast mass – T2 (tumor greater than 2 cm but not greater than 5 cm)
- Matted ipsilateral axillary lymph nodes – N2 (metastasis in ipsilateral ALN, fixed or matted, or ipsilateral internal mammary LN)
- No evidence of distant metastasis – M0

| T | Description |
|---|---|
| Tx | Cannot be assessed |
| T0 | No evidence |
| Tis | Carcinoma in situ |
| T1 | Tumor 2 cm or less in diameter |
| T2 | Tumor greater than 2 cm but not greater than 5 cm |
| T3 | Tumor greater than 5 cm |
| T4 | Any size with direct extension to the chest wall (4a) or skin (4b) |

| N | Description |
|---|---|
| Nx | Cannot be assessed |
| N0 | No regional LN metastasis |
| N1 | Metastasis to movable ipsilateral ALN |
| N2 | Metastasis in ipsilateral ALN, fixed or matted, or ipsilateral internal mammary LN |
| N3 | Metastasis in ipsilateral ALN and internal mammary LN, or infraclavicular LN, or supraclavicular LN |

| M | Description |
|---|---|
| Mx | Metastasis cannot be assessed |
| M0 | No distant metastasis |
| M1 | Distant metastasis |

**Stage grouping**

| Stage | T | N | M |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Tis | N0 | M0 |
| I | T1 | N0 | M0 |
| IIA | T0 | N1 | M0 |
| IIA | T1 | N1 | M0 |
| IIA | T2 | N0 | M0 |
| IIB | T2 | N1 | M0 |
| IIB | T3 | N0 | M0 |
| IIIA | T0 | N2 | M0 |
| IIIA | T1 | N2 | M0 |
| IIIA | T2 | N2 | M0 |
| IIIA | T3 | N1 | M0 |
| IIIA | T3 | N2 | M0 |
| IIIB | T4 | N0 | M0 |
| IIIB | T4 | N1 | M0 |
| IIIB | T4 | N2 | M0 |
| IIIC | Any T | N3 | M0 |
| IV | Any T | Any N | M1 |

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman has a 2 cm tumor in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast with no palpable axillary nodes. What is the most appropriate surgical management?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Breast-conserving surgery + sentinel lymph node biopsy**

For T1–T2 tumors with clinically negative nodes, breast-conserving surgery (lumpectomy) with sentinel lymph node biopsy is appropriate. Mastectomy is not mandatory for this stage.

**Specific management plans for breast cancer**

*LCIS*
- Observation
- Chemoprevention (tamoxifen)
- Prophylactic bilateral total mastectomy

*DCIS*
- Low grade: lumpectomy alone
- Intermediate grade: lumpectomy + radiotherapy
- High grade: mastectomy

*Early invasive breast cancer (Stage I, IIA, IIB)*
- Breast-conserving surgery + sentinel lymph node biopsy +/- adjuvant chemotherapy/radiotherapy
- Lumpectomy
- Axillary node assessment (SLNB)
- Radiotherapy

*Advanced locoregional breast cancer (Stage IIIA, IIIB, IIIC)*
- Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (Adriamycin–taxane containing), then either BCT or MRM
  - Plus adjuvant chemo/RT/trastuzumab (HER2+)
  - Plus antiestrogen therapy (ER/PR+)

*Stage IV*
- Palliative approaches: antiestrogen therapy, chemotherapy, surgery, radiotherapy, breast-conserving surgery
- Clinical trials

questions.stem: A basal cell carcinoma most commonly occurs in which region?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Sun-exposed face and neck**

Basal cell carcinoma commonly arises on sun-exposed areas like the face and neck, especially in fair-skinned individuals.

**Nonmelanoma skin cancers (NMSC)**
- More common
- Typically a disease of fair-skinned people lacking in melanin
- Correlate closely with sun exposure
- Risk factors:
  - Primary risk factor: sun exposure (UV-B > UV-A rays)
  - X-ray exposure
  - Arsenic exposure
  - Immunosuppression
  - Previous non-melanoma skin cancer

**Basal cell carcinoma**
- Most common type of skin cancer
- Most common subtype: nodular ("rodent ulcer")
- Most aggressive form: morpheaform
- Tumor characteristics: slow growing, rarely metastasizes, yet locally invasive
- Most common malignant eyelid tumor, and usual cause of upper lip malignancy

questions.stem: What is the most important prognostic factor in melanoma?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Breslow thickness**

Breslow thickness (depth of invasion) is the most important prognostic indicator for survival in melanoma.

**Malignant melanoma**
- Occurs in all ethnic groups
- Associated with increased sun exposure and decreased melanin content
- Responsible for the majority of deaths from skin cancer
- Correlates more with the intensity of prior sun exposure than cumulative exposure (in contrast to nonmelanoma skin cancer)
- Risk factors:
  - A history of five or more sunburns in early life has been associated with a doubled risk of developing malignant melanoma later in life
  - Fair skin and light eyes
  - Dysplastic nevi and multiple (>50) nevi
  - Prior history of melanoma or family history of melanoma
  - Immunosuppression (transplant patients)
  - Xeroderma pigmentosum — impaired nucleotide excision repair
- Pathology:
  - Migration of melanocytes upward to the dermo-epidermal junction
  - Development of melanoma is associated with exposure to UV radiation or malignant transformation of precursor lesions
  - Depth of invasion dictates management and prognosis

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT TRUE about erythema multiforme?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — The onset of a rash during the prodromal period occurs within 3 days, with centrifugal spreading**

Erythema multiforme lesions spread centripetally, not centrifugally, so this statement is false, making it the correct answer to this "NOT true" question. The rest of the choices are correct statements about erythema multiforme.

Source: Hafsi, W., Badri, T. (2024). Erythema Multiforme. StatPearls [Internet].

questions.stem: Which hernia passes through the deep inguinal ring and is lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Indirect inguinal hernia**

Direct hernia = medial; indirect hernia = lateral. Indirect hernias pass through the deep inguinal ring and lie lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. They are the most common type in both genders.

| Type | Remarks | Relationship to inferior epigastric vessels (IEV) | Covered by internal spermatic fascia? | Onset and etiology |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Direct inguinal hernia | Occurs in the floor of the inguinal canal, through Hesselbach's triangle; does not traverse the internal ring (traverses directly through the abdominal wall); rarely strangulates | Medial or inferior to the IEV | No | Adulthood (associated with chronic straining → weakness in musculature) |
| Indirect inguinal hernia | Most common subtype of groin hernia in men and women (Schwartz); passes through the internal inguinal ring and down the inguinal canal; can extend into the scrotum; commonly strangulates | Lateral or superior to the IEV | Yes | Congenital (usually due to patent processus vaginalis), or adulthood |
| Femoral hernia | Situated in the femoral ring (not the inguinal canal); occurs when intra-abdominal contents protrude along the femoral sheath into the femoral canal; 70% of femoral hernia repairs are performed in women, though the most common subtype of groin hernia overall is still indirect inguinal hernia (Schwartz) | — | — | — |

questions.stem: Which connective tissue disorder is not associated with inguinal hernia?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Churg-Strauss syndrome**

Microscopic examination of the skin of inguinal hernia patients demonstrated significantly decreased ratios of type I to type III collagen. Additional analyses of similar skin revealed disaggregated collagen tracts with decreased collagen fiber density.

Churg-Strauss syndrome, also known as eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA), is a rare autoimmune disorder and is not a connective tissue disease — it is a type of vasculitis affecting small- and medium-sized systemic blood vessels, often associated with eosinophilic tissue infiltration.

Source: Schwartz Principles of Surgery, 11th ed., p. 1606.

questions.stem: A newborn is found to have exposed bowel loops protruding through a defect right of the umbilicus with no covering membrane. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Gastroschisis**

Gastroschisis is a full-thickness defect of the abdominal wall, usually to the right of the umbilicus, with exposed bowel and no sac. Omphalocele is midline and covered by peritoneum and amnion.

| Feature | Omphalocele | Gastroschisis |
|---|---|---|
| Location | Umbilical ring | Right of umbilicus |
| Fascial defect | Variable (if more than 4 cm — giant) | <4 cm |
| Sac | Present, possibly ruptured | Absent |
| Intestines | Grossly normal | Leathery, shortened |
| Liver | Often herniated | Rarely herniated |
| Associated anomalies | Cloacal exstrophy, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, Cantrell pentalogy | Intestinal atresia, undescended testis, malrotation |

questions.stem: A hernia containing a Meckel's diverticulum is known as:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Littre's hernia**

Littre's hernia involves a Meckel's diverticulum. Amyand's hernia contains the vermiform appendix. Maydl's hernia contains two loops of bowel. Richter's hernia contains the antimesenteric border of the bowel.

**Hernia eponyms**

| Hernia | Description |
|---|---|
| Obturator hernia | Herniation at the obturator foramen; Howship-Romberg sign and Hannington-Kiff sign |
| Richter hernia | Herniation of the antimesenteric border of the bowel through the fascial defect |
| Littre hernia | Herniation of a Meckel diverticulum |
| Pantaloon hernia | Ipsilateral concurrent, direct, and indirect inguinal herniation |
| Maydl hernia | Herniation of two loops of bowel in the sac |
| Amyand hernia | Herniation of the vermiform appendix |
| Grynfeltt-Lesshaft hernia | Herniation of abdominal contents through the back (superior lumbar triangle) |
| Petit hernia | Herniation of abdominal contents through the back (inferior lumbar triangle) |
| Morgagni hernia | Herniation of abdominal contents through the anterior aspect of the diaphragm (via foramen of Morgagni) |
| Bochdalek hernia | Herniation of abdominal contents through the posterolateral aspect of the diaphragm |
| Spigelian hernia | Also known as lateral ventral hernia; herniation through the linea semilunaris (Spigelian line) along the arcuate line |

questions.stem: What is the most common non-traumatic cause of esophageal rupture?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Iatrogenic injury**

Esophageal rupture is a life-threatening condition caused by traumatic and non-traumatic factors.

Traumatic esophageal ruptures are most often caused by foreign body insertion, the most common being fish bone; other causes can be gunshot wounds or blunt injuries.

Non-traumatic esophageal ruptures can be divided into iatrogenic (after endoscopic intervention, NGT placement, or intubation — the most common cause of non-traumatic esophageal rupture) and non-iatrogenic.

- **A. Spontaneous rupture** — Spontaneous esophageal perforation (Boerhaave syndrome) is caused by forceful vomiting, which leads to an increase in intraesophageal pressure.
- **C. Congenital defect** — Rare; not usually a cause of rupture but rather of structural anomalies.
- **D. Caustic ingestion** — Can cause delayed rupture, but is less common.

Source: Kim, J. D. (2021). Prognostic factors of esophageal perforation and rupture leading to mortality: A retrospective study. *Journal of Cardiothoracic Surgery*, 16(1). https://doi.org/10.1186/s13019-021-01680-y

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a physiologic area of narrowing of the esophagus?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Level of the laryngeal prominence**

There are three normal areas of physiologic narrowing of the esophagus:

| Location | Level | Diameter / Comment |
|---|---|---|
| Cricopharyngeus muscle | C6 | Narrowest point of the esophagus (1.5 cm) |
| Main stem bronchus and aortic arch | T4 | 1.6 cm |
| Hiatus of the diaphragm | T10 | 1.6–1.9 cm; caused by the gastroesophageal sphincter mechanism |

- **A. Level of cricopharyngeus muscle** — one of the three normal areas of narrowing.
- **B. Level of the main stem bronchi and aortic arch** — one of the three normal areas of narrowing.
- **C. Level of the hiatus of the diaphragm** — one of the three normal areas of narrowing.
- **D. Level of the laryngeal prominence** — not one of the three normal areas of narrowing (correct answer).
