questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of a third-degree corrosive esophageal burn?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Pseudomembrane formation**

Third-degree corrosive esophageal and gastric burns are characterized by sloughing of mucosa, deep ulcers, massive hemorrhage, complete obstruction of the lumen by edema, charring, and perforation.

- **A. Sloughing of mucosa** — a characteristic of a third-degree burn.
- **B. Pseudomembrane formation** — a characteristic of a *second*-degree esophageal burn, together with limited hemorrhage and exudative ulceration, not a third-degree burn (correct answer).
- **C. Deep ulcer** — a characteristic of a third-degree burn.
- **D. Complete obstruction of lumen by edema** — a characteristic of a third-degree burn.

*Schwartz's Principles of Surgery, 11th ed., p. 1086.*

questions.stem: Which type of gastric ulcer is located closest to the esophagus?
questions.rationale:
The Johnson classification of gastric ulcers categorizes ulcers by location within the stomach and by whether they are associated with increased acid secretion.

| Type | Location |
|---|---|
| I | Lesser curvature of the stomach (body) |
| II | One gastric ulcer (body) + one duodenal ulcer; associated with increased acid secretion |
| III | Pre-pyloric region; associated with increased acid secretion |
| IV | Proximal lesser curvature, near the GE junction — closest to the esophagus |
| V | Anywhere in the stomach; associated with NSAID use |

**Correct answer: D — Type IV**, as it is located closest to the esophagus.

choices.text: Ulcer situated high on the lesser curvature

questions.stem: Which type of ulcer is associated with increased acid output?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Prepyloric ulcer**

Gastric ulcers can be classified by location and mechanism:

| Type | Feature |
|---|---|
| I | Antral, lesser curvature (most common) |
| II | Type I ulcer + duodenal ulcer |
| III | Prepyloric ulcer |
| IV | High on the lesser curvature |
| V | NSAID-induced |

- Ulcers associated with **increased acid output**: Type II and Type III (prepyloric — Choice D).
- Ulcers associated with **decreased mucosal protection**: Type I and Type IV.

Per choice:
- **A. Antral lesser curvature ulcer** — Type I; associated with decreased mucosal protection, not increased acid output.
- **B. Ulcer situated high on the lesser curvature** — Type IV; associated with decreased mucosal protection, not increased acid output.
- **C. NSAID-induced ulcer** — Type V; not among the ulcers associated with increased acid output.
- **D. Prepyloric ulcer** — Type III; associated with increased acid output (correct answer).

questions.stem: Which tumor marker may be elevated in a patient with gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST)?
questions.rationale:
Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) is a malignant neoplasm of the stomach that arises from the interstitial cells of Cajal. It is usually asymptomatic, but may present with bleeding, early satiety, and abdominal pain or fullness.

**Correct answer: A — CD117**

- **A. CD117** — the tumor markers elevated in GIST are c-KIT (CD117) and CD34 (correct answer).
- **B. CEA** — may be elevated in medullary thyroid carcinoma, invasive breast carcinoma, gastric adenocarcinoma, gallbladder carcinoma, or colorectal carcinoma.
- **C. CA 19-9** — usually elevated in biliary or pancreatic cancer.
- **D. CA-125** — elevated in ovarian cancer.

questions.stem: Which of the following liver lesions appears as a central scar on CT?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Focal nodular hyperplasia**

- **A. Hemangioma** — presents as asymmetrical nodular peripheral enhancement that is isodense with large vessels, with progressive centripetal fill-in enhancement over time.
- **B. Adenoma** — usually has sharply defined borders and can be confused with metastatic tumors on CT.
  - With venous phase contrast, it can appear hypodense or isodense relative to background liver.
  - With arterial phase contrast, subtle hypervascular enhancement is often seen.
- **C. Focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH)** — a solid, benign liver lesion believed to be a hyperplastic response to an anomalous artery. A good-quality biphasic CT scan is usually diagnostic, showing a well-circumscribed lesion with a typical central scar (correct answer).
- **D. Hepatocellular carcinoma** — often appears hypervascular during the arterial phase and relatively hypodense during the delayed phases, due to early washout of contrast by arterial blood.

*Schwartz's Principles of Surgery, 11th ed., p. 1375–1376.*

questions.stem: A patient came in the ER for right upper quadrant pain. Imaging done revealed low-density round lesions with peripheral edema. Fluorescent antibody test for E. histolytica was done and turned out to be positive. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.rationale:
The primary consideration in this case is amebic liver abscess. Unlike pyogenic liver abscess, amebic liver abscess presents with a positive fluorescent antibody test for *E. histolytica*.

**Correct answer: C — Metronidazole**

- **A. Exploratory laparotomy** — a treatment option for pyogenic liver abscess, depending on severity or if initial therapies fail; not for amebic liver abscess.
- **B. Laparoscopic surgery** — a treatment option for pyogenic liver abscess, depending on severity or if initial therapies fail; not for amebic liver abscess.
- **C. Metronidazole** — 750 mg three times a day for 7–10 days is the treatment of choice for amebic liver abscess and is successful in 95% of cases (correct answer).
- **D. Percutaneous drainage** — a treatment option for pyogenic liver abscess, depending on severity or if initial therapies fail; not for amebic liver abscess.

*Schwartz's Principles of Surgery, 11th ed., p. 1369–1370.*

choices.text: Second and third part of the duodenum junction
Junction of the neck and body of the pancreas

questions.stem: Which of the following locations does not comprise Passaro Triangle?
questions.rationale:
Most gastrinomas are found within the Passaro triangle, which is formed by three points:

**Correct answer: D — Head of the pancreas**

- **A. Cystic duct and CBD junction** — one of the three points forming the Passaro triangle.
- **B. Second and third part of the duodenum junction** — one of the three points forming the Passaro triangle.
- **C. Junction of the neck and body of the pancreas** — one of the three points forming the Passaro triangle.
- **D. Head of the pancreas** — not part of the Passaro triangle (correct answer).

questions.stem: A 35-year-old presents with moderate to severe right upper quadrant (RUQ) pain radiating to the back. She has no fever or jaundice. Ultrasound shows gallstones with no gallbladder wall thickening. Liver function tests are normal. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Biliary colic**

- **A. Choledocholithiasis** — incorrect, as it would typically show elevated LFTs and often jaundice.
- **B. Acute cholecystitis** — usually presents with fever, RUQ tenderness, and gallbladder wall thickening.
- **C. Biliary colic** — caused by temporary obstruction of the cystic duct by gallstones. Pain is episodic, radiates to the back or shoulder, and occurs without signs of inflammation (i.e., no fever or wall thickening) (correct answer).
- **D. Cholangitis** — typically presents with Charcot's triad: fever, jaundice, and RUQ pain.

questions.stem: Which of the following antibiotics is most appropriate for the initial treatment of emphysematous cholecystitis?
questions.rationale:
Emphysematous cholecystitis is a severe, life-threatening infection of the gallbladder by gas-forming organisms such as *Clostridium*, *E. coli*, and *Klebsiella*.

**Correct answer: C — Piperacillin-tazobactam**

- **A. Clindamycin** — has good anaerobic coverage but lacks Gram-negative coverage.
- **B. Amikacin** — has good Gram-negative aerobic coverage but no anaerobic coverage.
- **C. Piperacillin-tazobactam** — broad spectrum, covering Gram-negatives, anaerobes, and some Gram-positives, making it the ideal empiric choice (correct answer).
- **D. Ampicillin-sulbactam** — may also be used but is less effective against resistant Gram-negatives.

*Schwartz's Principles of Surgery, p. 1405.*

questions.stem: What type of choledochal cyst is being described?
questions.rationale:
Choledochal cysts typically present with abdominal pain, jaundice, and a right upper quadrant mass. Involvement of the extrahepatic and intrahepatic ducts characterizes Type 4a choledochal cysts.

**Correct answer: C — Type 4a**

| Type | Feature |
|---|---|
| 1 | Fusiform diverticulum (most common type) |
| 2 | Saccular diverticulum |
| 3 | Choledochocele(s); multiple cysts |
| 4a | Extrahepatic and intrahepatic duct involvement |
| 4b | Extrahepatic duct involvement only |
| 5 | Intrahepatic duct involvement only (Caroli disease) |

- **A. Type 2** — saccular diverticulum; not the type described.
- **B. Type 3** — choledochocele(s)/multiple cysts; not the type described.
- **C. Type 4a** — extrahepatic and intrahepatic duct involvement, matching the case described (correct answer).
- **D. Type 4b** — extrahepatic duct involvement only; not the type described.

*Figure 32-27, Schwartz's Principles of Surgery, 11th ed., 2019.*

questions.stem: What is the management for this case?
questions.rationale:
For Type 4a choledochal cysts, management involves segmental liver resection, excision, and Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy.

**Correct answer: D — All of the above**

| Type | Management |
|---|---|
| Types 1 and 4b | Excision + Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy |
| Type 2 | Excision; defect in the CBD closed over a T-tube |
| Type 3 | Sphincterotomy |
| Type 4a | Segmental liver resection, excision, and Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy |
| Type 5 | Liver transplantation |

- **A. Segmental liver resection** — part of the management for Type 4a choledochal cysts.
- **B. Excision** — part of the management for Type 4a choledochal cysts.
- **C. Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy** — part of the management for Type 4a choledochal cysts.
- **D. All of the above** — all three procedures together comprise management of Type 4a choledochal cysts (correct answer).

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most common indication of splenectomy?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Trauma**

- **A. Trauma** — the most common indication for splenectomy overall (correct answer).
- **B. Hereditary spherocytosis** — the most common type of hemolytic anemia for which splenectomy is indicated, but not the most common indication overall.
- **C. Malignancy** — the most common primary tumors of the spleen are sarcomas, but malignancy is not the most common indication for splenectomy.
- **D. Infection** — the most common complication after splenectomy, not an indication for it.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old female was scheduled for elective splenectomy. The following vaccines were given EXCEPT?
questions.rationale:
The most feared infectious complication after splenectomy is Overwhelming Postsplenectomy Infection (OPSI). Vaccination should be given 2 weeks prior to surgery (for elective splenectomy) or 2 weeks after surgery (for emergent splenectomy).

**Correct answer: C — Tetanus toxoid**

- **A. Meningococcal vaccine** — given against *Neisseria meningitidis* as part of OPSI prophylaxis.
- **B. Haemophilus influenza (vaccine)** — given as part of OPSI prophylaxis.
- **C. Tetanus toxoid** — not among the vaccines given for OPSI prophylaxis (correct answer).
- **D. Pneumococcal vaccine** — given against *Streptococcus pneumoniae* as part of OPSI prophylaxis, along with the influenza vaccine.

choices.text:
Epigastric pain radiating to the back with nausea
and vomiting
Pain occurring 6-10 hours after a meal

questions.stem: Which of the following is not consistent with the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Pain occurring 6-10 hours after a meal**

- **A. Grey Turner sign** — flank ecchymosis, seen in acute pancreatitis from blood dissecting among tissue planes.
- **B. Epigastric pain radiating to the back with nausea and vomiting** — the classic presentation of acute pancreatitis.
- **C. Pain occurring 6-10 hours after a meal** — incorrect; the pain of acute pancreatitis usually begins 1-4 hours after a meal (correct answer).
- **D. Ecchymosis of the inguinal ligament** — also known as Fox sign, seen in acute pancreatitis from blood dissecting among tissue planes.

Other signs from blood dissecting among tissue planes include Cullen sign (periumbilical ecchymosis) and Bryan sign (bluish discoloration of the scrotum).

questions.stem: Which is not a manifestation of a Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide-Secreting Tumor?
questions.rationale:
A Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide-Secreting Tumor (VIPoma) is often associated with the WDHA syndrome, also known as the Verner-Morrison syndrome: watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria.

**Correct answer: D — Hypoglycemia**

- **A. Hypokalemia** — a feature of WDHA/Verner-Morrison syndrome, seen in VIPoma.
- **B. Watery diarrhea** — a feature of WDHA/Verner-Morrison syndrome, seen in VIPoma.
- **C. Achlorhydria** — a feature of WDHA/Verner-Morrison syndrome, seen in VIPoma.
- **D. Hypoglycemia** — not a manifestation of VIPoma; it is a typical manifestation of insulinoma, often characterized by the Whipple triad: (1) symptomatic fasting hypoglycemia, (2) serum glucose <50 mg/dL, and (3) relief of symptoms with glucose administration (correct answer).

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most common cause of chronic pancreatitis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Alcohol**

- **A. Alcohol** — the most common cause of chronic pancreatitis (correct answer).
- **B. Hyperlipidemia** — may also cause chronic pancreatitis, but is not the most common cause.
- **C. Trauma** — may also cause chronic pancreatitis; trauma and pancreatitis are also the most important cause of pancreatic pseudocyst.
- **D. Gallstones** — may also cause chronic pancreatitis, but is the most common cause of *acute* pancreatitis, not chronic.

questions.stem: A 28/F presents to the ED with a 1-day history of abdominal pain and fever. The pain started at the umbilicus with eventual migration to the RLQ. Patient denies nausea and loss of appetite. Abdominal examination showed direct RLQ tenderness with no rebound tenderness. Laboratory tests were done showing leukocytosis and immature neutrophilic predominance. What is the Alvarado score of the patient?
questions.rationale:
**Alvarado score components**

| Feature | Score |
|---|---|
| Migration of pain | 1 |
| Anorexia | 1 |
| Nausea | 1 |
| Tenderness in RLQ | 2 |
| Rebound pain | 1 |
| Elevated temperature | 1 |
| Leukocytosis | 2 |
| Shift of WBC count to left | 1 |
| **Total** | **10** |

**Correct answer: A — 7**

Applying the score to this patient: migration of pain (1) + RLQ tenderness (2) + elevated temperature (1) + leukocytosis (2) + shift of WBC count to left (1) = 7. The patient has no anorexia, no nausea, and no rebound tenderness, so those points are not added.

questions.stem: What is the likelihood of villous adenoma to progress to malignancy?
questions.rationale:
The risk of malignant degeneration of adenomatous polyps relates to both the size and type of the polyp.

**Correct answer: C — 40%**

- **A. 5%** — this is the malignancy rate cited for tubular adenomas.
- **B. 20%** — tubulovillous adenomas carry an intermediate risk, cited as approximately 22%.
- **C. 40%** — villous adenomas may harbor cancer in up to 40% of cases (correct answer).
- **D. 60%**

*Schwartz's Principles of Surgery, 11th ed., p. 1290.*

questions.stem: If villous adenoma turned out to be malignant, what will be used to check the local invasion in rectum and regional nodal metastasis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Pelvic CT scan**

- **A. Pelvic CT scan** — useful (along with MRI, at times) in large rectal tumors and in recurrent disease to determine the extent of local invasion and regional nodal metastasis (correct answer).
- **B. PET scan** — may be useful in evaluating lesions seen on CT and in patients for whom a risky or highly morbid operation is planned.
- **C. Gastrografin enema** — a water-soluble contrast study that may be useful for delineating the degree of obstruction.
- **D. Flexible proctoscopy** — for rectal cancers, DRE and rigid or flexible proctoscopy with biopsy should be performed to assess tumor size, location, morphology, histology, and fixation.

*Schwartz's Principles of Surgery, 11th ed., p. 1296.*

questions.stem: Which of the following agents is commonly used for bowel preparation prior to a colonoscopy?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Polyethylene glycol (PEG)**

- **A. Lactulose** — also a laxative, but not as frequently used for colonoscopy preparation; more commonly used to treat chronic constipation and hepatic encephalopathy.
- **B. Polyethylene glycol (PEG)** — a non-absorbable osmotic laxative commonly used for bowel cleansing before colonoscopy. It draws water into the colon, causing loose stools and clearing the bowel for examination (correct answer).
- **C. Docusate** — an emollient laxative that softens stool by lowering surface tension; not typically used as the primary agent for bowel preparation before a colonoscopy.
- **D. Mineral oil** — a lubricant laxative, but not commonly used for bowel prep before colonoscopy.

*Schwartz's Principles of Surgery, p. 1279.*

questions.stem: An isolated tumor located at the descending colon would require what extent of resection?
questions.rationale:
Tumors found in the descending colon require a left hemicolectomy.

**Correct answer: B — Left hemicolectomy**

| Tumor location | Standard resection |
|---|---|
| Cecum | Right hemicolectomy |
| Ascending colon | Right hemicolectomy |
| Hepatic flexure | Extended right hemicolectomy |
| Splenic flexure | Extended left hemicolectomy |
| Descending colon | Left hemicolectomy |
| Sigmoid colon | Rectosigmoid resection |

questions.stem: A 58-year-old male presents with a 6-month history of change in caliber associated with blood-streaked stools. DRE reveals a hard, irregular mass 8cm from the anal verge. What is the most important diagnostic procedure?
questions.rationale:
The case above is a suspected colorectal cancer, given the patient's age, change in stool caliber, blood in the stools, and a DRE showing a hard, irregular mass.

**Correct answer: A — Colonoscopy**

- **A. Colonoscopy** — the gold standard for evaluating suspected colorectal cancer, as it allows direct visualization of the colon and biopsy of the mass (correct answer).
- **B. Abdominal ultrasound** — can assess abdominal organs but is not useful for assessing intraluminal colonic lesions.
- **C. Flexible sigmoidoscopy** — can visualize the rectum and sigmoid colon, but cannot assess the entire colon and will likely miss proximal pathology.
- **D. Fecal occult blood test** — used as a screening test for colorectal cancer, not a diagnostic one. It can identify blood in the stool, suggesting cancer, but does not provide information on the location or size of the mass.

questions.stem: Which condition is characterized by acute colonic pseudo-obstruction without a mechanical cause?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Ogilvie's syndrome**

- **A. Meckel's diverticulum** — a congenital anomaly in which a small pouch forms in the ileum; a cause of mechanical obstruction, not pseudo-obstruction.
- **B. Ogilvie's syndrome** — colonic pseudo-obstruction: massive dilatation of the colon (predominantly the right and transverse colon) without mechanical obstruction. It commonly occurs in hospitalized patients and is associated with narcotic use, bed rest, and comorbidities (correct answer).
- **C. Hirschsprung disease** — a congenital disorder due to absence of ganglion cells, causing functional obstruction.
- **D. Gardner's syndrome** — a subtype of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) with extraintestinal tumors; it does not involve colonic pseudo-obstruction.

questions.stem: 35-year-old male presents with persistent perianal discharge. On workup, a perianal fistula that encompasses a portion of the internal and external sphincter was visualized. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient?
questions.rationale:
A transsphincteric fistula encompasses a portion of the internal and external sphincter.

**Correct answer: C — Ligation of Intersphincteric Fistula Tract**

- **A. Fistulotomy** — used for superficial fistulas.
- **B. Seton** — used for superficial fistulas.
- **C. Ligation of Intersphincteric Fistula Tract (LIFT)** — the management of choice for transsphincteric fistulas, which encompass a portion of the internal and external sphincter, as in this patient (correct answer).
- **D. Advancement flap** — generally used for recurrent, complex, or high fistulas.

| Type | Description |
|---|---|
| Type 1 (Intersphincteric) | Travels along the intersphincteric plane |
| Type 2 (Transsphincteric) | Encompasses a portion of the internal and external sphincter |
| Type 3 (Suprasphincteric) | Encompasses the entire sphincter apparatus |
| Type 4 (Extrasphincteric) | Extends from a primary opening in the rectum, encompasses the entire sphincter apparatus, and opens onto the skin overlying the buttock |

questions.stem: An 80-year-old woman presents with hematochezia. On assessment, you note a fleshy mass that protrudes through the anal canal, but not beyond the anal verge. Which of the following is NOT indicated in the patient?
questions.rationale:
The lesion described is consistent with Grade I internal hemorrhoids.

**Correct answer: D — Milligan-Morgan procedure**

- **Grade I** (protrudes through the anal canal but not beyond the anal verge) — medical management, infrared photocoagulation, sclerotherapy, and rubber band ligation (RBL) are all indicated.
- **Grade II** (protrusion with spontaneous reduction) — medical management, infrared photocoagulation, sclerotherapy, and RBL are all indicated.
- **Grade III** (protrusion requiring manual reduction) — medical management is indicated; infrared photocoagulation and sclerotherapy may be used in selected cases; surgery is also indicated.
- **Grade IV** (protrusion that cannot be reduced; at risk for strangulation) — surgery is indicated, whether closed (Parks-Ferguson procedure) or open (Milligan-Morgan procedure).

Per choice, for this Grade I patient:
- **A. Infrared photocoagulation** — indicated for Grade I and II internal hemorrhoids.
- **B. Sclerotherapy** — indicated for Grade I and II internal hemorrhoids.
- **C. Rubber band ligation** — indicated for Grade I and II internal hemorrhoids.
- **D. Milligan-Morgan procedure** — an open surgical technique reserved for Grade III and IV internal hemorrhoids; not indicated for this Grade I patient (correct answer).

*Surgery Platinum, 1st ed., 2018, p. 325.*

questions.stem: What is the Hinchey Stage of the patient?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Stage I**

The table below describes each Hinchey stage for rectosigmoid diverticulitis:

| Hinchey stage | Description |
|---|---|
| I | Diverticulitis with a pericolic abscess |
| II | Diverticulitis with distant abscess (retroperitoneal, pelvic) |
| III | Purulent peritonitis |
| IV | Fecal peritonitis |

choices.text: Resection with primary anastomosis and diversion

questions.stem: What is the management for this case?
questions.rationale:
Percutaneous drainage of the abscess is recommended for Stage I diverticulitis. Segmental ileocecal resection is the management of choice for right-sided diverticulitis, which does not apply here.

**Correct answer: B — Percutaneous drainage of the abscess**

| Hinchey stage | Management |
|---|---|
| I | Percutaneous drainage of abscess; resection with primary anastomosis without diverting stoma |
| II | Percutaneous drainage of abscess; resection with primary anastomosis ± diversion |
| III | Hartmann procedure; diverting colostomy plus percutaneous drainage (in unstable patients) |
| IV | Hartmann procedure; diverting colostomy plus percutaneous drainage (in highly unstable patients) |

- **A. Hartmann procedure** — management for Stage III/IV diverticulitis, not Stage I.
- **B. Percutaneous drainage of the abscess** — the management for Stage I diverticulitis (correct answer).
- **C. Resection with primary anastomosis and diversion** — management for Stage II diverticulitis, not Stage I.
- **D. Segmental ileocecal resection** — the management of choice for right-sided diverticulitis, not for this presentation.

questions.stem: What is the most common cause of injury related to endotracheal intubation?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Excessive endotracheal tube cuff pressure**

All options can contribute to airway injury; however, the most frequent cause is excessive cuff pressure, which may cause pressure necrosis of the tracheal mucosa, leading to injury and irritation.

*AK, A. K. (2023, July 4). Post-intubation laryngeal edema. StatPearls [Internet].*

choices.text: Medical management with blood pressure control

questions.stem: What is the most appropriate management for an uncomplicated DeBakey Type IIIa aortic dissection?
questions.rationale:
Aortic dissection is the most common catastrophic event involving the aorta. It results from disruption of the aortic wall into a true lumen and a false lumen, usually progressing distally; if it progresses proximally, this causes proximal extension or retrograde dissection.

**DeBakey classification**

| Type | Description |
|---|---|
| I | Originates in the ascending aorta and extends at least to the aortic arch, often into the descending aorta |
| II | Involves the ascending aorta alone (confined to this segment) |
| III | Begins in the descending aorta, usually just distal to the left subclavian artery |

**Stanford classification**

| Type | Description |
|---|---|
| A | Involves the ascending aorta (with or without extension into the descending aorta) |
| B | Does not involve the ascending aorta; includes dissections that involve the aortic arch but not the ascending aorta |

**Correct answer: D — Medical management with blood pressure control**

- Acute ascending aortic dissection is an absolute indication for surgical repair.
- **Type A dissections** — managed with emergency surgery.
- **Uncomplicated Type B dissection** — managed with initial medical therapy (blood pressure control).
- **Complicated Type B dissection** — managed with surgery or thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR).

- **A. Immediate surgical repair** — indicated for Type A or complicated Type B dissections, not for an uncomplicated Type IIIa (Type B) dissection.
- **B. Endovascular stent placement** — an option (TEVAR) for complicated Type B dissection, not for an uncomplicated one.
- **C. Emergent aortic root replacement** — reserved for Type A dissection involving the aortic root, not for a DeBakey IIIa (Type B) dissection.
- **D. Medical management with blood pressure control** — the appropriate initial therapy for uncomplicated Type B (DeBakey IIIa) dissection (correct answer).

questions.stem: Which of the following commonly metastasizes to the brain?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Lung CA**

The most common primary source of brain metastasis is lung cancer, followed by breast cancer, colorectal cancer, and then melanoma.

*Singh, M., Manoranjan, B., Mahendram, S., McFarlane, N., Venugopal, C., & Singh, S. (2014). Brain Metastasis-Initiating Cells: Survival of the Fittest. International Journal of Molecular Sciences, 15, 9117–9133.*

questions.stem: A 6-year-old patient was managed with a spica cast. Which of the following was most likely fractured in the patient?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Hip**

- **A. Medial epicondyle** — medial epicondyle fractures of the elbow are usually treated conservatively unless severely displaced.
- **B. Lateral epicondyle** — a displaced lateral condylar fracture needs anatomical surgical reduction.
- **C. Hip** — a spica cast, which includes the abdomen, lower back, pelvis, and lower limb, can be used in pediatric patients with hip fractures (correct answer).
- **D. Ankle** — pediatric ankle fractures have several types. Salter-Harris I and II fractures are usually managed with casting; Salter-Harris III or IV fractures are managed with closed or open reduction and internal fixation.

*Schwartz's Principles of Surgery, 11th ed., p. 1916.*

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child, diagnosed with Hirschsprung disease, underwent surgical treatment involving a side-to-side anastomosis between the normal proximal colon and the aganglionic distal rectum. Which of the following procedures was most likely performed?
questions.rationale:
Hirschsprung disease is a defect in the migration of neural crest cells, the embryonic precursors of the intestinal ganglion cells.

**Correct answer: A — Duhamel procedure**

- **A. Duhamel procedure** — side-to-side anastomosis; a residual pouch of aganglionic bowel is left intact, with the ganglionic bowel attached behind it (correct answer).
- **B. Swenson procedure** — resection of the aganglionic segment with end-to-end anastomosis.
- **C. Soave procedure** — the mucosa of the aganglionic segment is stripped, but the outer muscular cuff is left, and anastomosis is done.
- **D. Nissen fundoplication** — a surgical procedure for treating GERD by wrapping the fundus of the stomach around the esophagus.

choices.text:
Initial colostomy followed by posterior sagittal
anorectoplasty (PSARP)
Posterior sagittal approach with primary repair

questions.stem: What is the most appropriate surgical management for a case of imperforate anus with the rectal pouch located below the levator ani muscle?
questions.rationale:
Imperforate anus results from failure of the rectum to descend through the external sphincter complex.

| Type | Location |
|---|---|
| High imperforate anus | Above the levator ani muscle |
| Low imperforate anus | Below the levator ani muscle |

| Type | Treatment |
|---|---|
| High imperforate anus | Colostomy, then anoplasty — favored procedure is posterior sagittal anorectoplasty (PSARP) |
| Low imperforate anus | Perineal approach without colostomy |

**Correct answer: A — Perineal approach without colostomy**

- **A. Perineal approach without colostomy** — the appropriate management for low imperforate anus, in which the rectal pouch is below the levator ani muscle (correct answer).
- **B. Initial colostomy followed by posterior sagittal anorectoplasty (PSARP)** — the favored procedure for high imperforate anus, not low.
- **C. Abdominoperineal pull-through** — too invasive for a low-type imperforate anus.
- **D. Posterior sagittal approach with primary repair** — too invasive for a low-type imperforate anus.

questions.stem: What is the most common complication associated with microsurgical resection of a vestibular schwannoma?
questions.rationale:
Vestibular schwannoma predominantly arises from the superior half of the vestibular portion of the vestibulocochlear nerve. Treatment is microsurgical resection.

**Correct answer: C — Facial nerve injury**

- **A. Cerebrospinal fluid leak** — may occur but is less common than facial nerve injury.
- **B. Meningitis** — a rare complication, secondary to CSF leak or infection.
- **C. Facial nerve injury** — the main complication, due to the close anatomical relationship between the tumor and the facial nerve. These tumors arise from Schwann cells of the vestibular portion of the eighth cranial nerve and are located in the cerebellopontine angle, where the facial nerve is closely associated with the tumor (correct answer).
- **D. Hearing impairment** — not the best answer, since most patients already have hearing loss before surgery; it is often pre-existing and not considered a surgical complication.

questions.stem: Which of the following craniosynostosis results in the abnormal fusion of the sagittal suture, resulting in a boat-shaped head?
questions.rationale:
Craniosynostosis is abnormal early fusion of a cranial suture line, resulting in restriction of skull growth in the affected area and compensatory bulging.

**Correct answer: B — Scaphocephaly**

- **A. Brachycephaly** — bilateral coronal synostosis, resulting in a broad, flattened forehead; often associated with maxillary hypoplasia and proptosis.
- **B. Scaphocephaly** — abnormal fusion of the sagittal suture, resulting in a boat-shaped head (correct answer).
- **C. Plagiocephaly** — unilateral coronal synostosis, resulting in ipsilateral forehead flattening and outward deviation of the orbit.
- **D. Trigonocephaly** — results from fusion of the metopic suture (between the frontal bones of the skull), producing a triangular forehead.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the management for Jefferson fracture?
questions.rationale:
A Jefferson fracture is a bursting fracture of the ring of C1 (the atlas) due to compression forces.

**Correct answer: B — Halo vest**

Jefferson fractures with less than 7 mm of dislocation are usually treated with a rigid collar, while those with 7 mm or greater dislocation are usually treated with a halo vest.

- **A. Cervical collar** — used for Jefferson fractures with less than 7 mm of dislocation.
- **B. Halo vest** — used for Jefferson fractures with 7 mm or greater dislocation (correct answer).
- **C. Axial contraction with collar ring** — used in patients with blunt trauma requiring cervical spine immobilization, not specifically indicated for this fracture pattern.
- **D. Cervical collar with anesthetic** — used in patients with blunt trauma requiring cervical spine immobilization, not specifically indicated for this fracture pattern.

*Schwartz's Principles of Surgery, p. 1843.*

questions.stem: Which of the following structures are typically injured in the “unhappy triad” of the knee?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — ACL, medial meniscus, MCL**

The unhappy triad occurs due to a lateral blow to the knee and involves injury to the ACL, MCL, and medial meniscus.

questions.stem: According to the Manual Muscle Testing (MMT) grading scale, what grade corresponds to full movement against gravity but not against resistance?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Grade 3**

*Source: [Manual Muscle Testing – Orthofixar](https://orthofixar.com/special-test/manual-muscle-testing/)*

return to activity

questions.stem: A Clay-shoveler’s injury involves injury of the C6, C7, T1 and T2. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.rationale:
A Clay-shoveler's injury can result from a motor vehicle accident or from shoveling soil or clay. Injury of C6, C7, T1, and T2 involves an avulsion fracture of the spinous process caused by paraspinal muscle forces.

**Correct answer: A — Immobilization, pain management, and gradual return to activity**

- **A. Immobilization, pain management, and gradual return to activity** — the appropriate treatment, since this is a stable avulsion fracture of the spinous process, managed conservatively with immobilization, analgesics, and supportive care (correct answer).
- **B. Emergency spinal surgery with internal fixation** — rarely needed, unless there is delayed or non-union of the fracture.
- **C. High dose corticosteroids and traction** — corticosteroids are not needed, since the spinal cord is not involved; traction, commonly used for alignment correction, is unnecessary since this is a stable avulsion fracture.
- **D. Immediate physical therapy and weight bearing exercises** — incorrect, as this may worsen pain or delay healing if done in the acute phase.

questions.stem: Which of the following terms describes a skin graft harvested from one part of the body and used to cover another part of the same individual’s body?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Allograft**

| Type | Definition |
|---|---|
| Xenograft | Skin harvested from another species |
| Allograft | Skin harvested from another person of the same species |
| Autograft | Skin harvested from one part of the body and used to cover another part of the same person's body |
| Isograft | Skin transferred between genetically identical individuals (e.g., monozygotic twins) |

- **A. Allograft** — skin harvested from another person of the same species (correct answer per the answer key).
- **B. Xenograft** — skin harvested from another species.
- **C. Isograft** — skin transferred between genetically identical individuals (e.g., monozygotic twins).
- **D. Autograft** — skin harvested from one part of the body and used to cover another part of the same person's body. Note: this definition is the one described in the question stem, though the source answer key designates Choice A (Allograft) as correct.

*Surgery Platinum, p. 529.*

questions.stem: The Mulliken method is the management for which of the following?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Bilateral cleft lip**

The Mulliken method is a surgical technique primarily used for bilateral cleft lip and nasal deformities. It is based on Mulliken's principle of constructing a philtral flap from the prolabium and forming the rest of the structure with lateral lip flaps. This technique has been widely accepted by surgeons, and most bilateral cleft lip surgeries performed today follow the Mulliken method, with some modifications.

choices.text: Mid-ureter at the level of the pelvic brim

questions.stem: What is the most common site of iatrogenic ureteral injury?
questions.rationale:
During hysterectomy, the ureter can be injured during ligation of the ovarian and uterine vessels, or during vaginal cuff closure.

**Correct answer: B — Distal third of the ureter**

- **A. Proximal third of the ureter** — injuries here are less common and typically associated with renal or upper abdominal surgeries.
- **B. Distal third of the ureter** — the most common site of iatrogenic ureteral injury (correct answer).
- **C. Mid-ureter at the level of the pelvic brim** — not the most commonly injured site.
- **D. Ureteropelvic junction** — rarely injured during surgery; injuries here are commonly associated with congenital anomalies or surgical procedures involving the kidney.

choices.text: At least 15 million spermatozoa per ml

questions.stem: The following statements are true of a normal semen analysis EXCEPT
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — At least 10% normal morphology**

Reference values for a normal semen analysis:

| Parameter | Reference value |
|---|---|
| Semen volume (mL) | ≥1.5 |
| Sperm concentration (million/mL) | ≥15 |
| Total sperm number (million/ejaculate) | ≥39 |
| Total motility (%) | ≥40 |
| Progressive motility (%) | ≥32 |
| Normal forms (%) | ≥4 |

- **A. Volume of at least 1.5 ml** — a true reference value for a normal semen analysis.
- **B. At least 15 million spermatozoa per ml** — a true reference value for a normal semen analysis.
- **C. At least 40% total motility** — a true reference value for a normal semen analysis.
- **D. At least 10% normal morphology** — incorrect; the reference value is at least 4% normal morphology, not 10% (correct answer).

questions.stem: Which ophthalmologic surgery involves removal of the entire globe and extraocular muscles are reattached to the donor sclera or implant?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Enucleation**

- **A. Evisceration** — the cornea and internal contents of the globe are removed, leaving only the scleral shell; the extraocular muscles remain attached to the sclera.
- **B. Enucleation** — the entire globe is removed, and the extraocular muscles are resewn to the donor sclera or a spherical implant/artificial eyeball (correct answer).
- **C. Exenteration** — the globe and orbital contents are removed down to the periosteum of the orbit, including the eyelids, fat, muscles, nerves, lacrimal gland, and surrounding skin.
- **D. Enodectomy** — not an ophthalmologic procedure.

questions.stem: Which type of cataract surgery uses an ultrasonic energy to emulsify and destroy the crystalline lens, which is then aspirated out of the eye?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Phacoemulsification**

- **A. Phacoemulsification** — uses ultrasonic energy to emulsify and destroy the lens, which is then aspirated through a small incision (correct answer).
- **B. Extracapsular cataract extraction** — extraction of the crystalline lens as a whole through an approximately 8 mm incision at the superior limbus or sclerolimbal border, expressing the lens material out while leaving the capsular bag intact.
- **C. Intracapsular cataract extraction** — the entire lens and capsule are removed through a large incision.
- **D. Laser assisted cataract surgery** — generally similar to phacoemulsification, but some steps are assisted by a femtosecond laser, such as creating the capsular opening and pre-cutting/chopping the lens nucleus.

questions.stem: A patient came into your clinic with eye irritation and dryness. On examination, you notice a fleshy mass on the nasal side of his left eye, gradually encroaching the cornea. Which of the following is the likely contributing factor to his condition?
questions.rationale:
The lesion described is a pterygium, typically characterized as a fibrovascular overgrowth of subconjunctival tissue. It often appears triangular in shape and extends onto the cornea.

**Correct answer: A — Ultraviolet (UV) light exposure**

- **A. Ultraviolet (UV) light exposure** — contributes to pterygium development by damaging limbal stem cells, which activates tissue growth factors, promoting angiogenesis and cell proliferation. As a result, the cornea undergoes conjunctivalization, and aggressive fibroblasts invade the corneal surface (correct answer).
- **B. Chronic contact lens use** — may lead to eye irritation and dryness, but does not directly cause pterygium or produce a fleshy mass.
- **C. Genetic predisposition** — although there may be a minor genetic component, it is not a primary cause of pterygium given its pathophysiology.
- **D. Inflammatory response** — the pathophysiology for *recurrent* pterygium, especially post-operatively; surgical trauma can amplify the inflammatory cascade, causing recurrence.

*Sakar, P. and Tripathy, K. (2023). Pterygium. StatPearls [Internet].*

questions.stem: A patient complains of new-onset double vision 3 months after pterygium surgery. What is the most likely cause?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Symblepharon**

- **A. Recurrence of pterygium** — incorrect, as recurrence typically causes redness or irritation, not diplopia.
- **B. Lateral rectus palsy** — rectus muscle palsies are rarely affected by pterygium removal.
- **C. Medial rectus palsy** — rectus muscle palsies are rarely affected by pterygium removal.
- **D. Symblepharon** — adhesion between the palpebral and bulbar conjunctiva, a known complication of pterygium surgery. It may restrict ocular motility, leading to diplopia (correct answer).

*Roy, F. H., Fraunfelder, F. W., & Fraunfelder, F. T. (2008). Roy and Fraunfelder's Current Ocular Therapy. Elsevier Saunders, p. 348–351.*

questions.stem: Which of the following does NOT typically affect the difficulty of intubation during anesthesia?
questions.rationale:
A protruding mandible usually indicates a longer thyromental distance, which typically indicates an easier intubation for the anesthesiologist.

**Correct answer: C — Protruding mandible**

- **A. Short muscular neck** — limits neck extension, making intubation more difficult.
- **B. Prominent upper incisors** — obstructs the view during intubation, making it more difficult.
- **C. Protruding mandible** — associated with a longer thyromental distance, which is generally associated with *easier*, not more difficult, intubation (correct answer).
- **D. Upper and lower dentures** — can obstruct the view during intubation if not removed beforehand, making it more difficult.

*Source: [Predicting Difficult Intubation](https://sleepworldmagazine.com/2022/07/01/predicting-difficult-intubation-what-the-rts-need-to-know/)*

questions.stem: An oligoclonal band can be seen in what condition?
questions.rationale:
CSF oligoclonal gamma globulin bands occur in association with a number of viral infections, with the associated antibodies often directed against viral proteins. Oligoclonal bands also occur commonly in certain noninfectious neurologic diseases, such as multiple sclerosis.

**Correct answer: C — Multiple sclerosis**

questions.stem: Which describes a swelling on the upper part of the lateral neck which contains opaque fluid and cholesterol crystals?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Branchial cyst**

- **A. Cystic hygroma** — Found on the lateral neck, but usually located on the posterior triangle of the neck and contains lymph, blood, or even pus.
- **B. Dermoid cyst** — Usually appears in the head and neck region and usually contains hair and sebaceous tissue.
- **C. Thyroglossal cyst** — Eliminated because it is located in the midline of the neck.
- **D. Branchial cyst** — Typically located in the anterior triangle of the neck and contains turbid, yellow-green liquid with cholesterol crystals.

questions.stem: In the ASA grading scheme, what is the grade that describes a patient with severe systemic disease without incapacitation but with limit of activity?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — III**

ASA III describes a patient with severe systemic disease without incapacitation but with limit of activity. All the other choices are wrong.

| ASA Classification | Definition | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| ASA I | A normal healthy patient | Healthy, non-smoking, no or minimal alcohol use |
| ASA II | A patient with mild systemic disease | Mild diseases only without substantive functional limitations. Current smoker, social alcohol drinker, pregnancy, obesity (30<BMI<40), well-controlled DM/HTN, mild lung disease |
| ASA III | A patient with severe systemic disease | Substantive functional limitations; one or more moderate to severe diseases. Poorly controlled DM or HTN, COPD, morbid obesity (BMI >40), active hepatitis, alcohol dependence or abuse, implanted pacemaker, moderate reduction of ejection fraction, ESRD undergoing regularly scheduled dialysis, history (>3 months) of MI, CVA, TIA, or CAD/stents |
| ASA IV | A patient with severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life | Recent (<3 months) MI, CVA, TIA or CAD/stents, ongoing cardiac ischemia or severe valve dysfunction, severe reduction of ejection fraction, shock, sepsis, DIC, ARD, or ESRD not undergoing regularly scheduled dialysis |
| ASA V | A moribund patient who is not expected to survive without the operation | Ruptured abdominal/thoracic aneurysm, massive trauma, intracranial bleed with mass effect, ischemic bowel in the face of significant cardiac pathology or multiple organ/system dysfunction |
| ASA VI | A declared brain-dead patient whose organs are being removed for donor purposes | — |

*Reference: [ASA Physical Status Classification System](https://www.asahq.org/standards-and-practice-parameters/statement-on-asa-physical-status-classification-system)*

choices.text: Just when the baby starts to talk

questions.stem: What is the desired age for cleft lip surgery?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — 3-6 months**

The desired timing for repairing a cleft lip is 3 to 6 months. It is worth noting that the desired timing for repairing a cleft palate is 6 to 12 months.

questions.stem: 60/F G6P6 who persistently wets her underwear when she coughs. What type of continence does she have?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Stress**

- **A. Psychological**
- **B. True** — Also known as total incontinence; characterized by the person having no control over their urinary flow, causing the person to constantly leak urine.
- **C. Paradoxical** — Also known as overflow incontinence or ischuria paradoxa; happens when urine leaks from a bladder that is full but cannot urinate. It is due to a blockade in the bladder or urethra, and the urine leaks out due to pressure buildup.
- **D. Stress** — Occurs when urine leaks during physical activity or exertion such as coughing (correct answer).

questions.stem: In herniorrhaphy, the surgeon will NOT use prosthetic mesh in what kind of hernia?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Strangulated**

In a strangulated hernia, the blood supply to the herniated tissue is compromised, and there is an increased risk of infection. Hence, a primary tissue repair without a prosthetic mesh is recommended to avoid the risk of mesh infection. While there are some studies that show that mesh repair may be done with strangulated hernias, it is not yet formally recommended (Tomauglu and Okmen, 2021), making Choice A the best option.

questions.stem: A patient came in the ER due to flank pain associated with sandy urine with hematuria at the end of stream. What is the BEST imaging to support your diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Helical CT**

The patient came in due to flank pain and hematuria with sandy urine, which points to a primary working impression of kidney or ureteral stones. Based on the choices, both KUB Ultrasound (Choice A) and Helical CT (Choice B) are imaging used to diagnose kidney or ureteral stones. However, since the patient passes sandy urine, suggesting the presence of small stones or particles, Helical CT (also known as CT Stonogram) is the gold standard imaging for diagnosing renal and ureteral stones because it has a high sensitivity for detecting stones, even small stones that are often missed by ultrasound or X-ray.

questions.stem: What is the mainstay treatment for Type I Choledochal cyst?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Total Excision**

Type 1 choledochal cyst is managed through excision + Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy. Based on the choices, D is the best answer.

**Choledochal cyst types**

| Type | Feature |
|---|---|
| Type 1 | Fusiform diverticulum (most common type) |
| Type 2 | Saccular diverticulum |
| Type 3 | Choledochoceles, multiple cysts |
| Type 4a | Extrahepatic and intrahepatic duct involvement |
| Type 4b | Extrahepatic duct involvement only |
| Type 5 | Intrahepatic duct involvement only (Caroli disease) |

*Figure 32-27, Schwartz's Principles of Surgery, 11th ed. 2019*

**Management by type**

| Type | Management |
|---|---|
| Types 1 and 4B | Excision + Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy |
| Type 2 | Excision; defect in the CBD is closed over a T-tube |
| Type 3 | Sphincterotomy |
| Type 4A | Segmental liver resection, excision & Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy |
| Type 5 | Liver transplantation |

*Surgery Platinum, 1st ed. 2018, p. 377*

questions.stem: Which diagnostic test is least helpful in the diagnosis of acute appendicitis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Plain Abdominal X-ray**

Acute appendicitis is diagnosed clinically and may use diagnostic tests and imaging to support the diagnosis.

- **A. CT scan of the abdomen** — Highly effective since it provides detailed images of the appendix and surrounding structures.
- **B. Plain Abdominal X-ray** — The least helpful in the diagnosis of acute appendicitis since it does not directly visualize the appendix.
- **C. Urinalysis** — Can be used to rule out UTI. Bacteriuria is generally not seen in acute appendicitis.
- **D. CBC** — Helpful in diagnosing acute appendicitis, as it typically shows leukocytosis.

questions.stem: Which is not associated with K+ levels below 3.5?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Addison’s disease**

Of all the choices, Addison’s disease (Choice B) is the only condition that presents with hyperkalemia. Due to low aldosterone levels, the body excretes sodium and retains potassium.

Gitelman syndrome, Bartter syndrome, and Cushing syndrome all present with hypokalemia.

**Bartter syndrome vs. Gitelman syndrome**

| | Bartter syndrome | Gitelman syndrome |
|---|---|---|
| Defect | Reabsorption defect in the thick ascending loop of Henle (Na-K-2Cl cotransporter) | Reabsorption defect in the distal convoluted tubule (Na-Cl cotransporter) |
| Diuretics mimicking the condition | Chronic loop diuretic use | Chronic thiazide diuretic use |
| Abnormalities | Metabolic alkalosis, hypokalemia, normal serum magnesium, hypercalciuria – increased risk for nephrolith formation | Metabolic alkalosis, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypocalciuria – no increased risk for nephrolith formation |
| Pattern of inheritance | Autosomal recessive | Autosomal recessive |

questions.stem: A 35-year-old male presents to the emergency department after a house fire. He sustained second-degree burns to his entire front torso (including chest and abdomen), both of his legs (anterior and posterior) and his right arm. He also sustained first degree burns on his face. Using the Rule of 9s, what is the total body surface area (TBSA) burned for this patient?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — 63%**

- Entire front torso + both legs + right arm = TBSA
- 18 + 36 + 9 = 63% TBSA
- Thus, Choice A is the answer.
- First-degree burns are not included in the calculation of the Rule of Nines.

**Rule of Nines (Rule of Wallace) — adult %BSA**

| Area | %BSA (adults) |
|---|---|
| Head | 9% |
| Chest | 9% |
| Abdomen | 9% |
| Upper back | 9% |
| Lower back or buttocks | 9% |
| Right arm | 9% |
| Left arm | 9% |
| Right thigh and leg | 18% |
| Left thigh and leg | 18% |
| Genitalia or perineum | 1% |

*Surgery Platinum, 1st ed. 2018, p. 161*

questions.stem: In patients suffering from burns, initial fluid resuscitation is important in improving outcomes. Why is Lactated Ringer’s preferred over plain NSS in initial fluid resuscitation for burn patients?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Lactated Ringer’s contains lactate, which helps in buffering metabolic acidosis.**

Lactated Ringer’s is preferred over plain NSS in burn patients because it is similar to the body’s fluids and contains lactate, which can help with metabolic acidosis. Hence, Choice C is the answer.

- **A. Plain NSS is more likely to cause hyperkalemia in burn patients.** — Incorrect, since plain NSS is not associated with hyperkalemia.
- **B. Lactated Ringer’s contains a higher concentration of sodium than plain NSS.** — A false statement, since Lactated Ringer’s contains less sodium than plain NSS.
- **C. Lactated Ringer’s contains lactate, which helps in buffering metabolic acidosis.** — Correct.
- **D. Lactated Ringer’s contains a lower concentration of sodium than plain NSS** — While this is a true statement, this is not the reason why Lactated Ringer’s is preferred over plain NSS for initial fluid resuscitation in burn patients.

**Composition of common IV fluids**

| Solution | Na⁺ | Cl⁻ | K⁺ | Ca²⁺ | Other | mOsm |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ECF | 142 | 103 | 4 | 5 | – | 280 |
| Lactated Ringer’s (LR) | 130 | 109 | 4 | 3 | Lactate | 280 |
| 0.9% PNSS | 154 | 154 | 0 | 0 | – | 308 |
| D5LR | 130 | 109 | 4 | 3 | Dextrose 50 g/L, Lactate 28 mEq/L | 560 |
| D5NS | 154 | 154 | 0 | 0 | Dextrose 50 g/L | 588 |
| D5 0.45% NaCl | 77 | 77 | 0 | 0 | Dextrose 50 g/L | 434 |
| D5 0.25% NaCl | 34 | 34 | 0 | 0 | Dextrose 50 g/L | 3577 |

questions.stem: For average risk individuals, screening for colorectal cancer should be done at what age?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — 50**

Beginning at age 50, men and women who are at average risk for developing colorectal cancer should be screened for colorectal cancer. They should have one of the five screening options below:

| Screening option | Interval |
|---|---|
| FOBT or fecal immunochemical test (FIT) | Every year |
| Flexible sigmoidoscopy | Every 5 years |
| FOBT or FIT + flexible sigmoidoscopy | Every year + every 5 years |
| Double-contrast barium enema | Every 5 years |
| Colonoscopy | Every 10 years |

questions.stem: Which disease is the triad of iron deficiency anemia, dysphagia, and esophageal webs commonly found?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Plummer-Vinson syndrome**

- **A. Plummer-Vinson syndrome** — (Kelly-Patteson syndrome) A rare disease of middle-aged women characterized by the classic triad of dysphagia, iron-deficiency anemia, and esophageal web. This is the correct answer.
- **B. Barrett Esophagus** — Defined as columnar-lined epithelium of the esophagus rather than squamous epithelium. This is usually asymptomatic; however, symptomatic patients experience symptoms related to GERD, such as heartburn, indigestion, and sour-tasting fluid backing up into the mouth.
- **C. Eosinophilic esophagitis** — An allergic condition that may cause dysphagia, but it is not associated with iron deficiency anemia or esophageal webs.
- **D. Esophageal cancer** — May cause dysphagia, but it is not typically associated with iron deficiency anemia or esophageal webs as a triad.

questions.stem: On patients with acute pancreatitis, what physical examination finding is described as bluish discoloration on the flanks?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Turner sign**

Grey Turner sign describes bluish discoloration on the flanks.

| Sign | Description |
|---|---|
| Grey Turner sign | Blood extends to the flank tissues → flank ecchymosis |
| Cullen sign | Blood dissects to the falciform ligament → periumbilical ecchymosis |
| Fox sign | Ecchymosis of the inguinal ligament |
| Bryan sign | Bluish discoloration of the scrotum |

questions.stem: What is the BEST imaging modality to determine perforation in hollow visceral organs?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — CT scan**

While upright abdominal X-ray (Choice D) and ultrasound (Choice C) are fast and easy screening tools for bowel perforation, CT scan (Choice B) is the primary imaging modality for the detection and localization of bowel perforation. Barium enema (Choice A) is contraindicated in bowel perforation since it could cause acute peritonitis.

questions.stem: What is the most common choledochal cyst type?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Fusiform diverticulum**

Type 1 choledochal cysts, characterized by a fusiform diverticulum, are the most common type.

**Choledochal cyst types**

| Type | Feature |
|---|---|
| Type 1 | Fusiform diverticulum (most common type) |
| Type 2 | Saccular diverticulum |
| Type 3 | Choledochoceles, multiple cysts |
| Type 4a | Extrahepatic and intrahepatic duct involvement |
| Type 4b | Extrahepatic duct involvement only |
| Type 5 | Intrahepatic duct involvement only (Caroli disease) |

*Figure 32-27, Schwartz's Principles of Surgery, 11th ed. 2019*

questions.stem: A 55-year-old female came into the ER with severe acute abdominal pain. History revealed that she has a history of thrombosis. On PE, her abdomen is soft with no distension and tenderness. Based on these clinical findings, what is your initial assessment?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Acute mesenteric ischemia**

The clinical findings of acute abdominal pain, history of thrombosis, and unremarkable PE point to a diagnosis of acute mesenteric ischemia (Choice D). While all the other choices also present with abdominal pain, the history of thrombosis and unremarkable PE make the other choices less likely.

choices.text: Multiple primary tumors of unknown origin

questions.stem: A 60-year-old male presents with a history of left-sided colon cancer, diagnosed 3 years ago, and is now found to have a right-sided renal mass on a routine follow-up imaging. There is no history of any other malignancy. Upon further investigation, the renal mass is confirmed to be renal cell carcinoma (RCC). What is the most likely relationship of these two tumors in this patient?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Metachronous tumors**

- **A. Synchronous tumors** — Two or more malignancies that occur within 6 months of each other.
- **B. Metachronous tumors** — Two or more malignancies that occur more than 6 months apart.
- **C. Triennial tumors** — Not a term used in oncology.
- **D. Multiple primary tumors of unknown origin** — Describes a scenario of multiple malignancies; however, it does not answer the question about the relationship between the two tumors.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old female with hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and morbid obesity is hospitalized after undergoing abdominal surgery. The wound has full-thickness skin loss, exposing the subcutaneous tissue. There is no visible muscle, tendon, or bone. The surrounding skin is red and inflamed, with some serosanguineous drainage. Based on the clinical findings, what is the most appropriate classification for this pressure injury?
questions.rationale:

questions.stem: A 2-day-old neonate is admitted to the NICU with a noticeable abdominal defect. Upon examination, the intestines are seen protruding outside the abdominal wall, to the right of the umbilicus, with no covering membrane or sac. The neonate has been otherwise healthy, and there is no history of other congenital abnormalities. The umbilical cord appears normal with no evidence of additional anomalies. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Gastroschisis**

- **A. Umbilical hernia** — Incorrect because it is typically covered by skin and is not usually seen as a defect with exposed intestines, as in gastroschisis.
- **B. Patent urachus** — Incorrect because it is a communication between the bladder and the umbilicus. The first sign of patent urachus is urine flow from the umbilicus.
- **C. Omphalocele** — Like gastroschisis, this is a protrusion of the abdominal organs; however, unlike gastroschisis, these are contained within a membrane or sac.
- **D. Gastroschisis** — Correct. It is a defect in the anterior abdominal wall through which the intestinal contents freely protrude, with no overlying sac. It is located at the junction of the umbilicus and normal skin and is almost always to the right of the umbilicus.

questions.stem: Using the Haggitt classification of colonic polyps, what level of invasion is described as cancer invading the neck of a pedunculated polyp?
questions.rationale:

| Level of invasion | Description | Risk of lymph node metastasis |
|---|---|---|
| Level 0 | Non-invasive (severe dysplasia, carcinoma-in-situ, or intramucosal carcinoma) | 0% |
| Level 1 | Cancer invading through the muscularis mucosa (limited to the head of the polyp) | <1% |
| Level 2 | Cancer invading the neck of a pedunculated polyp | <1% |
| Level 3 | Cancer invading the stalk of a pedunculated polyp | <1% |
| Level 4 | Cancer invading into the submucosa of the bowel wall below the stalk of a pedunculated polyp. All sessile polyps with invasive cancer are Level 4 | 12–25% |

*Surgery Platinum, 1st ed. 2018, p. 329*

questions.stem: This breast biopsy technique is the diagnostic technique of choice for patients who will receive preoperative systemic therapy:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Core needle biopsy**

- **A. Fine needle aspiration biopsy** — While often used for rapid diagnosis, it may not provide sufficient tissue for subtyping or receptor testing, making it less ideal for patients who will undergo preoperative therapy.
- **B. Core needle biopsy** — Considered the diagnostic technique of choice for patients who will receive preoperative systemic therapy (such as neoadjuvant chemotherapy) because it provides adequate tissue sampling to assess both the histological type and grade of the tumor, as well as to evaluate receptor status.
- **C. Stereotactic biopsy** — Used to help guide a biopsy in non-palpable breast lesions. Like fine needle aspiration, it provides a small tissue sample.
- **D. Wire or needle-directed excisional biopsy** — Generally used for diagnostic purposes in small, non-palpable lesions. It provides a larger sample than FNA, but it is more invasive.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with rapidly worsening breast erythema, swelling, and pain in her right breast over the past two weeks. She reports a sensation of warmth and has noticed that her breast has become heavier. On physical examination, the breast is reddened, with pitting edema (peau d'orange), and there is a firm mass in the lower quadrant. Presence of axillary lymphadenopathy is noted, and there is significant induration of the skin. The patient is afebrile and denies any trauma or recent breastfeeding. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Inflammatory breast carcinoma**

- **A. Mastitis** — A differential based on the presentation of tenderness and redness. It typically presents with fever and lacks the peau d’orange presentation.
- **B. Breast abscess** — Much like mastitis, this also presents with redness, swelling, and pain, but it typically involves a localized collection of pus. It also lacks the peau d’orange presentation.
- **C. Inflammatory breast carcinoma** — A highly aggressive form of breast cancer that often presents with rapidly worsening breast erythema, swelling, and pain, as seen in this patient. The presence of peau d’orange also points to this diagnosis.
- **D. Phyllodes tumor** — Can be a benign, borderline, or malignant tumor. It usually presents as a palpable, mobile mass, and it does not cause skin changes.

questions.stem: The following viruses are commonly found in surgical patients, EXCEPT:
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Coxsackie virus**

Among the choices, Coxsackie virus (Choice C) is the least common among surgical patients. Common viruses in surgical patients include Cytomegalovirus (Choice A), Epstein-Barr virus (Choice B), Hepatitis A, B, and C, Herpes simplex virus, Human immunodeficiency virus, and Varicella zoster virus (Choice D).

**Common pathogens in surgical patients**

- Gram-positive aerobic cocci
  - Staphylococcus aureus
  - Staphylococcus epidermidis
  - Streptococcus pyogenes
  - Streptococcus pneumoniae
  - Enterococcus faecium, E faecalis
- Gram-negative aerobic bacilli
  - Escherichia coli
  - Haemophilus influenzae
  - Klebsiella pneumoniae
  - Proteus mirabilis
  - Enterobacter cloacae, E aerogenes
  - Serratia marcescens
  - Acinetobacter calcoaceticus
  - Citrobacter freundii
  - Pseudomonas aeruginosa
  - Stenotrophomonas maltophilia
- Anaerobes
  - Gram-positive: Clostridium difficile; Clostridium perfringens, C tetani, C septicum; Peptostreptococcus spp.
  - Gram-negative: Bacteroides fragilis; Fusobacterium spp.
  - Other bacteria: Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare; Mycobacterium tuberculosis; Nocardia asteroids; Legionella pneumophila; Listeria monocytogenes
- Fungi
  - Aspergillus fumigatus, A niger, A terreus, A flavus
  - Blastomyces dermatitidis
  - Candida albicans
  - Candida glabrata, C paropsilosis, C krusei
  - Coccidioides immitis
  - Cryptococcus neoformans
  - Histoplasma capsulatum
  - Mucor/Rhizopus
- Viruses
  - Cytomegalovirus
  - Epstein-Barr virus
  - Hepatitis A, B, C viruses
  - Herpes simplex virus
  - Human immunodeficiency virus
  - Varicella zoster virus

*Reference: Brunicardi, F., Andersen, D., Billiar, T., Dunn, D., Hunter, G., Kao, L., Matthews, J., Pollock, R. (2019). Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery (11th ed., p. 163, Table 6-3). McGraw-Hill Education.*

questions.stem: Which is NOT a common source of extracellular volume deficit in surgical patients?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: D — Renal insufficiency**

- **A. Nasogastric suctioning** — Incorrect, since the most common cause of volume deficit in surgical patients is loss of GI fluids from nasogastric suctioning, vomiting, diarrhea, or enterocutaneous fistula.
- **B. Sequestration due to burns** — Incorrect, since this is known to cause third-space or non-functional ECF losses.
- **C. Prolonged surgeries** — Incorrect, since this is also known to cause third-space or non-functional ECF losses.
- **D. Renal insufficiency** — Correct, since renal insufficiency more commonly causes fluid retention, which leads to volume overload rather than volume deficit.

**Extracellular volume deficit vs. excess**

**Extracellular volume deficit** — most common fluid disorder in surgical patients.

- Acute volume deficit is associated with cardiovascular and central nervous system signs.
- Chronic volume deficit displays tissue signs such as decreased skin turgor and sunken eyes, in addition to acute signs.
- Most common cause of volume deficit in surgical patients is loss of GI fluids from nasogastric suction, vomiting, diarrhea, or enterocutaneous fistula.
- Third-space or nonfunctional ECF losses that occur with sequestration secondary to soft tissue injuries/infections, burns, and intraabdominal processes such as peritonitis, obstruction, or prolonged surgery can also lead to massive volume deficits.

**Extracellular volume excess**

- May be iatrogenic or secondary to renal dysfunction, congestive heart failure, or cirrhosis.
- Both plasma and interstitial volumes are increased.
- Symptoms are primarily pulmonary and cardiovascular.
- In healthy patients, edema and hyperdynamic circulation are common and well tolerated. However, the elderly and patients with cardiac disease may quickly develop congestive heart failure and pulmonary edema.

questions.stem: A 6/M came in your clinic with a 6 month history of a left inguinal mass. The patient denied any abdominal pain or changes in bowel movement. On physical exam, the mass was noted to be manually reducible. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Indirect inguinal hernia**

- **A. Femoral inguinal hernia** — Incorrect, since the mass is not situated in the femoral ring and does not protrude along the femoral sheath into the femoral canal.
- **B. Indirect inguinal hernia** — Given the age of the patient (6/M) presenting with a reducible left inguinal mass, the most likely diagnosis is an indirect inguinal hernia, which is usually congenital in nature, following a patent processus vaginalis.
- **C. Direct inguinal hernia** — Would also present as an inguinal mass; however, it usually occurs in adulthood due to weakness in musculature.
- **D. Strangulated inguinal hernia** — Incorrect, since the mass would be nonreducible (incarcerated) with associated vascular disorders or pain.

questions.stem: Which inhaled anesthetic agent should be avoided in patients with liver disease due to increased risk for hepatotoxicity?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Halothane**

Volatile inhaled anesthetic agents are more soluble in blood than nitrous oxide, are more potent, and require lower inspired concentrations.

- **A. Sevoflurane** — Has a relatively rapid uptake and elimination and is commonly used for inhalational induction.
- **B. Isoflurane** — The most inexpensive and widely available among the choices.
- **C. Halothane** — An older volatile agent that is no longer widely used, since it has been associated with hepatotoxicity.
- **D. Desflurane** — Has the most rapid uptake and elimination among the volatile agents, but is also the most expensive, requires a heated-electric vaporizer, and is an airway irritant.

*Reference: Brunicardi, F., Andersen, D., Billiar, T., Dunn, D., Hunter, G., Kao, L., Matthews, J., Pollock, R. (2019). Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery (11th ed., p. 2030). McGraw-Hill Education.*

questions.stem: A 62-year-old male presents with a colonic mass that invades the subserosa. No noted nodal involvement nor metastasis to other distant organs. What is the tumor staging for the patient?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: B — Stage II**

Based on the case given, the TNM staging of the patient is T3N0M0, which falls under Stage II.

**Colorectal carcinoma staging**

| Category | Definition |
|---|---|
| T1 | Invades submucosa |
| T2 | Invades muscularis propria |
| T3 | Invades subserosa or nonperitonealized pericolic/perirectal tissues |
| T4 | Invades other organs or structures |
| N1 | 1 to 3 nodes |
| N2 | 4 or more nodes |
| N3 | Any node along a major named vascular trunk |
| M0 | No metastasis |
| M1 | Distant metastasis |

| Stage | TNM |
|---|---|
| I | T1–2, N0, M0 |
| II | T3–4, N0, M0 |
| III | T(any), N+, M0 |
| IV | T(any), N(any), M1 |

questions.stem: A 66-year-old female presents to your clinic with a solitary firm mass on the right breast. Core needle biopsy was done showing low grade dysplastic epithelial cells without invasion of the basement membrane. What is the best management for the patient?
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: A — Lumpectomy**

CNB findings of low-grade dysplastic epithelial cells without invasion of the basement membrane are indicative of ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS).

- **A. Lumpectomy** — Correct, since this is the recommended management for low-grade DCIS.
- **B. Lumpectomy + radiotherapy** — Incorrect, since this is the recommended management for intermediate-grade DCIS.
- **C. Modified radical mastectomy** — Incorrect, since mastectomy is only recommended for high-grade DCIS.
- **D. Halsted mastectomy** — Incorrect, since mastectomy is only recommended for high-grade DCIS.

**Specific management plans for breast cancer**

**LCIS**
- Observation
- Chemoprevention (tamoxifen)
- Prophylactic bilateral total mastectomy (TM)

**DCIS**
- Low grade: Lumpectomy alone
- Intermediate grade: Lumpectomy + radiotherapy
- High grade: Mastectomy

**Early invasive breast cancer (Stage I, IIA, IIB)**
- BCS + SLNB ± adjuvant chemotherapy/radiotherapy
- Lumpectomy
- Axillary node assessment (SLNB)
- Radiotherapy

**Advanced local regional breast cancer (Stage IIIA, IIIB, IIIC)**
- Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (Adriamycin–Taxane containing)
  - Then either BCT or MRM
    - + Adjuvant chemo/RT/Trastuzumab (HER2+)
    - + Antiestrogen therapy (ER/PR+)

**Stage IV**
- Palliative approaches:
  - Antiestrogen
  - Chemotherapy
  - Surgery
  - Radiotherapy
  - Breast-conserving surgery
- Clinical trials

questions.stem: Which sign is described by increasing tenderness in the right lower quadrant as the patient moves from supine position to a left recumbent position
questions.rationale:
**Correct answer: C — Rosenstein sign**

- **A. Kocher sign** — Refers to the migration of pain from the umbilical region to the right iliac region.
- **B. Massouh sign** — Occurs when the patient grimaces as the examiner performs a swish across the epigastrium to the right iliac fossa.
- **C. Rosenstein sign** — Occurs when tenderness in the RLQ increases as the patient moves from a supine position to a recumbent posture on the left side.
- **D. Iliopsoas sign** — Elicited by slowly extending the right thigh, stretching the iliopsoas muscle, causing pain.

**Special signs on physical examination**

| Sign | Description |
|---|---|
| Aaron sign | Referred pain or feeling of distress in the epigastrium or precordial region on continued firm pressure over the McBurney point |
| Bassler sign | Sharp pain elicited by pinching the appendix between the thumb of the examiner and the iliacus muscle (chronic appendicitis) |
| Blumberg sign | Transient abdominal wall rebound tenderness |
| Bryan sign | Exacerbation of pain when the uterus is shifted to the right side (acute appendicitis in pregnancy) |
| Cutaneous hyperesthesia | In the area supplied by spinal nerves on the right (T10, T11, T12) |
| Dunphy sign | Increased abdominal pain on coughing |
| Kocher (Kosher) sign | Migration of pain from the umbilical region to the right iliac region |
| Markle sign | RLQ pain on dropping from standing on toes to heels |
| Massouh sign | Grimace when examiner performs a firm swish with index and middle finger across the abdomen from the epigastrium to the right iliac fossa |
| Rosenstein sign | Tenderness in the RLQ increases when the patient moves from a supine position to a recumbent posture on the left side |
| Rovsing sign | Pain at the RLQ when palpatory pressure is exerted at the LLQ |
| Iliopsoas sign | Patient lies on the left side; examiner slowly extends the right thigh, stretching the iliopsoas muscle (positive if extension produces pain) |
| Obturator sign | Performed by passive internal rotation of the flexed right thigh with the patient supine (positive if there is hypogastric pain on stretching the obturator internus muscle) |
| Summer sign | Increased abdominal muscle tone on exceedingly gentle palpation of the right iliac fossa (early appendicitis) |
| Ten Horn sign | Pain caused by gentle traction of the spermatic cord |

Specific physical signs (with their eponyms) that discern the location of the appendix:

- **Rovsing sign** — Pain in the right lower quadrant after release of gentle pressure on the left lower quadrant (normal position).
- **Dunphy sign** — Pain with coughing (retrocecal appendix).
- **Iliopsoas sign** — Pain with flexion of the hip (retrocecal appendix).
- **Obturator sign** — Pain with internal rotation of the hip (pelvic appendix). Pain with rectal or cervical examinations is also suggestive of pelvic appendicitis.
