questions.stem: What is the primary role of the hypodermis?
questions.rationale: **B. Insulation and fat storage.** The hypodermis (subcutaneous tissue) contains abundant adipose tissue, which stores energy, cushions deeper structures, and limits heat loss. Epidermal cell division occurs in the stratum basale, not the hypodermis.

questions.stem: What of the following muscles is NOT part of the levator ani muscle?
questions.rationale: **A. Sacrococcygeal muscle.** The levator ani consists of **puborectalis, pubococcygeus, and iliococcygeus**. The coccygeus (ischiococcygeus), sometimes called the sacrococcygeal muscle, is an adjacent pelvic diaphragm muscle but is not a subdivision of levator ani.

questions.stem: Hair follicles are implanted into which layer during transplantation?
questions.rationale: **D. Hypodermis.** Terminal scalp hair follicles extend deep through the dermis, with their bulbs reaching the **subcutaneous tissue (hypodermis)**. A follicular graft must be placed deep enough to accommodate the bulb without damaging it. Depth varies with follicle type, so the entire follicle is not confined to one skin layer.

questions.stem: Sweat glands are primarily located in which layer of the skin?
questions.rationale:
- **Papillary layer**
  - More superficial layer of dermis; composed of areolar connective tissue; forms dermal papillae; contains subpapillary vascular plexus
- **Reticular layer**
  - Deeper layer of dermis; dense irregular connective tissue surrounding hair follicles, sebaceous glands and sweat glands, nerves, and deep plexus of blood vessels extending into subcutaneous layer

questions.rationale:

**TERRIBLE TRIAD OF THE ELBOW**

- Posterior dislocation

questions.stem: A surgeon following Langer's lines is doing so to promote:
questions.rationale: **B. Better wound healing.** Orienting an incision parallel to **Langer’s lines** reduces tension and edge separation during healing, generally improving scar appearance. These lines are guides to skin tension rather than landmarks for vessels or nerves.

questions.stem: Giant platelets are a characteristic feature of:
questions.rationale:
**BERNARD-SOULIER SYNDROME**

- Deficiency of the Gp1b-IX-V receptor complex which bonds to the vWF to facilitate initial platelet adhesion
- Triad:
  - Thrombocytopenia
  - Prolonged bleeding time
  - Abnormally large platelets

questions.stem: During the surgical closure of a deep, full-thickness laceration, which of the following layers is closed first with high-tensile strength suturing material to approximate the deep margins, eliminate dead space, and provide underlying structural support?
questions.rationale: **D. Muscle fascia.** In a deep laceration that has disrupted fascia, the **deep fascial layer** is repaired first with sutures that restore structural continuity. Subsequent closure of subcutaneous tissue and skin reduces dead space and completes wound approximation; the precise sequence depends on which layers were injured.

questions.stem: Which nerve is vulnerable to injury during evacuation of pus in ischiorectal abscesses?
questions.rationale:

- Wedge shaped
- fat filled spaces; fat supports the anal canal and allows it to distend during defecation
- Boundaries:

  - Lateral - obturator internus muscle and fascia
  - Medial - levator ani, anal canal
- Contents: Fats, PUDENDAL CANAL (containing Pudendal nerve and Internal Pudendal vessels); Inferior rectal vessels and nerve

questions.stem: A patient presents with "winging" of the scapula when asked to push against a wall. The nerve responsible for this action arises from which part of the brachial plexus?
questions.rationale:

- Paralyzed serratus anterior owing to injury to the long thoracic nerve (C5-C7)
- Medial border of the scapula moves laterally and posteriorly away from the thoracic wall especially when leaning on a hand or pressing the upper limb against a wall
- When the arm is raised, the medial border and inferior angle of the scapula pull markedly away from the posterior thoracic wall
- Unable to abduct arm above horizontal

questions.stem: Which muscle of the lateral forearm compartment serves as an elbow flexor, particularly when the forearm is in a mid-prone position?
questions.rationale: **A. Brachioradialis.** This lateral forearm muscle flexes the elbow most effectively when the forearm is **mid prone (thumb upward)**. It is innervated by the radial nerve, so weakness can accompany a humeral shaft fracture even when elbow flexion by brachialis and biceps remains.

questions.stem: Ray is a 27-year-old student who accidentally aspirated a stone after shouting "Darna!" while upright. Radiographic imaging is ordered to locate the object. In which of the following lung locations is the aspirated object most likely to lodge?
questions.rationale:
**CLINICAL CORRELATION: FOREIGN BODY ASPIRATION**

- More likely to enter the right main bronchus because it is shorter, wider and more vertical than the left main bronchus
- In a patient who is standing or sitting, the foreign body tends to become lodged in the posterobasal segment of the inferior lobe of the right lung

| Supine | Superior BPS of the right lower lobe |

questions.stem: Pocholo, a 27-year-old male undergoes an elective circumcision at a local medical mission. One week after, he presents with severe pain, purulent discharge, and erythema along the surgical incision. On physical examination, which of the following lymph node groups is most likely to be enlarged and tender?
questions.rationale: **B. Superficial inguinal lymph nodes.** The **penile shaft and overlying skin** drain mainly to superficial inguinal nodes, so infection at a circumcision wound can cause their enlargement and tenderness. The glans and deeper penile structures have important drainage to deep inguinal nodes.

questions.stem: What type of dominance is observed when the circumflex artery supplies the posterior interventricular artery?
questions.rationale:
- RIGHT DOMINANCE (67%)
- LEFT DOMINANCE (15%)
- CODOMINANCE
- Origin and distribution of the posterior interventricular artery in the *right dominance*
- Origin and distribution of the posterior interventricular artery in the *left dominance*

questions.stem: Which artery supplies the prostate?
questions.rationale: **B. Inferior vesical.** The **inferior vesical artery**, usually a branch of the internal iliac system, supplies the prostate as well as the bladder base and seminal vesicles. Prostatic arterial supply is variable and may also involve middle rectal or internal pudendal branches.

questions.stem: A patient presents with a mid-shaft humeral fracture. Physical examination reveals wrist drop and the patient can still flex their elbow with significant strength, however it is noticeably weaker when the forearm is in a neutral position. Which muscle flexes the elbow and is situated on the lateral side of the forearm?
questions.rationale: **B. Brachioradialis.** Located on the lateral forearm, brachioradialis is a **radial nerve** muscle that flexes the elbow, especially with the forearm in neutral position. A midshaft humeral fracture may injure the radial nerve in the spiral groove, producing wrist drop and weakening this part of elbow flexion while other flexors remain active.

questions.stem: Which type of grip is used when holding a bag by its handles?
questions.rationale:
- **A** The hook grip is a type of power grip where the fingers are flexed into a hook shape to support a heavy load. In this grip, the force is primarily managed by the long flexors of the fingers (flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus).
- **B** "Palmar grip" is a general term for a power grip where the object is held against the palm for stabilization. Palmar tuck is not a standard anatomical term
- **C** Also known as a "key/pinch grip". Involves pressing an object between the pad of the thumb and the lateral side of the index finger.
- **D** This involves the tips of the fingers and thumb working together for fine motor tasks (eg. pen holding)

questions.stem: A patient is diagnosed with subacute infective endocarditis. Peripheral signs like Roth spots and Osler nodes are noted. What is the primary immunopathological manifestation responsible for these findings?
questions.rationale:
- **A. Cytokine production** - cause fever, malaise, constitutional symptoms
- **B. Overproduction of antibody** - antibodies form immune complexes, but the actual tissue injury is mainly from immune complex deposition with complement activation.
- **C. Complement Activation** - in infective endocarditis, immunologic phenomena such as Osler nodes, Roth spots, and Glomerulonephritis typically occur as a result of immune complex deposition and subsequent activation of complement, leading to vasculitis.

> “The clinical manifestations of IE—other than constitutional symptoms, which probably result from cytokine production—arise from damage to intracardiac structures; embolization of vegetation fragments leading to infection or infarction of remote tissues; hematogenous infection of sites during bacteremia; and tissue injury due to the deposition of circulating immune complexes or immune responses to deposited bacterial antigens.” (HPIM 22nd Ed., p. 1038)

- **D. Direct bacterial invasion** - causes valvular vegetations, abscess, local tissue destruction.

questions.stem: An ECG on a patient with sharp chest pain shows diffuse, concave ST-segment elevation and PR-segment depression. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
- **A. Acute Myocardial Infarction** - typically presents with ST-segment elevation representing a vascular territory (localized)
- **B. Acute Pericarditis** - typically presents with diffuse ST-segment elevation with PR depression
- **C. Atrial Ischemia** - classically presents with PR-segment deviation, especially PR elevation in aVR/V1
- **D. Pulmonary Embolism**
  - Most common abnormality in ECG in PE: T-wave inversions in leads V1-V4 (right precordial leads)
  - Most frequently cited abnormality in ECG in PE: Sinus tachycardia > S1Q3T3 sign (McGinn-White sign) (S wave in Lead I, Q wave in Lead III, T-wave inversion in Lead III)

questions.stem: A patient with a history of prostatic disease underwent a TURP procedure and later developed subacute endocarditis. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.rationale:
- **A. Staphylococcus aureus** - causes acute, aggressive endocarditis, often in IV drug users or bacteremic patients
- **B. Enterococcus faecalis** - associated with endocarditis s/p GU (e.g., TURP) or GI procedures.
- **C. Streptococcus pyogenes** - classically causes pharyngitis, cellulitis, necrotizing fasciitis, rheumatic fever. Rarely causes endocarditis.
- **D. Coxiella burnetii** - causes culture-negative endocarditis, often associated with exposure to farm animals, parturient cats/sheep/goats, or unpasteurized animal products. Also the causative agent of Q fever.

**RECALL MUST KNOW IE ORGANISMS**

**INFECTIVE ENDOCARDITIS IN…**

- IV Drug user: Staphylococcus aureus
- Prosthetic valve: Staphylococcus epidermidis
- s/p GU or GI procedures: Enterococcus faecalis
- (+) GI Malignancy: Streptococcus bovis/gallolyticus
- Dental procedures: Viridans streptococcus

**VALVULAR INVOLVEMENT:** Mitral Valve: most frequent valve involved EXCEPT in IV drug users (Tricuspid Valve)

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male with chronic bronchiectasis and recurrent infections is noted to have significant digital clubbing. What is the underlying cause of this physical finding?

choices.text: Chronic hypoxia and increase in growth factor

questions.rationale:
- **A. Viral destruction of alveoli** - alveolar destruction is more associated with emphysema, not clubbing from bronchiectasis. Viral infection may trigger lung disease but is not the mechanism of clubbing.
- **B. Interstitial fibrosis** - another possible cause of digital clubbing if with chronic hypoxia, however it is not the direct mechanism that causes clubbing.
- **C. Chronic hypoxia and increase in growth factor** - causes of chronic hypoxia such as chronic suppurative lung disease causes platelet-derived growth factor release in distal digits.

> “Although the mechanism of clubbing is unclear, it appears to be secondary to humoral substances that cause dilation of the vessels of the distal digits as well as growth factors released from platelet precursors in the digital circulation.” (HPIM 22nd Ed., p. 279)

- **D. Autoimmune destruction** - may be associated with some lung diseases, but the pathogenesis of digital clubbing itself is not due to autoimmune destruction.

**Correlate Recalls:**

*Is clubbing seen in COPD?* No! Clubbing is never seen in COPD unless there are other coexisting conditions such as lung malignancy, bronchiectasis, congenital heart disorders . If present, you RULE THEM OUT!

**MOST COMMON CAUSES OF COPD EXACERBATIONS**

- **MNEMONIC:** So Much Hate for COPD and Viruses
- Streptococcus pneumoniae
- Moraxella catarrhalis
- Haemophilus influenzae
- Chlamydophila pneumoniae
- Viruses

**3 INTERVENTIONS FOR COPD WITH KNOWN MORTALITY BENEFIT**

- Smoking Cessation
- Oxygen Therapy
- Lung Volume Reduction Surgery

questions.stem: A hospital administrator wants to prevent an outbreak of Legionella pneumophila. Which is the most effective way to prevent the spread of this pathogen in a facility?

choices.text: Clean air conditioner and replace water sources regularly

questions.rationale:
- **A. Hospital-grade masks, B. Cough etiquette** - Masks are for respiratory droplet/airborne spread. Cough etiquette prevents person-to-person respiratory spread. Legionella is not usually transmitted person-to-person and is acquired from water aerosols.
- **C. Clean air conditioner and replace water sources regularly** - Legionella spreads by aerosolized contaminated water, classically from air-conditioning, water systems, showers, and plumbing. Prevention is by water system maintenance/disinfection.

> “(Legionella) Infection of debilitated or immunocompromised humans commonly follows inhalation of the bacteria from aerosols generated from contaminated air-conditioning systems, shower heads, and similar water sources.” (Jawetz Medical Microbiology 28th Ed., p. 316)

- **D. Prophylactic antibiotics** - Not used for facility outbreak prevention. Prevention is environmental control of water sources.

**Correlate Recalls: Legionella pneumophila**

- Gram negative rod that affects the respiratory tract
- Facultative intracellular bacteria
- Poorly gram staining, seen in SILVER STAIN, grows in CHARCOAL YEAST AGAR
- Associated with aerosols from air-conditioning systems
- May cause PONTIAC FEVER (mild flu-like illness) or ATYPICAL PNEUMONIA (Legionnaire’s Disease)
- Treatment: Azithromycin or Erythromycin
- Other key facts: associated with HYPONATREMIA in patients with legionella pneumonia; patients may have a positive LEGIONELLA URINARY ANTIGEN when infected

questions.stem: Imaging of a patient with a history of TB reveals a well-defined mass within a lung cavity, surrounded by a crescent of air (Monod sign). What is the diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
- **A. Aspergilloma** - an aspergilloma is a fungal ball that grows inside a preexisting lung cavity, classically after TB, sarcoidosis, or bronchiectasis. Imaging may show a mobile intracavitary mass with surrounding air (Monod sign).
- **B. Coccidioidomycosis** - no particular radiologic finding, can cause lung nodules or cavities.
- **C. Lung Abscess** - typically shows a cavity with air-fluid level, usually from aspiration/anaerobic infection.
- **D. Pleural Effusion** - typically appears on chest x-ray as blunting of the costophrenic angle, with a homogeneous basal opacity that may form a meniscus sign.

questions.stem: A patient has atypical pneumonia. The organism lacks a cell wall. Why is Mycoplasma pneumoniae resistant to beta-lactam antibiotics?

choices.text: Due to lack of cell wall which is the target of other drugs

questions.rationale:
- **A. Due to lack of cell wall which is the target of other drugs** - Mycoplasma pneumoniae has no cell wall and no peptidoglycan. Beta-lactams act by inhibiting bacterial cell wall synthesis, so they are ineffective against Mycoplasma. This is also the reason that the DOC for these cases include Macrolides (e.g., Erythromycin, Azithromycin).
- **B. Thick peptidoglycan layer** - Incorrect. Mycoplasma has no cell wall.
- **C. Production of beta-lactamase** - Mycoplasma’s resistance to beta-lactams is due to the absence of a cell wall.
- **D. Hiding inside mitochondria** - Mycoplasma pneumoniae is an extracellular respiratory pathogen, not an organism that hides inside mitochondria.

**Correlate Recalls: BETA-LACTAM ANTIBIOTICS**

- MOA: Disruption of bacterial cell wall synthesis by inhibiting transpeptidation (Penicillin Binding Protein), leading to cell death (bactericidal).
- Note: These antibiotics will NOT WORK against bacteria that have no cell wall (e.g., Mycoplasma).
- Examples: Penicillins, Cephalosporins

**PROTEIN SYNTHESIS INHIBITORS**

- MOA: Disrupts protein synthesis by inhibiting either the 30S or 50S ribosomal subunit of the bacteria.
- Examples:
  - 30S inhibitors: Tetracyclines, Aminoglycosides
  - 50S inhibitors: Macrolides, Clindamycin, Chloramphenicol, Linezolid

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child presents with a barking cough, hoarseness, and inspiratory stridor. What is the most likely viral causative agent?
questions.rationale:
- **A. Parainfluenza** - barking cough, hoarseness, and stridor in a pediatric patient is the classic description of croup or laryngotracheobronchitis (LTB), which is most commonly caused by parainfluenza.
- **B. S. pneumoniae** - common causative agent of bacterial pneumonia
- **C. M. pneumoniae** - common causative agent of atypical pneumonia (“walking pneumonia”)
- **D. Bordetella pertussis** - causative agent of Pertussis “whooping cough”

questions.stem: Microscopy of a sample from a lung cavity mass reveals regularly divided (septated) hyphae. This finding is characteristic of:
questions.rationale:
- **A. Aspergilloma** - Aspergillus forms fruiting bodies (usually in lung cavities) and septate filaments, 5 to 10 µm thick, branching at acute angles (40 degrees)
- **B. Coccidioidomycosis** - main diagnostic feature is the presence of spherules (filled with endospores)
- **C. Lung abscess** - microscopy sample would show presence of causative bacteria (typically anaerobes) with abscess formation
- **D. Pleural Effusion** - varied microscopy results depending on cause/type of effusion (e.g., Tuberculous, Parapneumonic, Hemorrhagic, Malignant, Chylous, etc.)

**RECALL: FUNGAL AGENTS AND CHARACTERISTIC MORPHOLOGY**

| Fungal agent | Characteristic morphology |
|---|---|
| Sporothrix schenckii | Cigar-shaped yeast |
| Coccidioides spp. | Spherule filled with endospores |
| Paracoccidioides spp. | Budding yeasts “captain’s wheel appearance” |
| Histoplasma capsulatum | Macrophage filled with histoplasma oval yeasts |
| Blastomyces | Broad-based budding of Blastomyces |
| Mucor spp. | Branching hyphae at obtuse or right angles (at least 90 degrees) “wide angles” |
| Aspergillus spp. | Septate hyphae with acute branching |
| Candida spp. | Yeasts and pseudohyphae |

questions.stem: A 28-year-old female presents with malodorous discharge. Wet mount identifies Clue Cells. Which of the following best defines a clue cell?

choices.text: Vaginal epithelial cells covered with bacteria

questions.rationale:
- **A. Lactobacilli overgrowth on basement membranes** - Incorrect. Bacterial vaginosis involves decreased lactobacilli with overgrowth of Gardnerella and anaerobes, not lactobacilli overgrowth.
- **B. Vaginal epithelial cells covered with bacteria**

> “(Gardnerella vaginalis) In wet smears, this “nonspecific” vaginitis, or bacterial vaginosis, yields clue cells, which are vaginal epithelial cells covered with many Gram-variable bacilli.” (Jawetz Medical Microbiology 28th Ed., p. 309)

- **C. Yeast cells invading superficial tissue** - a vaginitis with yeast cells suggests Candida vaginitis, which causes thick, curdy discharge and pruritus.
- **D. Leukocytes with intracellular diplococci** - WBCs with intracellular gram-negative diplococci suggest Neisseria gonorrhoeae, not bacterial vaginosis.

questions.stem: A student must differentiate Trichomoniasis from Bacterial Vaginosis (BV). What is the primary difference between these two regarding their relationship to normal flora?

choices.text: BV is related to lactobacilli deficiency; Trichomoniasis is an exogenous infection
Trichomoniasis is associated with a pH of 4.0

questions.rationale:
- **A. BV is related to lactobacilli deficiency; Trichomoniasis is an exogenous infection** - Correct. BV is related to overgrowth of G. vaginalis and lactobacilli (normal vaginal flora) deficiency. Trichomoniasis is an exogenous infection caused by T. vaginalis, a protozoa.
- **B. BV shows pear-shaped organisms** - Incorrect. BV shows clue cells, while Trichomoniasis would show pear-shaped motile trichomonads.
- **C. Trichomoniasis is associated with a pH of 4.0** - Incorrect. Candidiasis is the only vaginitis associated with a low pH among the three.
- **D. Both require lactobacilli for growth** - Incorrect. Presence of lactobacillus is protective against vaginitides due to its acidifying effect on vaginal pH.

**VAGINITIS**

| Parameter | Bacterial vaginosis | Candidiasis | Trichomoniasis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Consistency of discharge | Thin, homogenous | Thick, curdy, “cottage cheese” | Frothy |
| Color of discharge | Clear to white | Clear to white | Yellow |
| pH of vaginal discharge | >4.5 | <4.5 | >4.5 |
| Wet mount features | Clue cells (>20%); Amine odor after addition of KOH | (+) hyphae, spores | (+) motile trichomonads |

questions.stem: A post-menopausal woman has recurrent cystitis. What is the most likely physiological reason for recurrent UTIs in post-menopausal women with estrogen and progesterone deficiencies?

choices.text: Estrogen deficiency leading to a decreased number of normal flora (Lactobacilli)

questions.rationale:
- **A. Increased vaginal acidity** - lack of estrogen leads to decreased Lactobacilli growth. Lactobacilli normally acidifies vaginal pH, hence, its absence decreases vaginal acidity.
- **B. Estrogen deficiency leading to a decreased number of normal flora (Lactobacilli)** - Estrogen is required for the formation of vaginal glycogen, which then promotes lactobacilli growth. Lack of estrogen would then lead to a decrease in lactobacilli, and a subsequent increase in vaginal pH, which allows uropathogen colonization.

> “At puberty, aerobic and anaerobic lactobacilli reappear in large numbers and contribute to the maintenance of acid pH through the production of acid from carbohydrates, particularly glycogen. This appears to be an important mechanism in preventing the establishment of other, possibly harmful microorganisms in the vagina… After menopause, lactobacilli again diminish in number.” (Jawetz Medical Microbiology 28th Ed., p. 178)

- **C. Progesterone deficiency causing anatomical changes, D. Mechanical Obstruction** - both do not directly influence vaginal normal flora growth (lactobacilli).

questions.stem: A 25-year-old male presents with a single, painless genital ulcer and non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
- **A. Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV)** - presents with PAINLESS solitary ulcer with PAINFUL lymphadenopathy. Caused by Chlamydia trachomatis (Serotypes L1-L3).
- **B. Syphilis** - presents with a chancre (PAINLESS solitary raised genital ulcer) with PAINLESS lymphadenopathy. Caused by Treponema pallidum.
- **C. Chancroid** - presents with PAINFUL multiple excavated ulcers with ragged, irregular edges. Caused by Haemophilus ducreyi.
- **D. Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV)** - presents with multiple vesicles and ulcers with erythematous edges.

**Correlate Recalls: SYPHILIS KEY RECALLS**

- CA: Treponema pallidum
- Most commonly used non-treponemal test: RPR
- Only test used for neurosyphilis: VDRL
- Screening tests: RPR VDRL
- Confirmatory tests: TP-PA, TPHA, MHA-TP, FTA-ABS
- Treatment: Penicillin G

**SYPHILIS LESIONS:**

- PRIMARY Syphilis: Painless chancre
- SECONDARY Syphilis: Condyloma lata, maculopapular rash
- TERTIARY Syphilis: Gummas

**OTHER LESIONS:**

- Granuloma Inguinale (Donovanosis): Painless ulcer with a RED AND BEEFY base. Caused by Klebsiella granulomatis.
- Condyloma Accuminata: Genital warts. Caused by HPV.

questions.stem: A patient is diagnosed with Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID). Regarding the mode of spread, which is the most accurate description of how the infection reaches the upper reproductive tract?

choices.text: Ascending infection from the lower genital tract

questions.rationale:
- **A. Ascending infection from the lower genital tract** - “The term pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) usually refers to infection that ascends from the cervix or vagina to involve the endometrium and/or fallopian tubes.” (HPIM 22nd Ed., p. 1104)
- **B. Lymphatic spread, C. Hematogenous spread, D. Direct extension from neighboring organ** - by definition, PID does not occur via these mechanisms.

> “The term pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) usually refers to infection that ascends from the cervix or vagina to involve the endometrium and/or fallopian tubes.” (HPIM 22nd Ed., p. 1104)
>
> “Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), also called salpingitis, is inflammation of the uterus, uterine tubes, and adnexal tissues that is not associated with surgery or pregnancy.” (Jawetz Medical Microbiology 28th Ed., p. 806)

**Correlate Recalls: PELVIC INFLAMMATORY DISEASE**

- Most common causes: N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis
- Major complication: Infertility due to uterine tubal occlusion (scarring secondary to inflammation)
- Treatment: Inpatient drug regimens include cefoxitin and doxycycline or gentamicin and clindamycin. Outpatient regimens include cefoxitin or ceftriaxone in single doses plus doxycycline, or ofloxacin plus metronidazole. (Jawetz Medical Microbiology 28th Ed., p. 807)

questions.stem: A 19-year-old female presents with pelvic pain and cervical motion tenderness. Which of the following is the most common causative agent of PID?
questions.rationale:
**NOTE:**

Jawetz Medical Microbiology 28th Ed., Robbins Pathologic Basis of Disease 9th Ed., and HPIM 22nd Ed., did not explicitly state which among the two (C. trachomatis vs N. gonorrhoeae) is more common. However, overall as an STI, C. trachomatis is known as the most common overall.

> “PID is the major consequence of endocervical N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis infections, and well over half of the cases are caused by one or both of these organisms.” (Jawetz Medical Microbiology 28th Ed., p. 806)
>
> “The agents most often implicated in acute PID include the primary causes of endocervicitis (N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis, and M. genitalium) and anaerobes associated with BV.” (HPIM 22nd Ed., p. 1104)
>
> “Neisseria gonorrhoeae continues to be a common cause of PID, the most serious complication of gonorrhea in women. Chlamydia infection is another well-recognized cause of PID.” (Robbins Pathologic Basis of Disease 9th Ed., p. 994)

- **A. Chlamydia trachomatis** - a common cause of PID along with N. gonorrhoeae.

> “Approximately 30% of women with documented acute cervicitis secondary to Chlamydia subsequently develop acute PID.” (Comprehensive Gynecology 8th Ed., p. 535)”

- **B. Escherichia coli** - does not cause cervicitis. Overall most common cause of UTI.
- **C. Neisseria gonorrhoeae** - also common cause of PID along with C. trachomatis. Based on comprehensive gynecology, C. trachomatis may be more associated than N. gonorrhoeae. (See choice A)

> “Approximately 15% of women with cervical infection by N. gonorrhoeae subsequently develop acute PID.” (Comprehensive Gynecology 8th Ed., p. 535)”

- **D. Staphylococcus aureus** - not a known common cause of PID.

questions.stem: A 28-week pregnant woman is diagnosed with Chlamydia trachomatis. Which of the following is the treatment of choice in this population?
questions.rationale:
- **A. Erythromycin** - the treatment regimen of C. trachomatis infection usually involves either Tetracyclines or Macrolides. In cases of pregnancy, a macrolide such as erythromycin is preferred over tetracycline due to its teratogenic effects (i.e., bone and teeth abnormalities).

> “Tetracyclines (e.g., doxycycline) are commonly used in nongonococcal urethritis and in nonpregnant infected women. Azithromycin is effective and can be given to pregnant women.” (Jawetz Medical Microbiology 28th Ed., p. 372)

- **B. Ertapenem** - a carbapenem antibiotic. Not given in cases of chlamydia.
- **C. Ciprofloxacin** - a fluoroquinolone antibiotic. Not given in cases of chlamydia.
- **D. Doxycycline** - a tetracycline. Should be avoided in pregnant patients due to teratogenic effects.

questions.stem: A 25/F patient with a chancre was noted to develop fever, chills, muscle pains, headache, and a general feeling of "worsening" a few days after starting treatment with Penicillin G. What is the most likely mechanism of the patient’s symptoms?

choices.text: Response to lipoproteins released by dying organisms
A hypersensitivity reaction to penicillin G

questions.rationale:
- **A. Response to lipoproteins released by dying organisms** - The phenomenon experienced by the patient is the Jarish-Herxheimer reaction, which is a self-limited response to the dead treponema lipoproteins.

> “A dramatic although self-limited reaction consisting of fever, chills, myalgia, headache, tachycardia, and increased respiratory rate may follow the initiation of treatment for syphilis. This reaction is thought to be a response to lipoproteins released by dying T. pallidum organisms. The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction occurs in ~50% of patients with primary syphilis, 90% of those with secondary syphilis, and a lower proportion of persons with later-stage disease.” (HPIM 22nd Ed., p. 1435)

- **B. A hypersensitivity reaction to penicillin G** - would present with signs of anaphylaxis or acute allergic responses rather than delayed fever and muscle pain.
- **C. Treatment resistance leading to septicemia** - Spirochetes (e.g., Treponema, Borrelia, Leptospira) typically do not develop resistance due to a conserved genome. Hence, the maintained susceptibility to Penicillin until today.
- **D. Development of a superinfection** - would progress to sepsis and not be self-limited.

questions.stem: A 47/M patient with advanced HIV presents with severe abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. Which of the following is the confirmatory diagnostic test for suspected CMV colitis?
questions.rationale:
- **A. Barium enema** - an imaging modality that utilizes contrast to anatomically assess the colon. Not confirmatory for CMV.
- **B. CMV stool assay, D. Stool Culture** - “Isolation of CMV from urine, stool, or saliva does not, by itself, constitute proof of acute infection, since excretion from these sites may continue for months or years after illness.” (HPIM 22nd Ed., p. 1515)
- **C. Endoscopic biopsy** - “CMV colitis presents as diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, and anorexia. The diarrhea is usually nonbloody, and the diagnosis is achieved through endoscopy and biopsy. Multiple mucosal ulcerations are seen at endoscopy, and biopsies reveal characteristic intranuclear and cytoplasmic inclusion bodies.” (HPIM 22nd Ed., p. 1161)

questions.stem: A patient presented to the ER with fever, further work-up revealed osteomyelitis as the source of the fever. Upon further history taking, you noted that the patient would often experience unprovoked episodes of torso pain and inflammation of the finger when she would go hiking. What is the most likely organism causing this patient’s osteomyelitis?
questions.rationale:
- **A. Staphylococcus epidermidis** - Osteomyelitis associated with prosthetic devices, catheters, and hardware infections.
- **B. Pseudomonas aeruginosa** - Osteomyelitis associated with burn injury.
- **C. Salmonella choleraesuis** - Torso pain episodes and finger inflammation suggest sickle cell disease with vaso-occlusive crises and dactylitis. In sickle cell disease, osteomyelitis is classically associated with Salmonella species.
- **D. Staphylococcus aureus** - Most common cause of osteomyelitis; also associated with osteomyelitis in IV drug users.

questions.stem: A patient presents with fever, rose spots, and pea-soup stools. Which of the following is the most likely causative agent?
questions.rationale:
- **A. Vibrio cholerae** - presents with “rice-water” non-inflammatory diarrhea. In patients with severe hypovolemia, may have sunken eyes, dry mouth, cold clammy skin, decreased skin turgor, or wrinkled hands and feet, aka “washerwoman's hands”.
- **B. Vibrio vulnificus** - associated with sepsis / wound infections after seafood or seawater exposure.
- **C. Vibrio parahaemolyticus** - associated with seafood-associated gastroenteritis
- **D. Salmonella Typhi** - classically described presentation: headache, stepladder (prolonged) fever, abdominal symptoms, rose spots, and diarrhea (> constipation). Also associated with Relative bradycardia (Faget Sign).

questions.stem: A patient has tingling and respiratory distress after consuming toxic mussels. What is the primary management for Paralytic Shellfish Poisoning (PSP)?
questions.rationale:
- **A. Supportive and respiratory support** - main management for cases of PSP.

> “Treatment is supportive and based on symptoms. If the victim seeks medical attention within the first few hours after ingestion, activated charcoal (50–100 g) can be administered in the absence of vomiting. Gastric lavage and cathartics have been attempted but there is no evidence of benefit, and most authors recommend against their use. The most serious concern is respiratory paralysis. The victim should be closely observed for respiratory distress for at least 24 h in a hospital.” (HPIM 22nd Ed., p. 3727)

- **B. Antidote for saxitoxin** - no established antidote for saxitoxin.
- **C. Penicillin G** - no role in treatment of PSP.
- **D. Emergency dialysis** - not indicated in the treatment of PSP.

questions.stem: A clinician suspects a Salmonella infection. During the first week of illness, which type of culture is most likely to yield the causative organism?
questions.rationale:
- **A. Blood culture** - best used during the first week of illness.

> “In enteric fevers and septicemias, blood culture results are often positive in the first week of the disease.” (Jawetz Medical Microbiology 28th Ed., p. 247)

- **B. Stool culture** - May become positive in the 3rd week of infection
- **C. Urine culture** - best used during the second week of illness.
- **D. Widal test** - an obsolete antibody test best used on the second week. Has inability to differentiate past and present infections.

**MNEMONIC: BONE MARROW CULTURE SURROGATES — TYPHOID FEVER - DIAGNOSIS**

Bone marrow culture - most sensitive (>80% sensitivity) diagnostic modality, but highly impractical and rarely indicated clinically.

“BUS” - surrogates for BM Culture

- Blood culture - 1st week
- Urine culture - 2nd week
- Stool culture - 3rd week

questions.stem: A patient in an area with poor sanitation develops massive, watery diarrhea. Which organism is classically associated with rice-water stools?
questions.rationale:
- **A. Vibrio cholerae** - presents with “rice-water” non-inflammatory diarrhea. In patients with severe hypovolemia, may have sunken eyes, dry mouth, cold clammy skin, decreased skin turgor, or wrinkled hands and feet, aka “washerwoman's hands”.
- **B. Vibrio parahaemolyticus** - associated with seafood-associated gastroenteritis
- **C. Vibrio vulnificus** - associated with sepsis / wound infections after seafood or seawater exposure.
- **D. Salmonella typhi** - classically described presentation: headache, stepladder (prolonged) fever, abdominal symptoms, rose spots, and diarrhea (> constipation). Also associated with Relative bradycardia (Faget Sign).

questions.stem: A patient develops acute watery diarrhea (non-rice water) 12 hours after eating raw oysters. Which Vibrio species is most likely responsible?
questions.rationale:
- **A. Vibrio parahaemolyticus** - associated with seafood-associated gastroenteritis (non-rice water).

> “V. parahaemolyticus is a halophilic bacterium that causes acute gastroenteritis after ingestion of contaminated seafood such as raw fish or shellfish. After an incubation period of 12–24 hours, nausea and vomiting, abdominal cramps, fever, and an explosive watery diarrhea occur. “ (Jawetz Medical Microbiology 28th Ed., p. 265)

- **B. Vibrio cholerae** - presents with “rice-water” non-inflammatory diarrhea.

> “Cholera is associated with poor sanitation, as well as direct contact with or consumption of contaminated water and/or food (e.g., water used for drinking, cooking, bathing, and crop irrigation)” (Jawetz Medical Microbiology 28th Ed., p. 265)

- **C. Vibrio vulnificus** - associated with sepsis / wound infections after seafood or seawater exposure.

> “V. vulnificus is a particularly virulent species and is primarily known to cause severe wound and soft tissue infections, as well as bacteremia/sepsis, rather than gastroenteritis.” (Jawetz Medical Microbiology 28th Ed., p. 265)

- **D. Vibrio alginolyticus** - associated with ear / wound infections from seawater.

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 22nd Ed. Table 138-4 Bacterial Food Poisoning

**Bacterial Food Poisoning:**

| Incubation period | Organism | Symptoms | Common food sources |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1–6 h | *Staphylococcus aureus* | Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea | Ham, poultry, potato or egg salad, mayonnaise, cream pastries |
| 1–6 h | *Bacillus cereus* | Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea | Fried rice |
| 8–16 h | *Clostridium perfringens* | Abdominal cramps, diarrhea (vomiting rare) | Beef, poultry, legumes, gravies |
| 8–16 h | *B. cereus* | Abdominal cramps, diarrhea (vomiting rare) | Meats, vegetables, dried beans, cereals |
| >16 h | *Vibrio cholerae* | Watery diarrhea | Shellfish, water |
| >16 h | Enterotoxigenic *Escherichia coli* | Watery diarrhea | Salads, cheese, meats, water |
| >16 h | Enterohemorrhagic *E. coli* | Bloody diarrhea | Ground beef, roast beef, salami, raw milk, raw vegetables, apple juice |
| >16 h | *Salmonella* spp. | Inflammatory diarrhea | Beef, poultry, eggs, dairy products |
| >16 h | *Campylobacter jejuni* | Inflammatory diarrhea | Poultry, raw milk |
| >16 h | *Shigella* spp. | Dysentery | Potato or egg salad, lettuce, raw vegetables |
| >16 h | *Vibrio parahaemolyticus* | Dysentery | Mollusks, crustaceans |

questions.stem: A 23/F accidentally forgot to remove her tampon for 3 days. She was then brought to the ER due to fever and loss of consciousness. Vital signs revealed the following: BP 60/40, HR 132, RR 34. Which of the following statements about her diagnosis is TRUE?

choices.text: Implicated antigen binds to MHC class I
Other symptoms include fever and a desquamative skin rash

questions.rationale:
Retained tampon with fever and profound hypotension suggests toxic shock syndrome due to Staphylococcus aureus TSST-1. TSST-1 is a superantigen causing massive T-cell activation and cytokine release. Classic findings include fever, hypotension, diffuse rash, and later desquamation.

- **A. Causes widespread B-cell stimulation** - TSST-1 causes widespread T-cell stimulation, not B-cell.
- **B. Implicated antigen binds to MHC class I** - TSST-1 binds to MHC class II molecules.
- **C. Other symptoms include fever and a desquamative skin rash** - True. This immune response results in symptoms such as fever, shock, and a desquamative skin rash. Other symptoms include strawberry tongue, altered sensorium, vomiting, nonpurulent conjunctivitis, and profuse watery diarrhea.
- **D. Mediated by a gram-negative organism** - mediated by S. aureus, a gram-positive cocci.

questions.stem: Which of the following Schistosoma species has eggs characterized by a prominent lateral spine on microscopy?
questions.rationale:
- **A. S. mansoni** - egg with a prominent lateral spine
- **B. S. japonicum** - egg with a small lateral knob
- **C. S. haematobium** - egg with a with a terminal spine at the posterior end
- **D. All of the above**

**MNEMONIC: SCHISTOSOMA EGGS**

- S. japonicum - small lateral “knob”
- S. manSoni - ManSIDE (lateral spine)
- S. haemaTobium - HaemaTERMINAL (terminal spine)

questions.stem: Which form of Chlamydia trachomatis is responsible for initiating infection by attaching to and entering host epithelial cells?
questions.rationale:
- **A. Reticulate bodies** - Reticulate bodies (RBs) are the non-infectious, metabolically active, replicative form that multiply inside the host cell that can be seen microscopically
- **B. Spore form** - Chlamydia does not form spores, which are more associated with fungi.
- **C. Elementary body** - Elementary bodies (EBs) are the infectious, metabolically inert form of Chlamydia trachomatis found intracellularly.
- **D. Cyst form** - Chlamydia does not form cysts, which are the infectious form of some protozoans.

**MNEMONIC: FORMS OF CHLAMYDIA**

- Elementary body = Enfectious, Enert (inert), Enters the cell via Endocytosis
- Reticulate body = Replicates in the cell by fission

questions.stem: An organism that produces a toxin was noted to cause paralysis in affected patients via prevention of acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction. What is the most likely organism?
questions.rationale:
- **A. Clostridium tetani** - Causes spastic paralysis, not flaccid paralysis. Its toxin blocks release of inhibitory neurotransmitters (GABA and glycine) from Renshaw cells, producing trismus, risus sardonicus, and opisthotonos.
- **B. Clostridium botulinum** - Botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, causing descending flaccid paralysis. Classically associated with canned foods, honey in infants, and wound botulism.
- **C. Clostridium perfringens** - Causes gas gangrene (myonecrosis) and food poisoning. Its alpha toxin is a lecithinase that destroys cell membranes and causes hemolysis and tissue necrosis.
- **D. Clostridioides difficile** - Causes pseudomembranous colitis, usually after antibiotic use. Its toxins damage colonic mucosa and lead to watery diarrhea.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child is diagnosed with meningitis caused by Haemophilus influenzae. The physician starts treatment with cefotaxime instead of ampicillin. What is the main reason cefotaxime is preferred?

choices.text: Most H. influenzae strains are resistant to ampicillin because of altered penicillin-binding proteins
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the preferred treatment, but it cannot be used because of sulfonamide allergy
Ampicillin is avoided because children commonly develop an immediate allergy to penicillins during treatment
Some H. influenzae strains produce plasmid-mediated beta-lactamase that can inactivate ampicillin

questions.rationale:
- **A. Most H. influenzae strains are resistant to ampicillin because of altered penicillin-binding proteins** - False. Resistance to ampicillin in H. influenzae is due to the presence of beta-lactamase.
- **B. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the preferred treatment, but it cannot be used because of sulfonamide allergy** - False. TMP-SMX is not the drug of choice for H. influenzae meningitis. Serious H. influenzae meningitis is treated with a third-generation cephalosporin.
- **C. Ampicillin is avoided because children commonly develop an immediate allergy to penicillins during treatment.** - Partially true if the patient is known to be allergic to penicillin, regardless of the organism. However, that is not the main reason why it is avoided in H. influenzae meningitis.
- **D. Some H. influenzae strains produce plasmid-mediated beta-lactamase that can inactivate ampicillin.** - True. “Many strains of H. influenzae type b are susceptible to ampicillin, but up to 25% produce a β-lactamase under control of a transmissible plasmid and are resistant.” (Jawetz Medical Microbiology 28th Ed., p. 277)

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy presents with a 2-day history of nasal congestion, watery rhinorrhea, sneezing, mild sore throat, and low-grade fever. His symptoms began after several classmates developed “colds.” Physical examination shows erythematous nasal mucosa without tonsillar exudates. He has no lower respiratory tract findings. Laboratory tests reveal a non-enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus. Which of the following is the receptor used by the most likely causative agent?
questions.rationale:
- **A. CD4 Receptor** - CD4 is the main receptor for HIV, with CCR5 or CXCR4 as coreceptors.
- **B. CD21 Receptor** - CD21 is the receptor for Epstein-Barr virus, which infects B cells and causes infectious mononucleosis.
- **C. Integrins** - Integrins/heparan sulfate are associated with CMV.
- **D. ICAM-1** - This is a case of common colds, most commonly caused by Rhinovirus, which is a non-enveloped, positive-sense ssRNA picornavirus. Most rhinoviruses attach to respiratory epithelial cells using ICAM-1.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman develops acute onset fever, malaise, anorexia, nausea, and jaundice after returning from a rural province where she drank water from a community well. Several other villagers reportedly had similar symptoms. Laboratory tests show elevated AST and ALT. Which virus is the most likely cause of her illness?
questions.rationale:
- **A. Hepatitis B** - Hepatitis B is transmitted mainly through blood, sexual contact, and perinatal exposure, not contaminated water.
- **B. Hepatitis C** - Hepatitis C is transmitted mainly through blood exposure, especially injection drug use or transfusion before screening.
- **C. Hepatitis D** - Hepatitis D is a defective RNA virus that requires HBV coinfection or superinfection because it needs HBsAg. It is not classically transmitted by contaminated water.
- **D. Hepatitis E** - Hepatitis B, C, and D are transmitted parenterally through blood and bodily fluids. Hepatitis E is the most likely cause of his symptoms because it is transmitted by the fecal-oral route, usually through contaminated water, and is common in outbreaks in areas with poor sanitation. May cause severe infection in pregnant women.

**MNEMONIC: VIRAL HEPATITIS**

- FECAL ORAL HEPATITIS: “TAE”
- Hepatitis A
- Hepatitis E

**OTHER MEMORY AIDS:**

- Hepatitis D - “Defective”; requires HBV
- Hepatitis C - “Chronic”
- Hepatitis E - may be severe in Expectant (pregnant) patients

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man, chronic alcoholic, presents with progressive dyspnea, bibasal crackles, and bipedal edema. Echocardiography reveals dilated cardiac chambers with global hypokinesia and reduced ejection fraction. He recalls having a recent self-limited illness with fever, malaise, and myalgias several weeks before the onset of heart failure symptoms. If the cause is infectious in origin, what is the most likely causative agent?
questions.rationale:
**NOTE:** Chronic alcohol use is a classic cause of dilated cardiomyopathy, which presents with systolic heart failure, four-chamber dilation, global hypokinesia, and reduced ejection fraction. If the question specifies for an infectious agent or asks for the most common viral cause of myocarditis leading to dilated cardiomyopathy, the answer is Coxsackievirus B.

- **A. Trypanosoma cruzi** - Can cause Chagas disease myocarditis and dilated cardiomyopathy, but it is classically associated with Latin America, reduviid bug exposure, megaesophagus, and megacolon. Not the most common infectious cause in general, but is one of the leading cause of heart failure in Latin America.
- **B. Coxsackievirus A** - Coxsackievirus A is more associated with herpangina and hand-foot-and-mouth disease.
- **C. Coxsackievirus B** - This is most likely a case of dilated cardiomyopathy, secondary to a previous viral myocarditis, which is more associated with Coxsackie B. “Coxsackie B viruses are the most commonly identified causative agents of viral heart disease in humans.” (Jawetz Medical Microbiology 28th Ed., p. 539)
- **D. Dengue Virus** - can rarely cause myocarditis, but its classic findings are fever, severe myalgia, thrombocytopenia, plasma leakage, and hemorrhagic manifestations

questions.stem: A 10-year-old child is brought to the clinic with fever and migratory joint pain 3 weeks after an untreated sore throat. The physician suspects acute rheumatic fever and applies the Jones criteria. Which of the following is not a major criterion in the Jones Criteria?
questions.rationale:
- **A. Carditis** - major criterion
- **B. Arthralgia** - should be ARTHRITIS, not arthralgia. Arthralgia is a minor criterion.
- **C. Chorea** - major criterion
- **D. Erythema marginatum** - major criterion

**JONES CRITERIA — For All Patient Populations with Evidence of Preceding Group A Streptococcal Infection:**

| Diagnosis | Manifestations |
|---|---|
| Initial ARF | 2 major manifestations or 1 major plus 2 minor manifestations |
| Recurrent ARF | 2 major or 1 major and 2 minor or 3 minor manifestations |

| Major criteria | Low-risk populations | Moderate- and high-risk populations |
|---|---|---|
| Carditis | Clinical and/or subclinical | Clinical and/or subclinical |
| Arthritis | Polyarthritis only | Monoarthritis or polyarthritis; polyarthralgia |
| Chorea | Chorea | Chorea |
| Erythema marginatum | Erythema marginatum | Erythema marginatum |
| SC nodules | SC nodules | SC nodules |

| Minor criteria | Low-risk populations | Moderate- and high-risk populations |
|---|---|---|
| Arthralgia | Polyarthralgia | Monoarthralgia |
| Fever | ≥38°C | ≥38°C |
| ESR/CRP | ESR ≥30 mm in the first hour and/or CRP ≥3.0 mg/dL | ESR ≥30 mm/h and/or CRP ≥3.0 mg/dL |
| PR interval | Prolonged PR interval, after accounting for age variability (unless carditis is a major criterion) | Prolonged PR interval, after accounting for age variability (unless carditis is a major criterion) |

questions.stem: Gram positive cocci were isolated from a blood culture. Final results within the laboratory reveal the following: catalase (-), with partial hemolysis, and has a negative reaction with optochin. Which of the following is the most likely organism?
questions.rationale:
- **A. Streptococcus pneumoniae** - gram positive cocci, catalase (-), alpha (partial) hemolysis, optochin sensitive
- **B. Viridans streptococci (e.g., S. mutans, S. mitis)** - gram positive cocci, catalase (-), alpha (partial hemolysis), optochin resistant/negative
- **C. Streptococcus pyogenes** - gram positive cocci, catalase (+), beta (complete) hemolysis, bacitracin sensitive
- **D. Staphylococcus aureus** - gram positive cocci, catalase (+), coagulase (+)

**GRAM-POSITIVE BACTERIA:**

- **Bacilli:** Aerobic: *Listeria*, *Bacillus*, *Corynebacterium*. Anaerobic: *Clostridium*, *Propionibacterium*.
- **Branching filaments:** Aerobic, weakly acid-fast: *Nocardia*. Anaerobic, not acid-fast: *Actinomyces*.
- **Cocci, catalase-positive (*Staphylococcus*):** Coagulase-positive: *S. aureus*. Coagulase-negative: novobiocin-resistant *S. saprophyticus*; novobiocin-sensitive *S. epidermidis*.
- **Cocci, catalase-negative (*Streptococcus*):**
  - Alpha hemolysis: optochin and bile-solubility negative viridans streptococci (*S. mutans*, *S. mitis*); positive *S. pneumoniae*.
  - Beta hemolysis: bacitracin-resistant group B *S. agalactiae*; bacitracin-sensitive group A *S. pyogenes*.
  - Gamma hemolysis: no growth in 6.5% NaCl nonenterococcus *S. bovis*; growth in 6.5% NaCl group D enterococci (*E. faecium*, *E. faecalis*).

*Enterococcus* may be alpha- or gamma-hemolytic.

questions.stem: Streptococcus pneumoniae may cause a disseminated form of the disease manifesting as meningitis, pneumonia, and endocarditis. This is known as:
questions.rationale:
- **A. Osler Triad** - Disseminated Streptococcus pneumoniae infection presenting with the triad of: Pneumonia, Meningitis, and Endocarditis. Also classically known as Austrian syndrome.
- **B. Saint's Triad** - Triad of gallstones, hiatal hernia, and colonic diverticulosis.
- **C. Carney's Triad** - Triad of gastric GIST, pulmonary chondroma, and extra-adrenal paraganglioma.
- **D. Gregg’s triad** - Congenital rubella syndrome: cataracts, cardiac defects, and sensorineural deafness.

questions.stem: In cases of severe cholera, rapid loss of fluids and electrolytes may lead to which type of primary acid-base imbalance and electrolyte problem?
questions.rationale:
- **A. Metabolic Acidosis, hypokalemia** - Severe diarrhea such as in cholera infection may lead to metabolic acidosis and hypokalemia via gastrointestinal loss of bicarbonate and potassium, respectively.

> “In cases of severe cholera the volume of diarrheal fluid loss can exceed 1 L/h. The rapid loss of fluid and electrolytes can lead to profound dehydration, painful muscle spasms, metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia, and hypovolemic shock with circulatory collapse, and anuria with associated renal failure.” (Jawetz Medical Microbiology 22nd Ed., p. 263)

- **B. Metabolic alkalosis, hypokalemia** - Incorrect. GI losses would lead to decreased bicarbonate (i.e., acidosis).
- **C. Respiratory acidosis, hypocalcemia** - Incorrect. Acidosis in this case is via loss of bicarbonate, not through retention of CO2. Hypokalemia should be present, not hypocalcemia.
- **D. Respiratory alkalosis, hypocalcemia** - Incorrect. Respiratory alkalosis is the expected response to metabolic acidosis, not the primary disorder in cases of severe diarrhea. Hypokalemia should be present, not hypocalcemia.

questions.stem: A daycare worker develops gastroenteritis after an outbreak at her workplace. What is the best way to prevent Entamoeba spread?

choices.text: Sand filtering and boiling water protocols

questions.rationale:
- **A. Sand filtering and boiling water protocols** - Entamoeba histolytica cysts are highly resistant to standard chemical water treatments like routine chlorination. Effective prevention depends on physical removal through sand filtration and destroying the cysts by boiling water protocols to secure a safe water supply.
- **B. Elimination of cockroaches only** - Relying on the elimination of cockroaches alone is insufficient to stop transmission. While mechanical vectors like cockroaches and flies can transport cysts, the primary route of transmission is direct fecal-oral spread via contaminated hands, food, or water.
- **C. Prophylactic Metronidazole** - Prophylactic use of antibiotics or amoebicides is not a standard or recommended public health measure for preventing Entamoeba outbreaks. Metronidazole is reserved for treating confirmed active intestinal or extraintestinal disease rather than preventing infection.
- **D. Using night soil** - "Night soil" refers to using human feces as agricultural fertilizer, which actively promotes the spread of Entamoeba histolytica. This practice contaminates crops and soil with infectious cysts, increasing the risk of widespread fecal-oral transmission rather than preventing it.

questions.stem: A patient tests positive for Anti-HCV with a high viral load. To prevent cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, what is the most appropriate management?

choices.text: Start antiviral therapy to prevent cirrhosis

questions.rationale:
- **A. Start antiviral therapy to prevent cirrhosis** - Active HCV infection (indicated by a high viral load) requires treatment with Direct-Acting Antivirals (DAAs). Eradicating the virus achieves a Sustained Virologic Response (SVR), which significantly halts disease progression, reverses fibrosis, and prevents the development of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)
- **B. Administer the Hepatitis C vaccine** - There is currently no vaccine available to prevent or treat Hepatitis C. While vaccines exist to protect against Hepatitis A and Hepatitis B, prevention of HCV relies on harm reduction, and management of an active infection requires therapeutic antiviral medications rather than immunization.
- **C. Administer immunoglobulin** - Immunoglobulin therapy is not effective for treating chronic Hepatitis C or preventing its long-term complications. Post-exposure prophylaxis with immune globulin is not recommended for HCV exposure, and it plays no role in managing a patient who already has an established, high-viral-load infection.
- **D. Observe only** - A "watch and wait" approach allows the virus to continuously replicate, leading to chronic liver inflammation, progressive fibrosis, and an elevated risk of liver failure or HCC. Given the high efficacy and safety of modern DAA therapies, immediate treatment is indicated rather than passive observation.

**HEPATITIS C:**

- Enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus; formerly called non-A, non-B hepatitis; genus *Hepacivirus*.
- Approximately 70–90% develop chronic infection, 10–20% cirrhosis, and 1–5% hepatocellular carcinoma.
- Transmission is mainly through blood; less commonly vertical, sexual, or through transplantation.
- Incubation period: 15–160 days. Acute infection is often asymptomatic with mild to moderate aminotransferase elevations.
- Extrahepatic findings: thyroiditis, autoantibodies, membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, porphyria cutanea tarda, diabetes mellitus, and essential mixed cryoglobulinemia.
- Anti-HCV does not distinguish acute, chronic, and resolved infections; positive HCV RNA detects active infection and monitors treatment response.
- Treatments listed: pegylated interferon and ribavirin; direct-acting antivirals including the pangenotypic combination sofosbuvir/velpatasvir.

questions.stem: A daycare worker is diagnosed with an acute liver infection after an outbreak of jaundice among children. What is the primary mode of transmission for HAV?
questions.rationale:
- **A** HAV is primarily transmitted through the fecal-oral route, typically via person-to-person contact or ingestion of contaminated food and water. In daycare settings, outbreaks frequently occur due to poor hand hygiene practices during diaper changes or toilet training, allowing the virus to spread rapidly among children and staff.
- **B** Bloodborne transmission of HAV is exceedingly rare. Unlike Hepatitis B or C, HAV causes an acute, self-limiting infection without a chronic carrier state, meaning the period of viremia is very brief and highly unlikely to be encountered in screened blood products.
- **C** Sexual contact is not the primary mode of transmission for HAV in a daycare outbreak scenario.
- **D** While sporadic HAV outbreaks can occur in marginalized populations due to poor sanitary conditions, the mechanism of spread remains fecal-oral rather than through shared needles.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the first serological marker or antigen detected during an acute Hepatitis B infection?
questions.rationale:
- **A. Anti-HBs** - Anti-HBs (Hepatitis B surface antibody) is a protective antibody that appears late in the course of the disease, long after the symptoms have resolved. Its presence signifies immunity to the virus, either from a cleared natural infection or from successful vaccination, rather than an active, acute infection phase.
- **B. HBeAg** - HBeAg (Hepatitis B envelope antigen) is not the first marker to appear, though it rises shortly after HBsAg. It serves as an indicator of active, high-rate viral replication and high infectivity, but its detection relies on the prior establishment of viral protein synthesis.
- **C. HBsAg** - HBsAg (Hepatitis B surface antigen) is the definitive diagnostic hallmark and the very first serological marker to appear in the serum during an acute infection. It can be detected as early as 1 to 2 weeks after exposure, well before the onset of clinical symptoms or biochemical liver abnormalities.
- **D. Anti-HBc IgM** - Anti-HBc IgM is an antibody directed against the core antigen, meaning it takes time for the host's immune system to mount this response. While it is the key serological marker used to confirm a diagnosed acute infection (especially during the "window period"), it appears weeks after HBsAg is already detectable.

**HEPATITIS B SEROLOGY:**

| Status | HBsAg | Anti-HBs | Anti-HBc |
|---|---|---|---|
| Early acute infection | + | − | − |
| HBV infection (acute/chronic) | + | +/− | + |
| Previous infection (immunity) | − | + | + |

questions.stem: A student was accidentally exposed to the stool of a patient with active Hepatitis A. What is the recommended management for post-exposure prophylaxis?

choices.text: Administer Hepatitis A vaccine or immunoglobulin

questions.rationale:
- **A** To be highly effective at preventing infection or lessening the severity of the disease, this intervention must be given as soon as possible, ideally within 14 days of the specific exposure.
- **B** Metronidazole is an antimicrobial medication targeting anaerobic bacteria and specific protozoal parasites, such as Entamoeba histolytica. It possesses absolutely no antiviral activity and plays no role in the prevention or management of viral hepatitis infections.
- **C** There are currently no approved or effective direct-acting antiviral medications tailored to treat or prevent acute hepatitis.
- **D** Relying on passive observation alone is an inappropriate clinical response when a documented, high-risk exposure has occurred.

questions.stem: A group of adults developed descending paralysis after consuming home-canned vegetables. What is the emergency treatment of choice for this botulism case?
questions.rationale:
- **A** Antibiotics like penicillin are not the primary emergency treatment for foodborne botulism.
- **B** This is the cornerstone of emergency management for adult foodborne botulism. It works by neutralizing the circulating neurotoxins (types A–G) in the bloodstream, preventing further binding to neuromuscular junctions and halting the progression of the descending paralysis
- **C** Standard human intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) does not contain specific neutralizing antibodies against botulinum neurotoxins. While a specialized product called Botulism Immune Globulin Intravenous (BIG-IV or BabyBIG) exists, it is specifically indicated only for infant botulism, not for adult foodborne cases.
- **D** Plasmapheresis is an apheresis therapy used to clear autoantibodies or immune complexes in conditions like Guillain-Barré syndrome, which mimics botulism presentation. It is completely ineffective at filtering out or neutralizing bacterial exotoxins like the botulinum toxin.

questions.stem: A patient with meningitis has a CSF Gram stain showing Lancet-shaped Gram-positive cocci in pairs. Which drug should be added to a 3rd generation cephalosporin?
questions.rationale:
- **A** The "lancet-shaped Gram-positive cocci in pairs" identifies Streptococcus pneumoniae, the leading cause of bacterial meningitis in adults. Due to the global rise of penicillin- and cephalosporin-resistant pneumococcal strains, empiric management requires adding vancomycin to a 3rd generation cephalosporin (such as ceftriaxone or cefotaxime) to guarantee synergistic bactericidal activity
- **B** Aminoglycosides like gentamicin penetrate the blood-brain barrier very poorly, making them ineffective for treating central nervous system infections like meningitis
- **C** Rifampicin is not part of the standard initial treatment regimen for acute pneumococcal meningitis. While it penetrates the central nervous system well, it is generally reserved as chemoprophylaxis for close contacts of patients with Neisseria meningitidis or Haemophilus influenzae, rather than direct therapy.
- **D** Macrolides like azithromycin play no role in the emergency management of bacterial meningitis due to poor central nervous system penetration.

**STREPTOCOCCUS PNEUMONIAE:** Gram-positive, lancet-shaped cocci in pairs or short chains; catalase-negative, alpha-hemolytic, bile-soluble and optochin-sensitive; positive Quellung reaction. Treatment noted: penicillin G; levofloxacin or vancomycin plus ceftriaxone for resistant infection.

questions.stem: A diabetic patient with a claw toe deformity and loss of sensation is at risk for osteomyelitis. This motor deficit is due to which neuropathy?
questions.rationale:
- **A** Sensory neuropathy involves the loss of protective sensation, such as the inability to feel pain, touch, or temperature changes. While it explains the patient's "loss of sensation" and heavily predisposes them to unnoticed trauma, ulceration, and subsequent osteomyelitis, it does not directly cause the motor structural changes like a claw toe deformity.
- **B** Diabetic motor neuropathy leads to the progressive atrophy and weakness of the intrinsic muscles of the foot. This muscular imbalance causes a relative dominance of the long extrinsic tendons, pulling the toes into a characteristic claw toe deformity (hyperextension at the metatarsophalangeal joints and flexion at the interphalangeal joints).
- **C** Autonomic neuropathy in the foot impairs the sympathetic nerve fibers that regulate sweating and vascular tone.
- **D** Optic neuropathy (such as diabetic papillopathy or advanced ischemic optic neuropathy) affects the cranial nerve path to the eyes, resulting in visual impairment.

questions.stem: A patient with recurrent UTIs and alkaline urine is found to have a staghorn calculus. Which organism is the most common cause (MCC) of these struvite stones?
questions.rationale:
- **A** Escherichia coli is a urease-negative organism. While it is overwhelmingly the most common cause of uncomplicated urinary tract infections overall, it does not split urea to raise urinary pH, meaning it does not typically promote the formation of alkaline-dependent struvite stones.
- **B** Pseudomonas aeruginosa is primarily associated with nosocomial or complicated UTIs related to indwelling urinary catheters and structural abnormalities. While some strains can produce urease, it is far less commonly isolated as the primary predisposing driver for staghorn calculi compared to classic urease-producing enterobacteria.
- **C** Although Klebsiella pneumoniae produces the urease enzyme and can cause alkaline urine leading to struvite stones, it is not the most common culprit. It serves as an important secondary cause of infection-induced stones but ranks behind the primary organism described in classic medical vignettes.
- **D** Proteus mirabilis is the most common cause of struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) staghorn calculi. It produces large amounts of the enzyme urease, which hydrolyzes urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide, significantly elevating urinary pH (alkaline urine) and creating the ideal chemical environment for these large, branching stones to precipitate.

**PROTEUS:** Facultative gram-negative rods; non-lactose-fermenting; urease-positive with swarming motility. Urease hydrolyzes urea to ammonia, raising the urine pH and promoting magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite) stones and staghorn calculi. Complicated urinary tract infections and urolithiasis.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old female presents with acute dysuria and frequency. Which of the following is the most common cause of Urinary Tract Infections (UTI) overall?
questions.rationale:
- **A** Escherichia coli is overwhelmingly the most common cause of both uncomplicated and complicated urinary tract infections overall.
- **B** Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus) is primarily a respiratory and cutaneous pathogen responsible for pharyngitis, cellulitis, and immune-mediated sequelae
- **C** Pseudomonas aeruginosa is typically an opportunistic, nosocomial pathogen rather than a common cause of community-acquired cystitis in a young female
- **D** Staphylococcus saprophyticus is well-known as the second most common cause of community-acquired UTIs in young, sexually active females, it still ranks significantly behind Escherichia coli.

**ESCHERICHIA COLI:** Facultative gram-negative rods; lactose fermenter on EMB and MacConkey agar, with a green metallic sheen on EMB. O (somatic) and H (flagellar) antigens. Colon flora may colonize the vagina and urethra and ascend to cause UTI; acquisition during birth may cause neonatal meningitis; fecal-oral transmission causes diarrhea. Community-acquired UTI and neonatal meningitis.

questions.stem: A sexually active woman with UTI symptoms has a dipstick test positive for nitrites. Which organism is the most likely causative agent?
questions.rationale:
- **A** Escherichia coli is the overall leading cause of urinary tract infections in young, sexually active women and belongs to the Enterobacteriaceae family, which produces the nitrate reductase enzyme. This enzyme converts dietary nitrates into nitrites, making a positive nitrite dipstick test highly characteristic of an E. coli infection.
- **B** While Proteus mirabilis is a Gram-negative rod that can produce a positive nitrite test, it is not the most likely causative agent in this scenario. It is less common than E. coli in young, healthy women and is strongly associated with urease production, alkaline urine, and staghorn calculi rather than uncomplicated cystitis.
- **C** Klebsiella species typically rank below Escherichia coli in frequency for community-acquired UTIs in young women. While it is a member of the Enterobacteriaceae family and will yield a positive nitrite test, it is more commonly implicated in healthcare-associated or complicated urinary tract infections.
- **D** Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a Gram-positive organism that lacks the nitrate reductase enzyme, resulting in a negative nitrite dipstick test.

questions.stem: A neonate presents with diffuse erythema and large flaccid bullae (SSSS). What is the specific toxin responsible for the cleavage of the epidermal layer?
questions.rationale:
- **A** Endotoxins are structural components (lipopolysaccharides) found exclusively in the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria, not Gram-positive organisms like Staphylococcus aureus.
- **B** While biofilms are structural matrices that help Staphylococcus aureus adhere to medical devices and resist mechanical clearing, they are not soluble toxins capable of inducing widespread epidermal sloughing.
- **C** Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS) is directly mediated by exfoliatin toxin (also known as exfoliative toxin A and B) produced by specific strains of Staphylococcus aureus. This exotoxin acts as a highly specific protease that cleaves desmoglein-1, a critical cell-adhesion molecule within desmosomes, causing a separation of the epidermis at the stratum granulosum.
- **D** PVL (Panton-Valentine Leukocidin) is a pore-forming cytotoxin that specifically targets and destroys white blood cells, such as neutrophils and macrophages. It is heavily associated with severe, necrotizing skin and soft tissue infections, such as furuncles, carbuncles, and abscesses, rather than the superficial, superficial peeling seen in SSSS.

**STAPHYLOCOCCUS AUREUS TOXINS:**

| Toxin | Effect |
|---|---|
| Exfoliatin A and B | Epidermal separation |
| Heat-stable enterotoxins | Food poisoning |
| Toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 (TSST-1) | Toxic shock syndrome |
| Alpha toxin | Skin necrosis and hemolysis |

questions.stem: A 55-year-old patient presents with a painful, vesicular rash in a dermatomal distribution. Which treatment should be initiated to shorten the duration of this Shingles outbreak?
questions.rationale:
- **A** Shingles will eventually resolve on its own, leaving it untreated increases the risk of prolonged pain and severe complications like postherpetic neuralgia.
- **B** Broad-spectrum antibiotics target bacterial pathogens and possess absolutely no antiviral activity against viral infections. They are only indicated if the vesicular lesions suffer a secondary bacterial infection from scratching, rather than as a primary treatment for the outbreak itself.
- **C** Tenofovir is a nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor specifically utilized to manage HIV and chronic Hepatitis B infections. It is completely ineffective against alpha-herpesviruses like the Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV)
- **D** Oral valacyclovir is a preferred first-line antiviral prodrug that effectively inhibits viral DNA polymerase. When initiated within 72 hours of rash onset, it significantly shortens the duration of viral shedding, accelerates lesion healing, and decreases the severity of acute pain.

questions.stem: A patient presents with persistent yellowing, thickening, and cracking of the nails. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
- **A** Onychomycosis is a fungal infection of the nail plate primarily caused by dermatophytes (such as Trichophyton rubrum). It characteristically presents with progressive subungual hyperkeratosis, leading to the yellowing, thickening, and cracking of the nails seen in this patient.
- **B** Tinea pedis, commonly known as athlete's foot, is a dermatophyte infection restricted to the skin of the feet, particularly the interdigital webs and soles. While it frequently co-exists with nail infections, it presents with scaling, erythema, and pruritus of the skin rather than structural nail abnormalities.
- **C** Tinea corporis, or ringworm, is a superficial fungal infection that manifests on the glabrous skin of the body, trunk, or extremities. It classically presents as annular, erythematous plaques with a raised, scaling border and central clearing, completely sparing the nails.
- **D** Paronychia is an inflammation or infection of the soft tissues immediately surrounding the nail fold, typically caused by bacteria like Staphylococcus aureus or yeasts like Candida.

**FORMS OF DERMATOPHYTOSIS:**

| Form | Site / description |
|---|---|
| Tinea pedis | Athlete's foot; feet; most prevalent |
| Tinea unguium (onychomycosis) | Nails; most difficult to treat; months of oral azole or terbinafine, with possible surgical removal |
| Tinea corporis | Body |
| Tinea cruris | Jock itch; groin |
| Tinea manus | Hands |
| Tinea capitis | Scalp; ectothrix spores surround the hair (*Microsporum* spp.); endothrix spores lie within the hair shaft (*T. tonsurans*, *T. violaceum*) |
| Tinea barbae | Facial hair |

questions.stem: An obese patient has itchy, well-defined red plaques in the groin and skin folds. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale:
- **A** Contact dermatitis is an inflammatory reaction caused by direct exposure to allergens or irritants, presenting as intensely pruritic, eczematous lesions that match the shape of the offending agent. While it can occur anywhere on the body, it lacks the specific predisposition for deep intertriginous skin folds seen in this patient.
- **B** Intertrigo is an inflammatory condition that develops in opposing skin-to-skin folds (such as the groin, axillae, or inframammary regions) due to moisture, friction, and maceration. Obesity is a major risk factor for this presentation, which typically manifests as itchy, stinging, well-defined erythematous plaques that are frequently secondarily infected by Candida albicans.
- **C** Tinea corporis, or ringworm, typically affects the glabrous (hairless) skin of the trunk and extremities rather than deep skin folds. It classically presents as annular (ring-shaped) plaques with a raised, scaling, active advancing border and a characteristic central clearing, which does not match this patient's diffuse plaque presentation.
- **D** Psoriasis characteristically affects the extensor surfaces of the body, such as the elbows and knees, presenting with thick, silvery scales. Although a variant called "inverse psoriasis" can target flexural skin folds, it presents as smooth, shiny, non-scaling red plaques and is far less commonly driven primarily by obesity and localized maceration compared to standard intertrigo.

**CANDIDA ALBICANS:** Normal flora of upper respiratory tract, gastrointestinal tract, and female genitourinary tract; pseudohyphae at room temperature and germ tubes at body temperature. In immunocompetent hosts: oral thrush, vulvovaginitis with cottage-cheese discharge, intertrigo with satellite lesions, skin infections, and onychomycosis. In immunocompromised hosts: esophagitis and right-sided endocarditis.

questions.stem: A clinician is reviewing the history of a patient in a dengue-endemic area. In which instance should the Dengue vaccine (Dengvaxia) be administered according to current protocols?

choices.text: The patient is below 12 years old
The patient must have a past dengue infection

questions.rationale:
- **A** Dengvaxia is a live-attenuated virus vaccine, meaning it is strictly contraindicated in individuals with severe immunodeficiency or immunosuppression.
- **B** Current global protocols generally restrict or heavily regulate the use of Dengvaxia in younger age groups. For instance, the US FDA and CDC recommend it specifically for children aged 9 to 16 years, while other endemic countries place the cutoff at 9 years or older, meaning it cannot be broadly given to anyone below 12 without qualifying criteria.
- **C** Re-vaccination screening is mandatory, and the vaccine must only be given to individuals with laboratory-confirmed evidence of a prior dengue infection. In seronegative individuals, the vaccine can act like a primary infection, paradoxically increasing the risk of severe dengue and hospitalization upon future natural exposure due to antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE).
- **D** Dengvaxia is NOT routinely indicated for all females of reproductive age as a blanket preventative measure.

**DENGVAXIA — Laboratory Testing Requirements for Vaccination with Dengvaxia — Dengue Vaccines**

- Dengvaxia is available for use in children and adolescents 9–16 years old who:
  - Have a laboratory-confirmed previous dengue virus infection, AND
  - Live in an area where dengue is endemic (occurs frequently or continuously)

Reference: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (2025)

questions.stem: A 10-week pregnant, unvaccinated woman is exposed to Rubella. According to standard CDC guidelines, what is the mandatory first step in her management?

choices.text: The patient must have a past dengue infection

questions.rationale:
- **A** This is the mandatory first step to establish the patient's immune status and check for active infection. Testing IgG determines if she has undetected immunity, while IgM detects an acute infection that poses a severe risk of Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS) to the fetus.
- **B** This is an incorrect, truncated option fragment with no clinical relevance to maternal viral exposure management.
- **C** This is incorrect as it applies strictly to the safety protocols for the Dengue vaccine (Dengvaxia), not Rubella.
- **D** This is incorrect because it describes a broad, preconception public health screening goal rather than the acute diagnostic action required for an active pregnancy exposure.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child presents with fever, Koplik spots, and a maculopapular rash. What is the next initial step specifically to reduce mortality of Measles?
questions.rationale:
- **A** World Health Organization (WHO) and CDC recommend immediate, high-dose Vitamin A administration for all children diagnosed with measles.
- **B** Systemic corticosteroids suppress the immune system. Administering them during an acute, highly contagious viral infection like measles can impair the body's natural immune response, prolong viral clearance, and increase the risk of severe secondary infections.
